headline_en: Tortured after BDT 46 lakh was taken on promise of Italy; finally dies
summary_en: Sajib Sardar (29) of Shibchar, Madaripur died in a Libyan hospital on 19 March 2025 after months of torture in captivity. His family contracted with broker Borhan Bepari for BDT 16 lakh to reach Italy; he was taken via Dubai to Libya in November 2024, sold twice to 'mafia', and the family paid BDT 30 lakh ransom in two instalments after receiving torture videos - BDT 46 lakh in all. The broker says his contract was only up to Libya; no complaint had yet been filed with police.

facts.statement: The family of Sajib Sardar (29) of Bagmara, Nilokhi union, Shibchar, Madaripur contracted with a local broker for BDT 16 lakh to deliver him to Italy; he left home in November 2024.
The broker took Sajib from Dhaka via Dubai to Libya; on arrival in Libya he was passed to another broker ring, and brokers in Libya detained him in a holding cell (bandishala).

The local broker told the family Sajib had been taken hostage by 'mafia' and demanded BDT 30 lakh ransom; videos of him being tortured were sent to the family's phone with threats to kill him if the money was not paid.
Sajib's family sold land and borrowed to pay BDT 30 lakh ransom in two instalments; with the BDT 16 lakh contract money his sister says the broker took BDT 46 lakh in instalments.
facts.source_in_article: Chanmia Sardar, father; Shamima Akter, sister

facts.statement: Locals say broker Borhan Bepari first took Sajib to Libya on a BDT 16 lakh contract for Italy, then he was sold to mafia on the pretext of a 'game' (the boat crossing of the Mediterranean) direct to Italy; Sajib was sold twice and beaten to extract BDT 30 lakh in two rounds.

Sajib was held about four months, chained with iron chains, beaten and not fed properly; when he became seriously ill he was released into the care of another broker in Libya who admitted him to a hospital in Libya, where he died on the night of Wednesday 19 March 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Chanmia Sardar, father; Julekha Begum, mother; local sources

facts.statement: Broker Borhan Bepari of Shirkhara area, Madaripur Sadar, said by phone: 'My contract was to take him as far as Libya. I don't know what happened after that. There is no use blaming me.'

Shibchar police OC Md. Ratan Sheikh said the family had not yet filed any complaint accusing a broker, and legal action would be taken if they complain; UNO Parvin Khanam said help would be given if the family asks and necessary steps would be taken to bring the body.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Ratan Sheikh, OC Shibchar; Parvin Khanam, UNO Shibchar

headline_en: Did Pratik Group chairman stage a BDT 730 crore 'remittance drama' to whiten black money?
summary_en: After the NBR chairman said on 17 March 2025 that a businessman had brought in BDT 730 crore as tax-free remittance with cash incentive, Prothom Alo found it was BDT 721 crore from China over nine years, brought by Pratik Group chairman Syed Mohammad Faruqui Hasan and shown as wage-earner income. Tax officials suspect laundered or commission money; his bank accounts have been frozen and NBR's tax intelligence unit is investigating. The article notes remittance is tax-free and earns a government cash incentive.

facts.statement: In Bangladesh there is no tax on remittance (expatriate income) brought into the country, and money brought as remittance also receives a government cash incentive; such money is shown as wage-earner income in the tax file and few questions are asked.

NBR chairman Abdur Rahman Khan said on Monday 17 March 2025 that a businessman had brought in BDT 730 crore as remittance using the tax exemption and cash incentive; Prothom Alo found the amount was BDT 721 crore from China, by a taxpayer of Dhaka Tax Zone-5, Pratik Group chairman Syed Mohammad Faruqui Hasan. His and his firms' bank accounts have been frozen and NBR's tax intelligence unit is investigating.
facts.source_in_article: NBR chairman; reporter's inquiry; Tax Zone-5

facts.statement: The money came over nine years as 'remittance' from three Chinese firms - Norinco International Corporation, China Shipbuilding and Offshore International Company: BDT 269 crore in FY2021-22, BDT 77 crore and BDT 81 crore in the two preceding years, and about BDT 300 crore in four earlier years - all shown as remittance in tax files, allegedly with tax officials' collusion.

Tax officials explain that money laundered abroad through trade or hundi, or commissions paid abroad by big companies, can be brought back as 'remittance', becoming legal in the tax file without tax and even earning the cash incentive.
facts.source_in_article: tax officials; a senior NBR official

headline_en: Women workers going abroad have been falling for two years
summary_en: BMET data show women's overseas employment fell from 105,466 in 2022 to 76,108 in 2023 and 61,158 in 2024. Most go to the Middle East as domestic workers (66% to Saudi Arabia in 2024); returnees describe unpaid or low wages, lack of food, beatings and untreated injury. BAIRA says training was lengthened from one to two months and Saudi employers are now hiring from African countries.

facts.statement: BMET data: 105,466 women workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2022, 76,108 in 2023 and 61,158 in 2024 - a fall of 28% from 2022 to 2023 and 20% from 2023 to 2024.

In the three years to 2024 more than 34 lakh workers went abroad in total, of whom fewer than 2.5 lakh were women. From 2015 to 2019 more than one lakh women went abroad every year; the number fell in 2020 due to Covid, rose for two years, then fell for two years.

BMET data: in 2024 women workers went to 56 countries; fewer than 10 went to each of 30 countries, only one each to 16 countries; more than 1,000 each went to five countries - Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Qatar, UAE and the United Kingdom. Saudi Arabia took 66% of all women workers in 2024, more than 40,000.
The pre-departure training for women workers going abroad has been increased from one month to two months, lengthening the process time for sending women workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, secretary general, BAIRA

facts.statement: BAIRA's secretary general said Saudi employers are no longer placing demand for Bangladeshi women domestic workers as before and are now taking workers from various African countries; negative publicity about sending domestic workers has also reduced interest in going.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, secretary general, BAIRA

facts.statement: Firoza of Manikganj returned ill in October 2024 after two years in Saudi Arabia: in the first year pay was low but regular; in the second year pay was raised but not paid for 11 straight months, and all of it was paid together when she left; food was a problem and she was beaten. She says women should not go to Saudi Arabia for housework.

Shahida Begum (40) of Faridpur returned in October 2024 after two years three months in one Saudi household: food was irregular, pay was low, the kafeel's (employer's) son sometimes beat her, and she got no treatment after spraining her leg on the stairs. Although the employer was supposed to give the return ticket, 700 riyals (BDT 17,500) was deducted from her pay.

Officials of BRAC, OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program) and Nari Sramik Kendra say returning women's complaints include being taken on false promises, being made to work in several houses, 14 to 16 hours of work, low and irregular pay, irregular food, and for some physical and mental torture; suicides have occurred, and some who fled the kafeel's house were detained by police and returned.
facts.source_in_article: officials of BRAC, OKUP and Nari Sramik Kendra

facts.statement: BRAC, OKUP (a grassroots migrants' organisation) and Nari Sramik Kendra provide various services to workers who return from abroad.

OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam said hardly any work opportunities have been created for women in sectors other than domestic work, and awareness that women regularly return abused from housework has made women unwilling to go on false promises.

headline_en: January: a call for unity to prevent human trafficking
summary_en: A reader-contributed opinion piece by Al Amin Noyon, a trafficking survivor and US 'TIP Hero', marking January as human trafficking prevention month. It gives general figures on trafficking, notes Bangladesh's Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 is weakly enforced, and calls for survivor-centred rehabilitation and global cooperation. It contains no practical migration details.

facts.statement: Bangladesh has the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act, 2012, but the writer says there are still many gaps where the law is not effectively enforced.
facts.source_in_article: Al Amin Noyon, writer (TIP Hero and rights activist)

facts.statement: The writer states that about 18,000 Bangladeshi citizens were trafficked in 2019, 75% of them women and children, and that about 2.5 million people are trafficked worldwide each year (no source given).
The writer says Bangladesh is regarded as a source, transit and destination country for human trafficking, with poverty, unemployment, climate change and internal insecurity as main causes.

key_quote_bn: বাংলাদেশ সরকার কিছু গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পদক্ষেপ গ্রহণ করেছে, যেমন মানব পাচার প্রতিরোধ ও দমন আইন, ২০১২, কিন্তু এখনো অনেক শূন্যস্থান রয়েছে যেখানে আইনের প্রয়োগ কার্যকর নয়।

headline_en: Human trafficking case in Sylhet filed on false allegations, press conference claims
summary_en: A case under the human trafficking law was recorded at Sylhet Kotwali police station on 4 December 2024 against 12 people for allegedly trafficking a Sunamganj youth, Ali Hossain (28), to Libya on a promise of Spain; his father says he paid about BDT 25 lakh and has had no contact for three and a half months. On 11 December a nephew of the main accused told a press conference the case is false and that the complainant and his son themselves hold people hostage in Libya.

facts.statement: Abdul Haque (55) of Sridharpasha village, Jagannathpur, Sunamganj filed a complaint petition on 27 November 2024 at the Sylhet Human Trafficking Crimes Suppression Tribunal alleging his son Ali Hossain (28) was trafficked to Libya on an assurance of being sent to Spain; on 4 December 2024 it was recorded as a case under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act at Sylhet Kotwali Model police station against 12 accused.

The main accused is Faysal Mia (45) of Akhalia area, Sylhet city; other accused named are his brother Mokbul Mia; Hasan Nur and Saiful Islam of Sridharpasha, Enam of Asampur, Shahin of Parargaon and Jilu Mia of Sridharpasha (all Jagannathpur); Nazrul Islam of Topoban area, Sylhet city; and Saleh of Doulatpur village, Derai.

Complainant Abdul Haque said the accused (Faysal and others) are holding his son hostage in Libya, that he has paid about BDT 25 lakh in all on promises of release, that they did not send the son back, and that he has had no contact with his son for three and a half months and does not know where he is.

At a press conference at Sylhet District Press Club on Wednesday 11 December 2024, Iqbal Hossain, nephew of main accused Faysal Mia, claimed the case is false; he alleged that Abdul Haque's son Ali Hossain has lived in Libya since 2015 and that father and son take well-off local boys to Libya in the name of sending them to European countries, hold them hostage and extract lakhs of taka, that two people have died in Libya from their torture, and that Abdul Haque and his wife were arrested over it. He demanded a fair investigation.

headline_en: Bangladeshis wishing to return from Lebanon must register
summary_en: On 9 October 2024 the Foreign Ministry said the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut has asked Bangladeshis who want to return home from war-hit Lebanon to register their names; about 1,000 migrant workers initially want to return. The government asked IOM to arrange chartered flights, but Beirut airport is not currently safe for flights, so alternative places outside the war zone are being sought.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut has asked Bangladeshis who wish to return home from Lebanon to register their names, according to a Ministry of Foreign Affairs press release of Wednesday 9 October 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs press release

facts.statement: According to initial information, about 1,000 Bangladeshi migrant workers want to return home from Lebanon.

The government says it is committed to bringing back all citizens who wish to return from Lebanon; the Foreign Ministry and the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment are making coordinated efforts, and a recent inter-ministerial meeting prepared a framework for bringing back Bangladeshis from Lebanon. Steps are also being taken for the safety of those who wish to stay.

Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said on Tuesday 8 October 2024 that the government has asked the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to arrange chartered flights to evacuate stranded Bangladeshis from Lebanon; the challenge is that Beirut airport is currently not safe for flights, and Bangladesh has advised finding alternative places outside the war zone for the evacuation.
Foreign Secretary Md. Jashim Uddin instructed the ambassador to ensure Bangladeshi citizens are brought home safely; the embassy is working closely with stakeholders on security and timely transport.

Israel began air strikes on Lebanon on 17 September 2024 and a ground attack through the southern border on 30 September 2024; attacks continued in Beirut and other regions and many countries were evacuating their nationals.

headline_en: Noor Ahmed is BOESL's new general manager
summary_en: A short jobs-section notice (12 September 2024) that Noor Ahmed has been promoted to General Manager of Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), the state company under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment. He joined BOESL in 2011 as assistant general manager and has Korean-language qualifications. No recruitment or migrant-facing information is given.

facts.statement: Noor Ahmed was appointed (by promotion) General Manager of Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), according to a BOESL notification; the promotion takes effect from his joining date. BOESL is described as being under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

Noor Ahmed joined BOESL in 2011 as Assistant General Manager; his 25-year career includes overseas employment and training work and Libya's 1,200-bed Benghazi Central Hospital construction project; he trained at Kyung Hee University, South Korea and AIT, Thailand, and holds a higher diploma in Korean from Dhaka University's Institute of Modern Languages.

headline_en: Al-Amin receives US 'TIP Hero' award for work against human trafficking
summary_en: On 24 June 2024 in Washington, US Secretary of State Antony Blinken gave the 'TIP Hero' award to Al-Amin (Noyon), manager of BRAC's Migration Welfare Centre, who was himself trafficked when he went to work in Malaysia in 2007. He assists returnees and trafficking victims at Dhaka airport and is said to have helped at least 34,000 people. A case filed against him in December 2023 was condemned by migrant organisations; he is on bail.

facts.statement: BRAC runs a Migration Welfare Centre whose manager, Al-Amin (Noyon), assists returnees from abroad and trafficking victims; he goes to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka whenever expatriates are in trouble, and when a mentally ill or addressless worker is found at the airport the Probashi Kalyan Desk or Airport Armed Police phone him.
As manager of BRAC's Migration Welfare Centre, Al-Amin is said to have assisted at least 34,000 returnees and trafficking victims; he began working in the BRAC Migration Programme in 2017.

Al-Amin went to Malaysia for work in 2007, became a victim of human trafficking and returned to Bangladesh the same year; after return he began a fight for his own rights and compensation and joined the movement for trafficking victims' and migrants' rights.
During the Covid pandemic Al-Amin worked on food, medical care and delivering returning expatriates to their families.
'Anirban Survivor Voice' (অনির্বাণ সারভাইভার ভয়েস) is described as the largest network of human trafficking survivors in Bangladesh; Al-Amin is its president.
A case was filed against Al-Amin in December 2023; all organisations working on migration condemned his arrest, calling the case false and harassing; he is currently on bail in the case.

The US State Department has honoured anti-trafficking individuals every year since 2004; in 2024 nine people were recognised as TIP Heroes (Bangladesh, Kenya, Mali, Philippines, Serbia, Spain, Suriname, Bolivia and Iraq), Al-Amin being the only one from South Asia; the award was handed over at the release of the annual Trafficking in Persons report in Washington.

headline_en: Remittances sent to siblings and in-laws also to be taxed
summary_en: Under the FY2024-25 budget proposal (reported 16 June 2024), cash, gifts and remittances received from anyone other than a spouse, children or parents would be treated as the recipient's income and taxed at up to 30%. An NBR official said tax can be avoided only if the sender declares the money as his own and the recipient shows it as a liability; NBR had given no formal clarification. PRI's Ahsan H Mansur criticised the move and suggested joint accounts.

facts.statement: According to the budget proposal, cash, gifts and remittances received from anyone other than husband/wife, son/daughter or mother/father would be taxable: remittance arriving in the bank account of a sibling, in-law, other relative or friend would be treated as that recipient's capital income (a gift), taxable at a rate of up to 30%, provided the recipient is within the tax net.
Under the proposal a gift recipient must show the gift in the annual income tax return and the giver must also report it in his or her return.

An NBR official explained the way to avoid the tax: the person who sent the remittance must show it as his own money (declare that it was given as a loan or kept in the recipient's custody), and the recipient must show it as a liability in the return; only then is it free of tax.

There is no tax on remittance in Bangladesh; so how the new budget would tax remittance money was unclear and NBR had given no formal explanation as of 16 June 2024; NBR officials said it might be clarified when the income tax circular (paripatra) is issued.

PRI executive director Ahsan H Mansur advised that a migrant who regularly sends money to siblings, friends or in-laws can open a joint bank account with them; alternatively, if the wife has no bank account the worker can send the money to a brother or brother-in-law who passes it on to the wife, but a written document is needed. He said the NBR proposal is inconsistent with the government's overall remittance policy.
facts.source_in_article: Ahsan H Mansur, executive director, Policy Research Institute

facts.statement: NBR officials said opening a bank account is now very easy, and with an account the parent, spouse or child to whom the money is sent would receive it directly. The article notes that in villages many elderly parents have no bank account, children are minors or wives do not open accounts, so migrants often rely on siblings', friends' or relatives' accounts, through legal channels.
By Bangladesh Bank's count USD 2,000 to 2,500 crore in remittances come through legal channels each year, besides large amounts through hundi or illegal channels.

By the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment's count, 1,125,833 workers went abroad with jobs in FY2022-23, the largest number, about 4.5 lakh, to Saudi Arabia; the number of Bangladeshis abroad is now about 1 crore.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

key_quote_bn: কর আরোপ না করার উপায় হলো, যিনি রেমিট্যান্স পাঠিয়েছেন, তাঁকে তা নিজের অর্থ হিসেবে দেখাতে হবে। যিনি পেয়েছেন, তাঁকে রিটার্নে তা দায় হিসেবে দেখাতে হবে।

headline_en: Oman will regularise 96,000 Bangladeshi workers: state minister
summary_en: After visiting Dubai, Qatar and Oman, State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said (ministry release, 11 June 2024) that Oman has assured it will reopen its labour market to new Bangladeshi workers and regularise 96,000 Bangladeshis living there illegally, waiving a fine of BDT 12,000 per worker per month at Bangladesh's request. Oman wants skilled workers in 12 sectors; unskilled workers can go after skilled sending begins.

facts.statement: Oman has given an assurance that it will open its labour market to take new workers from Bangladesh, the State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare said after visiting Oman from 24 to 31 May 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: The state minister said 96,000 Bangladeshi workers are living illegally in Oman and the Omani government has assured it will regularise them; each worker was supposed to pay a fine of BDT 12,000 per month for this, but it has been waived at Bangladesh's request.
Oman wants to take skilled workers in 12 sectors; once sending of skilled workers begins, unskilled workers will also be able to go, according to the ministry's press release of 11 June 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: The state minister met Qatar's labour minister Ali bin Samikh Al Marri and discussed various worker issues; sending more workers to the United Arab Emirates was discussed during his Dubai visit.

key_quote_bn: এর জন্য প্রত্যেক কর্মীকে মাসে ১২ হাজার টাকা জরিমানা দেওয়ার কথা থাকলেও বাংলাদেশের অনুরোধে এটি মওকুফ করা হয়েছে।

headline_en: Why they were left out is being investigated: Prime Minister in Parliament
summary_en: In Parliament on 5 June 2024, PM Sheikh Hasina said the government is investigating why many workers could not travel to Malaysia despite special flights, and action will be taken against anyone responsible. Opposition chief whip Mujibul Haque said Malaysia takes workers from 14 countries and only for Bangladesh must workers go through a few selected agencies. Hasina urged people not to sell land and to take Probashi Kallyan Bank loans instead. The rest of the article covers unrelated parliamentary answers.

facts.statement: PM Sheikh Hasina told Parliament on 5 June 2024 that the government had started special flights to send workers to Malaysia and sent people by special flights linked with other flights, but many were still left out; the reason is being investigated and action will be taken if anyone is responsible.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Hasina, Prime Minister, in Parliament

facts.statement: Opposition chief whip Mujibul Haque told Parliament that Malaysia takes workers from 14 countries; in 13 of them all licensed legal agencies can send workers, and only in Bangladesh's case must workers be sent through a few specific agencies arranged by some people of Malaysia and Bangladesh together (a 'ring'). He asked why all legal Bangladeshi agencies cannot send workers.
facts.source_in_article: Mujibul Haque, opposition chief whip, in Parliament

facts.statement: Sheikh Hasina said that whenever the government negotiates and fixes how many will go, a class of manpower businessmen in Bangladesh, linked with some people in Malaysia, rush to send people and create an abnormal situation; those who go find their work, job and wages are not as promised and fall into danger there - and this happens in many places, not only Malaysia.

Sheikh Hasina said people need not sell land and houses and spend lakhs of taka to go abroad; if needed they can take a loan from Probashi Kallyan Bank, which gives loans without collateral where necessary, provided the person specifies that he is going and that his job is definite.

The Prime Minister said some people want to go abroad through brokers and get into trouble, while those who go following the rules do not face problems; some sell everything in the race to go first and end up destitute or in danger abroad.

key_quote_bn: যদি দরকার হয়, প্রবাসী কল্যাণ ব্যাংক থেকে ঋণ নিতে পারেন। প্রয়োজনবোধে বিনা জামানতে ঋণ দেওয়া হয়।

headline_en: 'The brokers gave dates two or three times and never kept their word'
summary_en: Meraj Mia of Debgram, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria sold land and paid a broker BDT 6.5 lakh a year earlier to send his son Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) to Malaysia for a supershop job. Flight dates on 19 January 2024 and again on Friday 31 May 2024 were cancelled at the last moment. Returning home by train that day, Tanvir fell from the train door into the Meghna at Bhairab and is presumed drowned; the family blames broker Alamgir Hossain.

facts.statement: Meraj Mia of Debgram, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria sold land and paid BDT 6.5 lakh about a year before June 2024 to broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village, Akhaura and his Malaysia-based brother to send his son Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) to Malaysia; the broker had promised a supershop job, and the son's passport was made on an urgent basis.
facts.source_in_article: Meraj Mia's family; Imran Hossain, maternal uncle

facts.statement: The broker first gave a flight date of 19 January 2024 and said at the last moment the flight was cancelled; after the broker sent 30 people to Malaysia a few days before, the family trusted him and went to Dhaka on Thursday 30 May 2024 for a flight due on Friday 31 May morning or noon, which was again cancelled. The uncle says the brokers gave dates two or three times and did not keep their word.
facts.source_in_article: Imran Hossain, maternal uncle of Tanvir

facts.statement: On Friday 31 May 2024, returning home on the intercity 'Upakul Express' train after the cancelled Malaysia flight, Tanvir fell from the train door into the Meghna river at the Bhairab rail bridge, Kishoreganj and went missing; Bhairab river police and Fire Service divers searched, the rescue was called off at noon on 2 June 2024, and rescuers presume he drowned.

Broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village, Akhaura could not be reached despite several calls to his mobile; Tanvir's uncle called him a 'killer' whose shifting words cost his nephew's life. Many others were supposed to travel along with Tanvir.
Tanvir's father sold 130 decimals of land to send his son abroad and for his own business.

headline_en: More than 1.5 crore workers went abroad in 48 years: state minister in Parliament
summary_en: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury told Parliament on 8 May 2024 that 16,312,324 workers went abroad for employment from 1976 to March 2024, to 176 countries; the ministry has no data on Bangladeshis living abroad illegally without passports. He also gave figures for FY2023-24 and for low- or no-cost government-channel migration. The article ends with unrelated answers from the labour and food ministers.

facts.statement: From 1976 to March 2024 (48 years), 16,312,324 (1 crore 63 lakh 12 thousand 324) workers went abroad from Bangladesh for overseas employment.
facts.source_in_article: Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare, in Parliament

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has no information on how many Bangladeshis without passports are living illegally in various countries.
The state minister said the number of workers sent abroad in FY2023-24 was 1,126,060 (11 lakh 26 thousand 60), and that the overseas labour market had recovered after Covid.
Workers have been sent from Bangladesh to 176 countries so far.
From FY2009-10 to FY2022-23, 127,557 workers went abroad through government channels at low or no cost.

key_quote_bn: ২০০৯-১০ থেকে ২০২২-২৩ অর্থবছর পর্যন্ত সরকারিভাবে স্বল্প বা বিনা খরচে ১ লাখ ২৭ হাজার ৫৫৭ জন কর্মী বিদেশে গেছেন।

headline_en: Video of youth being tortured in Libya sent, BDT 10 lakh ransom demanded
summary_en: Rubel Hossain of Gabtali, Bogura went to Libya in mid-January 2024 through broker Mizanur Rahman alias Dholu of Temaria village, Akkelpur, Joypurhat after paying BDT 4 lakh. Moved elsewhere in Libya on a promise of better work, he was confined and beaten; a video was sent by WhatsApp on 27 March 2024 and a Bangladeshi caller demanded BDT 10 lakh ransom. The broker, who lives in Libya and recruits through his father and brother, is unreachable and his family has fled.

facts.statement: Rubel Hossain of Ameshwarpur Nishipara village, Gabtali, Bogura sold his land and gave BDT 4 lakh to relatives of broker Mizanur Rahman alias Dholu; he went to Libya in the second week of January 2024.

Broker Mizanur kept Rubel idle in Libya; about 10 days before 31 March 2024 Rubel was taken to another place in Libya on the promise of good work, confined there and beaten. On 27 March 2024 a video was sent to a relative's WhatsApp showing him in a room with hands and feet tied together and cloth stuffed in his mouth being beaten with a stick.
facts.source_in_article: Aktarun, elder sister of Rubel's wife

facts.statement: An unknown-voiced Bangladeshi phoned from Libya demanding BDT 10 lakh ransom for Rubel and threatening to kill him otherwise; on Saturday 30 March 2024 Rubel's wife was phoned again with the BDT 10 lakh demand.
facts.source_in_article: Aktarun, elder sister of Rubel's wife

facts.statement: Villagers say broker Mizanur Rahman alias Dholu of Temaria village, Akkelpur, Joypurhat spent 10 years in Saudi Arabia, returned three years ago, ran fish and poultry farms, went to Libya a year and a half ago and then began taking people to Libya; his father Abdur Rahman and younger brother Shahin went around recruiting people to send to Libya.

After a video of four youths from Anwara, Chattogram being tortured in Libya spread, people from various places began coming to Mizanur's house; on Tuesday 26 March 2024, 20-25 strangers on eight motorcycles took away his son Romim, who was recovered by relatives that night; on Friday 29 March his parents and brother locked the house and left for an unknown place. Mizanur cannot be reached by phone.
facts.source_in_article: villagers; Aktarun; UP member Fazilatun Nesa

facts.statement: Gopinathpur UP reserved woman member Fazilatun Nesa said Mizanur took many people to Libya and she now hears he is confining people in Libya and demanding ransom; Hafizar Rahman of Temaria said Mizanur took his son to Libya two weeks earlier and the family cannot now trace him.
facts.source_in_article: Fazilatun Nesa, UP member; Hafizar Rahman

headline_en: UAE and UK are now the main sources of remittance; why?
summary_en: In the first eight months of FY2023-24 (July to February) the UAE and the UK overtook Saudi Arabia and the United States as Bangladesh's top remittance sources, per Bangladesh Bank data. Bankers credit better rates and incentives for formal transfers; analysts suspect some laundered money in Dubai is being routed back as remittance to collect the incentive. RMMRU's Tasneem Siddiqui says Saudi remittances fell because of hundi and because many workers who recently went to Saudi Arabia on valid visas found no jobs and came back.

facts.statement: In the first eight months of FY2023-24 (July to February) the largest remittance to Bangladesh came from the United Arab Emirates, followed by the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, the United States and Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data cited by the reporter

facts.statement: In the two fiscal years before FY2023-24, Saudi Arabia was first and the United States second as remittance sources for Bangladesh, with the UAE third and the UK fourth.

Bangladesh received a total of USD 1,508 crore in remittance from July to February of FY2023-24: about USD 291 crore from the UAE, about USD 188 crore from the UK, USD 179 crore from Saudi Arabia, USD 168 crore from the United States and about USD 100 crore from Italy; these five countries made up about 61 percent of the eight-month total.

Remittance to Bangladesh from the UAE was about USD 207 crore in FY2021-22, about USD 303 crore in FY2022-23, and about USD 291 crore in just the first eight months of FY2023-24, an average of USD 36 crore 32 lakh a month; at that average another USD 145 crore could come in the remaining four months, taking the FY2023-24 total above USD 435 crore.

Remittance to Bangladesh from the UK was about USD 204 crore and about USD 208 crore in the previous two fiscal years, and about USD 188 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; at the current monthly average it could exceed USD 250 crore by the end of the fiscal year.

Remittance from Saudi Arabia has been falling for more than a year and a half: USD 454 crore in FY2021-22 (when Saudi Arabia was the top source), USD 376 crore in FY2022-23, and about USD 179 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; people in the sector expect the FY2023-24 total to stay below USD 300 crore.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, from Bangladesh Bank data; sector people

facts.statement: Remittance from the United States was about USD 344 crore in FY2021-22, USD 352 crore in FY2022-23 and about USD 168 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; if the trend continues the year-end figure may be around USD 250 crore.

Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, said many migrant workers who recently went to Saudi Arabia on valid visas are not getting jobs, and many of them are returning to Bangladesh without work; she gave this as one reason remittance from Saudi Arabia has fallen.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair, Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU)

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said many expatriates are sending money through hundi because of the exchange-rate difference and a lack of trust in banks.

Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said money sent from the United States to Bangladesh rose abnormally over the previous two years out of fear that the US might impose sanctions on Bangladesh, and has fallen again now that the fear has passed.

For remittances the official dollar rate at banks is BDT 110; on top of that the government gives a 2.5 percent incentive per dollar and various banks give an equal amount of incentive, so expatriates sending money through legal channels get more than BDT 115 per dollar. Because of the dollar shortage some banks are buying remittance at more than BDT 120.
facts.source_in_article: people in the sector, to the reporter

facts.statement: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director of Mutual Trust Bank, said expatriates now get good benefits for sending money through legal channels, banks are encouraging them in various ways, and a lot of promotion was done in the UAE in particular, which is why remittance from the UAE rose.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: Analysts say Dubai has become a favourite destination of Bangladesh's rich, entrepreneurs and political figures and Bangladeshi businesses there are growing; some suspect part of the money laundered from Bangladesh to Dubai is being brought back as remittance to collect the incentive and is then laundered out again illegally, which would explain the sudden rise in legal-channel remittance from the UAE.

A top executive of a bank, speaking anonymously, said many Bangladeshis have built huge assets in the UAE with laundered money and that through some banks part of that money is coming back in the name of remittance to take the incentive.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed top executive of a bank

facts.statement: Former Bangladesh Bank governor Mohammed Farashuddin said at a BIBM event in Mirpur, Dhaka, that a large part of the government's remittance incentive is going to 'big fish' and middlemen, who give part of the incentive to the people sending remittance and keep the rest while bringing money in through illicit routes.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammed Farashuddin, former governor, Bangladesh Bank

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসী আয়ে ব্যাংকগুলোতে এখন ডলারের আনুষ্ঠানিক দাম ১১০ টাকা। এর বাইরে প্রতি ডলারে সরকার আড়াই শতাংশ প্রণোদনা দেয়।

headline_en: Plan to send 6 million workers abroad in five years, state minister for expatriates' welfare tells parliament
summary_en: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury told parliament on 27 February 2024 that there is a plan to send 60 lakh workers abroad in the next five years. He gave overseas employment totals for 2022 and 2023 and a country breakdown for 2023 for five Middle East destinations. The rest of the article covers an unrelated food-stock answer.

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury told the Jatiya Sangsad on Tuesday 27 February 2024 that there is a plan to send 60 lakh workers abroad in the next five years.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, in reply to MP Nurunnabi Chowdhury

facts.statement: 1,135,873 workers went abroad for employment from Bangladesh in 2022, and the number rose to 1,305,453 in 2023.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury in parliament

facts.statement: Workers are being sent from Bangladesh to about 176 countries.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, in reply to independent MP Abdullah Nahid Nigar

facts.statement: In 2023 Bangladesh sent 497,674 workers to Saudi Arabia, 127,883 to Oman, 98,422 to the United Arab Emirates, 56,148 to Qatar and 36,548 to Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, in reply to independent MP Muhammad Saiful Islam

facts.statement: The state minister said Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates are among Bangladesh's main labour markets, and that Bangladesh's labour market in the Middle East is not at risk because of the Rohingya.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury in parliament

headline_en: Seven challenges facing the new foreign minister in a difficult time
summary_en: A column by former foreign secretary Md. Touhid Hossain lists seven diplomatic challenges for new foreign minister Hasan Mahmud after the January 2024 election: relations with the US, EU, UK, India, the India-China balance, Myanmar and the Rohingya, and human rights. Migration appears only briefly: US remittance of USD 352 crore in FY2022-23, and a closing note that the overseas labour market and human trafficking, though under other ministries, end up as problems the foreign ministry must handle.

facts.statement: Remittance of USD 352 crore came to Bangladesh from the United States in FY2022-23, placing the US right after Saudi Arabia as a remittance source.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain, former foreign secretary

facts.statement: Former foreign secretary Md. Touhid Hossain wrote that the overseas labour market has its own ministry, but the task of handling the irregularities and problems that arise in it falls on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; human trafficking is a Ministry of Home Affairs matter, yet the foreign minister will also come under pressure over it at various times.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain, former foreign secretary

facts.statement: The United States announced a visa restriction policy in May 2023 for officials of the administration, law enforcement, politicians and even the judiciary who would obstruct a fair election in Bangladesh, and said the restriction took effect from 22 September 2023.

The columnist notes that the Rohingya camps have become a centre of armed conflict, drugs and human trafficking, and that no progress was made in five years on returning more than 10 lakh Rohingya refugees.
The columnist notes that the UK is the third largest destination for Bangladeshi export goods and that a huge Bangladeshi community lives there.

key_quote_bn: কিন্তু এ ক্ষেত্রে যত অনিয়ম ও সমস্যার সৃষ্টি হয়, তা সামাল দেওয়ার দায়িত্ব পররাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের ওপরই বর্তায়।

headline_en: Migrant workers get insurance money easily only when they die abroad
summary_en: The article explains the compulsory 'Probashi Kormi Bima' (expatriate worker insurance) run by the Wage Earners' Welfare Board with Jiban Bima Corporation: who is covered, what it pays, what it excludes, and how few claims are made. Death payouts reach the family's bank account without an application, but disability and early-return benefits must be claimed and most workers do not know the insurance exists. Families of workers whose foreign death certificate says 'suicide' get no insurance, and rights groups want suicide, HIV/AIDS deaths and health cover included.

facts.statement: The government introduced compulsory 'Probashi Kormi Bima' (expatriate worker insurance) for Bangladeshi workers going abroad at the end of 2019. The Wage Earners' Welfare Board, under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, signed the agreement with the state-owned Jiban Bima Corporation on 12 December 2019 and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina inaugurated it on 19 December 2019; the initial insurance term was two years.

A new expatriate worker insurance agreement was signed on 12 March 2023 setting the sum insured at BDT 10 lakh; workers aged 18 to 55 going abroad are covered for five years, counted from the date they receive emigration clearance (bohirgomon chharpotro).
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: Under the new expatriate worker insurance agreement, benefits are payable within the insurance term for the worker's death, permanent disability, partial permanent disability, or if the worker loses the job and returns to Bangladesh within six months.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: If a worker dies of natural causes or by accident during the insurance term or within 90 days after it expires, the full insured sum of BDT 10 lakh is paid.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: A worker who is dismissed and returns to Bangladesh within six months gets BDT 50,000 under the expatriate worker insurance; this benefit does not apply if the worker went abroad entirely at the employer's cost.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: The expatriate worker insurance does not pay if the worker dies by suicide or self-harm within six months of the insurer taking on the risk; for death or illness from HIV/AIDS or similar diseases; for death in risky sports or adventurous activities (motor racing, boxing, scuba diving, horse racing, mountain climbing and others); for death due to alcohol or drug addiction; for death in war or riot or by an attack by miscreants; or for a worker executed under a court sentence.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: A worker going abroad has to pay the applicable insurance premium together with the other fees paid for emigration clearance; the article does not state the premium amount.

When a worker dies abroad, no application is needed for the insurance after the body arrives in Bangladesh: the insurance money is deposited in the dead worker's bank account. In other cases (disability, early return) the insurance has to be claimed.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources

facts.statement: By Jiban Bima Corporation's count, 3,224,343 workers went to various countries for work from the start of the insurance to the end of 2023, and in that time 1,397 workers or their family members claimed insurance money.

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board's 2022-23 annual report says 1,125,836 workers came under the compulsory insurance in that fiscal year, and the families of 860 workers were paid BDT 31 crore 72 lakh 10 thousand as death insurance.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board annual report 2022-23

facts.statement: Government bodies have no information on workers who return with a disability or who come back within six months, the Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources said; claims other than for death abroad have not risen much.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources

facts.statement: Although the insurance is compulsory, people concerned say there is no special effort to inform workers about it before they go abroad; many workers do not know the process, the rules for getting the money or the policy, and so miss out.

Md. Mosharraf Hossain, manager of expatriate worker insurance at Jiban Bima Corporation, said meetings have been held on how to make workers aware of the insurance before they leave and emphasis is being put on telling workers about it during various trainings.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Mosharraf Hossain, manager, expatriate worker insurance, Jiban Bima Corporation

facts.statement: Shariful Islam of Tangail went to Saudi Arabia in October 2023 at a cost of BDT 5 lakh, worked for 22 days, was then detained by police and was sent back to Bangladesh in December on an outpass. He says he does not know why he was sent back, does not know whether he paid any insurance money when leaving, has not applied anywhere since returning and nobody told him to.

Sima of Madaripur, who went to Kuwait to work as an aya at a school leaving three small children with her mother, died there in a road accident. Her mother Manju Begum, who did not know about the insurance, received BDT 35,000 at the airport when the body arrived, later BDT 3 lakh, and after that BDT 10 lakh as insurance compensation.
facts.source_in_article: Manju Begum, mother of the deceased

facts.statement: Amirun Begum of Narsingdi went to Saudi Arabia in November 2022; the death certificate sent from there says she died by suicide on 4 September 2023, and her body reached Bangladesh two months after the death.

On 14 January 2024 Harunur Rashid of Narsingdi came to Probashi Kallyan Bhaban in Dhaka to ask when he would get the BDT 3 lakh due for his daughter Amirun Begum's death. In front of the reporter a person working there looked at the death certificate and said, 'Oh, the daughter committed suicide, so she won't get the insurance money.'
facts.source_in_article: reporter's own observation at Probashi Kallyan Bhaban

facts.statement: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), said that when the destination country writes 'suicide' on the death certificate the worker's family can do nothing more; demands have been raised to bring deaths by suicide and from AIDS or related diseases under the insurance and to give workers health insurance. The article says these demands have been under discussion but not resolved.
A study by the private research body RMMRU done in 2023 found that 31 percent of women migrant workers' unnatural deaths abroad are from accidents and suicide.

Professor Tasneem Siddiqui, chair of Dhaka University's political science department and founding chair of RMMRU, said bringing workers under insurance for early return and other reasons, not just death, is very good, but if workers are not told about it the insurance will not be of use.

headline_en: What a grim example of the rule of law!
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial asks why about 95 percent of cases under the human trafficking prevention law end in acquittal. Citing a home ministry report for January to September 2023 (332 cases, accused acquitted in 316), it blames poor investigation, paid out-of-court settlements and police taking money from both sides. It calls for field-level awareness, accountability for investigators, and notes the government's own report that the high cost of going abroad through official channels pushes people to brokers.

facts.statement: A Ministry of Home Affairs report on human trafficking for January to September 2023 says 332 cases were filed in that period and the accused were acquitted in 316 of them; the editorial describes this as 95 percent of cases under the Prevention of Human Trafficking law being dismissed.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Home Affairs report, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In 2021-2022 the accused were not convicted in a single human trafficking case in Bangladesh, the editorial says.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing its own report

facts.statement: Stakeholders say accused in trafficking cases are being acquitted because cases are not investigated properly and because of compromise settlements with trafficking rings in exchange for money.
facts.source_in_article: stakeholders quoted in Prothom Alo's report

facts.statement: Salma Ali, president of the Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association, said human trafficking cases are very profitable for police: investigating officers take money from both victims and accused and hold up the investigation for a long time, and members of trafficking rings are highly influential, so the accused are not punished.
facts.source_in_article: Salma Ali, president, Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association

facts.statement: The Ministry of Home Affairs said it has issued investigation guidelines because trafficking cases are being dismissed wholesale; the editorial asks that investigators who do not follow them be held accountable.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Home Affairs, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: The United States' 2023 Trafficking in Persons report said Bangladesh did not meet the minimum standards for preventing human trafficking but is making efforts, and that the capacity of tribunals, legal action and the involvement of law enforcement members need to increase.
facts.source_in_article: US 2023 human trafficking report, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: In 2023 the government, together with the United Nations, published the 'National Study on Trafficking in Persons'.

The government's own report says trafficking happens more in areas with economic crisis and climate change risk, and that because the cost of going abroad through official channels is high, people fall into brokers' hands and get trafficked.
facts.source_in_article: government report, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: The editorial cites a case of trafficking and rape of a woman in which trial and sentence were completed in India while the same case has been pending in Bangladesh for three years; in another case the trafficked woman is serving jail time in India and her father, who complained against the traffickers, is in jail in a false case while the traffickers were acquitted.
The editorial says aspiring migrants should be made aware at field level that going abroad illegally through brokers may mean spending the rest of their life in jail.

headline_en: 112 workers to be recruited for Malaysia through the government at no cost; salary BDT 52,000
summary_en: Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) published a notice to recruit 112 skilled male workers for DHL Supply Chain (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd. at zero migration cost, in two posts: Operations Assistant and Technical Skill Workers. Applications are online only from 6 November 2026 10 am to 8 November 2026 4 pm; 300 are picked by software lottery and the employer then selects 112 by technical and oral tests.

facts.statement: BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) published a notice for government-channel recruitment of 112 skilled male workers for Malaysia at zero migration cost, for the employer DHL Supply Chain (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd., in two posts: Operations Assistant and Technical Skill Workers.
The salary in the BOESL notice for DHL Supply Chain (Malaysia) is 1,700 Malaysian ringgit (about BDT 52,000 as printed).

The job term is three years, renewable; work is eight hours a day, six days a week, with overtime available according to the company's needs and Malaysian labour law. The employer provides accommodation, primary medical care and transport.

Operations Assistant post: minimum SSC or equivalent, with vocational or higher degree holders preferred; ability to read, write and communicate in English; physical fitness for warehouse work and one to two years of real experience in related work; skill in operating forklift, power pallet truck and reach truck counts as an extra qualification.

Technical Skill Workers post: minimum HSC or equivalent; vocational, polytechnic or graduate degree holders who studied electrical subjects get special preference; good knowledge of warehouse network cabling, racking and IT equipment is required.

Applicants must be aged 22 to 35, and their passport must be valid for at least 18 to 24 months. A valid driving licence counts as an extra qualification, candidates with related experience at home or abroad are preferred, and a candidate may apply for only one post.
Applications must be made online at https://employee.oep.gov.bd/employee/registration, from 6 November 2026 at 10 am until 8 November 2026 at 4 pm.

First, 300 candidates are chosen by a software-based lottery and their list is published on BOESL's website; then the employer's representatives finally select 112 workers through technical and oral tests.
Selected workers will not have to spend any money at any stage of the recruitment process; BOESL warned people not to make any payment to any person or organisation in the name of this recruitment.
Details of the notice are at https://boesl.gov.bd/pages/reports/6aecae21862c6f28f3c9ac77 ; the application site is https://employee.oep.gov.bd/employee/registration .

headline_en: Claim that the Japanese government will take 100,000 workers a year from Bangladesh is not true
summary_en: A fact-check finds no agreement under which Japan will take one lakh Bangladeshi workers every year for five years, a claim that spread on Facebook and X after Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on 27 October 2026. Japan's foreign ministry spokesperson denied it; the joint statement speaks of Japanese investment creating two lakh jobs inside Bangladesh. A separate employment and skills cooperation memorandum signed on 17 October 2026 has no numerical target, and the 'one lakh' figure traces to a May 2025 report about a five-year target.

facts.statement: There is no agreement between Bangladesh and the Japanese government for Japan to take one lakh workers from Bangladesh each year; the claim that an agreement was signed giving one lakh Bangladeshis a year the chance to go to Japan for the next five years is false.

Kitamura Toshihiro, press secretary and director general for press and public diplomacy of Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on X on 29 October 2026 that social media claims that the Japanese government agreed to take one lakh workers from Bangladesh are false and have no truth, and that no such decision or agreement was made at the Japan-Bangladesh summit of 27 October.
facts.source_in_article: Kitamura Toshihiro, Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on X

facts.statement: The joint statement of the Japan-Bangladesh summit on Japan's foreign ministry website does not mention taking one lakh Bangladeshi workers a year; it says up to one trillion yen of Japanese private investment in Bangladesh is expected over the next five years, which is hoped to create two lakh jobs in Bangladesh. The summit discussed creating jobs in Bangladesh through Japanese investment and increasing facilities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan.
facts.source_in_article: Japan-Bangladesh joint statement, as checked by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Japan signed the 'Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development' (ESDP-MoC) on 17 October 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release; media reports

facts.statement: Several media outlets reported on 19 October 2026 that under the ESDP-MoC Japan would start recruiting Bangladeshi workers from 1 April of the following year (2027).
facts.source_in_article: media reports of 19 October 2026, cited in the fact-check

facts.statement: The ESDP-MoC with Japan has an initial term of five years and extends automatically for another five years, for an overall term of 10 years; it speaks of ensuring protection of Bangladeshi workers, strengthening cooperation in sending and receiving workers, and creating skill-development opportunities through employment. It contains no target or guarantee of taking one lakh Bangladeshi workers a year.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: A report published on 29 May 2025 titled 'Japan to take 1 lakh workers from Bangladesh' said Japanese authorities and businesspeople had spoken of recruiting at least one lakh workers from Bangladesh over the next five years to meet Japan's growing labour shortage; the fact-check says this was a five-year target, not one lakh a year, and not a Japanese government guarantee.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo fact-check, citing the 29 May 2025 report

facts.statement: The false claim spread on Facebook and X with a photo of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman shaking hands with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi; one X post carrying the claim had been viewed 18 lakh times when the fact-check was written, and some news outlets also reported that Japan had agreed to take one lakh workers a year.

key_quote_bn: প্রতিবছর বাংলাদেশ থেকে এক লাখ কর্মী নেওয়ার বিষয়ে জাপান সরকারের সঙ্গে বাংলাদেশের কোনো চুক্তি হয়নি।

headline_en: Why Bangladesh's workers are at the centre of the discussion in the Saudi-Houthi war
summary_en: A column by Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah on the October 2026 Houthi-Saudi conflict explains its background and what it could mean for Bangladesh, for which Saudi Arabia is a critical labour market. He warns that a long conflict could cut new hiring, slow construction projects and make wages and overtime uncertain, especially for workers who borrowed to go, and that domestic workers and those at isolated sites may be hard to reach. He urges sector- and region-based preparation: updated embassy contact with workers, wage-recovery arrangements, repatriation if needed, reintegration and alternative markets.

facts.statement: A Houthi-Saudi conflict flared in October 2026; the column refers to attacks on Saudi oil installations and to reports that Aramco quickly restored operations after a recent attack.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: A published report quoting a BMET official's figures said more than seven and a half lakh Bangladeshis went to Saudi Arabia for work in 2025.
facts.source_in_article: report citing a BMET official, quoted by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist warns that if the Saudi-Houthi conflict is prolonged, new recruitment may fall, construction projects may slow, and wages and overtime income may become uncertain; for a worker who went on loans even a few months without income is a major disaster.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: The columnist says it may be hard to get safety information and help to domestic workers and to workers at isolated workplaces in Saudi Arabia during the conflict.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: The columnist says not all sectors will shrink equally: there may still be demand for labour in repair, health care, transport or emergency supply, so Bangladesh's preparation should be sector- and region-based rather than panic-based.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: The columnist recommends that Bangladesh plan together for up-to-date embassy contact with workers, a system for recovering unpaid wages, repatriation where necessary, rehabilitation of returning workers, and real investment in alternative labour markets and skills, because over-dependence on one country is safe neither for a family nor for the state.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: Background given in the column: a Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in Yemen in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised Yemeni government; a UN-mediated truce reduced violence in 2022; commitments on a nationwide ceasefire came in late 2023 but were not turned into a working peace; the Houthis' formal name is Ansar Allah.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: A World Bank assessment of May 2026 said about three quarters of Yemen's people are below the poverty line.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank May 2026 assessment, cited by the columnist

key_quote_bn: সংঘাত দীর্ঘ হলে নতুন নিয়োগ কমতে পারে, নির্মাণ প্রকল্প ধীর হতে পারে, বেতন ও অতিরিক্ত কাজের আয় অনিশ্চিত হতে পারে।

headline_en: 'They hand you a weapon and say you won't have to fight, just go forward and back'
summary_en: Thirty Bangladeshis who went to Russia together as construction workers on 7 May 2026 did not get the promised jobs and were sent by deception to fight for Russia; Prothom Alo spoke with 15 of them or their families. At least 20 have died, six are still at the front, two fled hospital and returned home, and two wounded men, Ali Hasan Sohel in Penza and Palash Sheikh in Moscow, are in hospital pleading to be brought back. Bodies of those killed do not come back and families get no compensation; the embassy in Moscow says the two have not contacted it.

facts.statement: Thirty Bangladeshis went to Russia together on 7 May 2026 as construction workers; their families say they did not get the promised jobs in Russia and were sent by deception to fight in the war on Russia's side.
facts.source_in_article: families of the men; Prothom Alo spoke with 15 of the 30

facts.statement: Of the 30 Bangladeshis who went to Russia on 7 May 2026, at least 20 have died, six are still on the battlefield, two escaped from hospital and returned to Bangladesh, and the remaining two are in two different hospitals pleading to return home.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo's own finding from families and the injured

facts.statement: Workers started going from Bangladesh to Russia in 2023 and the flow has multiplied several times over three years; many of them end up in the war, mainly as 'bait', and some die. The exact number is not known, but Prothom Alo has obtained information on the deaths of at least 54 people.

Families of the dead and the injured say the 30 men were taken to an army camp and split into three groups, one of 16. Ali Hasan Sohel says that after only five days of training, five men were sent to the battlefield on the sixth day; they walked mile after mile for three days eating the dry food they carried and reached a tunnel that was an underground army camp, where the other 11 of his group later joined them.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel and families of the dead

facts.statement: Ali Hasan Sohel says men who refuse to fight are confined, beaten and punished until they are forced to go; they are handed a weapon and told they will not have to fight, only move forward and back, right and left. He calls this bait and a death trap: whoever goes is hit by Ukrainian drone attacks; some die and the injured who make it back are taken to hospital for treatment.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel, by video call from hospital in Penza

facts.statement: Ali Hasan Sohel says they were given weapons, dressed in army uniform and sent forward one at a time; of his group of 16, 14 are now missing and the other two are in hospital.

Md. Ali Hasan Sohel of Goalanda upazila, Rajbari, has been under treatment for 1 month 10 days at a hospital in Penza, Russia, about 700 km from Moscow; he said he does not know if he will be able to stand on his feet within a year. He said he contacted the Bangladesh embassy, which told him it would try to bring him home when he recovers, but he fears he will be sent back to the war once well.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel, video call with Prothom Alo on Wednesday 21 October 2026

facts.statement: Md. Palash Sheikh of Gopalganj Sadar upazila, who was in the first group of five sent to the front with Ali Hasan, lost one hand in a drone attack and has been in a Moscow hospital for 24 days. His cousin Abu Saleh Islam said the embassy also said it would try to return him when he recovers, and that Palash wants to return by any means.
facts.source_in_article: Abu Saleh Islam, cousin of Palash Sheikh

facts.statement: Ali Hasan's wife Aklima Khatun applied to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare on 26 July 2026 asking for his rescue and financial help for the family, saying he was cheated and fell into the hands of the Russian army and that the family is under pressure from creditors over loan instalments. Palash Sheikh's sister Chumki Khanam sent a letter to the same ministry on 26 July 2026 asking for diplomatic steps to rescue him and financial help, saying he went to Russia on 7 May on borrowed money and high-interest loans and was handed to the army by force and trickery.
facts.source_in_article: the applications, as described by the reporter

facts.statement: A responsible official of the Bangladesh embassy in Moscow told Prothom Alo that nobody who was injured in the war, is in hospital and wants to return home has yet contacted the embassy about being returned; this contradicts what Ali Hasan and Palash's cousin said about contacting the embassy.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed official, Bangladesh embassy in Moscow

facts.statement: The bodies of Bangladeshis killed in Russia do not come back to Bangladesh, and the families get no compensation.

Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, said the Bangladesh embassy must contact the Russian government and take responsibility for the two hospitalised men, recover all their treatment costs, dues and compensation from Russia, and arrange their return as soon as they recover.
Prothom Alo asked the Russian embassy in Dhaka by email on 21 October 2026 for comment on Bangladeshis being sent to war after being promised work in Russia; no reply is reported in the article.

headline_en: Riyadh flights will resume when the Saudi authorities give permission: aviation minister
summary_en: Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat said on Monday 19 October 2026 that Riyadh-bound flights are suspended by decision of the Saudi authorities and will resume when permission is given, with work under way to carry some passengers via Dammam or Madinah. Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury handed over luggage trolleys for migrant workers, spoke about two Bangladeshis executed in Makkah and Umrah pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia, and described a cooperation agreement signed with Japan on worker protection.

facts.statement: Flights to Riyadh are suspended for now by decision of the Saudi authorities, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat said on Monday 19 October 2026 at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport; flights will resume when permission to operate the route is received.
facts.source_in_article: Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat

facts.statement: To reduce passengers' suffering while Riyadh flights are suspended, work is under way to arrange carrying some passengers on the Dammam or Madinah route as an alternative.
facts.source_in_article: Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat

facts.statement: Many Umrah pilgrims are stranded in Saudi Arabia because of the current situation; some tried to come by alternative routes but many cannot return because of flight cancellations. The expatriates' welfare minister said they will be brought home when the situation becomes normal.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: Of two Bangladeshis executed in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, one was a migrant worker and the other an Umrah pilgrim; their bodies will be brought back when air links and the overall situation become normal.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board supplied 200 trolleys to the country's three international airports for carrying migrant workers' luggage inside the airport: 150 at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (handed over by the minister on 19 October 2026) and 25 each at Chattogram and Sylhet airports.

Passengers at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport told the aviation minister they are getting their luggage within 15 to 20 minutes; a live baggage monitoring system has been introduced at the airport.
facts.source_in_article: Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat

facts.statement: Bangladesh signed a cooperation agreement with Japan on Saturday 17 October 2026 to increase legal protection, skill development, higher pay and long-term residence opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan.
Under the cooperation agreement with Japan, Bangladeshi workers will get the same legal protection as local Japanese workers, the expatriates' welfare minister said.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The minister said the Japan agreement gives special weight to women workers' rights: equal opportunity for men and women at work, no dismissal of or discrimination against a woman worker because of pregnancy or childbirth, and no provision in the agreement for compulsorily sending a woman worker home for those reasons.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

headline_en: BDT 1,000 crore in loans for skill development of workers going abroad; how to get up to BDT 10 lakh
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank has launched a BDT 1,000 crore special pre-finance scheme, disbursed through Probashi Kallyan Bank, for skill and language training of Bangladeshis going abroad for work. A worker can borrow up to BDT 10 lakh without collateral at up to 9 percent interest, with two guarantors. The article sets out eligibility, what the loan covers, required documents and the online application process; by 4 October 2026, 481 people had received BDT 13.03 crore.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank launched a BDT 1,000 crore special pre-finance scheme to support skill development and language learning for Bangladeshis going abroad for employment; the fund is given through Probashi Kallyan Bank, and workers going abroad can take a collateral-free loan of up to BDT 10 lakh from it.

The BDT 1,000 crore fund will be given to Probashi Kallyan Bank in five equal instalments of BDT 200 crore; the next instalment is released only after checking that the previous one was properly used.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Salahuddin Tafadar, additional director, Bangladesh Bank, in a podcast on Bangladesh Bank's Facebook page

facts.statement: The loan carries a maximum interest of 9 percent. The initial term is three years including a six-month grace period, and the term can be extended to five years if needed.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: One person can borrow a maximum of BDT 10 lakh under the scheme. No collateral is needed, but two guarantors are required: one a close family member and the other a person established in society and able to repay the loan.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: The loan covers the tuition fee for language or job-skill training taken in the destination country after going abroad and, in specified cases, living and food costs; the air ticket is not covered.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: Bangladeshis who want to go abroad legally for employment can apply for the loan; students going abroad to study are not eligible.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank managing director Wahida Begum said Bangladeshis going abroad for employment through any legal channel, government or private, can get a loan under the bank's migration loan policy.
facts.source_in_article: Wahida Begum, managing director, Probashi Kallyan Bank

facts.statement: Documents needed for the loan: valid passport, visa, the required Certificate of Eligibility, and a certificate of qualification for the language or skill training; an offer letter from the training or educational institution is important and must state the tuition fee, how many months it is needed for, and who will bear living and food costs.

The loan application is made through Probashi Kallyan Bank's website, with no need to visit a branch to apply, and the applicant can track progress online. The information and papers are first verified at branch level, then sent to the bank's head office; if approved, an approval letter is sent to the branch, and after final approval the applicant must go to the branch in person to give consent to take the loan.
According to Probashi Kallyan Bank, BDT 13.03 crore had been disbursed to 481 people under the scheme up to 4 October 2026.
A two-tier monitoring system is in place so the loan money is used for its set purpose; Bangladesh Bank's SME and Special Programmes Department oversees the fund.

headline_en: Arabic is the 'language of remittance', so why is it so neglected in training?
summary_en: A column argues that Arabic should be a core part of training for workers going to the Middle East, since language protects workers from fraud, wage theft and harassment. It notes the three-day pre-departure orientation cannot teach a language, and that Arabic instructors appointed at 32 TTCs have no clear policy on their duties or future. The writer proposes a separate Arabic trade with one- to three-month courses, compulsory for certain occupations and visas.

facts.statement: According to Bangladesh Bank, a record USD 35.59 billion in remittance came to Bangladesh in FY2025-26, about 60 percent of it from the oil-rich Middle East countries; Saudi Arabia alone sent USD 5.85 billion and the United Arab Emirates USD 4.58 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Workers going to the Middle East currently have a three-day pre-departure orientation (PDO) training; the columnist says basic skill in a language cannot be gained in three days.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: Arabic language instructors have been appointed at 32 TTCs (technical training centres) in Bangladesh, but there is no clear policy on their duties and future: sometimes they are told to teach Arabic, sometimes to take classes of other trades, and there are rumours they may be dropped.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: The columnist says a worker who knows the language can speak about their rights, understand the employer's instructions, ask about the contract and explain their situation in danger; without it they depend on others, which exposes them to fraud, wage deprivation, workplace discrimination and harassment.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: The columnist proposes a separate Arabic trade at TTCs, a one- to three-month basic Arabic course for Middle East-bound workers, making it compulsory for certain occupations and visas, testing language skill after training, a permanent policy and job structure for the instructors, and coordination among BMET, the expatriates' welfare ministry and the TTCs. These are proposals, not decisions.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

key_quote_bn: বর্তমানে মধ্যপ্রাচ্যগামী কর্মীদের জন্য তিন দিনের প্রাক্‌-বহির্গমন ওরিয়েন্টেশন বা পিডিও প্রশিক্ষণ রয়েছে। কিন্তু তিন দিনে একটি ভাষার মৌলিক দক্ষতা অর্জন সম্ভব নয়।

headline_en: What steps to bring back Sheikh Hasina? Parliamentary committee asks for a report
summary_en: The parliamentary standing committee on the foreign ministry met on Thursday 17 September 2026 and asked for a detailed report on efforts to bring Sheikh Hasina back from India; it also discussed the Rohingya issue, irregular migration and human trafficking. On migration, the meeting was told that past worker-sending had serious systemic weaknesses from lack of verification, and the committee recommended building a system to send workers through verified recruiting agencies.

facts.statement: At the 17 September 2026 meeting of the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs it was said that the process of sending workers abroad in the past had serious systemic weaknesses, and that long-standing problems caused by the lack of proper verification now have to be dealt with; work is being done with emphasis on ensuring proper attestation of expatriate workers' information and documents.

The committee recommended taking the initiative to build a system for sending workers abroad through recruiting agencies verified by a transparent and effective process, in coordination with the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
The committee meeting, chaired by Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, also discussed irregular migration and human trafficking, along with Sheikh Hasina's extradition and the Rohingya problem.

headline_en: Licences of 49 recruiting agencies cancelled
summary_en: The government cancelled the licences of 49 recruiting agencies, including agencies of four former Awami League MPs linked to the syndicate formed around the Malaysian labour market. The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment issued the gazette notification on Sunday 19 July 2026 after a court accepted charges against the agencies. The short article names no agency.

facts.statement: The government cancelled the licences of 49 recruiting agencies, including the agencies of four former Awami League members of parliament involved in the syndicate formed around the Malaysian labour market; the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment issued the notification on Sunday 19 July 2026 because a court had accepted charges against these agencies. The article does not name the agencies.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notification, as reported

facts.statement: Sending workers to the Malaysian labour market stopped in June 2024 over various allegations and irregularities against the syndicate; the last date for approved workers to travel to Malaysia was 31 May 2024.
