headline_en: Give remittance fighters due respect and dignity
summary_en: A reader's opinion piece by a university student argues that expatriate workers who sustain Bangladesh's economy are neglected at home and abroad, citing remittance figures for 2019-20 through 2024 and that 53,633 expatriates' bodies came home in 31 years. He calls for legal protection abroad, humane airport and banking services, and loans and training for returnees.

facts.statement: According to the central bank as cited by the writer, Bangladesh's highest fiscal-year remittance was USD 24.77 billion in 2020-21, up from USD 18.20 billion in 2019-20.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh as cited by the writer: USD 2,207 crore in 2021 (over BDT 1 lakh 89 thousand 367 crore), USD 21.28 billion in 2022, USD 21.82 billion in 2023, and about USD 27 billion in 2024, which was 23 percent more than the previous year.
December 2024 remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2.63 billion, a one-month record and 33 percent more than December 2023.
The writer says that per Bangladesh Bank's latest report, remittance in 'the last 11 days' (of January 2025) was BDT 8,839 crore, and the daily average is USD 9 crore 55 lakh.
In the past 31 years 53,633 bodies of expatriates have come to Bangladesh from various countries (no source is given by the writer).
A VIP lounge for expatriates has been inaugurated at the airport in the presence of the Chief Adviser; the writer says it is not enough and that airport staff must treat expatriates with respect.

The writer says expatriate workers face harassment and exploitation at work, fraud in job contracts, poor housing and declining health abroad, and airport harassment and complicated banking at home; he calls for assured proper contracts and legal protection abroad, humane services on return, and special loans, entrepreneurship training and business support for returnees.
facts.source_in_article: Nurunnabi Sohan, student, Patuakhali Science and Technology University

facts.statement: Citing Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), the writer says about BDT 28 lakh crore was laundered abroad from Bangladesh in the last 15 years, an average of BDT 1 lakh 80 thousand crore.

headline_en: Stipend for children of expatriate workers, apply quickly
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board has invited online applications from 25 November to 24 December 2024 for education stipends for children of expatriate workers who passed SSC in 2024 or HSC in 2023. The article gives the eligibility, minimum GPA by group, stipend duration, conditions and the application websites.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board is giving education stipends to children of expatriate workers who passed SSC or equivalent in 2024 and are studying in class 11 or equivalent or a diploma course (first semester/year), and those who passed HSC or equivalent in 2023 and are studying in a university or medical college (first semester/year) in Bangladesh. Online applications run from 25 November to 24 December (2024).

Eligible for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend are children of expatriate workers who took emigration clearance through BMET's database or took Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, and children of deceased expatriate workers who have received or will receive a financial grant from the Board.

Minimum results for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend: in SSC/equivalent 2024, GPA 5.00 in science and 4.75 in humanities and commerce; in HSC/equivalent 2023, GPA 4.80 in science and 4.50 in humanities and commerce. Children of workers who died abroad can apply with GPA 4.00 in either exam.

Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend: SSC-category students get it for two years through classes 11 and 12, or four years for diploma students; HSC-category students get three years for a pass degree, four years for honours and five years for medical. Session jam is not taken into account. The article does not state the stipend amount.

Applications for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend are online only (no in-person or postal applications), with scanned copies of required documents uploaded; the student's mobile number and a mother's/father's/guardian's mobile number must be given.

A Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend application is cancelled if the name in the expatriate worker's passport does not match the father's or mother's name on the applicant's certificate, or if information is incomplete or wrong; the authority's decision on awarding stipends is final.
To apply for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend the notice gives www.wewb.gov.bd or http://stipen.wewb.gov.bd/stipend (as printed).

IOM Bangladesh deputy chief of mission Fatima Nusrat Ghazali said the United Nations sponsored the expatriate workers' lounge at Shahjalal airport and that IOM has sponsored about 100 volunteers to assist migrants at the airport.

headline_en: Seafarers, pilots and cabin crew can buy as many Wage Earners Bonds as they like
summary_en: The Internal Resources Division issued a notification on Sunday 3 November 2024 lifting the investment ceiling on the Wage Earners Development Bond for expatriate Bangladeshis from 1 December 2024 and allowing reinvestment for two further terms. Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew working for foreign-owned shipping and airline companies regain eligibility. The article sets out where the bond is bought, profit rates, tax status and the death-risk benefit.

facts.statement: By an Internal Resources Division (IRD) notification of 3 November 2024, from 1 December 2024 expatriate Bangladeshis can buy any amount of Wage Earners Development Bonds; the investment ceiling is removed, as it already was for the US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond.

Under the IRD notification, someone who buys a Wage Earners Development Bond with remittance income for one term gets reinvestment for two consecutive further terms, so investment can run for three terms totalling 15 years.

Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed in the overseas offices of foreign-owned shipping and airline companies get the opportunity to invest in the Wage Earners Bond under the IRD notification.

Two months before the notification, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment wrote to the IRD secretary saying the ceiling on Wage Earners Development Bond investment should be cancelled or relaxed to increase expatriates' investment and remittance flow.
This article says the five-year Wage Earners Development Bond was introduced in Bangladesh in 1981.

Wage Earners Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks; a foreign currency (FC) account is not required to buy them.
Profit on the Wage Earners Development Bond is income-tax-free and loans can be taken against the bond; it is a five-year bond paying simple interest.

The Wage Earners Development Bond can be bought by the foreign-currency earner (wage earner) personally or in the name of a person the wage earner nominates; government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad can also invest.

The Wage Earners Development Bond carries a death-risk benefit of 40 to 50 percent, paid to the nominee if the bondholder dies before maturity; it is capped at BDT 20 lakh, the bondholder must be under 55, and the nominee must apply within three months of the death. At maturity after the holder's death, the heirs get the principal and profit.

Wage Earners Development Bond profit rates: 12 percent on investment equivalent to up to BDT 15 lakh in foreign currency; 11 percent from BDT 15 lakh 1 to BDT 30 lakh; 10 percent from BDT 30 lakh 1 to BDT 50 lakh; 9 percent from BDT 50 lakh 1 to BDT 1 crore.

Under the Wage Earners Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 23 May 2015) any amount could be invested; on 3 December 2020 the Internal Resources Division set a combined ceiling of the foreign-currency equivalent of BDT 1 crore for the Wage Earners Development Bond, US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond; on 4 April 2022 the ceiling was lifted for the two dollar bonds but stayed for the Wage Earners Development Bond, which also had no automatic reinvestment, forcing expatriates to withdraw earlier investments.

headline_en: Three types of professionals to regain the chance to invest in Wage Earners Bonds
summary_en: A meeting at the Secretariat on Tuesday 15 October 2024 chaired by IRD secretary Abdur Rahman Khan decided to restore the right of seafarers, pilots and cabin crew to invest in the Wage Earners Development Bond, which was taken away in 2020; a notification is to follow. The Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association had long demanded this, arguing seafarers have no pension and cannot prove residence in one country.

facts.statement: A meeting on 15 October 2024 chaired by Internal Resources Division (IRD) secretary Abdur Rahman Khan, with Bangladesh Bank, Finance Division, Financial Institutions Division and Savings Directorate officials, decided to let seafarers, pilots and cabin crew invest again in the Wage Earners Development Bond after more than four years; the secretary said a notification would be issued soon.

In August 2020 the IRD and in September 2020 Bangladesh Bank issued separate notifications saying that Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed by foreign-owned shipping or airline companies, and those appointed to overseas offices of Bangladeshi-owned shipping/airline companies and earning foreign currency, could not buy the Wage Earners Development Bond. Four state-owned banks had discouraged them since late 2019.
facts.source_in_article: IRD and Bangladesh Bank notifications as quoted by reporter

facts.statement: The opportunity to buy the Wage Earners Development Bond was never closed for any citizen staying abroad, government employees on lien, or people working at Bangladeshi embassies and high commissions.

This article says the five-year Wage Earners Development Bond was introduced in 1988 and that seafarers, pilots and cabin crew could invest for 32 years until 2020; the same article cites the 'Wage Earners Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 2015)', and other Prothom Alo articles give 1981 as the start year.

Seafarers, pilots and cabin crew send their wages home through foreign banks or money exchanges, bringing about USD 60 crore a year into Bangladesh; the number of Bangladeshi seafarers is now over 12,000.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association

facts.statement: According to the Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association (BMMOA), seafarers have no pension, provident fund or post-retirement benefit; their contracts usually run 4 to 9 months; while on a foreign-flag ship a Bangladeshi marine officer is under that flag country's jurisdiction and cannot show proof of residence in any one country for the full service period.

BMMOA vice-president Golam Mohiuddin Kadri said they had made the demand for many years, the previous government ignored repeated letters, and restoring the bond would certainly increase remittance through legal channels.

headline_en: Remittance has risen; USD 222 crore came in August alone
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh reached USD 222 crore in August 2024, after the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August, compared with USD 191 crore in July 2024 and USD 160 crore in August 2023. The article explains the July dip (bank closure, internet shutdown, calls to boycott remittance, gold-bar buying in the Middle East) and the new governor's widening of the crawling-peg band that lets banks pay up to BDT 120 per dollar.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in August 2024 was USD 222 crore, USD 31 crore more than July 2024 (USD 191 crore) and USD 62 crore more than August 2023 (USD 160 crore).

In January to July 2024 the highest monthly remittance was USD 254 crore in June, the highest single month in three years (the previous high was USD 259 crore in July 2020); the second highest of 2024 so far was USD 225 crore in May.

After Ahsan H. Mansur became Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions was widened from 1 percent to 2.5 percent, so that under the crawling peg the dollar's mid price ranges from BDT 117 to a maximum of BDT 120; banks can now pay somewhat more for dollars.

Banks were closed from 19 to 23 July 2024 and broadband internet was off for 5 consecutive days and mobile internet for 10 days, nearly stopping foreign transactions; in the first week of August internet and banking were effectively shut and many expatriates announced they would not send remittance, then campaigned to send more after the government fell on 5 August.

It is reported as hearsay that in July 2024 many Bangladeshis in the Middle East turned to buying gold bars instead of sending remittance, hoping to get somewhat more money by bringing the bars home, sometimes with the possibility of a free return air ticket; when gold-bar buying rises legal-channel remittance falls.
Bank treasury officials said the competition to buy remittance at raised prices has eased and that reduced central-bank strictness has created a level field for all banks, increasing remittance.
Bangladesh received USD 21.61 billion (USD 2,161 crore) in remittance in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 23.91 billion (USD 2,391 crore) in 2023-24.

key_quote_bn: এই মাসে মোট প্রবাসী আয় এসেছে ২২২ কোটি ডলার।

headline_en: Remittance is falling; will it fall further?
summary_en: Economic analyst Mamun Rashid's column (10 August 2024) discusses the fall in remittance to USD 1.91 billion in July 2024, the lowest in 10 months, amid the quota movement, bank closures and internet shutdown. He describes how hundi works and why exchange-rate controls pushed expatriates to it, gold-bar buying by Middle East expatriates, and Bangladesh Bank's push to banks to pay up to BDT 120 per dollar.

facts.statement: According to World Bank research and related surveys cited by the columnist, Bangladesh's potential remittance is USD 40 to 45 billion; former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal said only 51 percent of that comes through official channels, the rest being settled in local cash through hundi.
facts.source_in_article: Mamun Rashid citing World Bank and former finance minister

facts.statement: The columnist says the main complaint against hundi is that its foreign currency never comes into Bangladesh but stays abroad and is used for under-invoicing or money laundering; he says many exchange houses under common ownership with banks cooperated, giving expatriates advance loans and delivering higher taka amounts door to door.

Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 1.91 billion, the lowest in 10 months (the previous low was USD 1.33 billion in September 2023); USD 1.43 billion came on 1-20 July and USD 471 million on 21-31 July. The column says that in the first 3 weeks of the month 'on average USD 400 to 500 million' came (the averaging period is not stated).
facts.source_in_article: central bank report as cited by columnist

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 2.54 billion to Bangladesh in June 2024, the highest single month in three years; the previous high was USD 2.59 billion in July 2020.

Citing Bangladesh Bank officials, the column says banks are obliged to distribute remittance within 24 hours once it is sent from abroad; if the sending-country remittance houses hold the money it takes some time to arrive, but usually not more than two to three days.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank officials as cited by columnist

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank called in the managing directors of 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance; banks had been paying BDT 117 to 118 per dollar for remittance and were advised to pay somewhat more, so the remittance dollar rate recently rose to BDT 120.

The columnist reports as hearsay that Middle East expatriates rushed to buy gold: if they bring gold bars instead of sending foreign-currency remittance they get a little more money, and it also covers the return air ticket and even the fare from the airport to their village home.

Banks were closed 19-23 July 2024 and broadband was off 5 days and mobile internet 10 days, nearly stopping foreign transactions with Bangladesh's banks; in some places demands were raised not to send remittance.

Remittance averaged USD 22 to 24 billion a year in the last three years; during Covid in 2020 monthly remittance averaged over USD 2 billion and total reserves passed USD 48 billion; fiscal-year remittance was USD 21.61 billion in 2022-23 and USD 23.91 billion in 2023-24.

key_quote_bn: কেউ বিদেশ থেকে প্রবাসী আয় দেশে পাঠিয়ে থাকলে ব্যাংকগুলো তা ২৪ ঘণ্টার মধ্যে বিতরণ করতে বাধ্য।

headline_en: India's remittance to rise to USD 160 billion
summary_en: A Reserve Bank of India report, cited via The Hindu, projects India's annual remittance at USD 160 billion by 2029; India is the world's top remittance recipient. The article is about India but gives global remittance figures, the SDG cost target for sending remittance, and notes Bangladesh ranks seventh in the world in remittance receipts.

facts.statement: Bangladesh ranks seventh in the world in receiving remittance, according to the article.

Global remittance flow reached USD 85,730 crore in 2023; India was top (expatriate Indians sent USD 11,500 crore last year), followed by Mexico (USD 6,620 crore), China (USD 4,950 crore) and the Philippines (USD 3,910 crore).
facts.source_in_article: Reserve Bank of India report via The Hindu

facts.statement: The average cost of receiving remittance in India was 5.01 percent in the first quarter of 2024, still above the Sustainable Development Goal rate; under the SDGs, sending USD 200 of remittance should cost 3 percent.

According to the UN migration agency (printed as 'IMO' in the article), 3.4 percent of the world's population are migrants; the World Bank says 60 to 95 percent of total remittance goes to low and middle income countries, with workers in 40 rich countries sending money to at least 125 countries.

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসী আয় পাওয়ার ক্ষেত্রে বিশ্বে বাংলাদেশের অবস্থান সপ্তম।

headline_en: 'Bankra', a locality transformed by remittance
summary_en: A feature (printed 22 July 2024) on Bankra in Jhikargachha, Jashore, where about 85 percent of families have one or two men abroad and remittance has built at least 30 multi-storey buildings known by the names of the countries their owners work in. Janata Bank's Bankra branch data show bank-channel remittance falling since 2019 while hundi rises. The piece recounts how Bankra's migration began in the 1990s, including brokers who took men bound for Japan through Thailand's jungle to Malaysia.

facts.statement: Bankra union in Jhikargachha upazila, Jashore has at least 5,000 families and over 19,000 voters; in 85 percent of families one or two men are abroad, so the union has at least 4,500 expatriates, according to the union parishad chairman.
facts.source_in_article: Anis Ur Rahman, Chairman, Bankra Union Parishad

facts.statement: Around Bankra bazar there are at least 30 multi-storey buildings built with expatriates' money, known locally by the owner's destination country: at least 7 'America buildings', 6 'Italy buildings' and 10 'Malaysia buildings'; 'Australia' buildings are also mentioned.

facts.statement: Bankra bazar has one full Janata Bank branch, one IFIC Bank sub-branch and agent banking of 13 government and private banks; the Janata branch has about BDT 100 crore in deposits and 33,792 accounts.

About 30 years ago, after the government tightened controls on border smuggling in the 1990s, two or three men from Bankra went to Japan and later to the United States; others then tried to reach Japan illegally through brokers, but the brokers took them to Thailand and through the jungle to Malaysia. They returned after three years and themselves began sending people to Malaysia, which is how Bankra's migration started.

In Bankra young men start preparing to go abroad around the time they finish secondary school, and there are hardly any young men left in the area; land in Bankra bazar now costs BDT 50 lakh to 1 crore per shotok (decimal) and is hard to find.
Despite the money in the area, Bankra still lacks good education, health and recreation facilities; a former MP said his plans for a 10-bed hospital and an administrative thana were not implemented.

headline_en: Bangladesh has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking
summary_en: The US State Department's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report 2024, released on Monday 24 June 2024, keeps Bangladesh on Tier 2: it does not fully meet the minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The report credits more investigations and convictions, victim-identification guidelines, an amended migrant worker policy and a first victim-compensation fund, but faults continued recruitment fees that leave migrant workers indebted, fines instead of jail for traffickers, and weak victim protection.

facts.statement: In the US State Department's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report 2024, published 24 June 2024, Bangladesh remains on Tier 2 (not fully meeting minimum standards for eliminating trafficking but making significant efforts); neighbours India, Bhutan and Sri Lanka are on the same tier.

The TIP Report 2024 says that because the Bangladesh government continued to allow recruitment fees to be set, many migrant workers are falling into debt, which increases their risk of being trafficked.

The TIP Report 2024 says the Bangladesh government amended its migrant worker policy to increase oversight and accountability of recruiting agents, formally adopted guidelines for identifying trafficking victims, and identified more victims than before.
The TIP Report 2024 says the Bangladesh government for the first time set up a fund to pay compensation to victims of trafficking.

The TIP Report 2024 says Bangladesh increased investigations, prosecutions and convictions of traffickers, but courts fined most traffickers instead of jailing them, which weakened deterrence and probably created safety concerns for victims; no new anti-trafficking tribunal was established.

The TIP Report 2024 says victim protection in Bangladesh remains inadequate: officials often lack a victim-centred approach, shelters lack specialised services, and there are only a few shelters outside Dhaka, especially for male victims; cases involving exploitation of Rohingya refugees and internal trafficking (sex trafficking, forced child labour) were not adequately investigated or prosecuted.

The TIP Report 2024 recommends that Bangladesh, among other things, impose adequate penalties including significant prison terms, strengthen anti-trafficking tribunal staffing, improve protection services for all victims, monitor migrant-worker recruitment companies and brokers and enforce the law regularly, investigate credible allegations of Rohingya trafficking, and improve the quality of pre-departure training for migrant workers.

headline_en: USD 205 crore in remittance came in 23 days: Bangladesh Bank data
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank sources say expatriates sent USD 205.2 crore in the first 23 days of June 2024, ahead of Eid-ul-Azha, including USD 13.8 crore on 23 June alone. Bankers link the rise to the May increase of the dollar rate to BDT 117 (banks paying BDT 118-119 in practice), Eid, and possibly laundered money returning as remittance.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 205 crore 20 lakh to Bangladesh in the first 23 days of June 2024 (the month of Eid-ul-Azha), of which USD 13 crore 80 lakh came on 23 June alone; the headline rounds the one-day figure to USD 14 crore. USD 146 crore came in the first 12 days. In 1-21 June 2023 the figure was USD 166 crore 60 lakh.

Remittance to Bangladesh in May 2024 was USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, an average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh a day; the first 23 days of June 2024 averaged USD 8 crore 92 lakh a day, about USD 1 crore 67 lakh a day more.

In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar price by BDT 7 in one step to BDT 117, after which legal-channel remittance rose; although the documented rate is BDT 117, banks are buying remittance dollars at BDT 118-119, and the bank that pays more gets more dollars from expatriates.

Some in the banking sector say many people are bringing back previously laundered money in the name of remittance; an unnamed bank managing director said the budget allows whitening of black money, offshore banking allows bringing money from abroad, and the government has told many to bring money back.
Social Islami Bank, one of the top five banks by remittance received in the first 23 days of June 2024, attributes the rise to increased manpower export and the usual increase before Eid-ul-Azha.
facts.source_in_article: Zafar Alam, Managing Director, Social Islami Bank

facts.statement: Bangladesh received USD 2,161 crore in remittance in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,137 crore in the first 11 months (July-May) of 2023-24.

During Covid in 2020 legal-channel remittance averaged over USD 200 crore a month and total reserves passed USD 48 billion; after the dollar crisis that began with the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022, total reserves have fallen to USD 24 billion, with actual (net) reserves of USD 13 billion as of June 2024.

headline_en: Foreign minister congratulates Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: At a community meeting in a Madinah hotel on Thursday 20 June 2024, then foreign minister Hasan Mahmud congratulated Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia for sending remittance legally and obeying the law, according to a press release. He said about 30 lakh Bangladeshis are in Saudi Arabia and pointed to the expatriates' pension scheme and offshore banking.

facts.statement: About 30 lakh Bangladeshis are in Saudi Arabia, according to then foreign minister Hasan Mahmud speaking in Madinah on 20 June 2024.

Hasan Mahmud said a special pension scheme has been introduced for expatriates whose benefits can be taken even by people aged 55, and that expatriates have offshore banking facilities in which a dollar account can easily be opened.

Hasan Mahmud urged Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to send remittance through legal channels, to obey the laws of the country they live in because an expatriate's crime gives the home country a bad name, and encouraged them to acquire business ownership abroad rather than only working in others' establishments.
The Madinah community meeting was attended by Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia Mohammad Javed Patwary and the consul general in Jeddah Mohammad Nazmul Haque.

headline_en: Greek coast guard throwing migrants into the sea, eyewitnesses allege
summary_en: A BBC analysis reported that more than 40 migrants died in the Mediterranean over three years because of the Greek coast guard, at least nine of them after being thrown into the sea. The Greek coast guard denies the allegations. The piece concerns migrants in general (witnesses cited are from Cameroon); the only Bangladesh link is embedded related-story headlines.

facts.statement: The BBC verified 15 incidents between May 2020 and May 2023 in which 43 migrants died after being forced out of Greek waters or pushed back to sea after reaching Greek-controlled islands; witnesses say at least 9 of them were deliberately thrown into the sea by the Greek coast guard.
facts.source_in_article: BBC analysis (sources: local media, NGOs, Turkish coast guard)

facts.statement: According to witnesses interviewed by the BBC, in four incidents migrants who had already reached Greek islands were sent back, and in several incidents migrants were put on engineless dinghies and pushed out to sea towards Turkey.

A Cameroonian man said that in September 2021 he reached the coast of Samos island, Greece, planning to apply for political asylum; five masked police (two in black, three in plain clothes) seized him and two others (one Cameroonian, one Ivorian), put them on a coast guard boat and threw them into the sea; his two companions died and he was pushed towards Turkey without a life jacket.

The Greek coast guard denies the pushback allegations, saying its own inquiry found no truth in any allegation of illegal conduct. Greece has long been accused of forcibly pushing Europe-bound migrants back towards Turkey, which the article calls a clear violation of international law.

A related-story headline embedded in the article states that 21% of migrants entering Europe across the Mediterranean are Bangladeshi; another states that 2,500 migrants died or went missing in the Mediterranean 'this year' (no further detail given).

headline_en: 35 Bangladeshis adrift in the Mediterranean cling to rescuers on sight
summary_en: Before dawn on Monday 20 May 2024 the charity ship Ocean Viking rescued 35 Bangladeshis from a fibreglass boat in waters between Malta and Italy; they had been at sea three days after leaving Benghazi, Libya, bound for Sicily. The ship was sent to the Italian port of Ortona. Italy listed Bangladesh as a 'safe country' that month, making asylum harder.

facts.statement: 35 Bangladeshis were rescued before dawn on Monday 20 May 2024 from an overcrowded fibreglass boat in waters between Malta and Italy by the charity rescue ship Ocean Viking, operated by SOS Mediterranee. They said they had been on the boat three days, had travelled about 600 km from Benghazi, Libya, and were heading for Sicily, Italy.

Of the 35 rescued Bangladeshis, three needed urgent medical help and one was unconscious; they were wet, barefoot and shivering. Red Cross/Red Crescent staff gave water, food, blankets and black tracksuits.

The rescued Bangladeshis repeatedly asked the crew whether they were being sent back to Libya; IFRC operations manager Sara Mancinelli said they were assured they were safe and would not be returned to Libya, and that they were mentally devastated.

After rescue the 35 were registered and housed in a container on the ship's deck; an IFRC crew member explained what would happen next. Only one of the Bangladeshis knew English and translated for the others. The ship was assigned the Adriatic port of Ortona, Italy, more than two days' sailing away.
Under a policy introduced by Italy's far-right government, rescue ships may carry out one operation at a time and must then go straight to the assigned port.
In May 2024 Rome listed Bangladesh as a 'safe country', which means it will be hard for rescued Bangladeshis to seek asylum in Italy.

According to the UN's International Organization for Migration, 622 migrants died or went missing in the central Mediterranean from January 2024 to the time of the report; IOM confirms this route is the most dangerous for migrants.
SOS Mediterranee says it has rescued about 10,000 people from the Mediterranean with the Ocean Viking since 2019.

headline_en: Applications open for allowance for disabled children of expatriate workers
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board invited applications for its allowance for disabled children of migrant workers: BDT 1,000 a month for five years, effective 1 January 2024. Online applications opened 16 May 2024 and the deadline was 27 June 2024; the article lists eligibility, documents, the postal address and the Probashbondhu call centre numbers.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board (under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment) gives an allowance for disabled children of migrant workers: if selected, BDT 1,000 a month (BDT 12,000 a year) for a five-year term, effective from 1 January 2024.

Eligible for the disabled-child allowance: children of migrant workers who took BMET emigration clearance / Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, and, for deceased workers, those whose family received a financial grant from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board. The child's father, mother or guardian applies; a worker with more than one disabled child must apply separately for each.

Documents for the disabled-child allowance application: photocopy of the parent's passport; for a worker who died abroad, the NOC issued by the Bangladesh embassy; two attested passport-size photos of the child for a paper application or one photo for an online application; attested photocopy of the Suborno Nagorik (disability) ID card issued by the upazila social services office; photocopy of the parent's passport including the BMET emigration clearance page; and a bank account statement (with bank routing number) of the parent/guardian who will receive the cheque.

The allowance can be applied for online through the board's website (online applications began 16 May 2024) or in person/by post; deadline 27 June 2024. Those who had already applied did not need to apply again.

For a paper application the form is free from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board head office, the board's website, Welfare Centres or District Employment and Manpower Offices; the completed form with documents had to reach: Wage Earners' Welfare Board, 9th floor (Despatch section), Probashi Kallyan Bhaban, Eskaton Garden, Ramna, Dhaka by 27 June.
Probashbondhu Call Centre for any information: 16135 toll-free from inside Bangladesh, +8809610101030 from abroad.

headline_en: No report of any Bangladeshi student being badly injured in Kyrgyzstan: Foreign Minister
summary_en: After mob attacks on foreigners in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, that also hit Bangladeshi students, Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on 19 May 2024 that concern had been conveyed to the Kyrgyz government and no Bangladeshi student was reported badly hurt. Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the embassy in Uzbekistan covers it.

facts.statement: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on Sunday 19 May 2024 (at an OCAB event at the press club, Dhaka) that Bangladesh had conveyed concern to the Kyrgyz government over attacks on Bangladeshi students, that there was no report of any Bangladeshi student being badly injured, and that he had told the ambassador to go to Kyrgyzstan and observe the situation.

Attacks on foreigners began in Kyrgyzstan after a clash between some Egyptian medical students and some locals; Bangladeshi students in the capital Bishkek were also attacked. At least 800 Bangladeshi medical students were living in insecurity; videos showed students of various countries hiding 15-20 to a room, a man being beaten, and locals patrolling the city in convoys of 20-25 cars.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladeshi students in Kyrgyzstan, by phone and email to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the Bangladesh embassy in Uzbekistan is responsible for Kyrgyzstan.
The Bangladesh embassy has no statistics on how many Bangladeshis are in Kyrgyzstan; it estimates 600 to 800 students and about a thousand workers.

headline_en: Cost of sending remittances from the UAE to rise
summary_en: Citing Gulf News, the article reports that UAE exchange houses will raise remittance fees by 15 percent (AED 2.5 per transaction) at their branches, probably from May 2024, the first rise in five years; digital and app transfers are not affected. The UAE is Bangladesh's largest remittance source.

facts.statement: Exchange houses in the UAE that belong to the Foreign Exchange and Remittance Group (FERG) agreed to raise the remittance fee by 15 percent, an increase of AED 2.5 per transaction, the first rise in five years. It applies only to transfers made at exchange-house branches; fees for online platforms and apps are not rising.
facts.source_in_article: Gulf News; Antony Jos, executive director of Joyalukkas Exchange

facts.statement: Under UAE consumer protection law, customers must be told at least two months before a fee increase.

Under the existing structure, sending remittance from the UAE to India or the Philippines costs AED 22 per transaction and to the UK AED 50, plus VAT. The fee to Pakistan equals India's but senders effectively pay nothing because the State Bank of Pakistan reimburses the fee. (The article does not give the fee to Bangladesh.)

Lulu Financial Holdings managing director Adeeb Ahamed said that even after the 15 percent rise the cost of remitting from the UAE is under 3.5 percent of the amount sent, against a global average of 6.2 percent.

Most people in the UAE still send money in person at exchange-house offices, which are usually near workers' factories and housing; few use digital channels. Exchange-house officials expect the fee rise to push workers towards cheaper digital transfers, as happened during Covid.

Remittances to Bangladesh from the UAE: about USD 2.07 billion in FY2021-22, about USD 3.03 billion in FY2022-23, and about USD 2.91 billion in the first eight months (July-February) of FY2023-24, when the UAE was the largest source, followed by the UK, Saudi Arabia, the USA and Italy.

headline_en: Wailing in the families of four workers kidnapped in Libya
summary_en: Four Bangladeshi masons from neighbouring villages of Lalmonirhat and Kurigram, working in Benghazi, Libya, were kidnapped on about 11 March 2024; callers demand ransom via bKash numbers in Bangladesh and threaten to kill them. The families accuse Libya-based fellow villagers, including the man through whom two of them migrated; the accused's father denies it. Two written complaints were filed at Lalmonirhat Sadar police station.

facts.statement: Four Bangladeshi workers who did masonry work in Benghazi, Libya, were kidnapped; families in Lalmonirhat and Kurigram were told by phone on 11 March 2024. They are Al Amin (23) of Sinduria village, Panchagram union, Lalmonirhat Sadar; his brother-in-law Hafizul Islam (40) of Ghorialdanga, Rajarhat, Kurigram; Al Amin (22) of Bhim Sharma village, Rajarhat; and his cousin Rakibul Islam (24) of Ramram village, Panchagram.

The kidnappers of Bangladeshi workers in Libya phone the families on imo and demand ransom be paid in instalments to bKash numbers held by the gang's members in Bangladesh, threatening to kill the captives and hide the bodies if not paid or if the family goes to the law.

Joynal Abedin said an unknown caller on his imo number at 8 am on 11 March 2024 demanded BDT 1 lakh ransom for his son Al Amin and son-in-law Hafizul, to be sent as BDT 50,000 each to two bKash numbers. Liton Mia, brother of the other Al Amin, said a caller from Libya at about 7:51 am the same day demanded BDT 5 lakh per person for the four. (The two demands differ.)

Joynal Abedin (60), a poor farmer of Sinduria village, Lalmonirhat, sold land and spent BDT 5 lakh three years earlier to send his only son Al Amin to Libya; the workers' families had borrowed, mortgaged or sold land to send them.

Families allege that Libya-based Mizanur Rahman (son of Abdul Monnaf, Sinduria village), through whom Al Amin and Hafizul went to Libya, is behind the kidnapping; Liton Mia also names Libya-based Md. Nazmul Huda (23, son of Samsul Haque, Ramram village) and Md. Sultan (32, son of Abu Bakkar Siddique, Ramram village). Mizanur's father Abdul Monnaf denies it, calling his son honest and the accusers jealous.

headline_en: Remittances of USD 630 million arrived in the first 9 days of February
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show USD 631.8 million in remittances through legal channels in the first nine days of February 2024, after USD 2.10 billion in January. The article repeats yearly totals for 2019-2023 and analysts' view that growth lags the number of workers going abroad.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 631.8 million (63 crore 18 lakh) through legal channels in the first nine days of February 2024: USD 69.1 million via state-owned banks, USD 29.6 million via one specialised bank, USD 531.6 million via private banks and USD 1.39 million via foreign banks.
Bangladesh received USD 2.10 billion in remittances in January 2024, the first month above USD 2 billion in six months.

Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.
Analysts say remittance growth is not meeting expectations because it is not rising in line with the number of workers sent abroad each year.

headline_en: Remittances cross USD 2 billion again, reserves fall
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 2.101 billion in remittances in January 2024, the highest in six months, while foreign reserves fell further. The article adds RMMRU figures: over 1.3 million workers went abroad in 2023, a record, up 13 percent, while remittances rose only 2.88 percent and female migration fell 27 percent.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 2,101.0 million in January 2024, the highest in six months (June 2023 had USD 2.19 billion); December 2023 brought USD 1,989.8 million and November 2023 USD 1.93 billion.

Bangladesh's gross foreign-exchange reserves were USD 25.09 billion on 31 January 2024 (USD 19.94 billion under IMF BPM6), down from USD 25.23 billion (BPM6 USD 20.02 billion) on 25 January, a fall of about USD 140 million in a week.

Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.

Because of the two-year foreign-currency crisis the official US dollar rate in Bangladesh rose from BDT 86 to BDT 110; banks were charging over BDT 120 per dollar for import payments because they were buying remittances at above the declared rate.

RMMRU told a press conference on Wednesday 31 January 2024 that more than 1.3 million (13 lakh) workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2023, the highest for any single year; overseas employment rose 13 percent over 2022 while remittances rose only 2.88 percent; male workers increased but female worker migration fell 27 percent from the previous year.
facts.source_in_article: Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU)

headline_en: Remittance growth only 3 percent in six months
summary_en: Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 21.90 billion in 2023, about 3 percent above 2022, despite record numbers of workers going abroad; July-December 2023 brought USD 10.80 billion, up about 2.75 percent. PRI's Ahsan H. Mansur blames continuing money laundering (hundi buyers purchasing expatriates' dollars abroad). The article gives the rates and incentives remitters receive.

facts.statement: Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.

In the first six months of FY2023-24 (July-December 2023) remittances totalled USD 10.80 billion against USD 10.51 billion in the same period a year earlier, growth of about 2.75 percent. December 2023 brought USD 1.99 billion, the highest in six months (June 2023: USD 2.19 billion).
According to BMET, more than 1,210,000 workers went abroad in the 11 months to November 2023, against 1,136,000 in all of 2022; the higher outflow did not show up in remittances.
facts.source_in_article: Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET)

facts.statement: Expatriates sending money through legal channels were getting BDT 109.50 per US dollar (it was BDT 110.50 a month and a half earlier), plus a 2.5 percent government incentive and an equal incentive from the banks. BAFEDA and ABB set the dollar rate on the central bank's advice, but some banks were buying remittances at up to BDT 123.

The official dollar rate rose 5 percent during 2023 to BDT 110, while banks charged over BDT 120 for import payments because they bought remittances above the declared rate; some banks bought remittances at high prices and sold the dollars to the central bank, which is how the central bank was raising reserves.

Ahsan H. Mansur, executive director of the Policy Research Institute (PRI), said expatriates are sending money but legal remittances are not rising because money laundering continues: launderers buy expatriates' dollars abroad, and no action is taken against anyone.
A World Bank and KNOMAD report had projected Bangladesh's formal remittances at USD 23 billion for 2023; the actual figure was USD 21.90 billion.

headline_en: Coming from India, Myanmar, Taiwan, Pakistan, China and committing crimes in Bangladesh
summary_en: A long report on foreign nationals arrested for crimes inside Bangladesh (633 arrested between 5 August 2024 and September 2026, including for running scam centres). Its only material on Bangladeshis abroad: police say a foreign ring that took Bangladeshis to Cambodia and built scam centres there is now trying to set up scam centres in Bangladesh, and that many Bangladeshis are victims of Cambodia- and Myanmar-based scam centres after being trafficked with promises of high pay.

facts.statement: The article notes that scam centres based in Cambodia and Myanmar have recently been in the news for trafficking people abroad with a promise of high pay and then holding them hostage, and that many Bangladeshi citizens are among the victims.

Additional IGP (Crime and Operations) Md. Ahsan Habib Palash of Police Headquarters said a foreign ring had taken some Bangladeshis to Cambodia and built scam centres there, and with that ring's help is now trying to set up scam centres inside Bangladesh; law enforcement has them under surveillance.
facts.source_in_article: Additional IGP Md. Ahsan Habib Palash

facts.statement: On 11 September 2026 police arrested 70 foreign nationals from a building in Jalalabad residential area, Khulshi, Chattogram, for scam-centre-style online fraud and seized 170 electronic devices; on the night of 3 September 2026 six foreigners of a similar ring were arrested at a hotel in Cox's Bazar town. Those arrested in the two cases include nationals of China, Pakistan, Laos, Nepal, Vietnam and Taiwan who police say were trying to set up scam centres in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh law enforcement arrested 633 foreign nationals in about two years (5 August 2024 to September 2026): India 346, Myanmar 62, Taiwan 61, Laos 35, Pakistan 24, China 22, one each from Vietnam and Nepal, and 81 from Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and other countries; alleged crimes include online fraud, fake crypto or investment schemes, running scam centres, drug and gold smuggling, and human trafficking. 127 had been released on bail.

According to Special Branch (SB) and law-enforcement data, 2,268,065 foreigners entered Bangladesh in the 26 months from 5 August 2024 to September 2026, and 7,088 people from 126 countries were overstaying expired visas, most of them Indian (2,164) and Chinese (1,995).

Online tricks used by foreign-run rings in Bangladesh, per law enforcement: promises of quick big profits from investing in gold or bitcoin, befriending on social media and promising an expensive gift from abroad, and offers of attractive online earnings (e.g. an Amazon-lookalike site in August 2023 promising BDT 18,000 a month for 20 minutes' work a day; a Nigerian-led ring arrested July 2025 took BDT 18-20 lakh from over a hundred people).

headline_en: Execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia is a lesson for us: Shama Obaed
summary_en: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on 17 October 2026 that Saudi Arabia's execution of two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar, for an 'immoral act' inside a Makkah mosque is a big lesson, and urged expatriates to obey host-country laws. Bangladesh was not informed beforehand and has written to Saudi authorities for details; return of the bodies depends on the reply.

facts.statement: The Saudi Press Agency, citing the Saudi interior ministry, confirmed on Wednesday (about 14 October 2026) that two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar, were executed in Saudi Arabia. Gulf News reported they had been arrested by Saudi security forces for immoral and indecent acts inside a mosque in Makkah.

According to Gulf News, the two Bangladeshis were sentenced to death under 'ta'zir' (discretionary punishment by the judge under Sharia law), the judge citing violation of the sanctity of the mosque and the circumstances of the offence; a higher judicial authority upheld the verdict and a royal order directed that it be carried out.

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said the labour wing of the Bangladesh mission in Saudi Arabia reported that the two were engaged in 'adultery' inside a mosque in Makkah, a grave offence under Saudi law, but the Bangladesh government had received nothing officially and had written asking for details.
facts.source_in_article: Shama Obaed Islam, State Minister for Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Shama Obaed Islam advised Bangladeshis abroad to obey the law of whatever country they are in, saying Saudi Arabia has its own legal framework and anyone who commits a grave offence is punished under it; she called the two executions 'a big lesson for us'.

A source at the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah said Saudi authorities did not formally inform Bangladesh before the executions; the consulate learned from the media and on Friday 16 October 2026 wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry asking for details. The state minister said how the bodies can be brought back will be known once Saudi Arabia replies.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Consulate Jeddah source; Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial of the two Bangladeshis ran for several months in a Jeddah court and two prominent Bangladeshi citizens helped as interpreters. Unnamed foreign ministry officials said it was mysterious that no one contacted the mission on the detainees' behalf.
facts.source_in_article: unofficial sources; unnamed foreign ministry officials

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; under Article 36, when a foreign national is arrested the detaining state must, at the detainee's request, inform his country's consulate without delay and allow consular assistance. It was not clear whether the two executed Bangladeshis had asked for the consulate to be informed.

headline_en: Boat sinking on illegal voyage to Malaysia; Navy ship rescues passengers, 11 detained
summary_en: On the night of Thursday 1 October 2026 the Bangladesh Navy ship BNS Khalid Bin Walid rescued 76 people from a sinking wooden boat about 81 km west of the St Martin's Island lighthouse; 65 men, women and children were being trafficked to Malaysia. Eleven alleged traffickers on board were detained and are being handed to Teknaf police.

facts.statement: A wooden boat carrying 76 people for an illegal sea crossing to Malaysia via the Myanmar and Thailand coasts suffered engine failure deep in the Bay of Bengal, drifted and began taking on water about 81 km west of the St Martin's Island lighthouse (Teknaf, Cox's Bazar) in Bangladesh waters on the night of Thursday 1 October 2026.

According to the Navy, the 65 men, women and children on the boat had been either lured with promises of good jobs or kidnapped, held in remote areas of Teknaf, and then loaded on the boat by traffickers to be sent to Malaysia.

Alerted by fishermen, the Navy ship BNS Khalid Bin Walid rescued all 76, gave first aid, food and humanitarian help, and after screening detained 11 of them as traffickers; the boat was seized, and the 11 and the boat were being handed over to Teknaf police station for legal action.

headline_en: Body of Libya expatriate returns home 8 months after death
summary_en: The body of Tarikul Islam (25) of Khetlal, Joypurhat, who died of illness in Libya on 3 January 2026, reached his village on Saturday 12 September 2026 after eight months of legal and administrative delay. A local union member said he had gone to Libya irregularly, which caused the delay.

facts.statement: Tarikul Islam (25) of Gurura village, Alampur union, Khetlal upazila, Joypurhat, who had gone to Libya about seven years earlier, died there of illness on 3 January 2026.

Tarikul Islam's body took eight months to be repatriated from Libya because of legal and administrative complications; it reached Dhaka airport at midday on Saturday 12 September 2026, the village about 4 pm, and was buried after a 5 pm janaza. UP member Abdul Mottaleb Hossain (ward 7, Alampur union) said the delay was because Tarikul had gone to Libya illegally.

headline_en: Was going to Italy by an illegal route; Bangladeshi youth dies in Hungary
summary_en: Faridur Rahman (32) of Daganbhuiyan, Feni, a Saudi returnee, agreed with a broker ring to be taken to Italy for BDT 18 lakh, left on 16 June 2026, and was moved via the UAE, North Macedonia and Serbia by road to Hungary, where he fell ill after being kept in a forest and died in hospital. Police told the family on 20 July 2026; the body is still in Hungary.

facts.statement: A broker ring took Faridur Rahman from Bangladesh on 16 June 2026 first to the United Arab Emirates, then through North Macedonia and Serbia by road to Hungary, on the way to Italy; in Hungary he was kept in a forest.
The broker ring agreed to take Faridur Rahman to Italy for BDT 18 lakh.

Faridur Rahman (32), of Purba Barahiguni village, Jayloskar union, Daganbhuiyan, Feni, fell ill after being kept in a forest in Hungary, was admitted to a local hospital and died under treatment; Daganbhuiyan police informed the family on Monday 20 July 2026 but could not say when he died. His body was still in Hungary. He leaves a five-year-old daughter.
facts.source_in_article: family; OC Muhammad Foyzul Azim, Daganbhuiyan thana

facts.statement: Brother Kazi Nazrul Islam last spoke to Faridur by phone on 24 June 2026; he then went to the home of Dulal, a member of the broker ring, who said Faridur was in hospital and could not talk by phone; on later visits Dulal was not found at home.

Police Headquarters asked Daganbhuiyan police station to verify Faridur's address; police went to his home, confirmed identity and told the family of the death. UNO Md. Shahidul Islam said the administration would give the family any help needed.
facts.source_in_article: OC Muhammad Foyzul Azim; UNO Md. Shahidul Islam

headline_en: EU interested in taking skilled workers from Bangladesh; ACU to expand cooperation in education
summary_en: On Wednesday 10 June 2026 an EU delegation told Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister and PMO spokesperson, that the EU is interested in recruiting skilled workers from Bangladesh and expanding legal migration. Mahdi Amin said the government plans an 'Expatriate Card' and is working to cut migration costs. An Association of Commonwealth Universities delegation separately discussed higher-education cooperation.

facts.statement: At a meeting at the Prime Minister's Office on Wednesday 10 June 2026 an EU delegation (Henrik Nielsen, Aleksandra Domanska, Baiba Zarina, Jurate Smalskyte Merville) expressed interest in recruiting skilled manpower from Bangladesh to meet Europe's labour-market demand and stressed expanding legal migration and bilateral cooperation. No numbers, sectors or agreement were announced.
facts.source_in_article: EU delegation, via PMO meeting report

facts.statement: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister, said the government has planned to introduce an 'Expatriate Card' to ensure better services and protection for migrant workers, and is working to reduce migration costs and protect workers' rights; he also described plans to expand technical and vocational training.
facts.source_in_article: Mahdi Amin, adviser to the Prime Minister

facts.statement: An Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) delegation led by Secretary General Prof. Colin Riordan, with BRAC University officials, met Mahdi Amin the same day and expressed interest in expanding cooperation between Commonwealth universities and Bangladeshi universities; no scholarships or programmes were specified.

headline_en: Bangladeshi workers at a Malaysian company unpaid for 3 months; passports allegedly withheld
summary_en: Bangladeshi workers at Malaysian bedding maker Aerofoam Manufacturing (1969) Sdn Bhd have not been paid for three months, about 35 have no valid work permit because the company did not renew it, and most have their passports held by the company, according to documents of the Migrant Welfare Network. The workers filed a formal complaint with Malaysia's labour department, Jabatan Tenaga Kerja (JTK).

facts.statement: All workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing (1969) Sdn Bhd, a Malaysian maker of bedding products employing Bangladeshis, had received no wages for three months as of June 2026; they cannot meet daily costs or send money home, and many who borrowed at high interest to migrate cannot pay instalments.
facts.source_in_article: Migrant Welfare Network (MWN) documents and workers' complaint

facts.statement: About 35 workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing have no valid visa or work permit (PLKS): they entered Malaysia legally but the company did not renew their work permits on time, leaving them in fear of arrest or fines.
The company holds most workers' passports, which the article says is contrary to labour law and restricts workers' freedom of movement.

Workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing allege they are forced to work overtime against their will without adequate rest, get no transport to the workplace, and the company has no effective grievance mechanism.

The affected Bangladeshi workers submitted a formal written complaint to 'Jabatan Tenaga Kerja' (JTK), the labour department of Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources, demanding prompt payment of arrears, regularisation of visas and work permits for the 35, return of passports, an end to forced overtime, a safe workplace, and investigation of high recruitment fees and irregularities in the migration process; they also asked that the company not retaliate.

headline_en: Three Bangladeshis killed in separate road accidents in the Middle East; families in mourning
summary_en: Two workers from Madarganj, Jamalpur, died in a road accident in Kurdistan, Iraq, on Sunday 24 May 2026, and Ripon Mia of Netrokona died near Madinah, Saudi Arabia, on about Wednesday 20 May 2026 when a lorry hit his taxi. Families, still carrying migration debts, ask the government to bring the bodies home.

facts.statement: Monohar Ali (35) of Ghughumari and Mohammad Bazlu (40) of Koalikandi, both Madarganj upazila, Jamalpur, who worked as labourers at a confectionery in Kurdistan, Iraq, died in a road accident on Sunday 24 May 2026 while returning home from work.

Monohar Ali went to Iraq about four years earlier, had no valid iqama, did assorted supply jobs and could not repay his migration loan in four years; Bazlu went about a year and a half earlier on borrowed money and had not improved the family's finances.

Ripon Mia (37) of Gobindasree Badda village, Madan upazila, Netrokona, who went to Saudi Arabia in October 2025 and worked as a labourer at a private company, was killed on the spot on Wednesday night near Madinah when a goods lorry rammed his taxi from behind on the way from 'Embo' (এম্বো) city to 'Fail' (ফাইল) city; the driver was seriously injured.
facts.source_in_article: family; brother Shamim Ahmed in Saudi Arabia

headline_en: Malaysia dream lost in the waves of the Andaman Sea
summary_en: A Malaysia-bound trawler from the Teknaf coast carrying at least 250 Bangladeshis and Rohingya sank in the Andaman Sea on 8 April 2026; only nine were rescued, and the six Bangladeshi survivors were charged under the human trafficking law and jailed. Seven young men from three villages of Rajakhali union, Pekua, who left Teknaf by trawler on 4 April have been out of contact since 8 April. An NGO head explains that brokers lure the poor with a free trip, payment on arrival and high wages.

facts.statement: A Malaysia-bound trawler that left the Teknaf coast of Cox's Bazar sank in the Andaman Sea on the morning of 8 April 2026 because of strong wind, rough sea and overloading; at least 250 Bangladeshi and Rohingya men and women were on board. The Coast Guard said no trace of the missing or wreckage had been found.

At midday on 9 April 2026 the Bangladesh-flagged merchant ship 'Meghna Pride' rescued eight men and one woman found floating with water drums and pieces of wood near the Andaman Islands; they were handed that night to the Coast Guard ship Mansur Ali and then to Teknaf police station.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Commander Sabbir Alam Sujon, Coast Guard media officer

facts.statement: Of the nine survivors, three were Rohingya (Md. Rafiqul Islam, 24; Enamullah alias Imran, 19; Rahela Begum, 25) whose statements were taken through court and who were sent back to the camps; the six Bangladeshis (Md. Hamid, 33, and Md. Akbar, 32, of Cox's Bazar Sadar; Md. Tofayel, 27, Md. Syed Alam, 27, and Md. Sohan Uddin, 19, of Teknaf; Md. Mohiuddin Hridoy, 42, of Mirsarai, Chattogram) were charged under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act and sent to jail, with 10-15 unnamed accused also in the case.
facts.source_in_article: Inspector Sukanta Chowdhury, Teknaf police station

facts.statement: Relatives said three trawlers left the Teknaf coast for Malaysia at about the same time; seven young men from Rajakhali union, Pekua, Cox's Bazar, boarded one on 4 April 2026, kept phone contact until 8 April, and have been unreachable since. The Teknaf brokers are not answering phones.

Brokers target unemployed, indebted young men of poor families and offer to take them to Malaysia by boat for free, saying payment can be made after arrival in Malaysia, and promise very high-paying jobs. Belal Uddin's wife said her husband had no money for Malaysia and went because brokers said he could go without paying.
facts.source_in_article: Parvez Siddiqui, executive director, Films for Peace Foundation; Sumi Akter

facts.statement: Rajakhali UP member Nezam Uddin Neju said he believes a local broker ring works with the Teknaf broker ring in trafficking, targeting young, unemployed, indebted and poor families' sons. No brokers are named.
Mohammad Didar (40), uncle of missing Rashed, said Teknaf police gave no effective help: they took a photo and address and sent the family away, saying they would inform them if anything was found.

The article recalls that mass graves were found in 2015 at traffickers' abandoned camps in dense jungle on the Malaysia-Thailand border. The NGO Films for Peace Foundation has worked on trafficking prevention in the Cox's Bazar region for four years; its head says rising unemployment is a major cause and calls for strict enforcement of the law.
facts.source_in_article: Parvez Siddiqui, Films for Peace Foundation

headline_en: Body of expatriate Tarek, killed in Bahrain, arrives home
summary_en: The body of S M Tarek, a Bangladeshi killed in Bahrain in the Middle East war, arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Friday 3 April 2026 on a Gulf Air flight from Dammam, Saudi Arabia. The expatriates' welfare minister said six Bangladeshis had died in the war and listed the Wage Earners' Welfare Board payments to the family. Ministers also mentioned efforts on visa extensions and on returning Bangladeshis held in camps in Greece.

facts.statement: The body of S M Tarek, a Bangladeshi killed in Bahrain in the Middle East war, was flown from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on a Gulf Air flight to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on Friday 3 April 2026 and received by Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, State Minister Nurul Haque and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the Wage Earners' Welfare Board gave the dead worker's family BDT 35,000 for burial and BDT 50,000 immediately, and that BDT 3 lakh in financial assistance and BDT 10 lakh in insurance would also be paid; he promised long-term support in coordination with the local MP.

facts.statement: Six Bangladeshis had died in the Middle East war as of 3 April 2026, according to the Expatriates' Welfare Minister; State Minister Nurul Haque said the bodies of three had reached Bangladesh so far.

The Expatriates' Welfare, Foreign Affairs, and Civil Aviation and Tourism ministries are coordinating with families and the countries concerned to speed up repatriation of bodies of Bangladeshis killed in the Middle East war; the ministry says it keeps constant contact with each family.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry says it continues to issue instructions and awareness messages asking Bangladeshis in the Middle East to stay on maximum alert; the government is making diplomatic efforts to get expatriates' visa validity extended in the war situation.

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said quick steps were being taken to bring home Bangladeshis held in camps in Greece, and that the government is taking a hard line to bring human traffickers to justice.

headline_en: Came abroad for a living, now helpless in the middle of a war
summary_en: A Middle East Eye feature on migrant workers in the Gulf during the war that followed the US-Israeli strike on Iran on 28 February 2026: delivery riders paid per delivery keep working under missile attack, every civilian killed in the UAE so far was a Bangladeshi, Nepali or Pakistani worker, and rights group Equidem says workers are left out of official safety guidance. Bahrain arrested five Pakistanis and one Bangladeshi for praising the attacks while filming, and filming security incidents carries prison risk in the UAE.

facts.statement: Since the war began after the US-Israeli strike on Iran on 28 February 2026, at least 12 civilians have been killed in Iranian attacks on Gulf countries; every civilian killed in the UAE so far was a migrant worker from Bangladesh, Nepal or Pakistan. One was Bangladeshi Saleh Ahmed (55), killed on the first day of the war while delivering water in the UAE.

Equidem executive director Mustafa Qadri said its researcher network in the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Jordan documented that migrant workers are effectively excluded from government safety communication: although some official statements mention 'all residents', workers say they got no workable guidance on shelters, safe evacuation routes or emergency help.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafa Qadri, Equidem, to Middle East Eye

facts.statement: Delivery riders in the UAE are paid only per delivery, so they have no income if they do not go out; a Pakistani rider in Dubai works 12-hour shifts and lives in a shared mess. Three riders on major UAE delivery platforms said they work at risk of death with no guidance, support or alternative, and workload multiplied after the war began as residents stayed indoors.
facts.source_in_article: delivery riders quoted by Middle East Eye

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi rider with two years at one company in Dubai said streets were empty on the day of the first attack but he had to go back out delivering the next day; customers were tipping somewhat more than usual.
Earlier in the week before 16 March 2026 Bahrain arrested five Pakistani and one Bangladeshi worker, accused of praising Iran's attack while filming its aftermath.

Mustafa Qadri warned that more workers may be arrested and face harsh administrative action for filming attack scenes, with the risk highest in the UAE, which has a record of jailing people for filming security-related incidents.

Qadri said labour-sending countries such as Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Kenya and Ethiopia have a historically weak record of meaningful diplomatic support for their citizens, and their response so far has been very inadequate; Western states under pressure to evacuate their own nationals put little pressure on Gulf states over migrant workers' safety.

Shaheen Abdullah, a shop owner in Doha, Qatar, said a burning splinter fell in front of his car during an explosion near his home, and that shops, restaurants and delivery services cannot close: 'no one can take even one day off'; evacuation, as European countries arrange for their citizens, is not something migrants with nothing to return to can consider.

Nepali workers are preferred for jobs on US and Western military bases in the Gulf because of Nepal's 'neutral' position; when risk rises Western civilians are evacuated but migrant workers are kept on to run cooking and cleaning services.

facts.statement: A foreign ministry notice said two Bangladeshis were killed and seven injured in missile and drone attacks in various Middle East countries over two days. In the UAE, Saleh Ahmed of Barlekha, Sylhet, died under rubble after an air strike on a civilian facility; in Bahrain one Bangladeshi was killed and three injured.

Four Bangladeshis were injured in a drone attack near the civilian airport in Kuwait: Aminul Islam of Nabinagar, Brahmanbaria; Rabiul Islam of Santhia, Pabna; Masudur Rahman of Begumganj, Noakhali; and Dulal Mia of Chandina, Cumilla.

At the inter-ministerial meeting chaired by Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman on 2 March 2026, the government promised that once the situation normalises and flights resume it will arrange travel for Middle East-bound passengers in the shortest possible time; flights were suspended and some workers were stuck in Bangladesh.

The mission in Manama is in contact with Bahraini authorities.

facts.statement: On 2 March 2026 the foreign ministers of Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE and Qatar's state minister for foreign affairs each phoned Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman about the crisis and the safety of Bangladeshi migrants; the Kuwait, Bahrain and UAE ministers expressed condolences and reaffirmed protection of civilians. Khalilur Rahman said the safety of Bangladeshis in the region is Bangladesh's priority and called for a diplomatic solution.

summary_en: Md. Fahad (18), a class-ten student from Chandanaish, Chattogram, was sent to South Africa through brokers for BDT 9 lakh. headline_en: Why should migration begin with debt and despair
summary_en: An op-ed by the ILO country director and IOM chief of mission in Bangladesh argues that recruitment cost is the biggest barrier to safe migration. It cites an average migration cost above USD 3,500 (about 10 months' earnings), Bangladeshis paying two to three times what Indians or Nepalis pay for the same jobs in the GCC and Malaysia, and calls for tighter control of recruiters and accountability for excess fees.

facts.statement: According to the Labour Force Survey 2024, the average cost of migration for a Bangladeshi worker is over USD 3,500 (BDT 462,000), which takes about 10 months of work to earn back.
facts.source_in_article: Labour Force Survey 2024, cited by ILO and IOM heads

facts.statement: In the GCC countries and Malaysia, Bangladeshi workers pay two to three times more than Indian or Nepali workers for the same job, a gap the authors say is well known to foreign employers and governments.

A worker named Shafiqul borrowed about USD 5,000 (over BDT 5 lakh), the price demanded by village brokers, to secure an ordinary construction job in Saudi Arabia the previous year; earning BDT 30,000-40,000 a month, he spent almost his entire first year repaying the loan.
BDT 30,000 to 40,000 a month is described as close to the average wage of low-skilled Bangladeshi migrant workers.
More than 13 million (1 crore 30 lakh) Bangladeshi workers are working in the Gulf, South-East Asia and elsewhere; in 2024 they sent home an estimated USD 26.9 billion, about 6 percent of GDP.

The authors say heavy migration debt forces workers to accept low wages, unsafe conditions and excess hours, limits their ability to bargain or complain, and leads to disputes, frequent changes of employer, overstaying and irregular work; they call for strict control of recruiters, an effective complaints system and clear liability for excess fees, noting the Labour Reform Commission has prioritised recruitment fees.

As human-rights and due-diligence laws tighten in major markets, companies are held accountable for fair recruitment too; since reimbursing excess fees is costly, employers are becoming more interested in hiring from countries with transparent, regulated recruitment systems.

headline_en: 15 injured in attack by rivals over human trafficking case in Madaripur
summary_en: At least 15 people were injured on the night of Friday 21 November 2025 in Purba Botla, Dasar upazila, Madaripur, in an attack that victims say was led by local broker Nasir Howlader against witnesses in a human trafficking case. The case was filed after Siam Howlader went missing two years earlier on the Libya route to Italy. Nasir denies it and police attribute the clash to a land dispute.

facts.statement: Siam Howlader, son of Habib Howlader of Purba Botla, Baligram union, Dasar, Madaripur, left home two years earlier to go to Italy by an illegal route with the help of local broker Nasir Howlader; he went missing on the way to Italy via Libya and has not been traced.
Siam Howlader's family filed a case under the human trafficking law against Nasir Howlader and five others (six accused) over his disappearance on the Libya-Italy route.

Injured witness Sabuj Howlader said that after a milad at Salam Howlader's house on Friday 21 November 2025, over a hundred people led by Nasir, with Rafiq, Salam and others, attacked Siam's relatives, who are witnesses in the trafficking case, with sticks and local weapons, vandalised and looted homes and threatened to kill them before going to jail. At least 15 were hurt and 11 seriously injured were admitted to Madaripur 250-bed Hospital. (The article's list of injured also includes a Nasir Howlader, 33.)

Nasir Howlader denied involvement, calling the trafficking case false. Dasar police OC Sheikh Md. Ehteshamul Islam said the attack arose from a land dispute within the Howlader clan, that neither side had filed a complaint, and police would act if one was filed.
facts.source_in_article: Nasir Howlader; OC Sheikh Md. Ehteshamul Islam

headline_en: New opportunity for sending workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On 28 October 2025 Malaysia sent Bangladesh a 10-point 'Recruiting Agent Selection Criteria' for private agencies that may send workers to Malaysia, following the third Joint Working Group meeting in Dhaka on 21-22 May. The ministry says the same criteria will apply to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Myanmar, and asked licensed agencies that meet them to apply to the ministry by 7 November 2025.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 28 October 2025 the Malaysian government sent Bangladesh its 'Recruiting Agent Selection Criteria' for choosing private recruiting agents to send workers to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: At the third Bangladesh-Malaysia Joint Working Group meeting held in Dhaka on 21 and 22 May (2025), the Malaysian side promised to set criteria for selecting private recruiting agents, after Bangladesh asked Malaysia to include all valid licensed agents to keep parity with other sending countries.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Previously fewer Bangladeshi recruiting agencies got the chance to send workers to Malaysia compared with other sending countries; the ministry says the same selection criteria will in future apply to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Myanmar.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 1 for Bangladeshi recruiting agencies: at least five years of satisfactory operation after getting the licence.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 2: proof of having sent at least 3,000 workers abroad in the last five years.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 3: experience of sending and placing workers in at least three different destination countries within the last five years.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 4: the agency must hold valid licences from all relevant Bangladeshi authorities for training, assessment, recruitment and overseas employment.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 5: the agency must have a good-conduct certificate from the proper authority of the sending country.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 6: the agency must have no record of involvement in forced labour recruitment, human trafficking, labour law violations, extortion of money, money laundering or other financial crime, or unethical migration practices.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 7: the agency must have its own training and assessment centre with full facilities, including accommodation, technical training facilities and an orientation module.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 8: the agency must have testimonials from five separate international employers saying it carried out migration activities satisfactorily.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 9: the agency must have a permanent office of at least 10,000 square feet, operated for at least three years, with infrastructure for selecting and recruiting workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 10: the agency must have proof that it previously followed the destination country's (including Malaysia's) recruitment conditions lawfully and procedurally when sending workers abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Bangladeshi licensed recruiting agents able to meet Malaysia's selection criteria were asked to apply with the supporting documents to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment by 7 November 2025; the Bangladesh government will then ask Malaysia to list every agent that meets the conditions without exception.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release
