headline_en: Scholarships for meritorious children of expatriate workers, applications close 25 November
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board (under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment) will give education scholarships to children of expatriate workers. The article lists the GPA thresholds for SSC 2025, HSC 2024 and Diploma in Engineering 2024, the documents required, the scholarship duration, and the online application deadline of 25 November 2025.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board will give education scholarships to children of expatriate workers; it is a scholarship of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, SSC and equivalent 2025: children of workers currently working abroad need GPA 5.00 in science or GPA 4.75 in humanities and business studies; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 4.00 in science, humanities or business studies.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, HSC and equivalent 2024: children of workers currently abroad need GPA 4.80 in science or GPA 4.50 in humanities and business studies; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 4.00 in any of the three groups.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, Diploma in Engineering 2024: children of workers currently abroad need GPA 3.50; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 3.00.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Documents required for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: proof that the mother or father is an expatriate worker; a certificate from the head of the educational institution including his or her mobile number; for children of workers who died abroad, a certificate from the embassy; a statement of the student's account at any bank with account number and routing number; one copy of the student's photo and signature; a copy of the student's NID card.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: SSC-category awardees get it for two years through classes 11 and 12, or four years if studying a diploma; HSC-category awardees get three years for a pass degree, four years for an honours degree and five years for medical; Diploma in Engineering awardees get four years.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Applications for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship must be made online; the online application deadline is 25 November 2025. (The article's application link and website address are not printed in the text.)
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

headline_en: Allegation of taking 5 times the fixed fee to send workers to Malaysia; cases against 13 companies
summary_en: On Sunday 14 September 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) filed cases against 31 people (chairmen, managing directors and directors) of 13 overseas recruiting companies for allegedly embezzling BDT 1,159 crore by charging Malaysia-bound workers five times the government-fixed BDT 78,990 through a syndicate. With earlier cases against 12 companies, the ACC has now acted in 25 cases against 64 accused over about BDT 2,288 crore.

facts.statement: The government-fixed cost for a Bangladeshi worker going to Malaysia was BDT 78,990, according to the ACC.
The ACC alleges that a syndicate of recruiting agency owners took five times the government-fixed BDT 78,990 from Malaysia-bound workers, taking extra money at various stages outside the agreement.

On Sunday 14 September 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) filed cases against 31 people, including chairmen, managing directors and directors of 13 overseas companies, for allegedly embezzling BDT 1,159 crore by sending workers to Malaysia at five times the government-fixed cost; charges are under several Penal Code sections and the Money Laundering Prevention Act.

According to the ACC, the accused formed a syndicate while holding various posts in BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), ignored the selection and financial conditions of the agreement when sending workers to Malaysia, and laundered the illegal money through transfer and conversion.
facts.source_in_article: ACC Director General Akhtar Hossain / case statement

headline_en: 'Probashi bond': profit on investment, tax-free income and extra security
summary_en: An explainer on the Wage Earner Development Bond ('probashi bond') for Bangladeshis working abroad: interest rates by slab, tax-free profit, death-risk benefit, loans against the bond, the five-year term renewable twice, removal of the investment ceiling from 1 December 2024, who may buy, the documents needed and where to buy.

facts.statement: The Wage Earner Development Bond (known as the 'probashi bond') is a one-time investment with the government by Bangladeshis working abroad, returned with profit after a fixed term, like a bank fixed deposit but with a higher rate, fully tax-free income and death-risk cover.

The Wage Earner Development Bond pays 12 percent simple interest a year, paid every six months (BDT 100,000 invested gives BDT 6,000 after six months, BDT 12,000 a year); it once paid compound interest but now pays simple interest, and the government can raise or lower the rate from time to time.

Wage Earner Development Bond profit slabs: 12 percent on investment up to the equivalent of BDT 15 lakh in foreign currency; 11 percent from BDT 15 lakh 1 to BDT 30 lakh; 10 percent from BDT 30 lakh 1 to BDT 50 lakh; 9 percent from BDT 50 lakh 1 to BDT 1 crore.
No source tax or income tax is payable on Wage Earner Development Bond income, unlike other savings certificates where tax is deducted.

If a Wage Earner Development Bond holder dies before maturity, the nominee gets a death-risk benefit, capped at BDT 20 lakh and only if the holder was under 55; the nominee must apply within three months of the death. The heirs receive the principal and profit at maturity.

A Wage Earner Development Bond can be used as collateral for a bank loan of up to 75 percent of the investment; the loan cannot be taken outside Bangladesh and the bond cannot be used as collateral for a third party.

The Wage Earner Development Bond has a five-year term and, under the government notification, a bond bought with remittance income can be reinvested for two further consecutive terms, so three terms and 15 years in total.

In November 2024 the government removed the investment ceiling on the Wage Earner Development Bond; from 1 December (2024) expatriate Bangladeshis can buy as much as they wish, as was already the case for the US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond.

Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed in the overseas offices of foreign-owned shipping and airline companies may invest in the Wage Earner Development Bond; so may government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad. The wage earner can invest in their own name or in the name of a person they nominate.

To buy a Wage Earner Development Bond one needs a national ID card, passport, a copy of a valid visa, proof of employment and a savings account in Bangladesh; business people need a trade licence and professionals a professional certificate. A foreign currency (FC) account is not required.
Wage Earner Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks.

headline_en: 36 Bangladeshis detained: Bangladesh will fully cooperate with Malaysia in the investigation
summary_en: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said on 5 July 2025 it will fully cooperate with Malaysia's investigation of 36 Bangladeshi workers arrested over alleged links to the Islamic State (IS). Five have been charged, 15 are to be sent back, 16 remain in police custody; three have already been returned and are being questioned in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said on 27 June (2025) that 36 Bangladeshis had been arrested for alleged links with the Islamic State (IS) militant group; the Bangladesh foreign ministry says they were arrested in a recent security operation the week before 5 July 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian Home Minister / Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Malaysia's police chief said all the 36 detained Bangladeshis were working in Malaysia's factory, construction and service sectors; they allegedly sent money to IS in Syria and Bangladesh, recruited members by targeting other Bangladeshi workers, and spread extremist ideology through social media and online messaging platforms.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: Of the 36 Bangladeshis detained in Malaysia over alleged IS links, five have been charged with being members of a terrorist organisation, 15 will be sent back to Bangladesh, and the remaining 16 are still in police custody under investigation.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: Malaysia's police chief said 100 to 150 people may be involved in the network; those with a low level of involvement will be sent back to their own country and those deeply involved will be dealt with under Malaysian law.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: After the arrests the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur contacted the Malaysian authorities and Bangladesh formally asked Malaysia for the identities of those detained and the charges against them; the ministry says the High Commission will give necessary help to expatriate Bangladeshis when needed.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs press release, 5 July 2025

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul told Prothom Alo on 4 July 2025 that three people had already been sent back from Malaysia and were being interrogated; everyone returned after being detained on this allegation will be interrogated and, if evidence of militancy links is found, put on trial.

headline_en: MoU signed to increase legal migration to Italy
summary_en: On Tuesday 6 May 2025 Bangladesh signed its first 'Migration and Mobility' memorandum of understanding with Italy, signed by adviser Asif Nazrul and Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi in Dhaka. Nazrul also said undocumented women workers in Saudi Arabia have got a chance to be regularised, and that women workers in Jordan who became irregular can regularise without a fine by declaring themselves to the authorities.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 6 May 2025 Bangladesh signed, for the first time, a 'Migration and Mobility' memorandum of understanding with Italy, aimed at stopping irregular migration and increasing legal migration; it was signed at the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment by adviser Professor Asif Nazrul and Italy's Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said Italy will take workers in two ways, 'seasonal' and 'non-seasonal'; a joint technical committee is planned that will meet once a year, and work is under way on Italian-language training at Technical Training Centres.
Asked how many people can be sent to Italy and in which sectors, Asif Nazrul said the MoU does not contain such details; the current quota will be increased and Italy will consider a quota increase.

At the Italy MoU signing, Bangladesh also discussed making the visa process easier for Bangladeshi students in Italy and removing Bangladesh from the Italian government's high-risk list for migration.
Asif Nazrul said memoranda of understanding have already been signed with six European countries including Portugal and Austria to increase legal migration to Europe.

After a recent visit to Saudi Arabia, Asif Nazrul said an opportunity has been created to regularise women workers living illegally in Saudi Arabia, and that there were fruitful talks with the Saudi government on sending more skilled and unskilled workers from Bangladesh.

Asif Nazrul said women workers in Jordan who became irregular for reasons such as changing their assigned workplace can become legal without a fine by contacting the relevant authority and making an admission; otherwise they will face a large fine.
Asif Nazrul said increasing the number of male workers in Jordan was discussed with the Jordanian government.

headline_en: A remittance fighter's self-reflection in the mirror of 1 May
summary_en: A May Day opinion piece by an expatriate writer arguing that Bangladesh gives returning migrant workers no pension, social insurance or mental-health support, unlike the Philippines' OWWA. He proposes a mandatory remittance pension scheme, reintegration and re-skilling, an entrepreneur fund, health units and national recognition; the rest is general political commentary.

facts.statement: The writer says more than 1.5 crore (15 million) expatriate Bangladeshi workers are spread around the world and send about USD 24 billion a year.

facts.statement: The writer says most expatriate workers return after working 20 to 30 years and find no permanent social security structure in Bangladesh: no pension, no social insurance, no mental-health support; he contrasts this with the Philippines' Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA).
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer Rahman Mridha (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

facts.statement: The writer proposes five measures for returning migrants: a mandatory national remittance pension scheme; a reintegration and re-skilling programme with jobs and training; an entrepreneur fund with easy-term loans; specialised mental and physical health units for post-migration crises; and an annual national honour.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer Rahman Mridha (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

He had been arrested on 20 October 2024 and remanded in a human trafficking case filed at Paltan police station.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 30 April 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) filed a case against former Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Imran Ahmad for BDT 90 lakh of illegal assets and BDT 6 crore of abnormal transactions.
facts.source_in_article: ACC Director General (Prevention) Md. Akhtar Hossain

facts.statement: Former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad was arrested by the Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Branch from Banani, Dhaka on the night of 20 October 2024; the next day he was taken on remand in a case filed at Paltan police station under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act (a related headline says three days' remand).

Imran Ahmad, five-time MP for Sylhet-4, became State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in 2018, full minister the next year, and held the same ministry again in the government formed after the 2024 election.

headline_en: Jordan to take 300 women workers through government channel, return airfare also provided
summary_en: State-owned BOESL announced recruitment of 300 women sewing machine operators for Tasker Apparel Company in Jordan, with free accommodation, food and medical care and airfare paid by the employer. The article gives the wage, contract terms, BOESL charges, documents to bring, and the interview on 7 March 2025 at the Women's Technical Training Centre, Mirpur, Dhaka.

facts.statement: Through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), Tasker Apparel Company (তাস্কার অ্যাপারেল) in Jordan will recruit 300 women workers as female machine operators.

Eligibility for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel machine operator jobs: women aged 20 to 35 with relevant work experience, practical experience of operating plain machines and overlock machines, and proficiency on at least two machines.
Monthly basic pay for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel female machine operator job is stated as BDT 21,311; duty is eight hours a day, six days a week, with overtime available.

The Jordan Tasker Apparel job contract is three years and renewable; the employer pays for accommodation, food, primary medical care and transport, the airfare to join, and the return airfare after three years of satisfactory service; other terms follow Jordan's labour law.

Anyone with a case against them in Bangladesh or Jordan is ineligible for the BOESL Jordan recruitment. Those who previously returned from Jordan need not apply, except those who worked at Tasker company, who can re-apply and attend the interview.

Selected women machine operators for Jordan must pay a BDT 1,000 medical fee, BDT 220 for fingerprints and a BDT 23,500 BOESL service charge, by pay order in the name of "BOESL, Dhaka" from Sonali Bank, Moghbazar branch, submitted at the BOESL office. No additional cost is needed anywhere else.
The BDT 23,500 BOESL service charge will be paid back to the worker by Tasker company three months after she goes to Jordan.
An application fee of BDT 100 is payable for the online application to BOESL for the Jordan jobs.
Interview for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel recruitment: 7 March (2025) at 8 am at the Women's Technical Training Centre (Mohila TTC), Darus Salam Road, Mirpur, Dhaka.

Candidates for the BOESL Jordan interview must bring four passport-size colour photos, the original passport, and four colour sets and four black-and-white sets of photocopies of the passport's photo page; anyone with more than one passport must bring them all. A CV is not needed.
Applying online to BOESL guarantees an interview but not the job; candidates must pass a trade test/examination.
BOESL has no agent or sub-agent and makes worker selection decisions itself.
For information on the BOESL Jordan recruitment: telephone 02-48319125 and 02-48317515, and the Probash Bondhu call centre 16135.

headline_en: Expatriate workers protest in front of T&T Bhaban with six-point demand
summary_en: On Monday 10 February 2025 workers returned from the UAE and other countries rallied in Dhaka with six demands, including rehabilitation, lifting of the UAE 'no entry' on them and a foundation for affected expatriates. They say they were jailed abroad for protesting during Bangladesh's July movement, then released and sent home, and cannot go back.

facts.statement: Returned workers say that when the movement began in Bangladesh in July (2024) they also protested while abroad, were jailed for it, and returned to Bangladesh after release, suffering financial loss.
Workers who returned to Bangladesh from the UAE after being jailed over the July protests say the UAE has put a 'no entry' on them, so they cannot go back to Dubai unless it is lifted.

The protesting returnees say arrests in the UAE in the same case are still continuing and some Bangladeshi expatriates are still held in UAE prisons in that case; they demand diplomatic talks to stop the arrests and bring the prisoners home.

The returnees' six demands: (1) jobs for affected returnees, sending those who wish abroad at government initiative free of cost, interest-free loans for former businesspeople and new entrepreneurs, and government allowances for the elderly; (2) state initiative to lift the UAE no-entry; (3) stop arrests and free those still jailed in the UAE; (4) identify and try those who gave lists of expatriates' names to foreign law enforcement, including diplomats of the time and Consul General B M Jamal; (5) a trust like the July Smriti Foundation to compensate affected expatriates and inclusion of jailed returnees in the list of the July Mass Uprising Directorate under the Liberation War Affairs Ministry; (6) permission for a seven-member delegation to meet the Chief Adviser to invite him to a thanksgiving event.

On Monday 10 February 2025 the returnee workers gathered at about 10:30 am in front of Hotel InterContinental in Dhaka and at about 1:30 pm rallied in front of the T&T Bhaban nearby; a six-member delegation set off to meet the Chief Adviser.

Khoori promised necessary cooperation.

facts.statement: On Wednesday (about 29 January 2025) Bangladesh's Consul General in Dubai, Mohammad Rashedujjaman, met Khalil Ibrahim Khoori, Under Secretary of the UAE Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and discussed creating job opportunities for Bangladeshis in Dubai and the Northern Emirates, easing visa issuance and visa transfer, and increasing facilities for expatriate workers; Khoori assured necessary cooperation from his ministry.
facts.source_in_article: Report in Prothom Alo's Dur Porobash section

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Consul General in Dubai asked the UAE ministry to recruit more Bangladeshis as engineers, doctors, nurses and in other sectors, and sought help in resolving difficulties Bangladeshi seafarers face getting sign-off/transit visas at Dubai and other UAE ports.

headline_en: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka receives recognition for diplomatic excellence
summary_en: On 28 January 2025 Saudi ambassador Essa Yousef Essa Alduhailan received the 'Bangladesh Diplomatic Excellence Medal', partly for his role in sending Bangladeshi workers to Saudi Arabia. The article carries figures on Saudi visas issued to Bangladeshi workers and the number of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: Saudi ambassador Essa Yousef Essa Alduhailan said the Saudi embassy in Dhaka issued visas for 22 lakh (2.2 million) Bangladeshi workers in the last three years and is issuing 7,000 visas every day.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi ambassador Essa Yousef Essa Alduhailan

facts.statement: A foreign ministry official said that during the ambassador's roughly five years in Dhaka about 14 lakh (1.4 million) Bangladeshi workers went to Saudi Arabia, that worker migration to Saudi Arabia was never fully stopped even during the coronavirus period, and that Saudi visas were made easier for Bangladeshi citizens. (The article thus carries two different figures: 14 lakh workers gone in about five years, and 22 lakh worker visas issued in three years.)
facts.source_in_article: An unnamed Bangladesh foreign ministry official

facts.statement: Foreign Adviser M Touhid Hossain said 30 lakh (3 million) expatriate Bangladeshis are in Saudi Arabia.
The ambassador was credited with an important role in including Bangladesh in Saudi initiatives such as the 'Route to Makkah Initiative'.

headline_en: 105 more Bangladeshis return from Lebanon
summary_en: 105 more Bangladeshis stranded in war-hit Lebanon returned on Thursday night 5 December 2024 on a government-chartered Emirates flight. A total of 963 have returned on 9 flights; the government pays repatriation costs for those who want to return.

facts.statement: 105 more Bangladeshis who had been stranded in Lebanon under Israeli aggression returned home at 11 pm on Thursday 5 December 2024 on Emirates Airlines flight EK-584 chartered by the Bangladesh government, with help from the foreign ministry, the expatriates' welfare ministry, the Bangladesh mission in Beirut and IOM.
In total 963 Bangladeshis have so far returned safely from Lebanon on 9 flights.
IOM gave each returnee from Lebanon BDT 5,000, necessary food and primary medical care at the airport.

The Bangladesh government is bearing the repatriation cost of Bangladeshis who wish to return from Lebanon; for those who want to stay, the Bangladesh embassy in Beirut is continuing efforts to ensure their safety.
An expatriate Bangladeshi was killed in an Israeli bomb attack in Lebanon a few days before 6 December 2024.

summary_en: An opinion piece by a Malaysia-based expatriate arguing that the main problem of expatriates is delay and harassment in renewing passports through Bangladesh missions, especially in Malaysia and the Middle East. He describes crowding and rough handling by private security guards at the e-passport office in Malaysia, says people turn to brokers and pay extra to avoid harassment, and calls for more consular offices and help with applications.

facts.statement: The writer says the main problem of expatriates is difficulty renewing passports through embassies, especially not getting the passport on time; delays in getting passports are reported for expatriates in Malaysia and various Middle East countries.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, a Bangladeshi expatriate in Malaysia for 21 years

facts.statement: The writer says about 15 lakh (1.5 million) expatriate Bangladeshis currently live in Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, a Bangladeshi expatriate in Malaysia for 21 years

facts.statement: The writer stresses that a passport is indispensable for an expatriate's visa or permit; no visa or permit can be had without a valid passport.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, a Bangladeshi expatriate in Malaysia for 21 years

facts.statement: The writer says expatriates who came for service at the office responsible for e-passports in Malaysia were (perhaps lightly) struck by security guards of the private company in charge of passports, amid crowding and pushing in the queue.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, a Bangladeshi expatriate in Malaysia for 21 years

facts.statement: The writer says that at Bangladesh missions officials expect expatriates to know all the rules and have no time to explain; to avoid harassment over passports, travel passes and document attestation many expatriates go to brokers and spend extra money.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, a Bangladeshi expatriate in Malaysia for 21 years

facts.statement: The writer urges the government to increase consular offices, spend more on serving expatriates, have embassy staff help people fill in applications correctly so they do not need brokers, and prepare in advance for surges in applicants or delays in printing passports in Bangladesh.

headline_en: Case in Barishal court over alleged trafficking of 23 young men to Saudi Arabia
summary_en: On Monday 28 October 2024 a case was filed at the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal against three people, including the managing director of the Dhaka recruiting agency SJ Group, for sending 23 men to Saudi Arabia on a false promise of solar-panel company jobs at 1,800 riyals a month; 12 were caught and deported and 11 are untraced. A separate case filed the day before accuses three people linked to M R International of sending a man to Saudi Arabia, giving him no job and handing him to a gang that demanded BDT 5 lakh ransom.

facts.statement: On Monday 28 October 2024 a case was filed at the Barishal Human Trafficking Offences Tribunal against three people including a recruiting agency director for allegedly trafficking 23 men from Barishal to Saudi Arabia with a promise of high-paid jobs; judge Md. Sohel Ahmed ordered the officer-in-charge of Mehendiganj police station to record it as an FIR and submit an investigation report. The plaintiff is Ershad Howlader of Darichar-Khajuria village, Mehendiganj upazila, father of one of the men.

Accused in the 23-man Saudi trafficking case: Araf Hossain alias Sifat, a Saudi-based expatriate and managing director of recruiting agency SJ Group of Purana Paltan, Dhaka; and Babul Howlader and Kuddus Howlader, sons of Samsul Haque Howlader of Badarpur village, Mehendiganj upazila, Barishal.

The accused lured Hasanuzzaman (son of plaintiff Ershad Howlader) and 22 other young men with jobs at a solar panel firm named in the case as 'Taj Al Nawar Trading East Company' (তাজ আল নাওয়ার ট্রেডিং ইস্ট কোম্পানি) in Saudi Arabia at a monthly salary of 1,800 riyals.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

facts.statement: Each of the 23 Barishal men paid BDT 4.5 lakh to the accused, BDT 1 crore 3 lakh 50 thousand in total, to go to Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

facts.statement: The 23 men were taken to Saudi Arabia on 4 May; instead of the solar panel company job they were made to work 1 month 15 days on a Hajj project and were paid 615 riyals.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

facts.statement: When the Hajj project ended, 12 of the 23 men were caught by Saudi police as illegal migrants and later sent back to Bangladesh; the other 11 had not been traced as of late October 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

facts.statement: On Sunday 27 October 2024 Kuddus Rarhi of Chunarchar village, Mehendiganj upazila, filed another case at the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal against three people for trafficking his son to Saudi Arabia and demanding money under threat of killing him; the judge ordered the OC of Kazirhat police station, Barishal, to record it as an FIR.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

Abdul Baten Sheikh of Phulbaria, Kapasia, Gazipur.
Md. Rubel paid BDT 3 lakh 80 thousand to Rana and Habiba under an agreement, after Abu Taher Sheikh proposed sending him to Saudi Arabia; he was sent to Saudi Arabia on 15 May 2024.

facts.statement: After arriving in Saudi Arabia on 15 May 2024 Md. Rubel was given no job and was handed over to a human trafficking gang in Saudi Arabia, whose members tortured him and demanded BDT 5 lakh from his father under threat of killing him; when told, the accused said Rubel would be killed if the money was not paid.
facts.source_in_article: Tuhin Molla, bench assistant of the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal, citing the case

headline_en: 12 Rohingya and 8 Bangladeshis rescued while being trafficked to Malaysia
summary_en: Late on Tuesday night 15 October 2024 police in Teknaf, Cox's Bazar rescued 20 people (8 Bangladeshis and 12 Rohingya) gathered in a house for trafficking to Malaysia by sea, and detained three brokers including a woman. On 14 October police and coast guard had detained 26 Rohingya at Inani beach in a similar attempt.

facts.statement: Late on Tuesday night 15 October 2024 police raided a house in Dakshin Lambari, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar and rescued 20 people (12 Rohingya including women and children and 8 Bangladeshis) who had been gathered for trafficking to Malaysia through the Teknaf sea coast.
facts.source_in_article: Teknaf Model police station OC Muhammad Gias Uddin

facts.statement: Police detained three brokers in the Teknaf raid: Luna Begum and Md. Riduan of Dakshin Lambari, Teknaf Sadar union, and Md. Abdullah of Kachubunia, Sabrang union; five or six people tried to run and the others escaped. Police are filing a case under the relevant law and arranging to return those rescued to their relatives.
facts.source_in_article: Teknaf Model police station OC Muhammad Gias Uddin

facts.statement: The Teknaf OC said an organised gang trafficking people by sea has become active and its members had gathered the victims for trafficking to Malaysia in exchange for large sums of money (amount not stated).
facts.source_in_article: Teknaf Model police station OC Muhammad Gias Uddin

facts.statement: The 8 Bangladeshis rescued in Teknaf were Abdul Mabud and Shahjahan of Patenga, Chattogram; Zahur Alam of Whykong union, Teknaf; Abdur Rahim of Ghonarpara, Cox's Bazar municipality; Touhidul Islam and Md. Sohel of Munshir Deil, Maheshkhali; Monirul Alam of Kauarkop, Ramu; and Monjur Alam of Nayapara, PM Khali, Cox's Bazar Sadar.

The 12 Rohingya rescued in Teknaf came from the Hakimpara, Balukhali, Kutupalong, Jamtoli, Shafiullah Kata and Thaingkhali camps in Ukhiya (named: Ayat Ullah, Nesar Ullah, Syed Kasim, Md. Nur Absar, Shafi Alam, Dil Kayes, Nur Alam, Md. Nazrul, Sabekunnahar, Dholu Begum, Umme Habiba, Minuara Begum).
On the morning of 14 October 2024 police and coast guard detained 26 Rohingya at the Inani beach area of Ukhiya while they were being trafficked to Malaysia; another 80 to 90 Rohingya escaped.

headline_en: A boat journey on the road to death... the chains of this modern slavery are still invisible
summary_en: A feature on sea trafficking from Cox's Bazar/Teknaf towards Malaysia, with accounts from victims and families: a son jailed in Malaysia, a brother missing for seven and a half years, a man jailed nearly a year in Myanmar after his trawler broke down, and another who drifted three months at sea and was held 11 months in Indonesia. It describes broker lures, ransom demands, killings at sea and UNHCR figures on Rohingya sea departures and deaths.

facts.statement: Local brokers mainly target teenagers and young men, promising that it will cost little and that jobs pay a lakh taka a month; better-off people, especially those aged 18 to 35, are also lured with onward travel via Malaysia and Indonesia to Australia, even America or New Zealand; women are told they will get good work in hotels, motels, parlours or shopping malls.

In April (2024) the government brought 173 Bangladeshis home from prison in Myanmar; the article says Mohammad Jamal was among them (though Jamal himself says he returned in July; the article carries both).
Mohammad Jamal of Cox's Bazar agreed a BDT 4 lakh deal with a broker named Ayub to go to Malaysia by sea.

In July 2023 Jamal and nine others were taken in a small boat from Garjania, Ramu upazila, Cox's Bazar and put on a 'ship' that was in fact a small fishing trawler carrying 73 people in all, including five females under 18.

After three days at sea the trawler's hull cracked in Myanmar (Burma) waters; after about two more days the passengers tied a red cloth to the trawler and deliberately surrendered to the Myanmar navy. Rohingya and Bangladeshis were kept in separate prisons; Jamal was held in a jail he calls 'Myo Myo Taung' (মিও মিও টং).

In the Myanmar prison Bangladeshi prisoners were made to do all the work, from growing vegetables to cooking, on scant food: rice starch at about 7 am, some rice with dried chilli at 11 am and rice again at 4 pm, with no fish or meat. Jamal says he served 11 months 19 days and returned with government help in July; those who said they were under 18 were still being held.

Kamal (pseudonym) of Teknaf made a BDT 1 lakh deal with a man named Abu to go to Malaysia, to be repaid after getting a good job there; during the voyage the brokers pressed for BDT 3 lakh ransom, and the total cost by the time he got home was BDT 2 lakh 30 thousand.

Kamal's trawler, carrying Bangladeshis and Rohingya, first reached the Bay of Bengal in Myanmar's waters and stayed seven days, then headed for Malaysia via Thailand; on reaching Malaysia it was chased by Malaysian police into Indonesian waters, and was sent back from there too.

On Kamal's trawler a Rohingya who protested was shot and thrown into the water; two Bengalis died in a clash with Rohingya; people who fell ill and died from lack of food were thrown into the sea; those who asked for food or water were beaten. Food was plain rice with chilli and one glass of water once a day, which had to last 28 hours.

After the Bengalis sank the trawler in anger and many passing ships did not rescue them, an Indonesian navy ship rescued Kamal's group; they were held in Indonesia for 11 months before the Bangladesh government brought them back. He had drifted at sea for three months in all.
Brokers on the sea route torture passengers and collect money from their families as ransom.

Sohel of Karachi Para village, Teknaf boarded a boat to go to Malaysia by sea and went missing; his widowed mother Hasina Akter says the government informed her that he is in prison in Malaysia and will bring him back once all papers are submitted; she has been running between the police station and the magistrate's office.

Manik Molla of Teknaf has been searching for his younger brother Shakil Molla for seven and a half years; Shakil, then 17, left by sea for Malaysia and was never heard from. About two years ago a broker told the family Shakil was in a Malaysian prison; they paid the broker money and he also vanished.
According to UNHCR, 8,312 Rohingya refugees tried to go to Malaysia by sea from 2018 to 2022; 589 of them drowned and many went missing.

Sufia, a 28-year-old Rohingya woman whose marriage was arranged with a Rohingya man in Malaysia, died of dehydration about two days into the boat journey; traffickers had demanded BDT 3 lakh from her relatives to deliver her, and the family learned of her death from someone on the boat while still raising the money.

Anti-trafficking experts stress teaching the public the difference between 'migration' and 'trafficking' and urge people to be open about their plans to go abroad instead of keeping them secret as brokers advise. Victim Kamal tells everyone to try to do something at home rather than go abroad the hard way.
People concerned believe that neither arrests of brokers, deaths in 'gunfights' nor deaths in trawler sinkings have been able to stop human trafficking by sea.

headline_en: Syndicate fee per worker for Malaysia was BDT 152,000
summary_en: At a press conference in Dhaka on Thursday 3 October 2024, members of BAIRA alleged that a syndicate charged a fee of BDT 152,000 per worker sent to Malaysia, that 95 percent of agencies were discriminated against, and that 50,000 workers could not go, including 17,000 who had completed all steps. They named former BAIRA secretary general Ruhul Amin alias Swapan as the mastermind and set out eight demands including keeping the market open to all agencies.

facts.statement: BAIRA members allege that the 'syndicate fee' for sending a worker to Malaysia was BDT 1 lakh 52 thousand per worker, which is why workers had to spend extra money to go.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA members' written statement at a press conference, read by joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam

facts.statement: BAIRA members say 95 percent of recruiting agencies were discriminated against because of the Malaysia syndicate, and that 50,000 workers could not go because of corruption and irregularities, including 17,000 who could not go even after completing all procedures.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA members' written statement at a press conference, read by joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam

facts.statement: BAIRA members name former BAIRA secretary general Ruhul Amin alias Swapan as the mastermind of the Malaysia syndicate, built with former MPs and ministers; the names raised include former MPs Benazir Ahmed, Nizam Hazari and Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury and Awami League leader Mohiuddin Mohi. The statement says no action had been taken against them.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA members' written statement at a press conference, read by joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam

facts.statement: BAIRA members' demands include: keep the Malaysia labour market open to all with no new syndicate; cancel the Malaysian government's power to select Bangladeshi recruiting agencies and let employers select the agency; the ministry should set up a central online system so all agencies can send workers at low or no cost; workers who could not go on time because of the syndicate should be re-sent to Malaysia at low cost without a syndicate; and those behind the syndicate should be tried.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA members' written statement at a press conference, read by joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam

headline_en: Expatriates' role in Bangladesh's socio-economic development and their demands to the government
summary_en: An opinion piece by the convener of an expatriates' group, written from Ethiopia, describing in general terms how expatriates contribute to Bangladesh and listing 15 demands to the government, covering airport treatment, remittance incentive, repatriation of bodies, embassy services, fees, training and voting.

facts.statement: Demands of the Swadhin Bangla Probashi Oikya Parishad include: a separate airport lounge for expatriate workers with food if they wait over two hours; an end to airport harassment and secure luggage; a minimum 5 percent incentive on remittances; and bodies of expatriates who die abroad, legal or undocumented, to be brought home quickly at government cost with the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's fixed amount paid to the family.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, convener of Swadhin Bangla Probashi Oikya Parishad, writing for expatriates in Ethiopia

facts.statement: Further demands of the group: embassies to help undocumented Bangladeshis regularise; embassies to be free of politics, bribery and nepotism and give fast, friendly service; document fees to be reviewed and some services such as birth and death certificates made free; embassy websites and social media to be kept updated; workers to be told their job terms and salary before departure; three to six months' training for every worker before going; voting rights for expatriates; and a government 'monthly pay and allowance card' for expatriates with at least five years abroad and valid papers.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer, convener of Swadhin Bangla Probashi Oikya Parishad, writing for expatriates in Ethiopia

facts.statement: The writer states that Bangladesh is the world's fourth largest remittance-receiving country (no source given).

headline_en: UAE to take two thousand taxi and motorcycle drivers a year
summary_en: On Thursday 27 June 2024 the then state minister said the UAE has begun taking motorcycle riders and car drivers from Bangladesh: Dubai Taxi, a UAE government-owned company, will take 1,000 motorcycle riders and 300 taxi drivers in 2024 and at least 2,000 a year from 2025. The UAE ambassador said the workers will be paid under UAE labour law.

headline_en: Results of education scholarships for children of expatriate workers published
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board published the final list of scholarship winners among children of expatriate workers who passed SSC/equivalent in 2023 and HSC/equivalent in 2022; applications had been taken online in January 2024. The article gives the scholarship duration and the Probash Bondhu call centre numbers.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives education scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers; in 2024 it awarded them to students who passed SSC/equivalent in 2023 and HSC/equivalent in 2022 and published the final selected list (by 18 April 2024).

Applications for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship were taken online in January 2024; eligible were students who passed SSC/equivalent in 2023 and study in class 11/equivalent or diploma first semester/year, and students who passed HSC/equivalent in 2022 and study in first semester/year at a university or medical college in Bangladesh, subject to conditions.

Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship duration: SSC-category awardees get two years (classes 11 and 12) or four years for diploma students; HSC-category awardees get four years at university and five years for medical; the student's session is not taken into account.
For details on the scholarship the Wage Earners' Welfare Board asks people to call the Probash Bondhu call centre: 16135 (from Bangladesh, toll free) and +8809610102030 (from abroad).

facts.statement: Through the 'Ami Probashi' platform recruiting agencies can post jobs, select aspiring migrants from the job portal and complete all government processes.

About 80 percent of Bangladesh's recruiting agencies have joined Ami Probashi; about 2,100 recruiting agencies can complete almost all migration-related government services online through its portal, including BMET clearance applications, bulk BMET database registration and Pre-Departure Orientation (PDO) enrolment.
Attestation of foreign job demand letters is to be added to the Ami Probashi platform soon, according to the press release.

Ami Probashi held a workshop on its 'Recruitment Management System and Job Portal' with representatives of more than 100 leading recruiting agencies; speakers were BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury, BAIRA joint secretary Akbar Hossain Manju and Sadia International proprietor Shamim Ahmed Chowdhury Noman.

headline_en: How did his father die in Kuwait? Selim has been seeking the answer for 14 years
summary_en: Md. Abdul Ali, a legally employed Bangladeshi driver in Kuwait since 1985, died on 27 November 2010 in Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh; his body came home on 14 January 2011 with head injuries and broken teeth. His son Selim has filed more than 11 applications to Bangladeshi offices over 14 years seeking the cause of death and compensation; the embassy reported that the employer (kafeel) refused to help with compensation, and the Kuwaiti death certificate gives the cause as 'under consideration'.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi worker Md. Abdul Ali died on 27 November 2010 in the Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh (গিলিব আল সুয়েখ) area of Kuwait; his body returned to Bangladesh on 14 January 2011. He had worked in Kuwait as a driver since 1985.

Abdul Ali's brother Abdul Mannan (34 years in Kuwait) and son Selim say the body had injury marks on the head, many broken teeth and blood stains on the beard, and they believe he was tortured and killed rather than dying naturally.
facts.source_in_article: Brother Abdul Mannan and son Selim

facts.statement: Abdul Ali had taken work under a new owner only two months before he died, and was working for an owner other than the employer through whom he had gone to Kuwait; Kuwaiti daily Al Shahid reported on 16 December 2010 on his unnatural death and said he had not been paid for those two months.

Abdul Mannan says that after the death those concerned hurried over the body and suggested burying it in Kuwait; when he considered finding the cause or filing a case he received threats by mobile phone and hints he could be framed in a case, and he got no help from embassy staff of the time.

In a letter dated 7 August 2011 to the BMET director general, the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait's First Secretary (Labour) K M Ali Reza wrote that the embassy contacted Abdul Ali's kafeel (employer) several times on mobile number 99056231 about compensation/financial benefit, that the kafeel said he could not cooperate on compensation, and that Abdul Ali had been working legally in Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: Embassy letter by First Secretary (Labour) K M Ali Reza

facts.statement: Selim says the number given in the embassy letter as the kafeel's is actually his uncle Abdul Mannan's number in Kuwait, raising doubt whether the embassy contacted the kafeel at all; his father's phone had two numbers of the kafeel but the embassy did nothing with them.

Selim wrote to the Bangladesh ambassador in Kuwait on 15 January (2024) saying the death certificate from Kuwait's birth and death registration branch does not give the real cause, stating 'condition under consideration' in the cause-of-death field.

Since 2011 Selim has filed more than 11 applications to government offices: on 5 February 2024 to the foreign and expatriates' welfare ministries demanding a fair investigation and maximum compensation, and on 11 February 2024 to the Principal Secretary of the Prime Minister's Office, the Secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry and the Director General of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board.

The article says BMET asked the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait on 27 June 2012 to re-investigate, that the embassy's First Secretary (Labour) replied on 7 August of that year, and that Abdul Ali's wife Kawsari Begum, dissatisfied, re-applied to BMET's Director (Welfare) on 4 April 2012 (dates as printed; the article elsewhere dates the embassy letter 7 August 2011).

Mostafa Jamil Khan, Director (Welfare) of the foreign ministry's Consular and Welfare wing, wrote to the Kuwait embassy on 6 February 2024 asking it to take necessary steps; he told Prothom Alo that after so many years it is hard to prove Abdul Ali was murdered in Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: Mostafa Jamil Khan, Director (Welfare), Ministry of Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: A Wage Earners' Welfare Board deputy assistant director in charge of the Kuwait desk said the family keeps re-applying because it is not satisfied with the embassy's reply, the board forwards the applications to the embassy and other places, and the matter is still unresolved.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board deputy assistant director (Kuwait desk)

facts.statement: Selim says that if his father was murdered he wants qisas or compensation under Kuwait's law.

headline_en: Case under migration law for anyone who tries to go abroad illegally
summary_en: Police in Cox's Bazar have begun filing cases under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act against Rohingya who flee the camps to go to Malaysia or elsewhere by sea. In the first such case, three Rohingya girls aged 12 and 14 rescued from a boat at Teknaf on 5 January 2024 were sent to jail along with an alleged trafficker, then bailed on 9 January and ordered back to the camp.

facts.statement: Police in Cox's Bazar say Rohingya who flee the Ukhiya camps and try to go to Malaysia or another country by sea will now be charged under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act and sent to jail; police say the step is meant to stop human trafficking and risky illegal sea crossings.

On the night of 6 January 2024 Sub-Inspector Sanjib Kumar Pal filed a case at Teknaf Model police station under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act against three Rohingya girls (two aged 12, one aged 14, from Balukhali camp, Ukhiya) and two alleged traffickers; all those held were sent to the district jail through the court. It is reported to be the first such case against a Rohingya who fled a camp.

The arrested alleged trafficker is Ariful Islam (19), son of Abdu Sattar of Adharghona village, Kalamarchhara union, Maheshkhali; Shamshul Alam (38), son of Amir Hamza of Lengurbil village, Teknaf Sadar union, is also accused and is absconding.

On the afternoon of 5 January 2024 at Lambarighat on the Teknaf Marine Drive, assistant judge Maitri Bhattacharya, returning from election inquiry duty, saw three Rohingya girls being put on a wooden boat for illegal trafficking to Malaysia; police with her rescued them, Teknaf police detained the trafficker and seized the boat.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Saiful Islam, bench clerk of the Cox's Bazar assistant judge court

facts.statement: Teknaf OC Muhammad Osman Gani said the three girls admitted in initial questioning that they were going abroad of their own will, which is why they were also charged. The Cox's Bazar children's court granted them bail on Tuesday 9 January 2024; they were to be sent back to the camp on 10 January and must appear in court from the camp as accused.
facts.source_in_article: Teknaf OC Muhammad Osman Gani; jail superintendent Md. Shah Alam Khan

facts.statement: According to police and Rohingya leaders, in the last five years law enforcers rescued at least 5,000 Rohingya being trafficked by trawler to Malaysia from the coasts of Teknaf, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar Sadar and Maheshkhali and returned them to the camps, and returned at least 60,000 Rohingya caught fleeing to other districts; no case was filed against any of them before.
There are 12.5 lakh registered Rohingya in 33 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf, of whom 8 lakh came in the months after 25 August 2017.

headline_en: No contact with family for four months, then a friend's message from Russia: 'Sagar is no more'
summary_en: Mohammad Sagar, 24, of Chandina, Cumilla went to Russia in mid-2025 for BDT 6 lakh and worked in a bakery, then was lured by a Bangladeshi broker in Russia into the Russian army and was sent to the Ukraine war in May 2026. His family lost contact, and on Saturday 17 October 2026 a friend in Russia messaged that 'Sagar is no more'; the death is unconfirmed.

facts.statement: Mohammad Sagar of Chhaykot, Chandina municipality, Cumilla went to Russia in mid-2025 at a cost of BDT 6 lakh with the help of Sohel, a shop manager and returnee migrant he knew; his father borrowed heavily to send him.
In Russia Sagar worked in a bakery and was earning about BDT 70,000 a month.

A Bangladeshi man Sagar met in Russia promised him a job in the Russian army and a one-time payment of BDT 30 lakh; lured by this, Sagar left the bakery job in May 2026 and joined the Russia-Ukraine war. His uncle says the broker gave false information to enlist him as a soldier although Sagar is illiterate.

After Sagar was sent to the Ukraine war in May 2026 his family lost contact; on Saturday 17 October 2026 his friend Rajon, who is in Russia, sent a message to Sagar's sister's phone saying only 'Sagar is no more', gave no details and could not be reached afterwards. The family cannot confirm the death, or when and how it happened.
Before going to the war Sagar sent BDT 3 lakh to his uncle Abdul Awal's bank account; contact stopped after that.

Chandina Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mohammad Ashraful Haque said on 19 October 2026 that he sent municipality staff to the family's house, that there is no confirmed information of Sagar's death other than the friend's message, and that they are keeping track.

headline_en: Boat sinks off Teknaf coast on the way from Myanmar to Malaysia; Rohingya mother and son die
summary_en: A boat carrying irregular migrants from Myanmar's Rakhine state capsized off Baharchhara, Teknaf (Cox's Bazar) at dawn on Tuesday 22 September 2026. A Rohingya woman and her 9-year-old son died, 16 people were rescued alive and one woman was missing. Eight of the rescued are Bangladeshis who say they were taken to Myanmar about a year earlier on a promise of being sent to Malaysia and were held there for a year.

facts.statement: A boat full of irregular migrants coming from Myanmar sank at dawn on Tuesday (22 September 2026) off the Boro Dail-Kachchhapia boat landing in Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar; the Bangladesh Coast Guard recovered the bodies of a Rohingya woman, Chhura Khatun (28), and her 9-year-old son.

In the Teknaf boat sinking, 16 people were rescued alive by the Coast Guard and local residents (13 men, 2 women and 1 child according to police), and one woman was still missing as of Wednesday afternoon, 23 September 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard; Inspector Md. Abu Sayed, in-charge of Baharchhara police investigation centre

facts.statement: The boat travelled from Myanmar's Rakhine state across the Naf river and the Bay of Bengal to the Baharchhara coast of Teknaf, where a large wave overturned it late at night as it was entering via the Baharchhara boat landing.

Eight Bangladeshis among those rescued told police they were taken from Bangladesh to Myanmar about a year earlier on the promise of being taken on to Malaysia; instead of being sent to Malaysia they were kept in various places in Myanmar for the past year.

According to police citing the rescued people, on Monday night (21 September 2026) they were put on a boat to be sent to Malaysia by sea and brought to the Baharchhara coast of Teknaf, where the boat sank after being hit by a wave.

The rescued Bangladeshis are Omar Faruk of ward 9 of Teknaf municipality; Kurban Ali of Majher Para, Shahporir Dwip, Sabrang union; Abu Rasel and Jamir Hossain of Naikhongchhari; Md. Mostafa of Katakhali, Hoaikyong, Teknaf; Abdul Kader of Uttar Nengulbil, Teknaf Sadar union; Mizanur Rahman of Morichya Ghona; and Apu Barua of Rajapalong union, Ukhiya.

Most of the Rohingya on the boat are reported to be registered residents of the Teknaf and Ukhiya refugee camps. The rescued Rohingya named are Md. Salim (Mochni camp, Hnila, Teknaf), Md. Hossain (Kutupalong camp, Ukhiya), Md. Saiful Karim (Akyab, Myanmar), Abdul Amin (Teknaf camp-26), Samjida (Chakmarkul camp-21, Hoaikyong), Lal Moti of Buthidaung, Rakhine and her 9-year-old son Hossain Johar, and Md. Idris (Jadimura camp-27).

The 16 people rescued were handed over to Teknaf Model police station at night; police were verifying their identities and said necessary action would be taken. The total number on the boat and the identity of the missing woman were not known.

Remittances exceeded USD 3 billion (300 crore) for six consecutive months from December 2025: December USD 322 crore, January 2026 USD 317 crore, February USD 302 crore, March about USD 375 crore, April USD 312 crore 70 lakh, May USD 342 crore 50 lakh (May was 15.34% above May 2025).

headline_en: Taken to Kazakhstan on a promise of Australia and tortured: how Sohel got back
summary_en: Sohel Rana alias Jewel (38) of Bagharpara, Jashore, gave up his restaurant business in Malaysia on a broker's promise of Europe, then agreed to go to Australia for BDT 16 lakh and paid BDT 12 lakh. He was flown via Dubai to Kazakhstan in January 2026, had his passport taken, was confined in an iron-smelting factory and asked for BDT 30 lakh, escaped, and came home on a travel permit on 20 April 2026 after his wife sent a further BDT 2.2 lakh. A trafficking case against the broker couple Md. Kaiyum and Nazma Akter was recorded on 6 April 2026; no one has been arrested.

facts.statement: Sohel Rana alias Jewel (38) of Ghop Durgapur village, Bagharpara upazila, Jashore, left Bangladesh for Australia on 15 January 2026 under a BDT 16 lakh contract; he had paid BDT 12 lakh to the broker from his savings, money borrowed against a promise to give paddy instead of interest, an NGO loan and other borrowing.
The broker Nazma Akter agreed to send Sohel Rana to Australia on the condition of a job paying USD 1,000 a month; after taking the money she kept stalling him.

Sohel Rana met broker Nazma Akter alias Nurjahan in 2014 in Bangladesh; she lured him with a promise of sending him to Europe within three to four months, so he returned from Malaysia in November 2024 (leaving two restaurants he had built there after going in December 2016 as a hotel cook), but she could not send him to Europe and then offered Australia.

Sohel Rana was first taken on 15 January 2026 to Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on a one-month business visa, and the next day, 16 January, to Kazakhstan, where he was told he would be taken to Australia after staying one month.

In Kazakhstan the abuse began at the hotel; the broker Nazma's representative took the passports of Sohel and two other Bangladeshis, and on 24 January 2026 they were driven about 900 km to a hilly area named Shimkyat (শিমক্যাট) and locked in an iron-smelting factory, given one piece of bread once a day.
The broker's representative demanded BDT 30 lakh from Sohel Rana and two other Bangladeshis to be let out of the factory in Kazakhstan where they were held, and threatened to kill them otherwise.

On 28 January 2026 Sohel Rana and one of the two other captive Bangladeshis escaped over the factory boundary wall with the help of a guard; the third Bangladeshi did not agree to escape. They then stayed in a hotel.
On 14 April 2026 Sohel Rana and his companion sent a text message to the mobile phone of a Bangladesh immigration officer describing their danger.

A South African lawyer demanded BDT 1 lakh 20 thousand to send Sohel Rana home from Kazakhstan; Sohel's wife borrowed and sent the lawyer BDT 1 lakh 20 thousand plus another BDT 1 lakh for the air fare, and Sohel returned to Bangladesh on 20 April 2026 with a travel permit.

Sohel's wife Mukta Begum applied on 9 March 2026 to the Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Prevention and Suppression Tribunal-1, Jashore, for a case; on the court's order the case was recorded at Bagharpara police station on 6 April 2026 against Md. Kaiyum (48) of Muslimnagar village, Keraniganj upazila, Dhaka, and his wife Nazma Akter (45). Police had not arrested anyone as of 22 June 2026.

The investigating officer, Sub-Inspector Md. Mizanur Rahman of Bagharpara police station, said accused Md. Kaiyum is outside the country and efforts are on to arrest the other accused, Nazma Akter; Nazma Akter's phone was found switched off on repeated calls by the reporter.
facts.source_in_article: SI Md. Mizanur Rahman, Bagharpara Thana

facts.statement: After returning on 20 April 2026 Sohel Rana says he has about BDT 15 lakh of debt and nothing left but his homestead; creditors come to his house daily and he sometimes stays in hiding. He wants the money returned.

headline_en: More than three billion dollars in remittances for six months running
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data published on 1 June 2026 show remittances of USD 342.5 crore in May 2026, 15.34% up on May 2025, making six consecutive months above USD 3 billion. The article gives bank-wise figures for May and the reserve position.

facts.statement: Bangladesh received USD 342 crore 50 lakh 30 thousand in remittances in May 2026, 15.34% more than the USD 296 crore 94 lakh 60 thousand of May 2025.

Monthly remittances were USD 322 crore in December 2025, 317 crore in January 2026, 302 crore in February, about 375 crore in March, 312 crore 70 lakh in April and 342.5 crore in May, six straight months above USD 300 crore.

Banking sector people said expatriates sent more money in March and April 2026 because of Eid-ul-Fitr and the US-Israel war with Iran, and in May ahead of Eid-ul-Azha; because of the Middle East crisis the taka had weakened somewhat against the dollar, so remitters were getting a higher price per dollar.
In July-May of fiscal 2025-26 Bangladesh received USD 3,275 crore 68 lakh in remittances, more than 19% above the USD 2,750 crore 69 lakh of the first 11 months of the previous fiscal year.
In May 2026 private banks brought about USD 238 crore 67 lakh in remittances; Islami Bank alone brought about USD 59 crore 21 lakh and BRAC Bank, second among private banks, about USD 41 crore.

In May 2026 the six state-owned banks brought about USD 56 crore 65 lakh in remittances, of which Agrani Bank brought the most, about USD 24.25 crore; the specialised Krishi Bank brought about USD 47 crore and is second overall.
On Monday 1 June 2026 Bangladesh's gross foreign exchange reserves were USD 3,477 crore (34.77 billion); under the IMF BPM6 method USD 3,011 crore (30.11 billion).

headline_en: Bangladeshis in Korea demand an Incheon transit on the Dhaka-Tokyo route
summary_en: Bangladeshis living in South Korea welcomed Biman Bangladesh Airlines' plan to restart direct Dhaka-Tokyo flights in June 2026 and demanded a short transit or stopover at Incheon International Airport on that route. Because there is no direct Dhaka-Korea flight, they travel via third countries at higher fares and longer times; they have opened an online petition portal.

facts.statement: Biman Bangladesh Airlines has taken an initiative to restart its direct Dhaka-Tokyo flight in June 2026.

There is no direct Dhaka-Korea flight, so Bangladeshi expatriates mostly have to travel through a third country, which takes more time, costs comparatively higher fares and often creates transit complications; passengers have to use various foreign airlines.

Bangladeshis in South Korea are demanding that Biman add a short transit or stopover at Incheon International Airport on the Dhaka-Tokyo route, so passengers could travel Dhaka-Incheon-Tokyo or Incheon-Dhaka.

Korea-based Bangladeshis launched an online opinion and petition web portal, https://petition2biman.com, where Bangladeshis living in Korea, people travelling between Bangladesh and Korea and future users of the route can join the petition by giving some basic information.

The expatriate community called on the Bangladesh Embassy in Seoul, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism and government policymakers to act quickly, and asked people to tag Biman and the Bangladesh Embassy Seoul in an online campaign.

The article says a large number of Bangladeshi workers, students, businesspeople, researchers and professionals live in South Korea, and many workers, students and businesspeople plan to go there from Bangladesh every year.

The UK says the company advertised high-paid service-sector jobs in Russia and that the Bangladeshis recruited were forced to fight on the front line against Ukraine.

headline_en: Uncertainty from the Middle East crisis: what should remittance-dependent families do
summary_en: A personal-finance piece advising families in Bangladesh who depend on remittances from the Middle East to prepare for a possible fall in income during the regional unrest. It lists five steps: review spending, build an emergency fund, reduce dependence on one income source, cut high-interest debt and divide a returning migrant's lump-sum savings.

facts.statement: Families dependent on remittances are advised to separate fixed and non-fixed spending, treat rent, education and medicine as priorities, postpone travel, festivals and unnecessary purchases, and work out the minimum cost of at least three months.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo personal finance desk)

facts.statement: Remittance-receiving families are advised to build a separate emergency fund equal to three to six months of expenses; if that is not possible at once, set aside 10 to 15% of the remittance in a separate bank account or short-term savings certificates (sanchayapatra).

The article's worked example: a family receiving BDT 50,000 a month in remittance with minimum spending of BDT 35,000 can target an emergency fund of at least BDT 1 lakh 5 thousand (three months' spending), reachable in one year by setting aside BDT 7,000 a month.

Families are advised to reduce total dependence on remittance by having another member earn part-time (work from home, small business, skill-based services) and to plan to pay off high-interest personal loans or credit cards first.

Keeping the risk of the migrant having to return in mind, the article advises not spending a migrant's lump-sum savings all at once but dividing it: one part emergency fund, one part income-generating investment, the rest in safe deposits.

The article says that when employment, wages or working hours fall in the Middle East it directly affects the cash flow of families in Bangladesh, and families relying solely on remittance are at comparatively higher risk; there is no certainty when the Middle East situation will normalise.
facts.source_in_article: the article, citing a review of Bangladesh Bank data

Remittances were USD 322 crore in December 2025, 317 crore in January 2026 and 302 crore in February 2026, falling month to month; in the five months before December 2025 they were below USD 3 billion each month.

Several bank officials, speaking anonymously, said remittances usually rise before the two Eids, but over the last two to three months the pace was good because of the recently held election; funds raised from Bangladeshis abroad for many candidates later came into the country as remittance.

In calendar 2025 Bangladesh received USD 3,282 crore in remittances in total, about equal to Bangladesh Bank's foreign exchange reserves; the record single month then was USD 329 crore in March 2025 (ahead of Eid-ul-Fitr) and December 2025's USD 322 crore was the second highest.

headline_en: What stands in the way of becoming a trillion-dollar economy
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Mohammad Nuruzzaman, CEO of Daffodil Group Ltd, arguing that Bangladesh should plan skills, overseas and domestic jobs, formal remittances and returnee reintegration together to create 10 million jobs in 2026-2030. He proposes demand-led skilling, turning embassies into labour-market intelligence units, a private skill development board under NSDA, compulsory destination-language training and upskilling madrasa graduates for Arab labour markets.

facts.statement: The columnist says the skills most in demand in the global labour market are human care workers, construction and infrastructure skills, electrical and welding trades, manufacturing and factory technicians, hospitality and service sector, and digital and remote services.
facts.source_in_article: Dr Mohammad Nuruzzaman, CEO, Daffodil Group Ltd (opinion)

facts.statement: The columnist sees real opportunities for Bangladesh in care and technical skills for ageing populations in Japan and Europe, manufacturing skills in East Asia, construction and services in the Middle East, and remote work in the global digital economy, and calls for demand-led skilling (identify demand first, train afterwards).

The columnist proposes turning Bangladesh's foreign missions and embassies into labour market intelligence units that work with local employers, chambers of commerce and trade bodies to build pipelines of legal jobs, which he says would reduce dependence on brokers and make overseas employment more transparent and safe.

The columnist says the National Skills Development Authority (NSDA) has limited capacity, staff and regulatory power, and that Bangladesh has thousands of small training centres many of which are uneven in quality and effectively unregulated; he proposes a Private Skill Development Board under NSDA for curriculum standardisation, trainer qualification checks, outcome-based accreditation and regular evaluation.

The columnist proposes 'train the trainers' programmes that turn skilled returnee workers, experienced technicians and industry professionals into trainers, because the trainer shortage is the biggest obstacle to skilling 10 million people.

The columnist says language skill is one of the biggest multipliers of income in the international labour market: for Japan, Korea, Germany or Arab countries knowing the language makes getting a job easier and raises pay significantly, so country-specific language training should be made compulsory alongside skills training.

The columnist says many madrasa-educated youths have basic Arabic but lack modern vocational skills; targeted upskilling in care, service, construction and hospitality could connect them quickly to Arab countries' labour markets, with higher retention because of cultural and linguistic fit.

The columnist says a large share of remittances still flows through informal or hundi channels and proposes, besides the cash incentive, tax breaks, faster service, priority loans for returnee entrepreneurs and easier digital transactions for remittances sent through formal banking and digital channels.

The columnist claims that if returnee workers are turned into SME entrepreneurs in a planned way, one worker can create three to five new jobs; he puts Bangladesh's youth population at close to 6 crore and the economy at about USD 450 billion.

Reserves peaked at USD 48 billion in 2021 and fell to USD 26 billion at the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, when the dollar reached BDT 128 in banks; it had fallen to BDT 122 by the end of 2025.
Banking sector people attribute the rise in remittances since August 2024 to lower money laundering reducing illegal hundi and a banking-channel dollar rate stable for several months.

key_quote_bn: বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংকের তথ্য অনুযায়ী, ২০২৫ সালের পুরো বছরে দেশে প্রবাসী আয় এসেছিল ৩ হাজার ২৮২ কোটি ডলার।

headline_en: Remittances pass 2 billion dollars in just 17 days
summary_en: In the first 17 days of December 2025 remittances passed USD 200 crore, 14% more than a year earlier, and reserves reached USD 32.57 billion. Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said reserves would reach USD 34-35 billion by end-December by buying dollars domestically rather than through IMF loans.

facts.statement: From 1 to 17 December 2025 Bangladesh received remittances the article prints as 'USD 200 crore 7' (২০০ কোটি ৭ ডলার), against USD 176 crore in the same days of 2024, a rise of 14%; USD 17 crore 70 lakh came on 17 December.

From July to 17 December 2025 Bangladesh received USD 1,505 crore in remittances against USD 1,290 crore in the same period a year earlier, a rise of 16.7%; November 2025 brought USD 288 crore 95 lakh.
Bangladesh received USD 3,033 crore in remittances in fiscal 2024-25 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal 2023-24; in July-October 2025 about USD 2.5 billion came each month.
Bangladesh Bank's foreign exchange reserves were USD 32.57 billion (3,257 crore) on Thursday 18 December 2025.

Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said at an event on Thursday 18 December 2025 that reserves would reach USD 34-35 billion by the end of December and would be built by buying dollars from within the country, not through loans from the IMF or any agency.
facts.source_in_article: Ahsan H. Mansur, Governor, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank officials said government and central bank initiatives against hundi and the incentive have played a big role in increasing remittances through the banking channel.
The single-month record as of December 2025 was USD 329 crore in March 2025; no month after that had exceeded USD 300 crore until December 2025, which bankers expected might do so.

key_quote_bn: বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংকের কর্মকর্তারা বলছেন, হুন্ডি প্রতিরোধে সরকার ও কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংকের উদ্যোগ, প্রণোদনা ব্যাংকিং চ্যানেলে প্রবাসী আয় বাড়াতে বড় ভূমিকা রেখেছে।

headline_en: Krishi Bank's big surprise in remittances
summary_en: Bangladesh Krishi Bank ranked second in collecting remittances in January-November 2025 (USD 277 crore), behind Islami Bank (USD 553 crore) and ahead of Agrani Bank (USD 265 crore). The article explains how the bank used its 1,038-branch rural network, agreements with foreign money-transfer firms, NGOs and MFS providers, expatriate savings schemes and round-the-clock direct account credit to grow, and names the transfer firms it gets most from.

facts.statement: In January-November 2025 Bangladesh received USD 2,958 crore in remittances, of which ten banks brought USD 2,063 crore (70%): Islami Bank 553 crore, Krishi Bank 277 crore, Agrani 265 crore, Janata 197 crore, BRAC Bank 191 crore, Trust Bank 160 crore, Sonali 145 crore, Rupali 110 crore, City 84 crore and Pubali 79 crore.

Bangladesh Krishi Bank has 1,038 branches and 5 sub-branches across the country, the widest network including remote areas of any bank; it has appointed Rajshahi Krishi Unnayan Bank as sub-agent in the northern region so it can provide remittance service across the whole country.

Other banks and mobile financial service providers formerly used Krishi Bank's network to distribute remittances for a small fee; after Ali Hossain Prodhania joined as managing director in 2018 the bank signed agreements with foreign money-transfer companies to use the network for itself.
During the coronavirus outbreak Krishi Bank kept all branches open and distributed remittances, which made it popular among expatriates.
Krishi Bank has launched several savings schemes for expatriates, in which about BDT 220 crore has been deposited.

Expatriates deposit money at money-transfer companies abroad and Bangladeshi banks collect remittances from those companies; money a bank collects for accounts outside itself is sent on to the relevant bank's account the same day.

Krishi Bank gets the most remittance from Merchantrade of Malaysia, followed by Instant Cash and Ria Money of the United States, CBL Money and NBL Money of Malaysia, Western Union, NEC Money of the United Kingdom, Home Remit of South Africa and EZ Remit of the United Kingdom.

Krishi Bank's general manager for international and accounts, Mostafizur Rahman, said customers earlier mainly received remittance using a secret PIN number, but now with greater financial inclusion they can have money credited directly to their own accounts, a service given 24 hours through Bangladesh Bank.
facts.source_in_article: Mostafizur Rahman, General Manager (International and Accounts), Bangladesh Krishi Bank

facts.statement: Mostafizur Rahman said Krishi Bank's agreements with MFS providers including bKash and Nagad and with important money exchange houses have made the service easier; its biggest strength is more than a thousand branches in remote areas.

Krishi Bank was tasked by the government during the dollar crisis with opening letters of credit for power, fuel and food imports and now pays USD 20-25 crore a month of government import liabilities, meeting the dollar demand from remittances; it earned about BDT 700 crore from foreign exchange business last fiscal year, targets BDT 1,000 crore this fiscal year, and had a loss of BDT 6,513 crore in fiscal 2023-24.
Krishi Bank signed agreements with NGOs under which NGOs can deposit the money they collect at any Krishi Bank branch free of charge and transfer it to their own bank.

headline_en: USD 289 crore in remittances came in November
summary_en: Expatriates sent USD 288.9 crore in November 2025, about 31.38% more than November 2024. The article gives the bank-category breakdown, the fiscal year-to-date total and the reserve position.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 288 crore 90 lakh to Bangladesh in November 2025, USD 69 crore more than the USD 219 crore 90 lakh of November 2024, growth of about 31.38%.
In November 2025 the six state-owned banks brought USD 58 crore 70 lakh in remittances, Krishi Bank USD 29 crore 59 lakh, private banks USD 199 crore 68 lakh and foreign banks USD 59 lakh.
From 1 July to 30 November 2025 (fiscal 2025-26) Bangladesh received USD 1,303 crore in remittances.
Bangladesh received USD 3,033 crore in remittances in fiscal 2024-25 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal 2023-24; July-October 2025 brought about USD 2.5 billion a month.
The article says Bangladesh Bank's gross reserves exceeded '31 billion or 3,200 crore dollars' (the two figures as printed do not match); under IMF BPM6 they were a little over USD 26 billion.

The reason given for higher remittances is that illegal hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell and the banking-channel dollar rate is stable; bank officials said that with good remittance inflows there is no problem opening letters of credit for imports.

headline_en: Remittances up 31 percent in the first 18 days of the month
summary_en: In the first 18 days of November 2025 Bangladesh received USD 190 crore in remittances, 31% more than the USD 146 crore of the same days in 2024. From 1 July to 18 November 2025 the total was USD 1,205 crore, 15.9% up.

facts.statement: In the first 18 days of November 2025 Bangladesh received USD 190 crore in remittances, 31% more than the USD 146 crore of the first 18 days of November 2024.

From 1 July to 18 November 2025 Bangladesh received USD 1,205 crore in remittances, up 15.9%; the article gives the year-earlier comparison as USD 1,040 crore but labels it 'export income' (রপ্তানি আয়) in the text.
Bangladesh received USD 3,033 crore in remittances in fiscal 2024-25 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal 2023-24; in each of the two months before November 2025 about USD 2.5 billion came.
Bangladesh Bank's gross reserves recently exceeded USD 32 billion (3,200 crore) but stood at USD 31 billion at the time of the article (21 November 2025).
