headline_en: Bangladesh to take steps to help fill Japan's shortage of 11 million workers
summary_en: The Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo, with JITCO, held a seminar and matching event in Nagoya on Friday 7 November 2025 on Bangladesh as a source of skilled workers for Japan, attended by about 250 sending and recruiting organisations. Senior Secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said 33 technical training centres have been designated for the Japanese market and a 'Japan Cell' formed in the expatriates' welfare ministry; four MoUs and agreements were signed.

facts.statement: On Friday 7 November 2025 the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo held a seminar titled 'Bangladesh: a highly promising source of skilled human resources for Japan' and then a matching event in an auditorium in Nagoya, Japan, in cooperation with the Japan International Trainee and Skilled Worker Cooperation Organization (JITCO); about 250 manpower exporting firms and recruiting organisations took part.

Senior Secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment said Japan will need about 1 crore 10 lakh (11 million) foreign workers by 2040, while Bangladesh currently has a surplus working-age population of 2 crore 50 lakh, a trend that will continue until 2040; he pledged all steps to help fill Japan's shortage.
facts.source_in_article: Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan, Senior Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: The Senior Secretary said 33 Technical Training Centres in Bangladesh have been designated to prepare workers according to the demand of Japan's labour market, and the number will be increased if needed.
The Senior Secretary said a 'Japan Cell' has been formed in the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare to act as the coordination and communication centre for the Japanese labour market.
At the Nagoya event four memoranda of understanding and agreements were signed between Bangladeshi manpower sending organisations and Japanese recruiting organisations.

Bangladesh's ambassador to Japan, Md. Daud Ali, promised all kinds of support from the embassy for sending skilled workers to Japan; JITCO senior vice president Shigeo Matsutomi gave a presentation on the international labour market and the prospects of Japan's labour market.

headline_en: The youth who hired a loudspeaker to abuse villagers after failing to go abroad is getting his wish
summary_en: Sarwar Hossain (27) of Hossainpur, Kishoreganj, had a visa for Saudi Arabia but could not raise the money or get a bank loan, and on 16 October 2025 hired a loudspeaker to abuse his neighbours; the video went viral. After media reports, Probashi Kallyan Bank's Kishoreganj branch verified his papers and gave him a BDT 2 lakh loan, repayable in instalments starting after two months; he was due to fly on 30 October 2025.

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank's Kishoreganj branch gave Sarwar Hossain (27), who had a visa for Saudi Arabia but no money to travel, a loan of BDT 2 lakh after verification of his papers; he will repay in instalments starting two months later.
facts.source_in_article: Mozammel Haque, General Manager, Probashi Kallyan Bank, Kishoreganj branch

facts.statement: Sarwar Hossain said that after media reports the Kishoreganj branch of Probashi Kallyan Bank phoned him, verified his documents and then gave him the BDT 2 lakh loan; he bought his ticket and was due to go to Saudi Arabia on 30 October 2025.

Sarwar Hossain of Dakshin Panan village, Gobindapur union, Hossainpur upazila, Kishoreganj, from a poor family, had tried repeatedly and failed to get a bank loan (he believed because neighbours did not cooperate) and appeals to NGOs and others also failed; on 16 October 2025 he hired a loudspeaker for BDT 500 and abused the villagers, then posted the video on Facebook himself.

headline_en: Remittances pass USD 2 billion in 25 days
summary_en: Bangladeshis abroad sent USD 203 crore 29 lakh home in the first 25 days of October 2025, according to Bangladesh Bank. The article breaks the inflow down by bank type, gives the reasons bankers cite for higher inflows through legal channels, and reports the foreign exchange reserve.

facts.statement: Bangladeshis abroad sent USD 203 crore 29 lakh to Bangladesh in the first 25 days of October 2025.
Bangladeshis abroad sent a total of USD 268 crore 50 lakh in September 2025; the article says October 2025 remittances may end up lower than September.

In the first 25 days of October 2025 remittances came through state-owned banks USD 38 crore 46 lakh, two specialised banks USD 19 crore 70 lakh, private banks USD 144 crore 63 lakh and foreign banks USD 48 lakh 70 thousand.

Bank officials say remittance inflow through legal channels has risen since the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, and the high dollar price also encourages sending through legal channels.
March 2025 set the record for remittances in a single month at USD 329 crore; since then no month has exceeded USD 300 crore (as of late October 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report citing Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: The reasons given for higher remittances are that illegal hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell, and the dollar exchange rate in the banking channel is stable, so more money comes by the legal route.
Bangladesh's gross foreign exchange reserve stood at USD 32.10 billion on 22 October 2025; under the IMF's BPM-6 method it was USD 27.35 billion.

key_quote_bn: অর্থ পাচার কমে আসায় অবৈধ হুন্ডি ব্যবসা কমে গেছে। এ ছাড়া ব্যাংকিং চ্যানেলে ডলারের বিনিময় হার স্থিতিশীল রয়েছে। এ জন্য বৈধ পথে আয় আসা বেড়েছে।

headline_en: Driven to New York by climate disaster at home, and fearing deportation there too
summary_en: A year-long Columbia Journalism Investigations and Documented investigation (republished by Prothom Alo) analysed more than 9 million US border-apprehension records from 2010 to 2024 and found that thousands of migrants who crossed the Mexico border into the United States came from areas hit repeatedly by storms, floods and droughts, including Feni and Noakhali in Bangladesh. It profiles three migrants in New York, including Hossain from Feni, who paid USD 41,000 and travelled nine months through 11 countries, applied for political asylum, and now fears deportation under the Trump administration. The article explains that US asylum has no provision protecting people fleeing climate disaster.

facts.statement: Hossain, a rice farmer from Feni, Bangladesh, left Bangladesh in February 2023 and crossed 11 countries by air and land over 9 months before surrendering to border officials in the US state of Arizona.
facts.source_in_article: Hossain, interviewed by CJI and Documented

facts.statement: Hossain from Feni sold his land and borrowed about USD 33,000 from relatives and friends, raising USD 41,000 in total for travel costs and the broker's fee for the journey to the United States via the Mexico border.
After Hossain surrendered to border officials in Arizona, they held him for three days in one room with 15 people; after release he moved to New York.

According to documents obtained, a legal organisation in Manhattan filed a political asylum application for Hossain in April 2024, based on his being a supporter of Bangladesh's opposition political party; the effect of climate-related floods on his income and livelihood is not admissible as a ground for asylum.
facts.source_in_article: documents obtained by CJI and Documented

facts.statement: While waiting for his hearing in the overloaded immigration court, Hossain received a work permit after seven months (the article does not say from which date the seven months are counted).

Hossain first worked as a kitchen helper in a local restaurant, then delivered food by bike on the streets of Brooklyn, and now works full time at a Bengali sweet shop and cafe in Kensington, Brooklyn ('Little Bangladesh'); he works six days a week and seven days during religious festivals, and shares a basement apartment with two roommates.

There is no specific provision in the United States protecting people who flee climate disasters, so such migrants face uncertainty over immigration; they had hoped to get asylum at the south-west border.

US President Donald Trump is stepping up operations to arrest, detain and deport migrants; the threat of deportation has spread panic among Bengalis in Brooklyn, and the streets of Kensington, once busy around 'Noakhali Deshi Bazar' and eateries such as 'Raj Mahal Restaurant + Sweets', have gone quiet.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained two Bangladeshis from Noakhali who were working in Buffalo, New York; the news spread quickly in Kensington, Brooklyn.

Hossain keeps copies of his asylum application and his court hearing notices in a plastic folder in his bedroom drawer, always within reach, and has put his lawyer's number on speed dial on his mobile phone in case ICE officers raid his home.

Hossain had hoped that once granted political asylum he could apply to bring his wife and daughter to him; he said that if he had known it was this hard now, he would not have come to the United States.

When Hossain's wife Sumaiya gave birth by caesarean in a Feni hospital in September 2022 he was handed a bill of USD 470 (about 57,500 taka) that he could not pay and had to borrow from relatives and a friend; his home had flooded five times in a decade and he could farm only one third of his land for several years.

In 2024 the worst flood in more than three decades hit Feni; Hossain's family home went under three feet of water and his wife and daughter had to move to a relative's house in Dhaka about 100 miles (160 km) away. He estimates rebuilding a home in Feni would cost about USD 45,000 (about 55 lakh taka).

Hossain said that because he joined opposition politics in Bangladesh, ruling-party members kept threatening him, while floods kept destroying his crops; together these forced him to leave. A friend advised him to go to Brooklyn because of its large Bangladeshi settlement, after he learned that many were getting asylum in the United States.
Border crossings from Bangladesh at the US-Mexico border rose 150 percent between 2019 and 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: In US border-apprehension records of Bangladeshis, Noakhali tops the districts of origin with more than 30 percent; more people from Bangladesh's coastal areas than from other areas migrated to the US southern border, and Feni town in disaster-prone Chattogram division is among the top 10 Bangladeshi towns from which the most people reached the US-Mexico border.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: CJI and Documented found that among those apprehended in 2024 alone, more than 520 were born in Guatemala, about 350 in Senegal and about 100 in Bangladesh (as the article states, in the context of the climate-hit areas it studied).
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: An estimated 1 lakh (100,000) Bangladeshis live in New York City. Newly arrived Bangladeshi migrants first settle around Bangladeshi groceries and restaurants in Kensington, Brooklyn; most come from Bangladesh's coastal areas.
More than 237,000 migrants and asylum seekers have arrived in New York City since April 2022, straining the city's shelter system; local hotels and large tents are used for emergency housing.

A recent survey by New York City community organisation Desis Rising Up and Moving (DRUM) found 135 newly arrived Bangladeshi and other migrants who had been forced to leave their countries because of climate disasters.

Bangladesh, Guatemala and Senegal did not receive Temporary Protected Status (TPS) from the United States between 2019 and 2024. Migrants eligible for TPS because of natural disasters usually fall into the 'inadmissible' category in US border data.

In a WhatsApp voice note shared by a Bronx imam, a migrant just back from immigration court warned that officials are giving migrants only two weeks to submit all required documents before deciding whether they can stay in the United States.
facts.source_in_article: voice note from a West African migrants' WhatsApp group, shared by Imam Sheikh Tidiane Ndao

facts.statement: Griselda, a Guatemalan migrant in New York, said she once applied for asylum in the United States but one of the people helping her with it embezzled several thousand dollars from her, after which she could not trust the system enough to try again.
Griselda's workplace gave her a red card with detailed instructions on what to do if confronted by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers; it is the only document she has.

Human smugglers often posed as travel agents and made TikTok and Instagram videos (in the Wolof language for Senegalese viewers) promoting the journey to the United States as very comfortable and saying a US work permit and job are very easy to get; reels showed migrants entering the US via Nicaragua. One smuggler advertised arranging visas and air tickets and connected people to other smugglers on the way.
facts.source_in_article: Mohamed, Senegalese migrant; CJI and Documented report

facts.statement: Mohamed, a Senegalese migrant, said he was told that once he reached the United States 'everyone is equal before the law; no one can deport you'.

Mohamed, 45, a farmer from Diourbel, Senegal, sold a horse, several cows and a horse cart for about USD 4,500 (about 5.5 lakh taka) by October 2023 and, with loans from relatives, spent more than USD 10,000 (about 12 lakh 21 thousand taka) in total to come to the United States.

Mohamed surrendered to Border Patrol agents in Arizona, who held him for one night and then released him; in New York he stayed at a migrant shelter near Times Square and was expelled within a month after another migrant complained that he had entered the women's toilet (he said by mistake, unable to read the sign); he then slept on the '2 train' subway.

Mohamed said he had no idea that climate disasters such as drought and flood would carry very little weight in his US asylum application, although he cited the climate disaster that destroyed his livelihood as the reason for migrating.

In recent months at least half a dozen WhatsApp groups linking several thousand West African migrants have formed in New York, working as support groups where members share job and room-rent information; migrants also wait outside a local Home Depot hoping to be called for odd jobs.

Griselda from Quetzaltenango, Guatemala mortgaged her father's land for a loan and, with a broker's help, travelled three weeks with two children to the US-Mexico border in 2018; in Texas US officials asked for the children's birth certificates and took them to a migrant shelter, and her husband later sent bus tickets to New York.

CJI and Documented analysed more than 9 million US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) apprehension records for 2010-2024, obtained by public-records request by University of Virginia researchers and CJI, which include birthplace; about 35 percent of records have the birthplace field blank, and CBP officers usually cannot speak migrants' languages so place names are often misspelt.

The investigation's final list of climate-hit origin areas with above-average migration to the US southern border contains 15 areas in Bangladesh, 96 in Senegal and 683 in Guatemala; about 55 countries with above-average migration were hit by three or more natural disasters in 2019-2024 according to the EM-DAT disaster database.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: More than 1,800 Senegalese migrants from western and central Senegal crossed the US-Mexico border between 2019 and 2024, from practically zero before.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: EM-DAT disaster data show about 300 people died in floods in Feni and surrounding areas in the last 10 years; Feni has 16 lakh residents.

Dhaka University geographer and disaster expert Sanjida Murshed said rising sea level due to climate change has worsened floods over the last two decades and cut food production in coastal areas like Feni because floodwater has nowhere to drain.

The Bronx imam Sheikh Tidiane Ndao said news of the threats facing migrants in the United States has not yet reached Senegal; he still gets more than 10 phone calls a month from Senegalese farmers seeking help, drawn by the lure of earning more in a week in the US than in several months in Senegal.

About 14 crore 30 lakh (143 million) people from low-income countries of the global South may be forced to leave their homes by 2050 because of climate change, with Latin America, South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa most affected.
facts.source_in_article: CJI and Documented report (source not named)

people_cases.outcome: Asylum case pending in immigration court; lives in fear of ICE and deportation; family home in Feni flooded in 2024; says he would not have come had he known how hard it is.

people_cases.outcome: No status; holds only a red know-your-rights card from her workplace; raising four children in East Harlem; does not want to return.

headline_en: Cost of sending remittances from Saudi Arabia is high and can be cut: Governor
summary_en: At the opening of the Saudi Arabia-Bangladesh Business Summit in Banani, Dhaka on 7 October 2025, Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said workers pay 6 to 10 percent to send remittances from Saudi Arabia and that the two countries' financial sectors could cut this cost. Other speakers discussed investment, exporting skilled nurses and workers, and the low share of skilled workers among about 21 lakh Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said expatriates in Saudi Arabia pay between 6 and 10 percent in costs to send their remittances to Bangladesh, which he called a huge burden on them.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Bank Governor said the cost of sending remittances from Saudi Arabia is comparatively much higher, and that a more efficient, lower-cost money transfer system is needed; financial institutions, central banks and related agencies of the two countries can work together on it.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Bank Governor said Saudi Arabia is the biggest source of remittances to Bangladesh and also the biggest source of its foreign currency inflow.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Governor said Bangladesh wants the lives of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia to improve and their incomes to rise, and that work is needed on trade, the economy, the financial transaction system and labour-market development between the two countries; some problems exist but can be solved.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: About 21 lakh Bangladeshis currently work in Saudi Arabia, but only 22 percent of them are skilled workers; joint initiatives with Saudi training and educational institutions could raise this rate.
facts.source_in_article: Masrur Reaz, chairman of private research body Policy Exchange, in a paper at the summit

facts.statement: BNP standing committee member Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said the remittance now coming from Saudi Arabia is commendable but could grow many times over if skill development programmes are taken up.
facts.source_in_article: Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, BNP standing committee member

facts.statement: Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said former president Ziaur Rahman first took the initiative to sign government-level agreements to send workers, which formally began the sending of workers from Bangladesh to Middle Eastern countries; before that workers went in a scattered way through private initiative.

The Saudi Arabia Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SABCCI), which organised the summit, said no joint business chamber had existed between the two countries in 53 years until now, and that it can now work to increase exports from Bangladesh including skilled nurses and workers.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Organised the Saudi Arabia-Bangladesh Business Summit in Banani, Dhaka on 7 October 2025; its president Ashraful Haque Chowdhury spoke of raising exports of skilled nurses and workers.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Bangladesh Bank Governor; said remittance-sending costs from Saudi Arabia are 6 to 10 percent and can be reduced.

headline_en: More than USD 2.5 billion in remittances came in September
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank sources say expatriates sent USD 268 crore 58 lakh in September 2025, USD 16.5 crore more than in August. The article gives comparison figures and the reasons cited for continued growth.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 268 crore 58 lakh in remittances in September 2025, which is USD 16.5 crore more than the previous month.
In the first 21 days of September 2025 expatriates sent USD 203 crore 10 lakh; in the same period of the previous year the amount was USD 163 crore 40 lakh.
Remittances were USD 242 crore 18 lakh in August 2025 and USD 240 crore 41 lakh in September 2024.

Bank officials say remittance inflow through legal channels has risen since the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024 and the high dollar price also encourages sending by the legal route.
March 2025 holds the single-month remittance record at USD 329 crore; no month since has passed USD 300 crore (as of early October 2025).
Reasons given for higher remittances: illegal hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell, and the dollar exchange rate in the banking channel is stable.

key_quote_bn: বিদায়ী সেপ্টেম্বর মাসে প্রবাসীরা ২৬৮ কোটি ৫৮ লাখ ডলারের প্রবাসী আয় পাঠিয়েছেন, যা আগের মাসের চেয়ে সাড়ে ১৬ কোটি ডলার বেশি।

headline_en: Krishi Bank is now third in collecting remittances
summary_en: Bangladesh Krishi Bank rose to third place among banks collecting remittances in January-August 2025, from 15th in 2023 and seventh in 2024. The article lists the top five banks, their volumes, and how Krishi Bank now delivers remittances through bKash, Nagad and exchange houses so recipients need not visit a branch.

facts.statement: Krishi Bank ranked third among banks in collecting remittances in the first eight months of 2025, collecting USD 197 crore 62 lakh, about 9.25 percent of all remittances that came to Bangladesh in that period.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report; Krishi Bank sources

facts.statement: State-owned Krishi Bank was 15th in remittance collection in 2023, rose eight places to seventh in 2024, and is third so far in 2025.
Krishi Bank collected USD 11 crore 60 lakh in remittances in January 2025 and USD 30 crore 19 lakh in August 2025.
Total remittances to Bangladesh in January-August 2025 were USD 21.45 billion (USD 2,145 crore).

Around 2018 Krishi Bank received only USD 5 to 7 lakh in remittances a month; it began building remittance capacity from 2018 by working with the world's large remittance-collecting companies and pushing branches that collected none.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hossain Prodhania, Krishi Bank chairman 2018-2021 (now BIBM supernumerary professor and NRBC Bank chairman)

facts.statement: The top five banks brought 49 percent of remittances in January-August 2025: in order Islami Bank, Agrani Bank, Krishi Bank, Janata Bank and BRAC Bank. Together they brought USD 10.5 billion (USD 1,050 crore) of the USD 21.45 billion total.
The three state-owned banks in the top five (Krishi, Agrani, Janata) brought USD 5.46 billion (USD 546 crore), 25 percent of all remittances in January-August 2025.
Sonali Bank was second in remittance collection in January 2025 with USD 17 crore 93 lakh but fell to seventh in August 2025 with USD 11 crore 75 lakh.

Krishi Bank has more than one thousand branches spread across remote areas. Previously recipients had to come to the bank to collect remittances; now, through agreements with MFS companies including bKash and Nagad and with money exchange houses, customers get the service at home.
facts.source_in_article: Mostafizur Rahman, General Manager, Krishi Bank

facts.statement: BRAC Bank was third in January 2025 with USD 16 crore 27 lakh in remittances and fell to fifth in August 2025 with USD 15 crore 87 lakh.

Islami Bank has consistently held first place in remittance collection: USD 28 crore 23 lakh in January 2025 and USD 55 crore 58 lakh in August 2025. Bankers say Islami Bank's presence in the Middle East and other countries with many Bangladeshi workers is better than any other bank's.

Remittances were USD 242 crore 20 lakh in August 2025 against USD 222 crore 41 lakh in August 2024, growth of about 9 percent; banking was disrupted in the first week of August 2024 by the student-public movement and change of government.

Bankers say the government's tough steps against sending money by illegal routes and the government incentive for sending by legal routes are playing a big role in remittance growth, and that the dollar crisis has largely eased.

headline_en: Technology-driven planning needed to raise remittances
summary_en: At a bKash-organised workshop on Bangladesh's changing remittance landscape at Bhawal Resort, Gazipur on 25 September 2025, bank and fintech officials said remittance sending has become faster through MFS, money transfer companies and digital platforms, and that AI, blockchain and stablecoins could increase legal inflows. Speakers gave figures on the diaspora, skills, digital share and smartphone use.

facts.statement: More than 1.5 crore Bangladeshi expatriates send income home each year; about 1.5 crore Bangladeshis are in 176 countries of the world.
facts.source_in_article: workshop speakers; Mohammad Zahidul Ahsan, head of remittance, bKash commercial division

facts.statement: More than 50 percent of Bangladeshi workers abroad are still unskilled, so remittance inflow is not rising at the expected rate.

About 70 percent of remittances to Bangladesh now come through digital channels, though demand for cash remittance has not completely gone; earlier remittance meant 'cash over the counter' collected at a distant bank branch or NGO office, costing more time and money.

bKash's chief commercial officer said bank representatives used to go abroad to increase workers' accounts and transactions, but now the whole process of sending remittances through MFS and money transfer companies has become digital.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Ahmed, Chief Commercial Officer, bKash

facts.statement: 92 percent of remittance-dependent households in Bangladesh now use a smartphone, and 77 percent of them are connected to the internet.
facts.source_in_article: Joyanta Sen, General Manager, marketing, bKash

facts.statement: Trust Bank's head of treasury said supervision and policy decisions sometimes negatively affect banks' remittance receipts.
facts.source_in_article: Zahurul Karim Chowdhury, head of treasury, Trust Bank

facts.statement: Speakers said modernising remittance sending with artificial intelligence, blockchain and stablecoins would increase remittances through legal channels; Taptap Send's head of growth said people now want to send money fast and easily.
facts.source_in_article: workshop speakers; Sudarshan Shubhashish Das, Head of Growth, Taptap Send

headline_en: Three held captive by traffickers in deep hills rescued, one detained
summary_en: BGB rescued three men from Ramu, Cox's Bazar who were held captive by a human-trafficking gang in the deep hills of Baraitali, Teknaf on the night of 25 September 2025, and detained a Rohingya youth. The men had been lured with a promise of being taken to Malaysia by sea via Thailand and were being held for ransom. The article lists four other anti-trafficking operations in Teknaf in September 2025.

facts.statement: BGB rescued three people held captive by a human-trafficking gang from the deep hills of the Baraitali area of Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar at about 9 pm on Thursday 25 September 2025, and detained a Rohingya youth, Md. Sadek (25), a resident of Jamtoli refugee camp in Ukhiya, on charges of involvement in trafficking.

The three rescued men were taken into the hills of Teknaf with the lure of being taken to Malaysia by sea via Thailand; the traffickers then tried to extract ransom from their families and threatened to sell them to a trafficking group based in Malaysia if ransom was not paid.
The three rescued men and the detained Rohingya youth were handed over to Teknaf police station; the BGB commander said action would be taken against them under the prevailing law.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Ashikur Rahman, commander, Teknaf-2 BGB Battalion

facts.statement: In September 2025 alone, law-enforcement operations in Teknaf detained members of trafficking gangs at least five times.
On Tuesday 23 September 2025 the Coast Guard rescued five abducted people from the deep hills of Kachchhapia, Baharchhara, Teknaf and detained two members of a human-trafficking gang.
On Monday 22 September 2025 a RAB and BGB operation in Teknaf detained three people with weapons and rescued 84 victims.
On 18 September 2025 the Coast Guard rescued 66 people in Teknaf (in an anti-trafficking operation).
On 16 September 2025 BGB detained 12 members of human-trafficking gangs and rescued 11 victims in Teknaf.

headline_en: 'He is my only son, how will I live without him'
summary_en: Sagar Bala (21) of Pakhulla, Rajoir, Madaripur, who reached Italy two and a half years ago by the irregular Libya-Mediterranean route and worked in a restaurant, went missing on 18 September 2025; police recovered his dismembered body on 23 September. His father, who sold all his land to send him, alleges his close friends in Italy killed him. Rajoir police promised help in bringing the body home.

facts.statement: Sagar Bala (21) of Pakhulla, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur was murdered in Italy: he was missing from 18 September 2025 and police recovered his dismembered body on 23 September 2025; relatives in Italy informed the family on 24 September.
facts.source_in_article: relatives (cousin Shuvo Bala and nephew Mithun Talukdar, in Italy)

facts.statement: Sagar Bala went to Italy about two and a half years before September 2025 by the illegal route, crossing the Mediterranean from Libya; he had worked in a restaurant in Italy for two years and sent money home every month.
Sagar Bala's father Kumod Bala, a farmer, sold all his land to send his only son to Italy and now farms other people's land (no amount given).
The father, Kumod Bala, alleged that his son's close friends who were in Italy killed him; the article reports no arrests or case.

The officer-in-charge of Rajoir police station said police were sent to the dead youth's home and that all kinds of cooperation would be given to bring his body back to Bangladesh and to support the family.

headline_en: Remittances pass USD 2 billion in 21 days
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank said on 22 September 2025 that expatriates sent USD 203 crore 10 lakh in the first 21 days of September, 24.3 percent more than a year earlier. Fiscal-year-to-date and August figures are also given, with the usual reasons for growth.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 203 crore 10 lakh in the first 21 days of September 2025, 24.3 percent more than the USD 163 crore 40 lakh of the same period a year earlier.
From July to 21 September of fiscal year 2025-26 remittances were USD 693 crore, against USD 577 crore 20 lakh in the same period of 2024-25, up more than 20 percent.
Remittances in August 2025 were USD 242 crore 20 lakh against USD 222 crore 41 lakh in August 2024, growth of about 9 percent.

Bankers say legal-channel remittance flow rose after the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024 and the high dollar price also encourages legal sending; hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell and the bank exchange rate is stable.
March 2025 holds the single-month record at USD 329 crore; no later month passed USD 300 crore (as of 22 September 2025).

key_quote_bn: চলতি মাসের প্রথম ২১ দিনে সব মিলিয়ে ২০৩ কোটি ১০ লাখ ডলার পাঠিয়েছেন প্রবাসীরা, যা গত বছরের একই সময়ের চেয়ে ২৪ দশমিক ৩ শতাংশ বেশি।

headline_en: Arakan Army is assisting drug smuggling
summary_en: At a press conference in Cox's Bazar on 15 September 2025 the BGB Ramu sector commander said the Arakan Army is assisting drug smuggling from Myanmar into Bangladesh and described border conditions. On migration, he said 47 human traffickers had been arrested during sea-route trafficking to Malaysia and 21 more are being sought. The rest of the article concerns drugs, arms, abducted fishermen and landmines.

facts.statement: BGB's Ramu sector commander said 47 human traffickers have already been arrested during trafficking to Malaysia by sea, and efforts are on to catch 21 more traffickers who are absconding.
facts.source_in_article: Colonel Md. Mohiuddin Ahmed, Sector Commander, BGB Ramu sector

facts.statement: BGB said it is active in preventing human trafficking by sea, but that drug smuggling and human trafficking still occur through remote hill paths, dense forest, rivers and the vast sea of the Cox's Bazar border area.

BGB said it uses radar, drones and night-vision devices to stop infiltration and border smuggling, and although it lacks capacity at sea it supports the Bangladesh Navy and Coast Guard with intelligence and digital data.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Sector Commander (deputy director general), BGB Ramu sector headquarters, Cox's Bazar; reported 47 traffickers arrested on the sea route to Malaysia and 21 absconding.

headline_en: USD 1 billion in remittances came in 9 days
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank sources said on 10 September 2025 that USD 101 crore 80 lakh in remittances came in the first nine days of September. The article gives year-earlier, fiscal-year-to-date, July and August figures and the reasons cited.

facts.statement: Remittances in the first 9 days of September 2025 were USD 101 crore 80 lakh, against USD 83 crore 30 lakh in the same period a year earlier (the article prints the difference as '18 crore 50 dollars').
From July to 9 September of fiscal year 2025-26 remittances were USD 591 crore 80 lakh, against USD 497 crore 10 lakh in the same period of 2024-25.
Remittances were USD 247 crore 78 lakh in July 2025 and USD 242 crore 20 lakh in August 2025 (August 2024: USD 222 crore 41 lakh; about 9 percent growth year on year but lower than July).
People concerned say remittances through legal channels have risen, and that the dollar price has been fluctuating for some time, which many may be taking advantage of.

March 2025 holds the single-month record at USD 329 crore; no later month passed USD 300 crore (as of 10 September 2025). Hundi has shrunk as money laundering fell and the bank exchange rate is stable.

headline_en: The government must take strong steps
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial says Cox's Bazar has become a regular sea route for human trafficking to Malaysia, mainly of Rohingya but also of Bangladeshi youths lured onto the unsafe route, and that traffickers become active when the sea calms after the monsoon and before winter. It cites 21 departure points, more than 657 Rohingya deaths at sea in 2024, and obstacles to prosecution, and calls for trawler tracking, faster trials and coordinated enforcement.

facts.statement: Cox's Bazar has become a regular route for human trafficking by sea in recent years; trafficking by sea takes place through 21 points in Teknaf, Ukhiya, Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar Sadar and other upazilas of the district.
Trafficking gangs become active in the period after the monsoon winds leave and before winter starts, when the sea is calm.
Because the Cox's Bazar sea route has become regular, traffickers are also luring a section of Bangladeshi youths to cross the sea to Malaysia on this unsafe route.

More than 657 Rohingya died on dangerous sea journeys in 2024; deaths in the jungles of Thailand on the way to Malaysia, torture by traffickers and deaths when food and water ran out on trawlers have been reported at various times in international media.
The editorial says human trafficking is having a negative effect on Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia and elsewhere in South-East Asia.

Cox's Bazar's Superintendent of Police said Rohingya girl children are the most trafficked, that victims are regularly rescued and traffickers arrested in joint-force operations, and that the number trafficked has fallen; the editorial questions how credible this claim is.
facts.source_in_article: Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police, quoted in editorial

facts.statement: At a meeting at the Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police's office on 2 September 2025, law-enforcement agencies, lawyers, journalists and NGO representatives called for advance preparation to stop human trafficking in the winter season.

About five thousand trawlers are engaged in sea fishing off Cox's Bazar and law enforcers have no specific data on which are involved in trafficking; the editorial urges installing GPRS systems on trawlers and bringing boatmen under an online database.
Trafficking cases stall because trafficked Rohingya families are unwilling to file cases, and because of slow case disposal and trial, lack of witnesses and intimidation by offenders.
More than 14 lakh Rohingya, old and new arrivals together, have taken shelter in Cox's Bazar.

headline_en: Remittances rose 9% in August

More than USD 30 billion in remittances came in fiscal year 2024-25, about USD 6.5 billion or 27 percent more than in 2023-24.

Bankers say the government's tough steps against sending money by illegal routes and various government incentives for legal sending are playing a big role in remittance growth; hundi has shrunk as money laundering fell and the bank exchange rate is stable.

Bangladesh Bank officials said all overdue foreign payments were cleared in the last few months, pressure on the dollar has eased with a better balance of payments, and foreign banks' confidence in Bangladesh has begun to return.

Gross foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 31.18 billion at the end of 'last Thursday' (about 28 August 2025) and USD 26.19 billion under BPM-6; on 24 August they were USD 30.86 billion gross and USD 25.87 billion under BPM-6.
March 2025 holds the single-month remittance record at USD 329 crore.

facts.statement: For the Kuwait nurse recruitment through BOESL, nurses proficient in English, skilled and experienced will get priority, and candidates must be within 39 years of age.

In addition to the BOESL service charge, selected nurses must pay for the medical test from GAMCA, the visa stamping fee at the Kuwait embassy in Dhaka and other incidental fees (amounts not given).
Finally selected candidates for the Kuwait nurse jobs must hold a valid certificate of Basic Life Support training (the article prints the abbreviation as 'BLN').

headline_en: United States now tops remittance sources; tax announcement raises worry
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show the United States was the largest single-country source of remittances to Bangladesh in January-March 2025 (USD 144.49 crore, about 18 percent). President Trump's proposed 5 percent tax on remittances sent by non-citizens from the US has raised concern, though some bankers say the effect would be limited because large exchange houses aggregate remittances from other countries and route them through the US. Country-by-country figures for the quarter are given.

facts.statement: In the January-March 2025 quarter remittances to Bangladesh recorded as coming from the United States were USD 144.49 crore, about 18 percent of the total and the highest of any single country.
Total remittances to Bangladesh in January-March 2025 were USD 801 crore against USD 627 crore a year earlier, growth of about 28 percent.

Remittances to Bangladesh by source country in January-March 2025: UAE about USD 109 crore (second), Saudi Arabia about USD 105 crore, United Kingdom USD 97 crore, Malaysia USD 63 crore, Kuwait USD 46 crore, Oman USD 44 crore, Italy USD 40 crore and Qatar USD 31 crore.
Remittances from the United States were USD 33 crore 7 lakh in April 2025 and USD 427 crore in the first 10 months (July-April) of fiscal year 2024-25.

US President Donald Trump proposed a 5 percent tax on remittances sent from the United States, under the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' approved in the House Budget Committee. It would apply to remittances sent by all immigrants other than US citizens, including green-card holders and H-1B visa holders, with no minimum threshold, so it would apply to money sent by Bangladeshis too.

headline_en: How remittances are rising even though the dollar price is not
summary_en: The article explains how money-transfer aggregators bid up the dollar after 2022 and how the post-August 2024 rate cap (BDT 122 plus up to BDT 1) and monitoring calmed the market. The central bank governor said Saudi remittances are being routed via Dubai by a ring that hoards and resells them at higher prices. In the first 15 days of March 2025 USD 166 crore arrived, with banks paying BDT 122.80 to 123.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh used to come directly into the recipient's bank account, and recipients could also collect remittances from banks and various private organisations using a one-time password; the article says this can still be done.

When the dollar shortage began in 2022, some overseas money-transfer companies began buying remittance dollars from customers and from smaller similar firms, pooling them and bargaining with Bangladeshi banks; the bank offering the highest price got the dollars, which drove the dollar price up sharply.

After the new government formed in August 2024 the dollar price was fixed at BDT 122; later it was decided that banks could buy and sell dollars at up to BDT 1 more, and the central bank tightened monitoring of the rates banks use.

Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H. Mansur said at several events that not all remittances from Saudi Arabia now come directly to Bangladesh but come via Dubai: a dishonest ring buys remittances in Saudi Arabia, hoards them and sells them to Bangladeshi banks at a higher price, trying to destabilise Bangladesh's dollar market from there. He said banks would not be allowed to buy dollars at higher prices from such firms.

headline_en: Western countries overtake the Middle East as top remittance sources
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's January 2025 source-country data show the United States first and the United Kingdom second, together sending USD 68 crore (31 percent) of USD 219 crore. Bankers say this is largely a recording effect: large money-transfer firms such as Western Union and MoneyGram aggregate remittances from many countries and send them from the country where they are registered or headquartered.

facts.statement: In January 2025 Bangladesh received about USD 219 crore in remittances, of which USD 68 crore or 31 percent was recorded as coming from the United States and the United Kingdom.

Remittances recorded from the United States to Bangladesh were USD 56.5 crore in December 2024 and about USD 41 crore in January 2025, a fall of about USD 15 crore, yet the US remained the top source; it has been top since September 2024, having overtaken the UAE which was top in August 2024.

The United Kingdom rose from fifth place in December 2024 (about USD 25 crore) to second place in January 2025 (about USD 27.25 crore) among remittance sources for Bangladesh, a rise of USD 2.25 crore or over 9.25 percent.

In December 2024 the UAE was the second largest remittance source for Bangladesh with USD 37 crore; Saudi Arabia was third with USD 29 crore; Malaysia fourth (the article says 'in May about USD 26 crore came from Malaysia'); the UK fifth with about USD 25 crore. Remittances from the UAE, Malaysia and Saudi Arabia fell notably in January 2025 compared with December.
Total remittances to Bangladesh fell from USD 264 crore in December 2024 to USD 219 crore in January 2025.

In January 2025 the Middle East countries UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Lebanon together sent USD 95 crore in remittances to Bangladesh, against USD 68 crore from the US and UK. Other large sources include Italy, France, Greece and Portugal.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said large remittance companies now collect income from all countries and then send it to the destination from one specific country, which is why remittances recorded from the US and UK suddenly rose. Bankers said Western Union, MoneyGram and others use an aggregated method, so remittances are recorded under the country where the company is registered or headquartered.

headline_en: Government giving scholarships to children of expatriate workers
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board is giving scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers who passed SSC in 2024 or HSC in 2023. The article gives the GPA thresholds, duration, eligibility, required documents, the online application sites and the 25 November to 24 December (2024) application window.

facts.statement: The government's Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers. Eligible to apply: children who passed SSC or equivalent in 2024 and enrolled in class eleven or equivalent or a diploma course in Bangladesh, or who passed HSC or equivalent in 2023 and are studying at a university or medical college in Bangladesh.

Results required for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: SSC or equivalent GPA 5.00 in science and GPA 4.75 in humanities and commerce; HSC or equivalent GPA 4.80 in science and GPA 4.50 in humanities and commerce. Children of workers who died abroad need only GPA 4.00 from any group.

Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: secondary-category recipients are covered for the next two years (those in higher secondary) and diploma students for four years; in the higher-secondary category, undergraduate students get 3 to 4 years and medical students 5 years.

Children of expatriates who are members of the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) or the Wage Earners' Welfare Board can apply for the scholarship; children of deceased expatriate workers who have received or will receive a financial grant from the Board are also considered.

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship application is online only. The application must give the student's and guardian's mobile numbers, and include proof that the mother or father is an expatriate worker, the student's photo and signature, a copy of birth registration or national ID, and a certificate from the current educational institution.

A scholarship application to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board is cancelled if the mother's or father's name on the student's certificate does not match the expatriate worker's passport, or if there is any other error.
Online scholarship applications to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board go through www.wewb.gov.bd or stipen.wewb.gov.bd/stipend (as printed).
The application window for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship (2024 round) was 25 November to 24 December.

headline_en: Canada's new work permit rules for students take effect in November
summary_en: Canada's immigration department IRCC announced revised Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) rules effective 1 November 2024. University degree graduates stay eligible for up to three years regardless of field, but college graduates must have studied one of 966 listed programmes in five fields, and all applicants must meet language scores (CLB 7 for university, CLB 5 for college). Tourism, hospitality and business studies are not on the list.

facts.statement: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) announced revised Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) rules effective 1 November 2024. Students who applied for or received a study permit before 1 November 2024 remain eligible under the existing rules; those who apply on or after that date fall under the new rules.
IRCC confirmed that university degree graduates remain eligible for a Post-Graduation Work Permit of up to three years with no restriction based on field of study.

From 1 November 2024, graduates of college programmes in Canada must have completed study in a designated field to qualify for a PGWP. IRCC listed 966 eligible programmes covering five fields: agriculture and agri-food; healthcare; science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM); skilled trades; and transportation.
Fields traditionally popular with foreign students such as tourism, hospitality and business studies are not on Canada's list of PGWP-eligible college programmes.

PGWP applicants must prove English or French ability through an approved language test: university graduates need Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 7 in English or the French equivalent NCLC 7; college graduates need CLB 5 or NCLC 5 in all four skills (reading, writing, listening, speaking).

A Toronto Star report said more than 105,000 students were given Post-Graduation Work Permits in the first half of 2024; 64 percent were college programme graduates; business studies graduates were 42 percent and all STEM fields 37 percent.

Karen Dancey, director of recruitment and international at Olds College, said on LinkedIn that hospitality's absence from the list would be disastrous for rural and remote communities. According to ICEF Monitor, Colleges Ontario president and CEO Marketa Evans raised the same concern in an open letter to IRCC minister Marc Miller in September, criticising lack of consultation with provinces (the article attributes the letter's quoted words to Marc Miller).

headline_en: Italy taking back 12 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants from Albania
summary_en: Twelve Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants whom Italy had sent to an asylum camp in Albania under a five-year Italy-Albania agreement left for Italy on 19 October 2024 after Italian judges ruled against the transfers. Sixteen had been sent on 16 October, four of whom were returned at once as vulnerable. Italy's interior minister said he would appeal.

facts.statement: Under a five-year Italy-Albania agreement signed in November 2023, male migrants arriving in Italy are to be sent first to Albania and held in an Albanian asylum camp until Italian courts finish examining their immigration cases.

On Wednesday 16 October 2024, 16 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants reached Albania's Shengjin port from Italy, the first group sent under the Italy-Albania agreement; four were immediately returned to Italy because their condition was 'vulnerable'.
On Saturday 19 October 2024 the remaining 12 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants left Albania on an Italian coast guard vessel to be taken to Brindisi in southern Italy.

On Friday 18 October 2024 Italian judges ruled against the Italy-Albania transfers, saying a recent European Court of Justice ruling means the male migrants sent to Albania must be brought back to Italy. Interior minister Matteo Piantedosi announced an appeal to a higher Italian court, and prime minister Giorgia Meloni said on social media she would do everything to stop illegal immigration.

headline_en: High Court orders inquiry and report on irregularities in sending workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On Wednesday 21 August 2024 a High Court bench ordered the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) and the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) to investigate allegations of irregularities, corruption and money laundering in sending workers to Malaysia and report within 90 days. The court also issued a rule asking why a full policy to ensure workers pay only the government-set cost of BDT 78,990 should not be ordered and why the more than 17,000 workers who could not travel in time should not be compensated.

headline_en: July remittance lowest in 10 months
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 191 crore, the lowest in 10 months, after banks and internet were shut during the quota reform movement. Bangladesh Bank called in the heads of 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance even at a higher price, and the remittance dollar rate rose to BDT 120.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 191 crore, the lowest in 10 months; the previous low was USD 133 crore 43 lakh in September 2023.

Because of the situation around the students' quota reform movement, banks in Bangladesh were closed from 19 to 23 July 2024 (government and general holidays); broadband internet was off for 5 consecutive days and mobile internet for 10 days, so foreign transactions with the country's banks almost stopped.

In the first 3 weeks of July 2024 remittance came at an average of USD 40 to 50 crore (per week); USD 142 crore 93 lakh came from 1 to 20 July and USD 47 crore 97 lakh from 21 to 31 July, of which USD 12 crore came on 31 July alone.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Bangladesh Bank officials say that when someone sends remittance from abroad, banks are obliged to disburse it within 24 hours; but if the remittance houses in the sending country hold the money, it can take some time to arrive, though usually not more than two or three days.

As remittance fell, Bangladesh Bank called in the managing directors of the country's 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance; banks had been collecting remittance at BDT 117 to 118 per dollar and were advised to increase legal inflow even by paying somewhat more, and the remittance dollar price rose to BDT 120.

Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended.
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

headline_en: Remittance inflow falls, only USD 13 crore 80 lakh came last week
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh fell sharply to USD 13 crore 80 lakh in the seven days from 21 to 27 July 2024, amid bank closures, internet shutdown and curfew during the quota reform movement. Bangladesh Bank urged a dozen top banks to bring remittances legally even at a higher price so that money does not shift to hundi, while expatriates were campaigning to leave banking channels.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the seven days from 21 to 27 July 2024 was only USD 13 crore 80 lakh. From 1 to 20 July USD 142 crore 93 lakh had come (USD 40-50 crore a week in the first three weeks), making USD 156 crore 74 lakh up to 27 July.
Another Bangladesh Bank source said remittance from 1 to 28 July 2024 was USD 165 crore 70 lakh.

The government imposed curfew from the night of Friday 19 July 2024; banks were closed from 19 to 23 July (until Tuesday) and online transactions stopped as there was no internet (broadband off 5 days, mobile internet 10 days). Banks reopened on 24 July after five days without transactions; that day the SWIFT system was disconnected so no remittance money came to many banks, and normal global transactions resumed the next day.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Bangladesh Bank officials say that when someone sends remittance from abroad, banks are obliged to disburse it within 24 hours; but if the remittance houses in the sending country hold the money, it can take some time to arrive, though usually not more than two or three days.

The managing directors of a dozen top banks were called in and urged to raise remittance; banks had been collecting remittance at BDT 117-118 per dollar and were told to bring it through legal channels even at a somewhat higher price and to watch that remittance does not shift to hundi because of the lower dollar price.

A bank managing director, speaking anonymously, said the central bank promised not to impose strictness over paying higher prices, that banks were desperately booking dollars with remittance houses, and that many expatriates had begun a campaign to move outside banking channels.

headline_en: Even six days did not bring one day's worth of remittance
summary_en: From 19 to 24 July 2024 Bangladesh received only USD 7 crore 80 lakh in remittances, about what had been arriving per day in the first 18 days of the month. Banks were shut and internet was off during the curfew, and money sent during the closure had not been credited on the first reopening day as expected.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the six days from 19 to 24 July 2024 was USD 7 crore 80 lakh, whereas in the first 18 days of July 2024 it averaged USD 7 crore 90 lakh per day.

Banking operated on only one day between 19 and 24 July 2024: curfew began on the night of Friday 19 July, banks were closed until Tuesday (23 July) and online transactions were off without internet; banks reopened on 24 July with transactions for four hours from 11 am to 3 pm. Remittance could not come through banks from 19 to 23 July, and money sent in that period was supposed to be credited on the first reopening day (Wednesday 24 July) but was not.

Bangladesh Bank officials say banks are obliged to disburse remittance within 24 hours of it being sent from abroad, but if remittance houses in the sending country hold the money it can take some time to arrive.

Remittance through legal channels from 1 to 24 July was USD 158 crore 60 lakh in 2023 and USD 150 crore in 2024; of the 2024 figure USD 142 crore 20 lakh came in the first 18 days and USD 7 crore 80 lakh from 19 to 24 July.
Remittance from 1 to 18 July was USD 129 crore 70 lakh in 2023 and USD 142 crore 20 lakh in 2024, a big jump before the shutdown.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said Bangladesh's financial transactions with the world were cut off for five days because the internet was off, so remittance could not come; money sent in that period should have arrived on Wednesday or Thursday, otherwise on the coming Sunday or Monday, and if it does not come in those two days it means remittance has taken a blow.

headline_en: USD 254 crore remittance in June, highest in three years
summary_en: Expatriates sent USD 254 crore 20 lakh to Bangladesh in June 2024, the month of Eid al-Adha, the highest single month in three years. Bankers link the rise to the higher dollar rate after the May 2024 crawling peg (BDT 117 official, BDT 118-119 actually paid), relaxed rules, and possibly previously laundered money returning as remittance.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore 20 lakh, the highest single month in three years (USD 259 crore came in July 2020); June 2023 was USD 219 crore 90 lakh.
Within June 2024, USD 146 crore came in the first 12 days, USD 205 crore 20 lakh up to 23 June, and USD 16 crore 70 lakh in the three days 28 to 30 June.

Discussion in the banking sector about the sudden jump: some say money laundered abroad earlier is being brought back as remittance; others say expatriates are encouraged to use formal channels because banks now pay a high dollar rate for remittance.

Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.
Expatriates usually send more remittance to relatives at Eid than in other months; Eid al-Adha was celebrated in Bangladesh on 17 June 2024.

Remittance in May 2024 was USD 225 crore. Bank officials say legal remittance started rising after Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar rate by BDT 7 in one jump to BDT 117 in May 2024; although the rate on paper is BDT 117, banks bought remittance dollars at BDT 118 to 119, and the bank that pays more gets more dollars from expatriates.

Bangladesh's foreign-exchange reserve rose to USD 2,715 crore at the end of June 2024, helped by the central bank buying dollars from local banks and by loans and budget support from development partners that arrived in the last week of June.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended.
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through banks from 1 to 12 June 2024 was USD 146 crore, against USD 84 crore in the same period of June 2023, an increase of USD 62 crore or about 74 percent.

Remittance in May 2024 was USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, an average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh per day; in the first 12 days of June 2024 the daily average was USD 12 crore 17 lakh, about USD 5 crore a day more.

Expatriate Bangladeshis send more remittance to relatives before Eid than in other months; Eid al-Adha was on Monday 17 June 2024. Banking-sector people expected June 2024 remittance to exceed USD 250 crore if the trend continued.
Banking-sector people say remittance through legal channels rose after Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar price by BDT 7 in one jump to BDT 117 in May 2024.
Remittance to Bangladesh in fiscal year 2022-23 was USD 2,161 crore; in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 (printed as 'July-June') it was USD 2,137 crore.

headline_en: 4 workers kidnapped in Libya rescued, relief for families
summary_en: Four Bangladeshi workers from Charbiaghat village in Gurudaspur upazila, Natore, who had been kidnapped in Libya and tortured for ransom, were rescued by the Libyan army in an operation at about 9 am local time on Sunday 9 June 2024 and are in Libyan police custody. The kidnappers, whom the victims said were Bangladeshi, had sent torture videos and demanded BDT 10 lakh each; none were caught.

facts.statement: Four kidnapped Bangladeshi workers were rescued by the Libyan army in an operation at about 9 am local time on Sunday 9 June 2024; they are in the custody of Libyan police, and the kidnappers could not be detained.
facts.source_in_article: Gurudaspur police station OC Ujjal Hossain; Natore SP Tariqul Islam

facts.statement: Kidnappers in Libya sent videos of the four workers being tortured to their relatives' mobile phones and demanded BDT 10 lakh ransom each; the video and demand were sent to the families on 2 June 2024, and the men had been tortured for more than a week after the kidnapping.
The four victims told their families that the kidnappers in Libya were Bangladeshi.

According to the families, the four workers (Sohan Pramanik 20, Sagar Hossain 24, Nazim Ali 36, Bidyut Hossain 26, all of Charbiaghat village, Gurudaspur, Natore) went to Libya two years before June 2024.

Natore Superintendent of Police Tariqul Islam confirmed the rescue at about 12 noon on 9 June 2024, and on his instruction the Gurudaspur police station officer-in-charge informed the workers' families.

Nazim Ali's wife Nadira Begum said the family borrowed money to send her husband to Libya, leaving two small children at home (amount not stated). Sohan Pramanik's mother Duli Khatun said the family had been preparing to raise the ransom money before the rescue.

headline_en: Stop the brokers' dominance in Mymensingh
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial on broker rings at the Mymensingh Regional Passport Office. It says flawed applications are accepted if the applicant gets a code number by paying extra at a computer shop near the office, while correct applications are rejected on pretexts so people are forced to use brokers, and that insiders in the office must be involved.

facts.statement: When a passport application form has missing information or the applicant forgets supporting papers such as copies of the national ID card or birth registration certificate, the passport office does not accept the application and tells the person to come back with it properly filled in and with all required documents.

At the Mymensingh Regional Passport Office, a flawed application becomes acceptable if the applicant obtains a code number by paying extra money or a bribe at a computer shop near the passport office; the application is accepted on sight of the shop's code without verification, even where the address is not right or the nationality or character certificate is doubtful.

Many passport applicants at Mymensingh complain that even when everything in their application is correct it is refused on some pretext of a defect, forcing them to go to a broker, which costs them extra money and hardship.

headline_en: USD 214 crore remittance came in May, growth 38 percent
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh through legal channels was USD 214 crore from 1 to 29 May 2024, about 38 percent above the same period of 2023. Banking-sector people attribute the rise to the crawling peg introduced on 8 May 2024, which lifted the dollar rate from BDT 110 to a mid-rate of BDT 117.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through legal channels from 1 to 29 May 2024 was USD 214 crore, against USD 155 crore in the same period of 2023, an increase of USD 59 crore or about 38 percent; April 2024 was USD 204 crore, so two consecutive months were above USD 200 crore.

On 8 May 2024 Bangladesh Bank introduced the crawling peg method for setting the dollar exchange rate, fixing a mid-rate of BDT 117 and telling banks to trade freely around it; before that the fixed price in the banking sector was BDT 110 per dollar, so the dollar price rose BDT 7 in one jump.
Banking-sector people believe expatriates increased sending through banks because they now get a good dollar price through legal channels.

The May 2024 figure is up to Wednesday 29 May; with Thursday 30 May added, the final May figure was expected to exceed USD 220 crore, which would be the highest single month of fiscal year 2023-24. The highest in July-April of that fiscal year was February 2024 at USD 216 crore.
Total remittance from July 2023 to 29 May 2024 was USD 2,126 crore, against USD 1,927 crore in the same period of fiscal year 2022-23, an increase of USD 199 crore or about 10.5 percent.

headline_en: Bank security guard took returnee migrant workers' money by deception, later returned some
summary_en: At the Akkelpur branch of Rupali Bank in Joypurhat, security guard Shahidul Islam took a cut of the BDT 13,500 incentive paid to each of 17 returnee migrant workers by opening their accounts, keeping their chequebooks with three signed cheques, withdrawing the full amount and giving them BDT 8,000 each. On Monday 20 May 2024 the workers protested; with the mayor present he returned BDT 3,000 each to four of them and promised to repay the others.

facts.statement: At Rupali Bank's Akkelpur branch (Joypurhat), security guard Shahidul Islam opened Rupali Bank accounts for 17 returnee migrant workers, kept each one's whole chequebook including three signed cheque leaves, and after the incentive money was credited used the signed cheques to withdraw the full BDT 13,500 incentive, giving each worker BDT 8,000.
The incentive money for returnee migrant workers credited to the bank accounts in this case was BDT 13,500 per person (the article does not name the scheme or the paying body).

On Monday 20 May 2024 the cheated returnees went to the branch to demand the rest; after an argument, and after they complained to the branch manager and then to the UNO, the guard returned BDT 3,000 each to four returnees at 4 pm in the presence of Akkelpur municipality mayor Shahidul Alam Chowdhury and promised to repay the others the same way.

The victims said about 20 days earlier the guard called 5 to 6 of them to the bank and handed over BDT 8,000 each, promising the rest on 20 May; on 20 May he misbehaved with them, they refused a BDT 3,000 settlement mediated by College Bazar traders' association president Kazi Shafiuddin, and then went to the UNO.

Akkelpur UNO Monjurul Alam said the returnees complained orally that they had been paid less by trickery; he told them to submit a written complaint and spoke to the Rupali Bank branch manager, after which the returnees did not come back to him. The guard said 'I have settled it'. No case or disciplinary action is reported.

headline_en: 21% of migrants entering Europe via the Mediterranean are Bangladeshi
summary_en: IOM Director General Amy Pope, visiting Dhaka, said on Tuesday 7 May 2024 that Bangladeshis top the list of people reaching Europe across the Mediterranean in the first four months of 2024: 3,425 of 16,200 arrivals, or 21 percent. She said 283 Bangladeshis have died on the route since 2014 and that traffickers use social media skilfully while information on legal routes and required skills is under-funded.

facts.statement: From January to 30 April 2024, 16,200 nationals of various countries reached Europe across the Mediterranean, of whom 3,425 were Bangladeshi (21 percent), putting Bangladesh at the top of the list.
In 2023 Bangladeshis were fourth on the list of irregular migration across the Mediterranean.
In 2023, 5,000 migrants died (worldwide); 524 of them died in the Mediterranean, on the route Bangladeshis usually take to Italy.
Since 2014, 283 Bangladeshis have died on the way to Europe across the Mediterranean.

Migration from Bangladesh to Europe via the Middle East is increasing; Amy Pope said many of these migrants were working in the Middle East, and that the tendency to cross to Europe via the Mediterranean has increased since 2015.
facts.source_in_article: IOM Director General Amy Pope; reporter's question

facts.statement: Amy Pope said human traffickers use social media in a sophisticated way, taking account of the situation worldwide.

Amy Pope said there are not enough legal pathways for would-be migrants, not enough is invested in informing people about legal ways to migrate, and people cannot properly learn what skills they need for legal migration and how to get them; to counter traffickers on social and digital media people must be properly informed about legal migration routes.

IOM's global report for 2024 says about 15 lakh people have been displaced in Bangladesh; Amy Pope said data and research are needed to understand whether large numbers are migrating because of climate change.
facts.source_in_article: IOM World Migration Report 2024; Amy Pope

headline_en: Remittance suddenly rose on the last day of April
summary_en: Remittance of USD 13 crore 50 lakh arrived on the last day of April 2024, taking the month to USD 204 crore 30 lakh, 21 percent above April 2023. Bankers say Bangladesh Bank let banks buy remittance at up to BDT 117 per dollar, which with the 5 percent total incentive makes about BDT 123, and that end-of-month account updating also played a part.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in April 2024 was USD 204 crore 30 lakh, 21 percent more than April 2023; USD 13 crore 50 lakh came on the last day (30 April), about double the roughly USD 6.5 crore daily average of the first 29 days.
Remittance was USD 128 crore 15 lakh in the first 19 days of April 2024 and, as printed, '190 crore 80 dollars' in the first 29 days.

A senior official of one bank said that because remittance was below expectation early in April 2024, Bangladesh Bank allowed banks to buy remittance at up to BDT 117 per dollar and many banks bought remittance dollars at the last moment.
If a remittance dollar is bought at BDT 117, with the total 5 percent incentive given by the government and the bank the value of the dollar comes to about BDT 123.

A bank managing director said remittance that arrives earlier is sometimes not added to the accounts for various reasons and accounts are updated at month end, which can also raise the last day's figure.
Eid al-Fitr was in April 2024, but unlike most years no extra Eid surge in remittance was seen, bankers said.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 210 crore in January 2024, USD 216 crore 60 lakh in February 2024 and USD 199 crore 68 lakh in March 2024.

Most banks were buying remittance at BDT 116.50 to BDT 117 per dollar and some crisis-hit banks at higher prices, although the official dollar rate was BDT 110; overall inflation was still above 9 percent.

Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 210 crore in January 2024, USD 216 crore 60 lakh in February 2024 and USD 199 crore 68 lakh in March 2024.

headline_en: Dhaka tops remittance receipts, followed by Chattogram, Sylhet, Cumilla and Noakhali
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's district-wise report for July 2023 to February 2024 shows most remittance arrives at bank branches in Dhaka district, followed by Chattogram, Sylhet, Cumilla and Noakhali. Bank officials say migrant-heavy districts receive less than expected because many expatriates have settled abroad and are selling assets at home and taking the money out.

facts.statement: District-wise remittance received in July 2023 - February 2024: Dhaka USD 523 crore, Chattogram USD 142 crore, Sylhet USD 87 crore, Cumilla USD 81 crore, Noakhali USD 46 crore, Brahmanbaria USD 38 crore, Feni USD 37 crore, Moulvibazar USD 36 crore, Chandpur USD 35 crore and Narsingdi USD 25 crore.
Expatriates sent USD 1,507 crore to Bangladesh in the eight months July 2023 - February 2024, including USD 216 crore 46 lakh in February 2024 and USD 210 crore in January 2024.

Bank officials say migrant-heavy districts should be receiving more than they do, but many expatriates have settled permanently abroad and are instead selling assets in Bangladesh and taking the money abroad, increasing money laundering.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh: USD 2,190 crore in 2023, USD 2,130 crore in 2022 (growth about 3 percent in 2023), USD 2,207 crore in 2021, USD 2,173 crore in 2020 and USD 1,833 crore in 2019. December 2023 was USD 198 crore 98 lakh and November 2023 USD 193 crore.

The official dollar price for buying remittance was BDT 110, but banks were buying at higher prices because of the dollar crisis, which is raising legal remittance; bank officials also think some people are bringing back laundered money by showing it as remittance.

The Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers Bangladesh (ABB), both bodies of commercial banks, have been setting the dollar exchange rate from time to time depending on supply and demand.
Banks in Bangladesh now give their own incentive on remittances equal to the government's 2.5 percent incentive (so 2.5 percent from government plus 2.5 percent from the bank).
