headline_en: Higher education in South Korea: a realistic budget idea for Bangladeshi students
summary_en: A guide piece by the CEO of CHS Education Limited sets out what studying in South Korea costs a Bangladeshi student: average tuition by university type, monthly living costs, and the total first-year budget with and without tuition waivers. It names three national universities to look at, points to the Global Korea Scholarship 2027 undergraduate guideline, explains the D-2 and D-4 visas and warns that part-time work is not guaranteed. It ends with seven questions to ask before deciding.

facts.statement: According to the Korean government's Study in Korea portal, average annual tuition at 4-year universities in South Korea is about 68.2 lakh won (given as 6.2 lakh taka); at national and public universities about 42.7 lakh won (given as 3.93 lakh taka); at private universities about 76.3 lakh won (given as 7.2 lakh taka). Actual payable amounts may differ because of bank exchange rates and transaction charges.
facts.source_in_article: Study in Korea portal, cited by writer Nazmul Hasan Raju

facts.statement: According to official guidance, an international student's monthly cost in South Korea is roughly 7.5 lakh to 10 lakh won, covering housing, food, transport and daily expenses; the article gives the 12-month total as 8.24 lakh to 11 lakh taka.
facts.source_in_article: Korean government guidance, cited by the writer

facts.statement: In the article's budget section, annual tuition is put at about 3.98 lakh taka at a national or public university and about 7.12 lakh taka at a private university, and 12 months of living costs at 8.40 lakh to 11.20 lakh taka. These taka figures differ slightly from those given earlier in the same article (3.93 lakh and 7.2 lakh tuition; 8.24 to 11 lakh living).
facts.source_in_article: Writer Nazmul Hasan Raju, CEO of CHS Education Limited

facts.statement: Without a scholarship, the total initial annual cost of studying in South Korea is put at 12.38 lakh to 15.18 lakh taka at a public university and 15.52 lakh to 18.32 lakh taka at a private university. These are national-average planning figures, not any university's specific figures.
The South Korea study budget excludes airfare, application and admission fees, visa cost, document translation and attestation, initial set-up and an emergency fund.

Fees differ by programme in South Korea: engineering, natural science and laboratory-based subjects can cost more than humanities or social science, and housing and local costs in big cities like Seoul need to be checked separately.

Pusan National University (Busan) is suggested for students interested in engineering, science and business; its admission guideline lists tuition and dormitory costs by department, and it has some English-medium programmes.

Kyungpook National University (Daegu) is suggested for business, IT, engineering and science; its international admission page has information on tuition and scholarships based on TOPIK (Test of Proficiency in Korean), but conditions must be checked for each admission session.

Seoul National University (Seoul) is described as known for high-quality academic and research-based education; admission is competitive and tuition differs by department. Fees published in 2025 cannot be taken as confirmed fees for 2027.

Before applying to a South Korean university, check four things together: whether the programme really runs in English, whether Bangladeshi students can apply, the actual tuition for 2027, and how much you must pay yourself if you get a scholarship.

The official guideline for the Korean government's Global Korea Scholarship (GKS) 2027 at undergraduate level has already been published, and university-based application notices have also come out; students are advised to check eligibility, the university list, application method and deadlines now.
South Korean universities give their own scholarships; Kyungpook and Pusan offer tuition waivers based on TOPIK results, but these are conditional and not guaranteed for everyone.

Illustration of tuition waivers at a South Korean public university: with no scholarship the total initial annual cost is 12.38 to 15.18 lakh taka; with a 50 percent tuition waiver 10.39 to 13.19 lakh taka; with a 100 percent tuition waiver only living costs remain, 8.40 to 11.20 lakh taka. The waivers are for comparison, not a promise of any specific scholarship; fully funded GKS benefits and conditions must be checked separately.
For South Korea, the D-2 visa generally applies to degree programmes and the D-4 visa to language training.

According to the Korean embassy's instructions, a student visa application is made by filling in the e-form on the Korea Visa Portal and submitting it with the required papers; proof of financial capacity, bank statements and admission documents are needed. Applicants should check the latest rules before applying.
facts.source_in_article: Korean embassy instructions, cited by the writer

facts.statement: Part-time work for students in South Korea depends on visa conditions, permission, language ability and applicable rules; getting work is not certain, so possible earnings should not be treated as a substitute for the family's initial financing.

Without Korean language, daily life, job hunting and a long-term career in South Korea may need extra preparation; even where a degree can be done in English, local language skill widens future opportunities.

Seven questions to ask before deciding on South Korea: do my results and subject match the programme's eligibility; have I checked the programme language and IELTS/TOEFL or TOPIK conditions; do I have a written account of all costs including tuition, housing, food and insurance; have I verified scholarship eligibility, benefits, deadline and renewal conditions; can I prepare the visa's financial proof and documents; do I have money to continue studying even without part-time work; have I thought about career, language preparation and a back-up plan after the degree.

headline_en: Promise of well-paid jobs and marriage to suitable grooms: how they fell into traffickers' trap
summary_en: Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) rescued nine people at South Lombori Ghat, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, on the evening of Saturday 7 November 2026 as they were being gathered for trafficking to Malaysia by sea. Ten to fifteen members of the trafficking ring escaped by boat. The rescued said men were lured with good jobs and women with promises of marriage to suitable grooms in Malaysia.

facts.statement: BGB rescued 9 people at about 6:30 pm on Saturday 7 November 2026 in a raid at South Lombori Ghat (দক্ষিণ লম্বরীঘাট) in Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, while they were being trafficked to Malaysia via the Teknaf sea coast; 10 to 15 members of the trafficking ring fled out to sea in a boat.

The nine rescued at Teknaf were Amir Hossain (45), Md. Jibon (19), Jannat Ara (17), Abdul Khalek (29), Foysal Karim (16), Ariful Islam (21), Nurul Islam (22), Ahmad Nabi (23) and Zahid Alam (18); some are residents of Rohingya refugee camps and the rest are from Cox's Bazar.

According to the rescued people's initial questioning, traffickers persuaded men to go to Malaysia by sea in wooden trawlers with the lure of good jobs, and promised women marriage to suitable grooms once taken to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Mohammad Tajul Islam Chowdhury, commander, Teknaf Battalion-2 BGB

facts.statement: The irregular sea route to Malaysia described: people are gathered at a boat landing (Lombori Ghat, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar) in the evening and sent by sea in wooden trawlers.
BGB said work was under way to establish the detailed identities of the nine rescued and efforts continued to catch the traffickers who fled.

headline_en: Family of West Bengal's Sahabuddin, who shared video of two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia, in anxiety
summary_en: After Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter, over alleged immoral acts inside a mosque in Mecca, the family of Sheikh Sahabuddin, an Indian migrant mosque cleaner from Murshidabad, fears for him. He was arrested in 2023 for posting video of the incident on social media and is serving a prison sentence in Saudi Arabia. Indian migrant-support groups have contacted India's foreign ministry and embassy.

facts.statement: In mid-October 2026 the Saudi Interior Ministry announced the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter, under 'tazir' law, on the charge of engaging in immoral acts inside a mosque in Mecca; the article says this was three years after the incident.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, citing Saudi Interior Ministry announcement

facts.statement: Sheikh Sahabuddin, an Indian migrant worker from Balarampur village, Murshidabad, West Bengal, who worked as a cleaner at the Mecca mosque, was arrested in 2023 on a charge of disrespectful conduct at the mosque; another young man present filmed the two Bangladeshis with Sahabuddin's mobile phone and Sahabuddin later spread the video on social media. A Saudi court sentenced him to imprisonment and he is now in a Saudi prison.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, citing Indian media and the family

facts.statement: Saudi authorities treated posting the video of the incident inside the Mecca mosque on social media as a serious offence that damaged the dignity of a holy place; the poster was arrested quickly and jailed.

Sahabuddin's family says he is innocent and posted the video on a whim without understanding its gravity; organisations and social workers helping Indian migrant workers have contacted India's Ministry of External Affairs and the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia to get him freed and returned.

Related headlines embedded in the article state that Bangladesh sent a letter to Saudi Arabia seeking answers to 6 questions about the execution of the two, and that a father spoke to his daughter for the last time the day before the execution.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry named them as Sajal Chandra Das of Cumilla and Mohammad Abdur Rahim of Noakhali; they fainted from heat and smoke, have no serious injuries and are in the Saudi-German Hospital in Dammam. The article cites Al Jazeera on a series of attacks on Saudi airports.

facts.statement: An attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, at about 9 pm on 21 October 2026 killed at least 2 people and injured 8 others, including 2 Bangladeshis.

facts.statement: CPB General Secretary Abdullah Kafi Ratan said the government should have had details of the charges, trial process and verdict against the two Bangladeshis executed in Mecca, but the Foreign Ministry said it knew nothing about these.

facts.statement: At a rally in front of the National Press Club, Dhaka, at about 11:30 am on 22 October 2026, CPB demanded a full investigation of every expatriate death abroad, action to free Bangladeshis jailed abroad, and effective diplomatic initiative, legal aid and accountability to protect Bangladeshis working abroad.

CPB presidium member Ragib Ahsan Munna demanded that the government make a list of Bangladeshis detained or imprisoned abroad, give expatriates legal aid at state expense, and set up regular prison visits and contact with prisoners' families; he called for urgent diplomatic steps to free Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia and other countries.

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia: embassy did not know
summary_en: A short item says the Bangladesh Embassy is angry at the execution of Bangladeshis Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter in Saudi Arabia, of which Saudi authorities did not inform it before or after; news came through the media on 14 October. They were detained in August 2023. The embassy has sent a diplomatic note asking for a copy of the verdict.

facts.statement: Saudi authorities did not inform the Bangladesh Embassy before or after executing Bangladeshis Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter; the news came through the media on 14 October (2026).

Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter were detained in Saudi Arabia in August 2023 on allegations relating to information technology and adultery, but a charge of violating the sanctity of a mosque in Mecca was brought.
The Bangladesh consulate said the list of detainees it received did not mention any punishment for the two, and that a death sentence on such charges is rare.
The Bangladesh Embassy sent a diplomatic note to Saudi authorities asking for a copy of the verdict in the case of the two executed Bangladeshis.

summary_en: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam told reporters on Monday 19 October 2026 that Bangladesh has asked Saudi Arabia for a copy of the verdict in the execution of two Bangladeshis, a man and a woman, and is awaiting a reply. She said Saudi authorities regularly send lists of jailed Bangladeshis and the ministry is checking whether the two were on it. The ministry had no details from the families yet.

facts.statement: Bangladesh has asked Saudi Arabia for a copy of the court verdict on the two executed Bangladeshis (one man, one woman), after first asking for information on the execution; Dhaka is awaiting the reply and will review the documents and decide next steps in discussion with Saudi authorities.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam

facts.statement: Saudi authorities send, at regular intervals, detailed information including names and identities of Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia to Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry and to the Bangladesh missions there; the ministry was checking whether the two executed people were on that list.

facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam

facts.statement: The state minister urged patience, and advised people not to reach conclusions from Facebook posts and to beware of misinformation and disinformation on social media about the two executions.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam

facts.statement: The state minister called Saudi Arabia's response 'very positive', and said Saudi Arabia is an important destination for Bangladeshi workers and one of the biggest sources of remittance, and that the government has a responsibility to ensure Bangladeshis there can work safely.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir said there was a lapse in information exchange and in the diplomatic communication process over the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia, and Bangladesh has asked Saudi authorities for a detailed explanation; the two sides are talking to find where the lapse was.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir

headline_en: Why barring three women from going abroad is not beyond legal authority: High Court
summary_en: On Tuesday 29 September 2026 a High Court bench issued a rule asking why stopping three adult women from travelling abroad should not be declared without lawful authority, and why authorities should not be directed to issue guidelines against blocking adult women's lawful travel for being unmarried or unaccompanied. The women were stopped at the airport despite valid passports, visas or entry permissions and tickets. The court ordered the police's Additional IGP to dispose of their complaint in seven days and immigration not to obstruct their next trip if papers are in order.

facts.statement: A High Court bench of Justice K M Kamrul Kader and Justice Fatema Anwar on 29 September 2026 issued a rule asking why the action of obstructing three women's travel abroad should not be declared beyond lawful authority, and why the authorities should not be directed to frame and issue guidelines not to obstruct adult women citizens' lawful foreign travel merely for being unmarried, travelling without a guardian or similar gender-based considerations.
facts.source_in_article: High Court order; lawyer Ishrat Hasan

facts.statement: Three adult women were stopped from leaving Bangladesh at the airport despite having valid passports, visas or entry permission and air tickets; immigration asked whether their families knew, told them to phone home (which they did), and said they were unmarried and travelling on their own. There was no court ban or other legal bar on their travel.
facts.source_in_article: Lawyer Ishrat Hasan; the writ petitioners

facts.statement: The three women filed a written complaint with the Additional Inspector General of Police on 30 August (2026) asking for an investigation into why they were stopped and action against those involved; getting no result, they filed a writ petition in the High Court.

The High Court directed the Additional Inspector General of Police to dispose of the three women's complaint within seven days and file a report, and directed the immigration authority not to obstruct the petitioners' next foreign trip if they have proper papers.

The petitioners' lawyer argued that stopping adult women from travelling for being unmarried or unaccompanied raises questions under Constitution articles 27 and 28 (equality and non-discrimination by sex), 31 and 32 (protection of law and personal liberty) and 36 (freedom of movement); the petitioners said whether an adult woman is unmarried or accompanied by parents or a guardian cannot be an independent legal basis to control a citizen's lawful travel abroad.

headline_en: The central bank between growth, inflation and the exchange rate
summary_en: An opinion column by Jyoti Rahman and Asif Khan on Bangladesh Bank's monetary policy argues that the economy is in stagflation and the central bank has turned expansionary despite high inflation. On remittances it argues that informal control of the exchange rate pushes remittances back to hundi, citing weak formal inflows in 2022 to 2024 despite record migration and record inflows after the taka stabilised following the 2024 political change.

facts.statement: The columnists say that from 2022 to 2024 overseas labour markets were strong and a record number of workers went abroad, yet remittance inflow through formal channels was weak because continued taka depreciation led many to use informal hundi channels.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists Jyoti Rahman and Asif Khan

facts.statement: The columnists say that after the 2024 political change, with the taka stable and the incentive to use hundi effectively gone, formal-channel remittances reached record levels.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists Jyoti Rahman and Asif Khan

facts.statement: The columnists describe Bangladesh's current exchange-rate system as a loosely managed float within an undeclared band, in which the central bank is reported to set acceptable exchange-rate limits for commercial banks by informal verbal instruction; they warn that when banks cannot legally transact above a set rate, remittances easily shift back to hundi and a foreign-currency black market forms.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists Jyoti Rahman and Asif Khan

facts.statement: Background given in the column: Bangladesh Bank announced a 60,000 crore taka stimulus package in May (2026), capped the spread between weighted-average lending and deposit rates in June, and cut the policy rate by 50 basis points on 30 July; July inflation was 8.3 percent.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists Jyoti Rahman and Asif Khan

headline_en: Number of Bangladeshis killed in Saudi factory fire rises to 16
summary_en: The number of Bangladeshis killed in a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Sunday 9 August 2026 rose to 16, according to a Foreign Ministry Facebook post on 10 August. Thirteen were from Atrai upazila of Naogaon, two from Naldanga in Natore and one from Bagmara in Rajshahi. The ministry said bodies would be brought home with the families' consent once identification is complete.

facts.statement: A fire broke out at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, at midday on Sunday 9 August 2026; the number of Bangladeshis killed rose to 16, according to a post on the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry's verified Facebook page at 8:17 am on Monday 10 August. An earlier related headline had put the toll at 10, all from Naogaon.

By the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry's information, the 16 Bangladeshis killed in the Riyadh sofa factory fire were 13 from Atrai upazila, Naogaon; 2 from Naldanga upazila, Natore; and 1 from Bagmara upazila, Rajshahi.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry

facts.statement: The 13 dead from Atrai, Naogaon are: Md. Rubel Pramanik (father Md. Saidur Rahman), Md. Kalimuddin (father Bazlur Pramanik), Md. Mohon and Md. Sumon (father Guffar Pramanik) of Gondogohali village; Majidul (father Majnu) and Abdul Jalil of Khorosrota village; Farid of Ujanpoi village; Shuvo and Sumon of Dubai village; Hridoy of Boala village; Shahin of Naogaon village; Sagor of Sadnagar village; and Minhaj of the same upazila.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry

facts.statement: The two dead from Naldanga, Natore are Shamim of Dighirpar village and Sabbir of Khajura village; the one from Bagmara, Rajshahi is Shyamol of Moru village (মরুগ্রাম).
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry

facts.statement: A second Foreign Ministry Facebook post at 11:27 am on 10 August 2026 said that once identification is complete, necessary steps will be taken to bring the bodies to Bangladesh in line with the families' consent.

Officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh went to the fire site right after hearing of it and are working closely with Saudi authorities on identifying the dead and completing formalities for the bodies; the Foreign Ministry said it is monitoring round the clock and giving help as needed.

headline_en: Lost land and homestead to brokers; now supports family selling eggs by bicycle
summary_en: A feature on Lal Mia (54) of Chhoto Amian village, Shalikha, Magura, who has sold eggs by bicycle for 32 years. Between 2002 and 2012 he paid brokers four times, about 10.5 lakh taka in total, to go to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia (twice) and Dubai, selling four bighas of farmland and his 12.5-decimal homestead; he never went abroad and never got the money back. He now lives in a house built on someone else's land.

facts.statement: Lal Mia of Chhoto Amian village, Shalikha upazila, Magura, says he paid a broker 1 lakh 30 thousand taka in 2002 to go to Saudi Arabia but could not go.
Lal Mia says he paid 2.5 lakh taka in 2006 to go to Malaysia, and again 3 lakh taka in 2010 to go to Malaysia; he did not get to go either time.
Lal Mia says that in 2012 a broker who said he would take him to Dubai coaxed 3 lakh 60 thousand taka out of him; he did not go abroad and did not get the money back.

Lal Mia handed brokers about 10.5 lakh taka in four payments over ten years for jobs abroad, raising it by selling four bighas of farmland and a 12.5-decimal homestead; he says the brokers spoke in such a way that he was compelled to believe them. He never went abroad and no money was returned; he now lives in a house on another person's land.

Lal Mia (54) now earns an average of 15 to 18 thousand taka a month buying and selling duck and chicken eggs by bicycle across about 50 villages in Shalikha (Magura) and Kaliganj (Jhenaidah), riding about 50 km a day; he says the income no longer covers household costs.

headline_en: Bangladeshi diaspora: the challenges of engaging expatriates in national development
summary_en: Second and final part of an opinion column by Mobasser Monem, chairman of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission, proposing a 'PIE' (Philanthropy, Investment, Expert Engagement) framework and a high-powered national platform under the Prime Minister's Office to engage the diaspora. He says the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry deals mainly with labour migrants' welfare and has no mandate or programme for diaspora engagement, and lists challenges such as the lack of a reliable database and undocumented expatriates' reluctance to share personal data.

facts.statement: The columnist says the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has long handled mainly labour migrants' welfare and overseas employment, has no mandate or structure for using the diaspora's knowledge, skills and investment, has taken no initiative yet on diaspora engagement in national development, and is very busy with labour migrants' problems with limited staff and resources.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Mobasser Monem, Chairman, Bangladesh Public Service Commission

facts.statement: The columnist proposes a 'PIE' framework (Philanthropy, Investment, Expert Engagement) and a high-powered 'National Platform for Diaspora Engagement in National Development' working from the Prime Minister's Office, possibly headed by the Prime Minister, with a Project Implementation Unit; the Economic Relations Division (ERD) could implement it in the short term. This is a proposal, not an existing scheme.

Challenges named by the columnist: there is no reliable long-term online database of expatriates; many expatriates live in countries where they have no legal residence permit and so are unwilling to disclose personal information; and many expatriate associations abroad are influenced by Bangladesh's national politics.

The columnist recommends a special bank account or fund-management structure with online tracking for expatriates' charitable donations, a prepared list of development projects, regular contact through embassies, missions and consulates, an annual conference and expatriate awards.

headline_en: Family overwhelmed to get back missing migrant Amir Hossain after 30 years
summary_en: Amir Hossain of Dinara village, Naria, Shariatpur, went to Malaysia through a broker in 1996, lost contact with his family after three years and was missing for 27 years. Six months ago two Bangladeshis found him mentally unwell in a tin hut in a forest in Penang and posted video; his wife recognised him. After the Bangladesh mission verified his identity through the Naria UNO, a birth registration was issued and the mission gave a travel pass; he landed in Dhaka at 12:20 am after the night of Tuesday 21 April 2026 and was received by BRAC Migration Programme and family.

facts.statement: Amir Hossain of Dinara village, Chamta union, Naria upazila, Shariatpur, sold inherited farmland and went to Malaysia through a broker in 1996, worked there as a painter, kept in touch and sent money home every month for three years, then contact stopped and the family had no trace of him for 27 years.

Six months before his return, an expatriate named Dipu and expatriate journalist Bappi Kumar Das found Amir Hossain in a mentally unbalanced state in a small tin hut in a forest in Penang, Malaysia, rescued him and posted photos and video on social media; his family recognised him from the video and contacted the person who posted it, then spoke to him on video calls several times. (The son's quote spells the journalist's name 'Pappi Kumar Das'.)

How an undocumented, long-missing Bangladeshi was repatriated from Malaysia: Bangladesh mission officials in Malaysia sent his photo and the information he gave to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) of Naria for verification; the UNO verified it with the family; with upazila administration help Chamta Union Parishad issued a birth registration for him; that birth registration and family members' documents were sent to the Bangladesh mission in Malaysia, which then issued a travel pass and arranged his return.
Amir Hossain arrived in Dhaka from Malaysia at 12:20 am in the night following Tuesday 21 April 2026, about 30 years after leaving; the whole effort took about six months.

At the Dhaka airport, BRAC Migration Programme and family members received Amir Hossain with help from Civil Aviation Security (AVSEC) and the Probashi Kallyan (expatriates' welfare) Desk; he was then taken to his younger son Shahidul Islam's home in Keraniganj, Dhaka.
Naria UNO Abdul Qayyum said the upazila administration would stand by the returnee in any problem.

BRAC Associate Director (Migration and Youth Platform) Shariful Hasan said the case shows the uncertainty of migrant life, that nobody knows how many others are in such a crisis, and that a database of every expatriate is not impossible in this age of technology but necessary.

After Amir Hossain went missing, his wife raised six children with help from relatives and neighbours; the children could not study for lack of money and worked as labourers from childhood, according to son Babu Talukdar, who was six when his father left.

headline_en: I could not even see my son one last time
summary_en: First-person account by Akhlus Mia of Sunamganj, whose son Shayek Ahmad was one of 22 people who died of lack of water and food on 21 March 2026 in a small boat crossing the Mediterranean to Greece. The father had earlier lost 4.5 lakh taka to a broker for a Serbia trip that never happened, then paid broker Azizul Islam of Ichhgaon 4.5 lakh taka up front and 7.5 lakh more after Shayek reached Libya via Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Egypt. In Libya Shayek was held in a crowded room, starved and tortured for money.

facts.statement: On 21 March 2026, 22 people died from lack of water and food while crossing the Mediterranean in a small boat on the way to Greece; one was Shayek Ahmad of Sunamganj.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo introduction; father Akhlus Mia

facts.statement: Akhlus Mia of Sunamganj says that two years ago he sold some land and paid a broker 4.5 lakh taka to send his son Shayek to Serbia; the trip kept being postponed and never happened, the money was lost and could not be recovered from the broker.

For the Libya-to-Greece trip arranged through broker Azizul Islam of Ichhgaon (ইছগাঁও), the terms were 4.5 lakh taka up front and the remaining 7.5 lakh taka after reaching Libya, before being put on the 'game'; the father paid the first 4.5 lakh, then sold the household cows and land to send the further 7.5 lakh taka (12 lakh taka in all by these figures). The agreement was verbal.

Shayek left home with several others from his village about four months before the account and travelled first to Saudi Arabia, then Kuwait, then Egypt, to Libya; the promise was that he would be sent from Libya to Greece in a large wooden boat.

'Game' is the word used for going by sea from Libya to Greece in small wooden or plastic boats at the risk of one's life; the father says he knew of hundreds of young men dying in 'games', including two boys from his own area two years earlier.

Brokers said the migrants were in a 'camp' in Libya, but it was one room into which everyone was crammed, with too little food: a kind of hostage situation. Many had their phones taken; they were beaten for money and photos and videos of the beatings were sent to families so that money would be sent quickly. Shayek too was tortured for money, was not given food and was at times cut off from contact.

Shayek once cried on the phone asking his father to arrange his return from the Libya 'camp', saying he would not survive; the broker ignored the father, saying time was up and the 'game' could be any time.

Shayek missed one boat departure because he fell and hurt his leg running on the seashore. On 21 March he phoned to say there was a 'game' that day that he probably would not be on and that he would go on the 23 March one; in fact he was on the 21 March boat.
On 23 March the father could not reach Shayek and the broker did not answer the phone; the family learned of the death only on 28 March from people in the area.
The father, Akhlus Mia, had himself worked in Kuwait for 18 years and wanted his son to study and stay in Bangladesh; he says the son became obsessed after seeing local boys leave for Europe.

headline_en: Language study abroad: Probashi Kallyan Bank giving loans of 10 lakh taka without collateral
summary_en: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched a 'loan for language learning and special skills for overseas employment' scheme giving up to 10 lakh taka without collateral for admission to language courses in countries including Japan, Korea, China and Germany. The loan covers tuition sent directly to the institution and living costs abroad. Conditions include age up to 40, an offer letter, a minimum language certificate, 11 percent annual interest and a term of up to three years; helpline 16238.

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched the scheme 'Loan for language learning and acquiring special skills for the purpose of overseas employment' (বৈদেশিক কর্মসংস্থানের উদ্দেশ্যে ভাষা শিক্ষা ও বিশেষ দক্ষতা অর্জনের জন্য ঋণ), under which eligible applicants get up to 10 lakh taka as a loan without collateral for admission to language courses in countries including Japan, Korea, China and Germany.

The Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan can be used to send tuition fees directly to the educational institution concerned and to send money for accommodation and food costs while abroad; easy terms are highlighted especially for students going to Korea, Japan, China and Germany.

To get the Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan the applicant must be a local resident of the branch's area and not more than 40 years old, and must show an offer letter issued by an educational institution in the destination country and a language certificate of at least intermediate level (for example N5 for Japan, TOPIK Level 3 for South Korea).

Documents to submit with the Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan application: passport-size photo, copy of national identity card, educational certificates and the necessary papers relating to the guarantor.
The Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan carries annual interest of 11 percent and a maximum term of three years; other fees and charges are set by the bank's policy.
For details on the language-study loan, contact the nearest Probashi Kallyan Bank branch or the helpline number 16238; information is also on the bank's website (address not printed).

named_actors.what_the_article_says: State bank offering collateral-free loans up to 10 lakh taka for language courses abroad at 11 percent annual interest for up to three years; helpline 16238.

headline_en: 5,000 women garment workers to be recruited for Jordan at no cost, with housing and other benefits
summary_en: BOESL, under the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, will recruit 5,000 skilled or semi-skilled women garment machine operators for garment companies in Jordan. The job is for 3 years (renewable), age 20 to 35, 8 hours a day with overtime, at 130 Jordanian dinars; the employer bears housing, food, primary medical care and airfare to Jordan. Selection tests are held every Friday at 7 am from 3 April at Bangladesh-Korea TTC and Mohila TTC, Mirpur, Dhaka.

facts.statement: A total of 5,000 skilled or semi-skilled women garment machine operators will be recruited through the government channel for various garment companies in Jordan, via BOESL under the supervision of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.
BOESL Jordan garment recruitment: women aged 20 to 35 who are skilled or semi-skilled in operating garment sewing machines are eligible.

headline_en: Amid war, Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East spend Eid in fear
summary_en: With the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February 2026 spreading to other Middle East countries, Bangladeshis in Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman describe an Eid-ul-Fitr under restrictions: movement limits, Eid prayers only inside mosques, police safety briefings and cancelled flights home. Several Bangladeshis have been killed in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the UAE and Iraq. Bangladesh embassies advise expatriates not to post war-related content on social media; in Bahrain people are being arrested for doing so.

facts.statement: The article says more than 50 lakh Bangladeshis live in the war-affected countries of the Middle East, and that during the war several Bangladeshis have been killed in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the Emirates and Iraq.

In Qatar the government continually sends warnings and emergency instructions by SMS to residents' mobile phones and tells people not to go outside when the situation worsens; police visit workplaces and have instructed staff how to move quickly to a safe place with customers if an alarm sounds.
facts.source_in_article: Kabir (pseudonym), accountant at a bank in Al-Shahaniya, Qatar, 7 years in the country

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi in Al-Shahaniya, Qatar, said bombs hit 10 to 15 km from his workplace, there were days with two or three attacks, and he had to stay indoors for 10 days in a row. Movement has been somewhat eased in Al-Shahaniya, but free movement remains stopped in areas such as Ain Khaled, Al Waab and Lusail City for fear of Iranian attack.
In Qatar, for security, Eid-ul-Fitr 2026 prayers have to be said inside mosques instead of in open fields, and free movement between most cities is stopped.

Aziz Ahmed (pseudonym) of Narsingdi, 9 years with a cleaning company in Al-Jahra, Kuwait, had a ticket home for 16 March 2026 but could not travel because airports and flights were temporarily shut after the war began.
Kuwait's administration announced that there would be no Eid congregation in the open or on large fields in 2026 and that everyone should pray in mosques.

Kuwait police called a meeting of expatriates and explained in Arabic and English what to do immediately and how to take shelter if a war warning or siren sounds; expatriates are told to follow the administration's instructions and warnings when commuting. The worker said he and colleagues also follow emergency instructions from the Bangladesh Embassy.

In Saudi Arabia there is fear in the eastern areas, especially those on the Gulf coast, and extra caution in Riyadh, while the situation is normal in the western cities of Mecca, Medina and Jeddah, where people are going to work and shopping for Eid. In Gulf countries, expatriates in areas with US bases are in the most frightening situation.
facts.source_in_article: Two Bangladeshi expatriates in Mecca and Jeddah; reporter

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi in Manama said an Iranian attack a few days earlier caused deaths in Bahrain and many now do not go out unless necessary.
A Bangladeshi in Manama said many people in Bahrain are being arrested for publishing anything war-related online.
A Bangladeshi in Manama said expatriates fear losing work, and that many Bangladeshi expatriates who have gone home to Bangladesh fear losing their jobs.
A Bangladeshi in Sohar, Oman, said he wanted to spend Eid in Bangladesh but could not return because of the war; the situation in his city is largely normal, though people fear an attack at any time.

Bangladesh embassies in various countries are advising expatriates to refrain from publishing war-related information or spreading news on social media. The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, in an urgent notice in the first week of March 2026, asked expatriates, in respect of Saudi local law, not to upload any related photo or video, or publish, share, like or comment on any such news on social media.

headline_en: How is the economy doing
summary_en: A question-and-answer explainer on Bangladesh's economy at the half-way point of fiscal year 2025-26, covering inflation, wages, GDP, credit, revenue, reserves, exports and imports. For migrants the usable part is the remittance and exchange-rate data: remittances topped USD 3 billion in December 2025, the first six months brought USD 16.26 billion (18% up), and the dollar is described as fairly stable at BDT 122.

facts.statement: Remittances sent by Bangladeshis abroad exceeded USD 3 billion in the month of December (2025), and inflows had been high for several months.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo explainer citing Bangladesh Bank and other government sources

facts.statement: The record for remittances received in a single month was set in 'last March' (2025), when USD 329 crore (3.29 billion) came into Bangladesh, the highest for any single month so far.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo explainer citing Bangladesh Bank and other government sources

facts.statement: In the first six months of fiscal year 2025-26 Bangladesh received USD 1,626 crore (16.26 billion) in remittances, 18 percent more than in the same period of the previous fiscal year.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo explainer citing Bangladesh Bank and other government sources

facts.statement: The article says remittances have kept a positive trend since the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024.
The article says the dollar shortage in Bangladesh is almost gone and the dollar price has become roughly stable at BDT 122; the shortage had peaked during the Ukraine war.

Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 31.18 billion at the end of December (2025), or USD 28.57 billion under the IMF's BPM method; remittance inflow and an improved current account are credited. Reserves had reached USD 48 billion in 2021 and had fallen to USD 26 billion when the Awami League government fell.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo explainer citing Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: Overall inflation in Bangladesh was 8.49 percent in December (2025), with food inflation 7.71 percent and non-food inflation 9.13 percent; rice inflation was 11.92 percent (12.26 percent in November); the national wage growth rate was 8.08 percent, below inflation.
Bangladesh's goods exports fell 14 percent in December (2025) to USD 397 crore from USD 462 crore a year earlier, the fifth straight monthly fall; imports that month were USD 5.80 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo explainer citing EPB and Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: GDP growth in the first quarter of fiscal year 2025-26 was 4.5 percent, against 2.58 percent a year earlier; the article says weak private credit (6.58 percent growth in November) is shrinking private-sector job opportunities at home.
facts.source_in_article: BBS and Bangladesh Bank, via Prothom Alo explainer

headline_en: Gunfight between two sides at a human traffickers' den, young woman killed
summary_en: On Friday 16 January 2026 an 18-year-old local woman was shot dead in Baharchhara, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar during a gunfight between armed men living in the hills and a human-trafficking gang. A local union member said the traffickers had gathered people in a hill hideout to send them to Malaysia by sea. Police said Baharchhara has become the main base of trafficking gangs; no one had been arrested.

facts.statement: Sumaiya Akter (18), daughter of Md. Siddique of Noakhaliya Para, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, was shot dead at about 6:30 pm on Friday 16 January 2026 at the foot of the hill in Noakhaliya Para during a gunfight between armed men in the hills and members of a human-trafficking gang; she had two bullet wounds and was declared dead at Teknaf Upazila Health Complex.
facts.source_in_article: Cox's Bazar district police spokesperson Additional SP (DSB) Alok Biswas; emergency doctor Nowshad Alam

facts.statement: According to a Baharchhara union ward 9 member, trafficking gang members had gathered some people in a hideout in the hills of Baharchhara, Teknaf, to traffic them to Malaysia by sea; armed men living in the hills raided the hideout on hearing of it, which started the gunfight.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Ilias, member, ward 9, Baharchhara Union Parishad

facts.statement: Cox's Bazar police say the coastal Baharchhara area of Teknaf has turned into the main base of human-trafficking gangs.
facts.source_in_article: Additional SP (DSB) Alok Biswas, Cox's Bazar district police spokesperson

facts.statement: Police and other law-enforcement forces were running an operation in the Baharchhara hills to catch the armed men and the traffickers, but as of the evening of 16 January 2026 no one had been arrested; Teknaf Model Thana OC Md. Saiful Islam said legal action would be taken and the body was being sent to Cox's Bazar Sadar Hospital morgue for post-mortem.
facts.source_in_article: Additional SP Alok Biswas; OC Md. Saiful Islam, Teknaf Model Thana

headline_en: Lakhs of Bangladeshis 'will be harmed' by US visa suspension
summary_en: The United States has suspended immigrant visas for applicants from 75 countries including Bangladesh from 21 January 2026; tourist and other short-term visas are not covered. Three US immigration lawyers told Prothom Alo that lakhs of Bangladeshis with pending family-based petitions will be affected, while student, visit and business visas remain open and may be processed faster. The article gives figures on US visas and permanent residence granted to Bangladeshis and on remittances from the US.

facts.statement: The United States has suspended immigrant visas for applicants from 75 countries including Bangladesh, effective 21 January (2026); tourist or short-term visa holders are not covered by the restriction.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report; US State Department statement

facts.statement: The article explains that a US immigrant visa is one with which a person enters the US directly with a green card and becomes a permanent resident; it covers family-based green cards (spouse, parents, children, siblings) and employment-based permanent residence. Non-immigrant visas are for temporary stay and include student visas, visit visas and work visas.

Under the suspension, processing of pending petitions by naturalised Bangladeshi-Americans to bring parents, siblings, spouses or children to the US will stay suspended and family members cannot go for now. New family petitions can still be filed, but visas will not be issued for now; US citizens who newly marry cannot bring their spouse for now.
facts.source_in_article: US immigration lawyers interviewed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Immigration law expert Dilli Raj Bhatta says those affected include people whose cases have been pending for many years, those on the waiting list for immigrant visa review, and those whose interviews were already scheduled. He said there is no specific announcement on how long the policy will last and that lawsuits challenging it are expected.
facts.source_in_article: Dilli Raj Bhatta, Nepali-origin US citizen and immigration law expert

facts.statement: Lawyers say visas outside the immigrant category are not suspended: temporary, tourist and business visas are unaffected, so people who want to travel, study or go on business to the US can apply and will get a visa if eligible.
facts.source_in_article: US immigration lawyers interviewed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: US immigration lawyer Raju Mahajan says that because immigrant visa processing is stopped, pressure on the embassy will fall and eligible applicants for other visas (travel, business, student) will get visas in less time than before; those who want to invest in the US can also apply as foreign investment is being encouraged.

Lawyer Moin Chowdhury called the suspension an inhumane decision: a wife married now cannot come, a child who passes age 21 will not be able to come, and a long suspension will create complicated problems.
facts.source_in_article: Moin Chowdhury, described as the first Bangladeshi-origin American lawyer licensed by the US Supreme Court

facts.statement: In US fiscal year 2023 about 59,254 US visas were issued to Bangladeshi nationals: 44,674 non-immigrant visas and 14,580 immigrant visas.
US Homeland Security statistics show Bangladeshis granted lawful permanent residence in the US: 14,890 in fiscal 2019, 9,010 in 2020, 6,180 in 2021, 10,140 in 2022 and 18,240 in 2023.
facts.source_in_article: US Office of Homeland Security statistics

facts.statement: Lawyers say some Bangladeshi families have petitions pending for 15 to 16 members, so by that reckoning several lakh people are waiting to immigrate to the US in stages.
facts.source_in_article: US immigration lawyers interviewed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladesh received its highest-ever remittances 'last year': USD 3,282 crore (32.82 billion). The United States was the fourth-largest source, with 11 percent of remittances.

The US State Department said in a statement that immigrant visa processing for 75 countries would stay suspended while it reassesses its immigration processing so that no foreign national enters who may take public welfare funds and benefits; lawyers said the reason is that many who take citizenship draw government allowances instead of earning.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department statement; US immigration lawyers

headline_en: May Bangladesh School Muscat meet Bangladeshis' expectations
summary_en: A reader's opinion piece by a Bangladeshi community figure in Oman about Bangladesh School Muscat after its governing-body election on 31 October 2025. It describes how the school was founded in 1996 with expatriates' donations collected through embassy services, how it is governed, its low fees, about 1,000 families using it, and complaints about falling standards, late audits and weak A-level teaching. It also notes a new, larger plot allotted for the school in Bowshar and the arrival of a new ambassador in February 2025.

facts.statement: Bangladesh School Muscat, a community school for children of Bangladeshis in Oman, was established on 3 September 1996 and formally inaugurated on 9 November 1996, with approval of Oman's Ministry of Education; it is run under Oman's policies for community schools.
facts.source_in_article: Writer Syed Mohammad Monjurul Islam, former joint secretary of Bangladesh Social Club

facts.statement: To build the school's new building, expatriate Bangladeshis in Oman gave donations to the Bangladesh embassy for 10 years: the writer says 5 rial was taken from each passport service, expatriates twice donated 10 rial, and the money was taken as a percentage from various embassy services over 10 years.

Bangladesh School Muscat is governed by five representatives directly elected by parents for two years plus three Bangladesh embassy representatives (one embassy representative and two highly educated Bangladeshi expatriates); the principal is ex officio member-secretary; the five elected members choose a chairman; the constitution requires a yearly audit.
The election of the governing body of Bangladesh School Muscat was held on 31 October (2025); five members won in the parents' vote.

The writer says Bangladesh School Muscat's tuition fees are much lower than other international schools in Muscat and about 1,000 families send their children there; teachers at the best schools are said to be paid three times what Bangladesh School pays.

Complaints listed about Bangladesh School Muscat: its standard has fallen (it once ranked number 4 in Oman, per the writer), there is a shortage of good A-level teachers and parents say A-level teaching is not up to standard, the 2023-24 audit was not done on time, there is waste and no proper accountability, the school ran for years without a principal, and its finances are fragile. Parents demand an audit of four years of alleged financial irregularities by a reputable firm.

Parents' wishes listed for the school include trained and better-paid teachers, a new building on a new site, a school bus, introduction of the English version of Bangladesh's national curriculum, and low-cost places for poor meritorious students; the writer says fees should be raised if needed. The article refers to O level and A level being taught there.

After a meeting at 11 am on 4 August 2024 between Bangladesh's ambassador to Oman Md. Nazmul Islam and Oman's Minister of Housing and Urban Planning Khalfan bin Said bin Mubarak Al-Shueili, the minister allotted a 9,079 square metre plot at Al Ansab in the Bowshar area for Bangladesh School Muscat's own building, larger than the plot allotted earlier.

Rear Admiral Khandaker Misbaul Azim became Bangladesh's new ambassador to Oman in February 2025; the writer says embassy service in Oman has visibly changed a great deal since his arrival, and that a retired Sri Lankan navy rear admiral (Pradeep Rathnayake) was appointed principal in August 2025. No Bangladeshi principal has been appointed since 2009.

headline_en: Immigration police stop 22 Bangladeshi workers at the airport
summary_en: On Saturday 1 November 2025 immigration police at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport stopped 22 of a group of 30 Bangladeshi workers travelling to Sri Lanka through China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) for an ADB-funded project. Police said their visas carried the words 'No work permit'; the company's recruitment representative said the group had BMET certificates and no-objection letters from both embassies and called it harassment, noting eight others left with the same documents.

facts.statement: At about 8 pm on Saturday 1 November 2025, immigration police at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, stopped 22 people who were leaving for Sri Lanka on worker visas; police said they were stopped because they had no permission to work.

The group of 30 Bangladeshi workers was going to Sri Lanka through China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) to work on a two-year project financed by the Asian Development Bank (ADB); they were to fly at 8:10 pm on an IndiGo flight via Chennai. Eight of the 30 departed; 22 were stopped.
The 22 workers stopped at Dhaka airport were told by the airport immigration authority, citing visa complications, to bring a clearance from the head office of the police Special Branch.

A Special Branch (immigration) police officer said the stopped workers' visas did not carry permission to work: the words 'No work permit' were written on the visas, and that was why they were stopped.
facts.source_in_article: An unnamed officer of police Special Branch (immigration)

facts.statement: CCECC's South Asian recruitment representative Mahbub Alam said the group had all valid papers, including BMET certificates and no-objection letters from the embassies of both countries, that the other eight went with the same documents, that it was plainly harassment, and that the workers suffered financial loss.
facts.source_in_article: Mahbub Alam, South Asian recruitment representative, CCECC

named_actors.what_the_article_says: South Asian recruitment representative of CCECC; said the workers had BMET certificates and both embassies' no-objection letters and called the stop harassment.

headline_en: Kuwait embassy's 'double holiday' policy makes expatriates' lives miserable
summary_en: A letter from a Bangladeshi social worker in Kuwait complains that the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait closes on Kuwait's weekend, all Bangladeshi public holidays and all Kuwaiti public holidays, leaving few service days for more than three lakh workers. He says e-passport appointments are often unavailable online or come four to five months later, and proposes limited Friday service, more staff and restarting mobile consular camps.

facts.statement: The letter writer says more than three lakh (300,000) expatriate Bangladeshis are currently working in Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Saiful Islam, social worker, Bangladeshi expatriate in Kuwait

facts.statement: Through the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait, expatriates mainly get passport renewal (e-passport service), national identity card (NID), birth registration, visa attestation and out pass (travel permit), among other essential services.

Since e-passport service began at the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait, expatriates face heavy crowds and wait for hours in long queues; an online appointment for an e-passport application is unavailable most of the time, and when one is obtained it is for four to five months later.

The Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait is closed on Kuwait's weekly holidays (every Friday and Saturday), on all Bangladeshi public holidays and on all Kuwaiti public holidays, which the writer says leaves very limited service days and makes it hard for workers who must take leave on a working day.
Mobile consular service or camps in different areas of Kuwait existed for some time earlier but, according to the letter writer, have been stopped for a long time.

The writer proposes that the embassy in Kuwait keep passport or selected urgent services open for limited hours on Fridays (with special allowance for staff), hire extra staff and digitise services, and hold frequent mobile consular camps in different areas of Kuwait.

key_quote_bn: অ্যাপয়েন্টমেন্ট পেলেও চার-পাঁচ মাস পরে পাওয়া যাচ্ছে।

headline_en: Professor Yunus to address the UN; reform and election may get emphasis
summary_en: A report on Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's programme at the 80th UN General Assembly in New York, including his planned speech and a dinner on labour reform. The migration-relevant part: on Thursday 25 September 2025 Albania's President Bajram Begaj told Yunus that Albania wants to recruit skilled and unskilled Bangladeshi workers, is considering e-visas for Bangladeshis, and that its universities will welcome Bangladeshi students; Bangladeshis currently have to go to New Delhi for Albanian visas.

facts.statement: Albania expressed deep interest in recruiting skilled and unskilled workers from Bangladesh to meet its growing labour demand; President Bajram Begaj made the proposal in a meeting with Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus at UN Headquarters in New York on Thursday 25 September 2025, on the sidelines of the 80th UN General Assembly.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report of the meeting

facts.statement: Albanian President Bajram Begaj said: 'Our country needs labour. Several Albanian companies have already applied to recruit workers from Bangladesh.' He said cooperation could expand, especially in tourism.
Chief Adviser Yunus noted that Bangladeshi nationals currently have to travel as far as New Delhi for an Albanian visa, and asked the Albanian government to simplify the visa process.
President Begaj said Albania is considering introducing e-visas for Bangladeshis.

Asif Nazrul, the adviser in charge of the expatriates' welfare ministry, said Bangladesh can supply a varied workforce from doctors and nurses to factory and agriculture workers, and stressed signing a memorandum of understanding with Albania; the article does not report an MoU being signed.
President Begaj said Albania's universities are ready to welcome Bangladeshi students under the existing arrangement for admitting international students.

At a dinner hosted by Bangladesh's permanent mission at UN Headquarters on Thursday 25 September 2025, Yunus reaffirmed the interim government's commitment to implement key labour reforms in line with ILO conventions before the national election due in February; BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami and NCP leaders agreed labour-sector reform should continue.

headline_en: Why new chairman Arifur Rahman left Premier Bank and came back
summary_en: A profile of physician Arifur Rahman, appointed chairman of Premier Bank in August 2025 after Bangladesh Bank installed a new board. He recounts how, while working as a doctor in Saudi Arabia, he became involved in recruiting Bangladeshi workers for Saudi employers, was detained for about three months by Saudi police because that broke his iqama rules, and then ran a recruiting business under Saudi royal sponsors until 2010. The rest concerns the bank's bad loans and alleged embezzlement by former chairman H B M Iqbal.

facts.statement: Arifur Rahman, a Bangladeshi physician who worked at Saudi Arabia's National Guard Medical Services (clinic between Dammam and Al Khobar), says a wealthy contractor named Al Khodari, who had won the Saudi government contract to clean Dammam city, told him he needed 2,700 people from Bangladesh; Rahman later connected him with Riazul Islam from Dhaka, and Al Khodari divided the job of bringing the 2,700 workers among several people.
facts.source_in_article: Arifur Rahman, chairman of Premier Bank, speaking to Prothom Alo on 30 August 2025

facts.statement: After that became known, businessmen Ali Asgar Lobi, Nur Ali, H B M Iqbal, A H M Mustafa Kamal and M A H Selim, among others, came to Arifur Rahman one after another; a further job to take 4,000 people then came and was also shared among several of them.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report quoting Arifur Rahman

facts.statement: Some Pakistanis filed a complaint that Arifur Rahman, though a doctor, was involved in manpower export from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia; the article says this was a breach of the rules of his iqama (Saudi residence permit), which he did not know.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report quoting Arifur Rahman

facts.statement: Following the complaint, Saudi police took Arifur Rahman away and interrogated him as a suspect; as the allegation was not proved he was released after about three months and rejoined his job.

Arifur Rahman says Saudi prince Mishari bin Saud bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, then head of the National Guard, asked him to run a business as recruiting manager for his elder brother Mishaal bin Saud bin Abdulaziz Al Saud; with Saudi policy support he obtained visas for Bangladesh, cutting into the shares of India, Pakistan and Thailand, and this continued until 2010.

Arifur Rahman claims that, combining cooperation with other recruiters of the time and his own work, about 17 lakh (1.7 million) Bangladeshis had got jobs in Saudi Arabia by then; he says a 2004 UNDP report described his contribution to sending 15 lakh people and the number later rose by two lakh.

Arifur Rahman bought a large share of Premier Bank with income from manpower export. Bangladesh Bank appointed a team led by him to the bank on 19 August 2025 and the new directors made him chairman on 21 August 2025; he says the bank's default loan rate is close to 23 percent and it could not pay a dividend this time.

headline_en: Malaysia may give Bangladeshi students the Graduate Plus visa
summary_en: On Wednesday 13 August 2025 Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus raised with Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abdul Kadir the introduction of Malaysia's Graduate Plus visa for Bangladeshi students. Adviser Asif Nazrul said the minister agreed in principle, but formalities remain before it takes effect. About 10,000 Bangladeshi students study in Malaysia and, unlike students of other countries, cannot enter its labour market.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abdul Kadir agreed in principle to give the Graduate Plus visa to Bangladeshi students studying in Malaysia, after Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus raised it at a meeting at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur, on Wednesday 13 August 2025; both sides must complete some formalities before the policy takes effect.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, expatriates' welfare and overseas employment adviser

facts.statement: At present Bangladeshi students in Malaysia are denied the opportunity to enter Malaysia's labour market, whereas students of other countries get it; the Graduate Plus visa would let thousands of graduates take high-skilled employment there.
About 10,000 Bangladeshi students are currently studying at various universities in Malaysia.

Malaysia's Education Minister Fadhlina binti Sidek met Yunus at a Kuala Lumpur hotel on 13 August 2025; they discussed increasing scholarships for Bangladeshi students at Malaysian universities and colleges.

headline_en: UK introduces e-visa for foreign students
summary_en: The UK has replaced paper visa documents with e-visas for students: those who applied for a UK student visa from Bangladesh on or after 15 July 2025 no longer get a visa sticker (vignette) in the passport. Dependants of students still get vignette stickers. The article lists what students should do before flying, including creating a UKVI account linked to the travel passport.

facts.statement: From 15 July (2025), people who apply for a UK student visa from Bangladesh no longer receive a visa sticker (vignette) in the passport; the UK has introduced an e-visa system in place of paper documents.
facts.source_in_article: UK government, cited via Economic Times

facts.statement: The UK has already abolished the Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) and replaced it with the e-visa; the Biometric Residence Card (BRC) and passport stamps or sticker visas will all be replaced by e-visas in phases.
facts.source_in_article: UK government, cited via Economic Times

facts.statement: All the student's visa information is stored in a secure digital account, which can be checked or updated at any time; on entering the UK students need to carry only the passport and their e-visa account details.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report citing the UK government

facts.statement: Most applicants will receive an e-visa, but applicants who are dependants of students (husband/wife, children) will still receive a vignette sticker.

Before boarding, students going to the UK should: create a UKVI account and link the passport they will travel with; confirm the e-visa has been issued and is correctly linked to the account; carry a printed or digital copy of the e-visa approval letter to show at the airport or immigration; and update passport details in the UKVI profile if they have a new or changed passport.

The UK Home Office says the aim of the change is to make access easier and more secure and to advance digitisation; with an e-visa the visa can be verified or details updated at any time from anywhere.

headline_en: Kushtia's Robijul, known for seven marriages, arrested in human trafficking case
summary_en: Police arrested Robijul Islam (40) of Kushtia on Sunday 20 July 2025; he faces at least six human trafficking cases. Police say he spent about twelve years in Libya, acted as the channel taking young men from Kushtia, Chuadanga, Jhenaidah and nearby districts to Libya, and that the ring filmed victims suffering in Libya and sent the videos to families to demand large sums.

facts.statement: Robijul Islam (40), of Patikabari village, Kushtia Sadar upazila, was arrested from Khoksa upazila, Kushtia, on the morning of Sunday 20 July 2025 by Islami University Thana police; there are at least six cases against him on human trafficking allegations, and he was to be taken to court on Monday 21 July with a remand application.
facts.source_in_article: OC Mehedi Hasan, Islami University Thana

facts.statement: Police sources say Robijul Islam was in Libya for about twelve years, acted there as the channel for taking young men from his area to Libya, and continued this after returning to Bangladesh; allegations of money dealings and human trafficking were raised against him at various times.

Police say Robijul lured village youths from Kushtia, Chuadanga, Jhenaidah and surrounding districts and sent them to Libya; after they arrived, ring members recorded videos of them suffering in Libya, sent the videos to the person's family and demanded large sums of money.
Police said Robijul was arrested after a preliminary investigation found the allegations true; he will be questioned about other members and police are working to identify the whole ring.
facts.source_in_article: OC Mehedi Hasan, Islami University Thana; police sources

headline_en: Five Bangladeshis in two Malaysian prisons; High Commission officials going to meet them
summary_en: Five Bangladeshis arrested in Malaysia and charged with terrorism-related offences are held in Selangor and Johor Bahru prisons, and Bangladesh High Commission officials were to visit them on Wednesday 9 July 2025 after prison authorities allowed consular access. Malaysia's home minister said 36 Bangladeshis were arrested over alleged links to Islamic State; High Commission sources put the number at 35, of whom 14 were visa overstayers handed to immigration and six of those have been sent back.

facts.statement: Five Bangladeshis arrested in Malaysia and charged with terrorism-related offences are being held in two prisons: two in Selangor prison and three in Johor Bahru prison.

Officials of the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur were to visit the five imprisoned Bangladeshis on Wednesday (9 July 2025) to give consular service, after Malaysia's prison authority gave permission; they will find out whether the men need legal or other basic assistance and hear any statement before deciding next steps.

On 27 June (2025) Malaysia's Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail told the media that 36 Bangladeshis had been arrested in Malaysia on allegations of involvement with the militant group Islamic State (IS); he said police carried out the operation in three phases from 24 April in the Selangor and Johor areas.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: Of the 36 arrested Bangladeshis, five were charged with terrorism-related offences, expulsion (deportation) orders were issued against 15, and further investigation into militant links continues against the remaining 16.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report of the Malaysian minister's account

facts.statement: Bangladesh High Commission sources in Kuala Lumpur say that in separate operations by the Royal Malaysia Police counter-terrorism division from April to June 2025, 35 Bangladeshis were arrested, not 36. The article thus carries two figures (36 from the Malaysian minister, 35 from the High Commission).

Of the 35, 14 were staying in Malaysia illegally after their visas expired; those 14 were handed over to immigration police and six of them have been sent back to Bangladesh. Five were charged with terrorism offences and 16 remain under further investigation.

While the operation was under way, several Malaysian law-enforcement-linked bodies informally asked about a few Bangladeshis, including whether any had past militancy allegations; Bangladesh replied that none on the list had any such allegation in Bangladesh. The High Commission was not told then that a counter-terrorism operation was running.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh High Commission source; diplomatic source

facts.statement: Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Kuala Lumpur say Bangladesh contacted Malaysia's foreign, home and human resources ministries from the start seeking assistance regarding the 35 detainees, but the High Commission did not get the expected response.
facts.source_in_article: Multiple diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Kuala Lumpur

headline_en: Ringleader of gang that sent people to the Ukraine war in the name of jobs arrested
summary_en: CID says it arrested Muhammad Alamgir Hossain (40), the alleged ringleader of a gang that lured Bangladeshis with chocolate-factory cleaner or cook jobs in Russia at BDT 2 to 2.5 lakh a month, sent them first to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, then to Russia where they were handed to the Russian army and forced to fight Ukraine. At least one man was killed and one badly injured; another group of 10 is stranded in Saudi Arabia without passports. A partner of Dream Home Travels and Tours Limited, Banani, was arrested earlier.

facts.statement: CID claims it arrested the ringleader, Muhammad Alamgir Hossain (40), of Amtali Majherpara village, Lohagara thana, Chattogram, late at night last Wednesday (about 11 June 2025) at Shah Amanat Airport, Chattogram; he was shown arrested in a human trafficking case filed at Banani thana on 4 February (2025), gave a confessional statement at the Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate court and was sent to jail.

According to CID, the ring lured people with jobs as cleaners or cooks in a chocolate factory in Russia at a salary of BDT 2 to 2.5 lakh a month, first sent 10 people to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, had them perform Umrah, then took them to Russia and sold them to 'a Sultan', who handed them as slaves to Russian soldiers.

In Russia the victims were given military training and forced to fight against Ukraine; those who refused were physically and mentally tortured and their food was stopped to break their will, after which they joined the fighting under compulsion.
In the fighting, Humayun Kabir of Singra upazila, Natore, was killed and a man named Aminul of Keraniganj, Dhaka, was seriously wounded.

Md. Akram Hossain (24), of Palash thana, Narsingdi, one of the 10 sent to Russia, escaped from the training camp and returned to Bangladesh on 26 January (2025) by his own arrangement, then contacted the victims' families.

On information from returnee Akram Hossain, Jhumu Akter, wife of the war-wounded Aminul, filed a case at Banani thana, Dhaka, under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act (the case is dated 4 February 2025).

CID found that another group of 10 is in Saudi Arabia; after learning that people were being forced to fight, they refused to go to Russia, so their passports were taken away, and they can neither work in Saudi Arabia nor return home.

On the night of 5 February (2025) CID arrested Fabiha Jerin alias Tamanna, described as a key member of the trafficking ring, at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, while she was fleeing to Nepal; she is a partner of Dream Home Travels and Tours Limited in Banani, Dhaka.

CID Additional Special SP Md. Mostafizur Rahman said Alamgir went to Russia on a student visa in 2008, married there and got Russian citizenship; so far he has taken 50 people from Bangladesh to Russia on three categories of visa, and in the past year took 11 on work permit visas saying they would work in a Russian army camp, then forced them to fight Ukraine in breach of the terms.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Mostafizur Rahman, Additional Special Superintendent of Police, CID headquarters

facts.statement: Alamgir also took away the money the men received there, giving a list of costs he said had been spent under various heads.

CID has learned that three Bangladeshis have so far been killed fighting for Russia against Ukraine; the Russian government has confirmed two Bangladeshi deaths and said the process of sending their bodies to Bangladesh is under way.
CID says it is contacting the relevant government and non-government bodies to bring the victims home.

headline_en: Chief Adviser on his way home from Tokyo
summary_en: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus left Tokyo on Saturday 31 May 2025 after a four-day official visit. Besides loan and grant announcements and six economic MoUs, two MoUs were signed on Thursday 29 May on raising Bangladeshi workers' skills and creating jobs for them in Japan, and Japanese authorities and businesses said they plan to recruit at least one lakh Bangladeshi workers over the next five years.

facts.statement: On Thursday 29 May 2025 two memoranda of understanding were signed between Bangladesh and Japan to increase Bangladeshi workers' skills and create employment opportunities for them in Japan, at a human resources seminar organised by the Bangladesh embassy at Hirakawacho, Chiyoda City, Tokyo, with Chief Adviser Yunus present.

At the Tokyo seminar Japanese authorities and business people said a plan has been made to recruit at least one lakh (100,000) Bangladeshi workers over the next five years to tackle Japan's growing labour shortage.
facts.source_in_article: Japanese authorities and business people at the seminar

facts.statement: On Friday 30 May 2025 Japan's Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba announced USD 106.3 crore (1.063 billion) of support for Bangladesh: USD 64.1 crore for railway development and reform, USD 41.8 crore for economic reform and climate resilience, and a USD 42 lakh grant for human development scholarships; the two leaders pledged to finalise a Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement within months.
Six memoranda of understanding on cooperation in economy, investment and other sectors were signed between Bangladesh and Japan at a 'Bangladesh Business Seminar' in Tokyo.

headline_en: 14 teenagers and young men rescued from traffickers' 'hostage house'
summary_en: BGB rescued 14 teenagers and young men at about 11:30 pm on Saturday 10 May 2025 from a locked room in a house at Uttar Lambori, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, where they were held for trafficking to Malaysia by sea while ransom was extracted from their families. Two victims from Cox's Bazar town said a CNG auto-rickshaw driver tricked them there from Inani; their families paid BDT 1 lakh each but they were still held 18 days. No one was detained.

facts.statement: At about 11:30 pm on Saturday 10 May 2025 a Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) team rescued 14 teenagers and young men from a house in the Uttar Lambori area of Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar; no one could be detained, and the rescued are in BGB custody.
facts.source_in_article: BGB; Lt Col Ashikur Rahman, commander, Teknaf-2 BGB Battalion

facts.statement: BGB says the 14 were kept locked in one room of the Teknaf house for the purpose of trafficking them to Malaysia by sea, and were held hostage there while money was extracted from their families.

Two rescued men, Mohammad Kasem and Mohin Uddin of Cox's Bazar town, said they had gone on an outing to the Inani area, where a CNG auto-rickshaw driver tricked them into going to the house in Teknaf; they were confined and beaten there.
facts.source_in_article: Victims Mohammad Kasem and Mohin Uddin

facts.statement: The families of Mohammad Kasem and Mohin Uddin were made to pay BDT 1 lakh each; even after the money was collected they were not freed but held in the house for 18 days, while attempts were made to sell them to brokers for trafficking to Malaysia by sea.
facts.source_in_article: Victims Mohammad Kasem and Mohin Uddin

facts.statement: BGB said it was trying to find out from the victims who was involved and would then take legal action against those responsible.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Ashikur Rahman, Teknaf-2 BGB Battalion
