headline_en: Why air ticket prices are higher in Bangladesh
summary_en: A report comparing air fares from Dhaka with fares from Kolkata, New Delhi and Colombo for the same dates, finding Dhaka consistently dearer (for example Dhaka to Jeddah USD 552 against New Delhi to Jeddah USD 307 for 1 May 2025). Ticket sellers blame airlines' excess profit and a ticket-blocking ring; airlines blame high taxes, airport fees, fuel prices and delays in repatriating ticket revenue. The civil aviation ministry issued 10 directives in February 2025, including discounted tickets for migrant workers.

facts.statement: A direct Dhaka to Jeddah air ticket for 1 May (2025) was priced at USD 552 (about BDT 67,000), while a New Delhi to Jeddah ticket the same day was USD 307 (about BDT 37,500).
The lowest Dhaka to Bangkok fare found for 1 May (2025) was USD 231 (about BDT 28,000 at BDT 122 per dollar), against USD 167 from Kolkata and USD 140 from New Delhi the same day.

On Trip.com the lowest Dhaka-Singapore return fare (out 1 May, back 8 May 2025) was USD 409 (about BDT 50,000), against USD 277 (about BDT 34,000) for Kolkata-Singapore return on the same dates; Colombo to Singapore the same day was USD 206 (about BDT 25,000).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo's own fare search on Trip.com

facts.statement: On one airline, Dhaka to Singapore on 1 May (2025) cost USD 271 (about BDT 33,000) while Singapore to Dhaka the same day cost USD 212 (about BDT 26,000) on Trip.com; on the airline's own website the fares were BDT 36,723 and BDT 26,817 respectively.
Before the Malaysian labour market closed in June of 'last year' (2024), ticket prices to Malaysia exceeded BDT 1 lakh; towards the end of that year a trade in tickets to Saudi Arabia began.

Ticket agencies say a ring formed during the previous Awami League government: state carrier Biman Bangladesh itself began charging more, blocking low-priced tickets and releasing only the higher-priced ones so everyone bought dear, after which the ring sold the low-priced tickets at high prices too; the practice has not fully stopped.

In February (2025) the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism issued 10 directives to prevent abnormal ticket prices; they say air tickets must be sold according to the price list approved by the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) and that discounted tickets must be given to expatriate workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism directive

facts.statement: A Home Ministry investigation committee recently found evidence of fraud behind high ticket prices and has submitted its report to the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism; a task force formed by the interim government is working on lowering ticket prices.

CAAB chairman Air Vice Marshal Md. Monjur Kabir Bhuiyan said CAAB does regular monitoring as regulator and has already written to all airlines to set the high and low ticket prices at a reasonable level.
facts.source_in_article: Air Vice Marshal Md. Monjur Kabir Bhuiyan, chairman, CAAB

facts.statement: Biman Bangladesh managing director Md. Safiqur Rahman said there is no longer any scope to block Biman tickets, anyone can book, Biman's ticket prices have fallen compared with before, and discounted tickets are being given to workers going abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Safiqur Rahman, managing director, Biman Bangladesh

facts.statement: Aviation businesspeople say taking off from Dhaka costs at least 3 to 4 times more than from other countries; going from Dhaka to Singapore the tax per passenger is more than BDT 10,000, while on the return from Singapore the tax paid there is about BDT 3,000.

Aviation expert Kazi Wahidul Alam says that on an international ticket of BDT 1 lakh from Bangladesh, BDT 40,000 is government tax, with other fees on top; on a BDT 3,000 domestic ticket the government tax is BDT 1,100. He says Bangladesh's airport service quality is the lowest and its fees the highest.
facts.source_in_article: Kazi Wahidul Alam, aviation sector expert

facts.statement: Members of the Board of Airline Representatives (BAR) Bangladesh say foreign airlines' ticket revenue is remitted weekly in India, Nepal and Sri Lanka (two to three weeks at worst) but takes six to seven months from Bangladesh, sometimes over a year in a dollar shortage, with no interest; airlines now buy dollars at BDT 120 to 125 when remitting. The interim government has already reduced the remittance time.
facts.source_in_article: Members of Board of Airline Representatives (BAR) Bangladesh

facts.statement: Airlines say 75 percent of Bangladesh's air transport business is held by foreign companies, whereas in every country at least 50 percent is normally held by domestic carriers; ground handling at the airport is done solely by Biman Bangladesh.

The article says lakhs of Bangladeshi workers go abroad for work each year and more than one crore (10 million) expatriates live abroad; they are the airlines' main passengers and a large part of their income goes on air tickets.

ATAB president Abdus Salam Aref said Biman Bangladesh Airlines' ticket prices fell somewhat after the government circular of February (2025), that prices here are still higher than in other countries, and that CAAB could fix maximum and minimum fare limits.
facts.source_in_article: Abdus Salam Aref, president, Association of Travel Agents of Bangladesh (ATAB)

named_actors.name: Biman Bangladesh Airlines
named_actors.what_the_article_says: State carrier; ticket agencies say it began charging more and blocked low-priced tickets under the previous government; it is the sole ground handler; its MD says tickets can no longer be blocked and workers get discounted tickets.

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসী কর্মীদের জন্য ছাড়ে টিকিট দিতে হবে।

headline_en: Land of the yellow fairy-4
summary_en: A travelogue by a Bangladeshi postdoctoral researcher living in Taiwan about a five-day family trip to Singapore for a virology congress in November 2024. Most of it is sightseeing; the usable parts are his observations that Bangladeshis live around Little India where there are many cheap Bangladeshi restaurants, that most Bangladeshis he saw were working as cleaning and construction labourers, and small practical notes (EZ transport card, halal food, a paid-photo trick at the Singapore Flyer).

facts.statement: The writer observed that Bangladeshis in Singapore live around the Little India area, where there are many Bangladeshi restaurants; food there is quite cheap, with one plate carrying enough rice for three people.
facts.source_in_article: Writer Badruzzaman Khokon, postdoctoral researcher in Taiwan

facts.statement: The writer says he saw many Indians and Bangladeshis on Singapore's streets: Indians working in shops, malls and tourist sites, but most Bangladeshis working on the streets as cleaning, construction and other labourers.

The writer bought a mobile SIM and three EZ cards from a shop beside his hotel; the EZ card is used on public transport (he used mainly public buses and metro rail), and he says halal food shops are plentiful in Singapore.

At the Singapore Flyer a person offered to take the family's photo, saying it could be downloaded by scanning a barcode; the writer calls it a scam because on the way back they had to pay 70 Singapore dollars to buy the photos.

The writer, a Bangladeshi resident in Taiwan, applied for Singapore visas for three people at the Singapore business and cultural centre in Taipei (which handles visa work) at midday on 28 October and received visa confirmation by email on the morning of 30 October.
The writer states that about 16% of Singapore's population follow Islam.

key_quote_bn: বেশিরভাগ বাংলাদেশিকে দেখেছি রাস্তায়—ক্লিনিং, কনস্ট্রাকশনসহ নানা শ্রমিক হিসেবে কাজ করতে।

headline_en: 'Tell the government to bring my Mona back to my arms'
summary_en: Abdur Rab (25) of Kabirhat, Noakhali, who went to Libya in January 2022 on borrowed money and worked at a medicine manufacturer, was abducted on 14 January 2025 on the way to Misrata by people posing as law enforcement. Since 26 January his family has received torture videos and audio on imo with a ransom demand of BDT 26 lakh payable into five Bangladeshi bank accounts. His father has applied to the Deputy Commissioner, the Superintendent of Police and the district manpower office.

facts.statement: Abdur Rahim of Sundalpur village, Kabirhat upazila, Noakhali, says he borrowed from people and spent BDT 10 lakh to send his elder son Abdur Rab to Libya on 9 January 2022; the next year he sent his younger son Abdur Rahman the same way. Both brothers worked at a medicine manufacturing company in Libya, and much of the debt is still unpaid.

On 14 January (2025), on the way from their workplace to the city of Misrata, Abdur Rab, his brother Abdur Rahman and two others (four in all) were detained by people identifying themselves as law enforcement; after checking papers three were released but Abdur Rab was kept, and his brother could get no trace of him from the law-enforcement agencies afterwards.

On 26 January (2025) the family got a call on the imo app; the caller said they had bought Abdur Rab for BDT 20 lakh and would release him for BDT 26 lakh. When the father said he had no money, torture began.

Although the abduction was in Libya, the kidnappers told the family to pay the ransom into five bank accounts in Bangladesh and sent the account numbers along with audio recordings of torture; the father later learned the accounts were opened in Chattogram and Khulna.

A neighbour says the kidnappers recently sent two torture videos: one shows Abdur Rab with hands and feet tied with cloth being beaten on the soles of his feet, the other shows him being jabbed in the hand with a blade; they threatened to torture him to death if ransom was not paid.

The father applied to the Deputy Commissioner, the Superintendent of Police and the district office of the manpower and employment bureau for his son's rescue. The district office's assistant director Mukit Hasan said a complaint had been lodged with his office and he would arrange to send it through the ministry to the embassy in Libya.
facts.source_in_article: Abdur Rahim; Mukit Hasan, assistant director, district manpower and employment office, Noakhali

facts.statement: Noakhali Superintendent of Police Abdullah-Al-Faruk said the family's complaint had not come to his notice, that such matters involving expatriates are usually handled by the police Criminal Investigation Department (CID), and that he would still help on seeing a written complaint.

people_cases.outcome: Still held as of 11 February 2025; family unable to pay; complaints filed with DC, SP and district manpower office

key_quote_bn: লিবিয়ায় অপহরণ করলেও বাংলাদেশের পাঁচটি ব্যাংক হিসাবে মুক্তিপণ পরিশোধ করতে বলা হয়।

headline_en: 163 human trafficking cases filed so far in Mymensingh division, only two disposed of
summary_en: A divisional workshop in Mymensingh on 28 January 2025 on the national referral mechanism for trafficking victims heard that 163 human trafficking cases have been filed in the division and only two disposed of, because there is no tribunal. A Home Ministry joint secretary said trafficking victims would be able to file complaints online from 12 February 2025, with police, BGB and other units automatically notified.

facts.statement: 163 human trafficking cases have been filed in Mymensingh division so far and only two have been disposed of; the lack of a tribunal is given as the reason they cannot be disposed of quickly. Up to 2024 the cases were: Mymensingh district 52, Jamalpur 12, Netrokona 89, Sherpur 10.
facts.source_in_article: Statistics presented at the Mymensingh divisional workshop, 28 January 2025

facts.statement: A Home Ministry joint secretary said that from 12 February (2025) victims of human trafficking will be able to submit complaints online; once the complaint form is filled in, police, BGB and other relevant units will automatically receive the information and assist the victim, so victims will not face harassment.
facts.source_in_article: Mu. Jasim Uddin Khan, joint secretary, Public Security Division, Ministry of Home Affairs

facts.statement: INCIDIN Bangladesh's executive director said the real number of trafficking cases is far higher than published statistics, as many victims do not dare to file cases because of social and legal complications, though Mymensingh division has comparatively fewer than other divisions.
facts.source_in_article: A K M Masud Ali, executive director, INCIDIN Bangladesh

facts.statement: The Mymensingh Deputy Commissioner said human trafficking is taking place through the two border upazilas of Mymensingh district, Haluaghat and Dhobaura, and that BGB needs to be more active.

The workshop, titled on the Bangladesh National Referral Mechanism framework for protection and assistance of trafficking victims, was organised by the Public Security Division of the Home Ministry and the Mymensingh divisional administration at the district council auditorium on Tuesday 28 January 2025.

key_quote_bn: আগামী ১২ ফেব্রুয়ারি থেকে মানবপাচারের ভিকটিমরা অনলাইনে অভিযোগ জমা দিতে পারবেন।

headline_en: National Expatriates' Day observed in Amman
summary_en: The Bangladesh embassy in Amman, Jordan, marked National Expatriates' Day and International Migrants Day on Wednesday 18 December 2024 with a discussion and cultural programme. The ambassador urged workers in Jordan to send remittances through legal channels and promised work on expatriate voting rights and remittance-related legal complications; the first secretary (labour) said many Bangladeshis work in Jordan's garment sector and as domestic workers, and asked them not to work illegally.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's ambassador to Jordan, Nure Helal Saifur Rahman, called on all Bangladeshi migrants working in Jordan to send remittances home through legal channels.

The ambassador said expatriate Bangladeshis face various legal complications in sending money home and the embassy is working to reduce them; he also said Bangladeshis working abroad are deprived of the right to vote in national elections and the embassy would work on steps to ensure it.

The embassy's first secretary (labour) said a large number of Bangladeshi workers are employed in Jordan's garment sector, and many Bangladeshis are also in domestic work, housing and other businesses.
facts.source_in_article: Umme Salma, first secretary (labour), Bangladesh embassy in Amman

facts.statement: The first secretary (labour) told Bangladeshi migrant workers in Jordan that the embassy is with them for any need and asked them not to work illegally in Jordan.
facts.source_in_article: Umme Salma, first secretary (labour), Bangladesh embassy in Amman

key_quote_bn: আপনাদের কাছে অনুরোধ জর্ডানে অবৈধভাবে কাজ করবেন না।

headline_en: Dollar price in the country crosses BDT 127
summary_en: In December 2024 banks in Bangladesh began buying remittance dollars at up to BDT 127.50, up from BDT 121-122 before December, because Bangladesh Bank ordered old import liabilities settled within the month; the open-market rate also passed BDT 127. The article lists the rates paid by named remittance houses and gives remittance inflow figures for December 2024, November 2024 and December 2023.

facts.statement: Before December (2024) banks bought remittance dollars from expatriates at BDT 121-122 per dollar; in December this rose to BDT 127.50. Banks were still selling cash dollars at BDT 123, and the card rate (credit and other cards) was BDT 123.

Remittance house sources say Sonali Exchange Company bought dollars at BDT 124, Ria Money Exchange at BDT 124.18, Taptap Send at BDT 124.70 and Western Union at BDT 125.60, so banks had to buy from them at higher prices.

In Dhaka's open (kerb) market the dollar was being bought at BDT 126.70 and sold at BDT 127.50; ten days earlier it was bought at BDT 122.50 and sold at BDT 123. The price rose at least BDT 4 in a little over a week.

In the first 14 days of December 2024 remittances of USD 138.13 crore came in, a daily average of about USD 9.8669 crore; in the whole of December 2023 remittances were USD 199.1260 crore (daily average USD 6.4234 crore); in November 2024 they were USD 220 crore.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report (Bangladesh Bank data implied)

facts.statement: Bank officials say Bangladesh Bank ordered banks to pay off old import liabilities within the month, so from early December several state-owned banks and one private bank began buying remittance dollars at higher prices and others had to follow; higher rates are bringing in more remittances.

Mutual Trust Bank MD Syed Mahbubur Rahman said dollars are not available from all remittance houses as before: some companies buy up dollars from smaller companies and banks must buy from them at higher prices. He said the rise is temporary and expected the price to fall in January.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank's foreign exchange reserves rose by USD 19 crore in a week to USD 2,494 crore on Wednesday (18 December 2024), from USD 2,475 crore the previous Wednesday, as the central bank bought dollars from commercial banks.
Sector people say one reason for the open-market rise is sharply higher demand for dollars from outbound travellers, as many go abroad for holidays in December.

key_quote_bn: ডিসেম্বরের আগে তারা প্রবাসীদের কাছ থেকে প্রতি ডলার কিনত ১২১-১২২ টাকায়। এখন তা বেড়ে ১২৭ টাকা ৫০ পয়সায় উঠেছে।

headline_en: EU-funded Talent Partnership project launched
summary_en: A EUR 3 million EU-funded Talent Partnership project was formally launched in Dhaka on Wednesday 11 December 2024. ILO, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and BMET will implement it over 2024-27 to train 3,000 workers to the skill standards EU labour markets need, upgrade the ministry's online job platform, cut migration costs and reduce irregular migration.

facts.statement: A EUR 30 lakh (3 million) Talent Partnership project funded by the European Union was formally launched in Dhaka on Wednesday 11 December 2024; it aims to address workers' skill gaps, reduce migration costs and widen opportunities for Bangladeshis wishing to migrate for work so as to supply skilled workers for the EU labour market.

The International Labour Organization (ILO), the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment (MoEWOE) and the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) will implement the project over three years, 2024-27.

The project's training programmes aim to prepare 3,000 workers with the skills required for employment in the EU, training them to the skill standards needed in various sectors of EU member states' labour markets, with emphasis on safe, dignified legal migration routes and reducing irregular migration.
The project will also make the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment's online platform fit for job matching (finding jobs).
The article states that more than 74 lakh (7.4 million) Bangladeshi migrant workers send EUR 200 crore (2 billion) in remittances every month.

EU ambassador Michael Miller said the EU-Bangladesh Talent Partnership will ensure safe and dignified migration and that, alongside creating legal migration pathways, work must be stepped up to end irregular migration and tackle trafficking and exploitation; ILO country director Tuomo Poutiainen said it aims to facilitate technical skills development and fair recruitment; adviser Asif Nazrul said it will ensure workers' safety and raise remittances.
facts.source_in_article: Michael Miller, EU ambassador; Tuomo Poutiainen, ILO country director; adviser Asif Nazrul

key_quote_bn: প্রশিক্ষণ প্রোগ্রামগুলো ইইউতে কর্মসংস্থানের জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় দক্ষতা পূরণের জন্য তিন হাজার কর্মীকে প্রস্তুত করার লক্ষ্যে কাজ করবে।

headline_en: The word 'non-resident' remains in the notification; fear that investment will be hampered
summary_en: The government has reopened the Wage Earners' Development Bond to seafarers, pilots and cabin crew after more than four years and removed the investment ceiling, by an Internal Resources Division notification effective 1 December 2024. The merchant marine officers' association fears the word 'non-resident' left in the notification will cause trouble, since seafarers on 4 to 9 month contracts cannot prove residence in any one country; the IRD secretary says a clarification will be issued if needed. The article restates the bond's terms.

facts.statement: By a notification of the Internal Resources Division (IRD), which this article dates 4 November (2024), the government reopened investment in the Wage Earners' Development Bond for seafarers, pilots and cabin crew after more than four years and removed the upper limit on investment in the bond; the notification takes effect from 1 December (2024).
facts.source_in_article: IRD notification, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The notification retains the word 'non-resident'; the Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association (BMMOA) fears it may be read as requiring the investor to reside in the country concerned, causing complications for seafarers. Its vice-president says they had asked IRD officials before the notification to drop the word and believe it was left in by mistake.

BMMOA argues that seafarers have no pension, provident fund or post-retirement benefit; a Bangladeshi marine officer on a foreign-flag ship is under that country's jurisdiction under international law; contracts usually run 4 to 9 months; and he cannot show proof of residence in any particular country for the whole period, though sign-on to sign-off records are internationally valid documents.

IRD secretary Md. Abdur Rahman Khan said the notification names the professions, so there should be no trouble investing in the bond; if there is, IRD will look into it and issue an amendment or clarification if necessary.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Abdur Rahman Khan, secretary, IRD

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment had recently written to the IRD secretary saying the ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond should be lifted to raise expatriates' investment alongside remittance flow.

The Wage Earners' Development Bond is a five-year bond introduced in Bangladesh in 1981 paying profit on a simple-interest basis; under the Wage Earners' Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 23 May 2015) any amount could be invested in it.

Wage Earners' Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks; a foreign currency (FC) account is not required to buy them.
Profit on the Wage Earners' Development Bond is income-tax-free, loans can be taken against the bond, and investment carries a death-risk benefit of 40 to 50 percent.

The foreign-currency earner (wage earner) can invest in the Wage Earners' Development Bond personally or in the name of a person he or she nominates; government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad can also invest.

On 3 December 2020 the Internal Resources Division (IRD) set a combined investment ceiling equivalent to BDT 1 crore in foreign currency for the Wage Earners' Development Bond, US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond, and at the same time barred seafarers, pilots and cabin crew from the wage earners' bond. On 4 April 2022 the ceiling on the two US dollar bonds was lifted, but the ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond stayed and its automatic reinvestment was also stopped.

key_quote_bn: এই বন্ডের মুনাফা আয়করমুক্ত। বন্ডের বিপরীতে ঋণ নেওয়ার সুযোগও আছে।

headline_en: Some new benefits for investing in savings certificates and bonds
summary_en: The interim government has announced new facilities for investors in national savings certificates and bonds, including expatriate Bangladeshis, by an IRD notification effective 1 December 2024. The ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond is withdrawn, it can be reinvested for two further terms, the US Dollar Premium and Investment Bonds for four, and seafarers, pilots and cabin crew of foreign-owned companies can again invest. The article also covers automatic reinvestment for domestic savings certificates and restates the bond's terms.

facts.statement: The investment ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond has been withdrawn; money can be invested for 1 term and reinvested for 2 terms. The IRD notification was issued on Sunday 3 November 2024 ('yesterday Sunday' in an article published 4 November) and takes effect from 1 December 2024.
facts.source_in_article: IRD notification; IRD secretary Abdur Rahman Khan

facts.statement: For the US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond, investment for 1 term and reinvestment for 4 terms has been allowed.

Non-resident Bangladeshi seafarers (mariners), pilots and cabin crew employed in the overseas offices of foreign-owned shipping or airways companies, whom the previous government had barred, can again invest in the Wage Earners' Development Bond, with no upper limit on the amount.
For national savings schemes with automatic reinvestment, the investment ceiling will apply from the date of reinvestment.

New facilities for domestic savings certificates: automatic reinvestment of principal for the Three-Monthly Profit Sanchayapatra and Paribar Sanchayapatra; for Pensioner Sanchayapatra automatic reinvestment of principal plus profit paid monthly instead of quarterly; for the five-year Bangladesh Sanchayapatra and Post Office Savings Bank fixed deposit, reinvestment of principal together with profit.

The government's target is to raise BDT 15,400 crore from savings certificate sales in fiscal 2024-25; the National Savings Directorate says net sales are trending negative again, meaning encashment exceeds sales.

BMMOA says the number of Bangladeshi seafarers (the profession barred from the bond in 2020) is now more than 12,000; they have no pension, provident fund or post-retirement benefit and usually work on 4 to 9 month contracts.

The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment wrote to the IRD secretary two months before (the November 2024 article) saying the ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond should be lifted to raise expatriates' investment alongside remittance flow.

The Wage Earners' Development Bond is a five-year bond introduced in Bangladesh in 1981 paying profit on a simple-interest basis; under the Wage Earners' Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 23 May 2015) any amount could be invested in it.

Wage Earners' Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks; a foreign currency (FC) account is not required to buy them.
Profit on the Wage Earners' Development Bond is income-tax-free, loans can be taken against the bond, and investment carries a death-risk benefit of 40 to 50 percent.

The foreign-currency earner (wage earner) can invest in the Wage Earners' Development Bond personally or in the name of a person he or she nominates; government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad can also invest.

On 3 December 2020 the Internal Resources Division (IRD) set a combined investment ceiling equivalent to BDT 1 crore in foreign currency for the Wage Earners' Development Bond, US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond, and at the same time barred seafarers, pilots and cabin crew from the wage earners' bond. On 4 April 2022 the ceiling on the two US dollar bonds was lifted, but the ceiling on the Wage Earners' Development Bond stayed and its automatic reinvestment was also stopped.

key_quote_bn: ওয়েজ আর্নার্স ডেভেলপমেন্ট বন্ডে বিনিয়োগের ঊর্ধ্বসীমা প্রত্যাহার করা হয়েছে।

headline_en: Growth in remittances is the main reason reserves rose
summary_en: A reader's opinion piece by a Bangladeshi in Kuwait saying the rise in remittances in July-August 2024 stopped the fall in Bangladesh's reserves, yet expatriates get no recognition. He alleges embassies do not help workers in trouble and that there are complaints of harassment, asks for respectful treatment at the airport, interest-free loans for people going abroad and simpler processing.

facts.statement: The writer says remittance flow rose considerably in July to August (2024), that this is the main reason foreign exchange reserves increased, and that Bangladesh Bank believes the fall in reserves has been halted.
facts.source_in_article: Writer Saif Al Rubel, Bangladeshi expatriate in Kuwait

facts.statement: The writer alleges that when expatriates fall into trouble abroad the Bangladesh embassy gives no help, and that there are also complaints of harassment in various ways; he asks that expatriates not be harassed at the airport and be treated politely.

The writer demands interest-free loans for people going abroad, simpler processing for going abroad, easier arrangement of work for Bangladeshis in different countries, and easier financial assistance for those who need it.

key_quote_bn: বিদেশগামীদের জন্য বিনা সুদে ঋণের ব্যবস্থা করা হোক

headline_en: Raising remittances through worker skills development: specific initiatives needed
summary_en: A reader-contributed opinion piece (Dur Porobash section) by Rahman Mridha, a former Pfizer director in Sweden, argues that remittances can grow if Bangladesh sets up corruption-free, international-standard 'special vocational training centres' for current and aspiring migrant workers. It lists occupations he says are in demand abroad, what the government and embassies should do, and proposes minimum education and language requirements for trainees. It contains proposals and general claims, not reported events.

facts.statement: The writer states that at present roughly more than one crore (10 million) Bangladeshis are working in various countries. No source is given for the figure.
facts.source_in_article: Rahman Mridha, opinion writer (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

facts.statement: The writer proposes setting up corruption-free, international-standard 'special vocational training centres' (বিশেষ ভোকেশনাল ট্রেনিং সেন্টার) to raise the skills of migrant workers and people wishing to migrate; this is a proposal, not an existing scheme.

The writer says skilled, trained workers generally get higher pay, more job security, more chance of promotion and the option of moving between different fields of work, and that technical skill is essential to compete in the international labour market.

The writer lists occupations he says are in demand abroad for Bangladeshi workers if trained: health care (nurses, doctors) in developed countries, needing proper training and language skills; engineering (construction, mechanical, electrical), needing advanced training and international-standard certificates; home and personal services (domestic workers, cooks, beauticians, child-care workers) in developed countries; security guards in various countries, needing training and language skills; and gardeners in many countries of the Middle East and Europe.

The writer claims demand for workers in old-age homes and personal care in China is steadily rising, and that a minimum knowledge of the Chinese language is essential for such work. (He also writes that the average life expectancy of China's elderly is about 100 years; this is the article's own claim.)

The writer claims worker demand in the Middle East is steadily rising and that with minimum Arabic-language skill Bangladeshi workers could work in old-age homes or personal care in Arab countries and earn significantly.

The writer says the government should keep training centres corruption-free through strict monitoring, neutral administration and regular inspection; provide infrastructure, international-standard equipment and trainers; allocate funds and open the way for private-sector partnership investment; and give incentives to workers who take training.

Under the writer's proposal, trainees would need a minimum educational qualification and basic language skill; workers with basic knowledge of the selected language would get priority at the training centre and their language skill would be checked through an internal test.

The writer says Bangladeshi embassies and ambassadors should build relations with host governments to create new jobs, do their utmost to protect workers' rights and give legal help when workers have problems, and build links with local employers as a main duty of the embassies.
The writer calls on the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other relevant ministries to jointly implement the skills-training proposal.

key_quote_bn: উন্নত প্রশিক্ষণপ্রাপ্ত কর্মীরা সাধারণত উচ্চতর বেতন পান এবং চাকরির ক্ষেত্রে তাঁদের নিরাপত্তা নিশ্চিত হয়।

headline_en: High Court order due Tuesday on writ seeking independent inquiry committee into mismanagement allegations (sending workers to Malaysia)
summary_en: On Monday 15 July 2024 a High Court bench fixed Tuesday 16 July 2024 for its order on a writ asking for an independent inquiry committee into alleged mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia after they had received final clearance. The writ was filed by Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed on the basis of two newspaper reports of 2 June. The Deputy Attorney General told Prothom Alo that a six-member inquiry committee's report has been submitted to the court.

facts.statement: On Monday 15 July 2024 a High Court bench of Justice Mostafa Zaman Islam and Justice S M Masud Hossain Dolon fixed Tuesday 16 July 2024 for its order on a writ seeking a direction to form an independent inquiry committee into alleged mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia after final clearance (চূড়ান্ত ছাড়পত্র).

Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed the writ attaching two newspaper reports printed on 2 June: one in a daily headlined '20 thousand crore taka looted, breaking the dreams of 30 thousand youths' about the Malaysia labour market, and one in an English daily on the subject 'Jobs in Malaysia: more than three thousand workers did not get tickets because of mismanagement'.
The writ asks for a three-member independent inquiry committee headed by an additional secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, and for it to submit a report.
The writ came up in court on 30 June 2024; that day the court told the state side to find out and report what action had been taken on the mismanagement allegations.

Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy, for the state, told the court on 15 July 2024 that an inquiry committee's report had arrived, and later told Prothom Alo that the report of a six-member inquiry committee had been submitted and the court had kept Tuesday for its order.
facts.source_in_article: Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy

headline_en: How 46 Bangladeshis held captive in the Sahara desert came back alive
summary_en: A column by former army officer Sheikh Masumul Hasan, who served as a UN military observer with MINURSO in Western Sahara in 2004-05, recounts how 46 Bangladeshis trying to reach Europe via UAE, Mali and Mauritania were pushed back by the Moroccan army and held at the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army camp at Tifariti in April 2005. He describes how he collected their details, obtained IOM voluntary return forms and, with UN colleagues, got them repatriated from Mauritania to Dhaka in January 2006, about 10 months later.

facts.statement: On 5 April 2005 the writer, then a UN military observer with MINURSO in Laayoune, was told by phone that 46 Bangladeshis had been detained by the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army in Western Sahara and were being held at Tifariti camp.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Masumul Hasan, former army officer and MINURSO observer (first-person account)

facts.statement: The 46 Bangladeshis told the writer they had each spent 10-12 lakh taka and travelled in small groups by the route Dhaka - United Arab Emirates - Mali - Mauritania to Western Sahara; some had left home 4 months earlier and some 12 months earlier, and their destination was Europe.
facts.source_in_article: The 46 migrants, as told to the writer

facts.statement: After the 46 Bangladeshis crossed Western Sahara and entered Morocco, the Moroccan army detained them and pushed them back to the Sahrawi side of Western Sahara, where the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army caught them and held them at its Tifariti camp.
facts.source_in_article: The 46 migrants, as told to the writer

facts.statement: While held at the Tifariti camp the Bangladeshis worked all day in the Sahrawi liberation army camp and got one meal of bread and lentils a day from it; some of them had earlier job experience in the Middle East and could speak Arabic.

The MINURSO chief operations officer told the writer that rescuing and repatriating the Bangladeshis was not in MINURSO's mandate and that the mission could only exchange information; only the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army and MINURSO military observers could go to the place.
facts.source_in_article: MINURSO chief operations officer (a Ghanaian lieutenant colonel), as quoted by the writer

facts.statement: The writer informed Bangladesh Army headquarters and the Bangladesh mission in Rabat, Morocco by email, then with permission of the acting UN Special Representative (a German woman the article names as ইনগুন্দে ফুউলাও) flew to Tifariti, took food, and collected the names and addresses of the 46; he scanned their handwritten letters and had a friend in Dhaka print and post them to their families.

The detained men all asked the writer to help them reach Europe; he told them he could only try for their return to Bangladesh and ask their captors to treat them well, and writes that in the end there was no way other than repatriation.

In the second week of June 2005 the writer met the Bangladesh ambassador at the Bangladesh permanent mission to the UN in Geneva, then kept contact with IOM headquarters in Geneva and the IOM office in Dhaka, collected IOM 'Voluntary Return Assistance' forms, filled them in for the 46 at Tifariti camp, had photos taken and printed (four sets of papers each), and sent all forms to the IOM regional office in Dakar, Senegal.

According to an email of 30 December 2005 from the UN official quoted by the writer, all 46 were to be handed over at Zouerate (জরেট) on 14 January 2006 and leave Mauritania for Dhaka on 15 or 16 January 2006; the writer says rescuing and returning them took about 10 months.
facts.source_in_article: Email from the acting SRSG, as quoted by the writer

headline_en: How many dollars expatriates sent ahead of Eid-ul-Azha
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show expatriates sent USD 72.62 crore through banks in the first week of June 2024, ahead of Eid-ul-Azha, a higher daily average than May 2024, when USD 225 crore arrived (the highest in 46 months). The article breaks the week's inflow down by bank type and leading banks, and gives BMET figures on yearly overseas employment and a ministerial statement on total migration since 1976. It attributes the rise to the central bank raising the official dollar rate by Tk 7 to Tk 117 in May.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshis sent USD 72 crore 62 lakh in remittances through banks in the first week of June 2024, a daily average of USD 10 crore 37 lakh.
Remittances in May 2024 were USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, a daily average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh; the first week of June averaged USD 3 crore 12 lakh a day more.

Of about USD 73 crore received in the first week of June 2024, USD 17 crore came through state-owned banks, USD 1 crore through specialised banks, USD 54 crore through private banks and USD 20 lakh through foreign banks.

In the first week of June 2024, among state-owned banks Janata Bank brought the most remittance (USD 6 crore) and Agrani Bank the second most (USD 5 crore 75 lakh); among private banks Islami Bank brought the most (USD 15 crore 91 lakh), followed by BRAC Bank (USD 5 crore 29 lakh) and Bank Asia (USD 3 crore 30 lakh).
Bangladesh received USD 2,161 crore in remittances in fiscal year 2022-23, and USD 2,137 crore in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 (the article prints the period as 'July-June').
According to BMET, more than 10 lakh workers went abroad in a year for the first time in 2017; more than 11 lakh 35 thousand went in 2022; and more than 13 lakh went in 2023, a record.
facts.source_in_article: Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET)

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury told parliament in May 2024 that 1 crore 63 lakh 12 thousand 324 workers went abroad for employment in the 48 years from 1976 to March 2024. The article adds that many expatriates are returning home 'failed'.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the official price of the US dollar by Tk 7 in one step to Tk 117; the article says remittance inflow rose because of the higher dollar price.
Bankers think strict action against money laundering and hundi is needed to raise remittances through the banking channel.

headline_en: Banks stop their own incentive on remittances
summary_en: After Bangladesh Bank announced the 'crawling peg' exchange-rate method on 8 May 2024 with a mid-rate of Tk 117 per dollar (previously Tk 110), banks stopped the extra 2.5 percent incentive they had been paying on remittances on top of the government's 2.5 percent. Remitters now get about Tk 120 per dollar; with the banks' incentive it would have been Tk 123. The government incentive stays. Monthly remittance figures for January to April 2024 are given.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank announced the 'crawling peg' method for setting the dollar exchange rate on 8 May 2024, fixing the mid-rate at Tk 117 per US dollar; the official rate before was Tk 110.

Banks had been paying an extra 2.5 percent of their own on remittances in addition to the government's 2.5 percent incentive; after the new exchange-rate method they stopped their own incentive. Remittances now fetch Tk 120 per dollar; had banks continued, it would be Tk 123.
Foreign exchange houses have set the price of remittance dollars between Tk 117 and Tk 117.50; adding the government's 2.5 percent gives about Tk 120.

In October 2023 a joint meeting of the Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers, Bangladesh (ABB) decided banks would give a 2.5 percent incentive of their own on remittances alongside the government's; state banks and some private banks then began paying it, but remittances did not improve much.

BAFEDA chairman and Sonali Bank managing director Afzal Karim said: after the new method we stopped giving the incentive, because with the government incentive alone the dollar price is close to Tk 120; other banks will decide for themselves.
facts.source_in_article: Afzal Karim, BAFEDA chairman and Sonali Bank MD

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Mezbaul Haque said banks have been advised to stop their own incentive because of the new dollar-pricing method; the government incentive will remain, and the government will decide on it.
Remittances received by Bangladesh: January 2024 USD 210 crore; February 2024 USD 216 crore 60 lakh; March 2024 USD 199 crore 68 lakh; April 2024 USD 204 crore 30 lakh.

headline_en: 'They have killed my boy'
summary_en: The bodies of eight Bangladeshis who died on a boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia while being taken from Libya to Italy reached Dhaka on Thursday 2 May 2024 on a Saudia flight; five were from Rajoir, Madaripur and three from Muksudpur, Gopalganj. Relatives say brokers packed 52 people into a boat for 30, forced the eight below deck and beat them back when they tried to come up for air. The family of Rasel Sheikh (23) says a local man named Sumon had promised to get him to Italy for 13 lakh taka. Police say no family has yet complained at Muksudpur police station.

facts.date: boat left Libya 14 February 2024; bodies arrived 2 May 2024
facts.statement: Eight Bangladeshis died on an engine boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia on the way from Libya to Italy; their bodies arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at midday on Thursday 2 May 2024 on a Saudia Airlines flight. Five were residents of Rajoir, Madaripur and three of Muksudpur, Gopalganj. One Pakistani national also died, and the local coast guard rescued several people alive.

The eight dead are: Rifat Sheikh (23), son of Dadon Sheikh, Bardia village, Muksudpur, Gopalganj; Md. Rasel (Rasel Sheikh, 23), Fatepatti village, Dignagar union, Muksudpur; Imrul Kayes Apon (22), son of Pannu Sheikh, Goylakandi village, Muksudpur; Sajib Kazi (19), son of Mizanur Rahman Kazi, Kodalia village, Rajoir, Madaripur; Mamun Sheikh (22), son of Yusuf Ali Sheikh, Paschim Swarmangal village; Sajal Bairagi (22), son of Sunil Bairagi, Sendiar village; Nayan Biswas (24), son of Paritosh Biswas (village given as Uttar Para in one place and Kadambari in another); and Kawsar (22), Keshardia village.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, from relatives, police and local sources

facts.statement: Several young men from Rajoir (Madaripur) and Muksudpur (Gopalganj) left home for Italy on 14 January 2024, flew via Dubai to Libya, and on 14 February 2024 set off from Libya for Italy through brokers on an engine boat.

Relatives said the brokers put 52 people in a small boat that could carry 30. The eight who died were forced below the deck planks; when they tried to come out because of lack of oxygen the brokers beat them and sent them back, and they died of torture and lack of oxygen.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives of the dead, speaking at Dhaka airport on 2 May 2024

facts.statement: Rasel Sheikh's mother Shilpi Begum said the brokers had agreed to take the migrants across the sea in a big fishing trawler, but instead pushed 52 people into the hold of a 30-capacity boat.
facts.source_in_article: Shilpi Begum, mother of victim Rasel Sheikh

facts.statement: Rasel Sheikh's uncle Md. Kabir Sheikh said Sumon of Kanuria village, Dignagar union (Muksudpur, Gopalganj) had said 'give 13 lakh taka and we will get Rasel to Italy'; a few days after they took him he was physically tortured and not given food for three days.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kabir Sheikh, uncle of victim Rasel Sheikh

facts.statement: Muksudpur police station OC Mohammad Ashraful Alam said the bodies had come home through the government, that no family had yet filed a complaint at the station, and that legal action would be taken in contact with the authorities if a complaint came.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Ashraful Alam, OC, Muksudpur police station

facts.statement: Rasel Sheikh was the only son among three children of Abul Kashem Sheikh, who runs a small tea shop in the Bhanga area of Faridpur; Rasel's grandmother died two days after he left home and the family got the news of his death on the day of her kulkhani.
facts.source_in_article: Abul Kashem Sheikh, father of victim

summary_en: The bodies of eight Bangladeshis who died in the Mediterranean on the way from Libya to Italy were flown from Tunisia to Dhaka on Thursday 2 May 2024. Relatives say brokers took 52 people in a boat for 30 and forced the eight below deck, beating them when they tried to come out. A murder case has been filed at Airport police station. One victim's brother-in-law says brokers took 8 lakh taka for the Libya-Italy leg.

facts.statement: The bodies of eight Bangladeshis who died in the Mediterranean while going from Libya to Italy were flown from Tunisia to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at midday on Thursday 2 May 2024. They are Mamun Sheikh, Sajal Bairagi, Nayan Biswas, Rifat Sheikh, Sajib Kazi, Imrul Kayes, Md. Kaisar and Rasel Sheikh; five were from Madaripur and three from Gopalganj.

Relatives waiting at the airport said brokers took 52 people in a small boat that could carry 30; the eight who died were forced below the deck, tried to come out because of lack of oxygen, and were beaten and sent back by the brokers, dying of torture and oxygen shortage.

facts.statement: A murder case has been filed at Airport police station (Dhaka) over the eight deaths, according to DMP Uttara Division Additional Deputy Commissioner Touhidul Islam, who said the bodies would be handed to families after due legal process.

facts.statement: Shaon Fakir, brother-in-law of victim Md. Kaisar, said brokers took 8 lakh taka to take Kaisar from Libya to Italy and had said they would take him in a big boat; because there were too many people, Kaisar and seven others were kept below the deck. Kaisar leaves two small daughters.

headline_en: Job opportunities for skilled workers in four European countries
summary_en: Four EU countries, Italy, Germany, Greece and Romania, have shown interest in taking skilled workers from Bangladesh in six sectors under the EU's Talent Partnership programme, and a roadmap is to be finalised by June 2024. The EU is initially giving Bangladesh EUR 30 lakh to build capacity. The article describes each country's sector demand, what the roadmap will contain, the open question of the recruitment process (Japan's SSW and Korea's EPS are cited as models) and Bangladesh's request that uncertified mega-project workers be recognised.

facts.statement: Four European Union countries, Italy, Germany, Greece and Romania, have expressed interest in taking skilled workers from Bangladesh in six sectors: shipbuilding, textiles and ready-made garments, information and communication technology, construction, tourism and agriculture.

A roadmap for sending skilled workers to the four EU countries is to be finalised by June 2024; Bangladesh and the EU have been discussing legal migration for about two years and held talks in Brussels on 4 and 5 March 2024. An inter-ministerial meeting on the roadmap, chaired by Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen, was held on Wednesday 3 April 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs officials; Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen

facts.statement: The EU is initially giving Bangladesh financial assistance of EUR 30 lakh to build its capacity to send skilled workers.

The EU started a specialised programme called Talent Partnership in 2021 to support legal migration to Europe by giving citizens of partner countries outside Europe skills and work opportunities; Bangladesh is one of seven countries under it. The Foreign Secretary called it a pilot project.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen

facts.statement: Italy wants Bangladeshi workers for the ready-made garment and shipbuilding industries.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Germany wants workers from Bangladesh for the tourism and information technology sectors.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Romania's demand from Bangladesh is for skilled construction workers.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Greece wants skilled agricultural workers from Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: The roadmap being drafted covers skills development in the six sectors according to the four countries' demand, a database of interested workers, building institutional training capacity, setting training subjects, certification after training, language and way-of-life training for those going to Italy, Greek-language training, and reintegration of workers who return from Europe.

The process by which workers will be sent to the four EU countries is still being discussed with the EU, because of past complaints of workers not being sent legally, going illegally through traffickers and being cheated. A government official said a model could build on Japan's Specified Skilled Worker (SSW) model and South Korea's Employment Permit Scheme (EPS), or the way workers were earlier sent to Hong Kong could be considered; whatever the process, control of recruitment will stay in Europe's hands.

At least 40 thousand workers have worked or are working on Bangladesh's mega projects (Padma Bridge, Rooppur nuclear power plant, metro rail and similar) and have special skills but no institutional certificate, which limits their job market; Bangladesh recently asked the EU that the lack of a certificate should not be a barrier to their getting jobs.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen said he hopes to finalise the roadmap by June and move to implementation, and that if the Talent Partnership is implemented properly many more European countries will show interest in taking workers from Bangladesh.

headline_en: One of four hostages in Libya escapes; traffickers move location with the rest
summary_en: Four young men from Raipur union, Anwara, Chattogram went to Libya legally in February 2024 through a local broker for Tk 4 lakh 10 thousand each, were told they had hospital jobs, had their passports taken, and were sold to another gang that demanded Tk 10 lakh ransom each. One, Md. Wasim (20), escaped by breaking a toilet ventilator and told local law enforcement, but the traffickers moved the other three before the raid. Families say the captives are being hung up and tortured and that the callers speak Bangla.

facts.statement: Four young men of Raipur union, Anwara upazila, Chattogram went to Libya by the legal route in February 2024: Naim Uddin on 14 February and the other three on 16 February.
The four went to Libya through a broker named Zahirul Islam of the Raipur area, paying Tk 4 lakh 10 thousand each.

After the four reached Libya, members of the trafficking gang said they had all got good jobs at a hospital and took their passports and papers; the four were then sold to another gang, which confined them and demanded Tk 10 lakh ransom each from their families.

The gang tortures the young men and sends videos of it to their families, saying they will be killed if the ransom is not paid. A brother said the captives are being hung up and tortured, that the gang's people spoke to the family in Bangla, and that they called every hour on Thursday 28 March 2024 for ransom.
facts.source_in_article: Victims' families; Salah Uddin, brother of hostage Borhan Uddin

facts.statement: Md. Wasim (20), son of Nurul Alam of Raipur union, escaped by breaking the ventilator of the toilet of the room where they were held, then told local law enforcement; they raided the house, but the traffickers had already moved the other three hostages (the move was on Wednesday 27 March 2024).
facts.source_in_article: Nasir Uddin, uncle of Wasim; Salah Uddin

facts.statement: Still held hostage are Borhan Uddin (21), son of the late Mozaher Mia; Jabedur Rahim (20), son of Abdur Rahim; and Naim Uddin (22), son of Jebal Hossain, all of Raipur union, Anwara, Chattogram. Naim's father asked for government help to rescue them.
Anwara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md. Ishtiaq Emon said he had spoken to the victims' families and informed higher authorities.

summary_en: At an event for expatriate Bangladeshis at a hotel in Jeddah on Wednesday 6 March 2024, Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud, in Saudi Arabia for an OIC meeting, urged Bangladeshis there to send remittances through legal channels and said about 30 lakh Bangladeshis live in Saudi Arabia. headline_en: USD 164 crore in remittances came in 23 days
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data published on Sunday 25 February 2024 show expatriates sent USD 164.61 crore in the first 23 days of February 2024. The article gives the breakdown by bank type, monthly figures for November 2023 to January 2024, and annual totals for 2019 to 2023. The official dollar rate for buying remittances is Tk 110, but banks are paying more than Tk 120.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 164 crore 61 lakh through the banking channel in the first 23 days of February 2024, about Tk 18,107 crore at Tk 110 per dollar. Bangladesh Bank published the update on Sunday 25 February 2024.
Of the 1-23 February 2024 remittances, state-owned banks brought USD 17 crore 55 lakh, one specialised bank USD 6 crore 30 lakh, private banks USD 140 crore 40 lakh and foreign banks USD 35 lakh.
Remittances were USD 193 crore in November 2023, USD 198 crore 98 lakh in December 2023 and USD 210 crore in January 2024.
Annual remittances to Bangladesh: 2019 USD 1,833 crore; 2020 USD 2,173 crore; 2021 USD 2,207 crore; 2022 USD 2,130 crore; 2023 USD 2,190 crore (a rise of about 3 percent over 2022).
The official dollar price at banks for buying remittances is Tk 110, but because of the dollar shortage banks are buying remittances at more than Tk 120.

headline_en: Conflicts of interest may arise (in parliamentary standing committees)
summary_en: A February 2024 report on the newly formed parliamentary standing committees of the 12th parliament finds that at least six committees, including the one on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, may face conflicts of interest because members have related businesses. For migration, it notes that committee member Nizam Uddin Hazari is linked to the manpower export business and is listed on BAIRA's website as chairman of 'Snigdha Overseas', and that former minister Imran Ahmad now chairs the committee. The rest concerns other committees and expert comment.

facts.statement: Nizam Uddin Hazari became a member of the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in the 12th parliament; he is reported to be involved in the manpower export business, and the website of the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (BAIRA) lists him as chairman of 'Snigdha Overseas' (স্নিগ্ধা ওভারসিস).
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's review of committee lists and the BAIRA website

facts.statement: Imran Ahmad, who was in charge of the expatriates' welfare ministry in the Awami League government's previous term, was made chair of the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment; he is one of 12 just-former ministers and state ministers made chairs of the committees for their old ministries.

Under the Rules of Procedure of the Jatiya Sangsad, no member may be appointed to a parliamentary committee if they have a personal, financial and direct interest in a matter the committee may consider. A standing committee's job is to review its ministry's work, investigate irregularities and serious allegations, and examine bills.
facts.source_in_article: Rules of Procedure of parliament, as cited by the reporter

facts.statement: Chief Whip Nur-E-Alam Chowdhury said many people have businesses and anyone may do business; what must be seen is whether they do business with the government. On ex-ministers chairing committees he said other members can investigate if allegations arise.

Parliament researcher and former Chittagong University professor Nizam Uddin Ahmed said it would have been better not to put people with personal interests on the related committee, and that with former ministers as chairs irregularities from the previous term may not be investigated.

headline_en: Government scholarship for children of expatriate workers: see how to apply
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board is giving education scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers who passed SSC in 2023 or HSC in 2022 and are in the first year of the next level. The article gives the eligibility conditions, how long the scholarship lasts, and the online application rule with a 31 January deadline.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives education scholarships to meritorious children of workers living abroad. Eligible to apply online: those who passed SSC or equivalent in 2023 and are studying in class 11 or equivalent or a diploma (1st semester/year) in Bangladesh, and those who passed HSC or equivalent in 2022 and are studying at a university or medical college (1st semester/year) in Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board notice, as reported

facts.statement: Conditions for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: the applicant must be (1) a child of an expatriate worker who took emigration clearance through the BMET database or took Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, or (2) a child of a deceased expatriate worker whose family has received or will receive a financial grant from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board notice, as reported

facts.statement: Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: SSC-category students get it for two years through classes 11 and 12, or four years if in a diploma course; HSC-category students get it for 4 years at university and 5 years for medical studies. The student's session is not taken into account.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board notice, as reported

facts.statement: All students must apply online for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, and the application must state the student's mobile number and the mobile number of the mother, father or guardian. The deadline for this round was 31 January (2024). The article links to the online application details without printing the address.

headline_en: 'Father, I am being tortured': body of the girl who sent this message from Dubai has come home
summary_en: A girl from Gazaria, Munshiganj, who her family says was 17 but shown as 21 on paper, was sent to Dubai on a visit visa on 16 August 2023 after a neighbour took Tk 3 lakh promising a hospital cleaner's job. She phoned her father to say she had been sold and was being tortured; she died on 8 September 2023, the papers with the body giving the cause as a fall from height. Her father filed a trafficking and murder case in Dhaka's Human Trafficking Tribunal in late December 2023 naming two women, Farzana and Sohagi; CID has been ordered to investigate but no investigating officer has yet been appointed.

facts.statement: According to the family, a girl from Gazaria, Munshiganj, actually 17 years old, was shown by the broker as 21 on paper and sent to Dubai on 16 August 2023 with the promise of a cleaner's job at a hospital in Dubai; she was not given that job but was sold in Dubai by human traffickers, sexually abused and killed.
The girl's father, a CNG auto-rickshaw driver, said neighbour Sohagi told the family her elder sister Farzana lives in Dubai and could take the girl there for Tk 3 lakh; the family paid this money.

According to the case statement, accused Sohagi used a broker to get the girl's passport made at a Narayanganj address (the family home is in Gazaria, Munshiganj) and then sent her to Dubai on a visit (travel) visa on 16 August 2023.

A few days after reaching Dubai the girl phoned her father and said she had been sold and was seriously ill from torture ('Father, I am being tortured'); he could not contact her again. According to the information that came with the body she died in Dubai on 8 September 2023, with the cause of death written as falling from above.
facts.source_in_article: Victim's father; Jatrabari police inspector Md. Azharul Islam

facts.date: 26 November 2023; body returned first week of December 2023
facts.statement: The family learned of the girl's death only on 26 November 2023, when the father went to Sohagi after failing to reach his daughter; he was not told why or how she died. The body arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, from Dubai in the first week of December 2023.

In late December 2023 the girl's father filed a complaint case in the Human Trafficking Offences Prevention Tribunal in Dhaka alleging human trafficking and murder and naming two women, Farzana and Sohagi, as accused. The tribunal ordered the Jatrabari police station OC to record it as an FIR and ordered CID to investigate.

Jatrabari police station inspector Md. Azharul Islam said a post-mortem was done in Bangladesh but the report has not come; forensic samples were sent to CID to find out whether the girl was raped before death; and although the court ordered CID to investigate, no investigating officer has yet been appointed. The father says police are not arresting the accused.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Azharul Islam, inspector, Jatrabari police station; victim's father

facts.statement: Accused Farzana, who recently returned to Bangladesh, told Prothom Alo by phone that she had told the girl that her employer (malik) in Dubai behaves well but makes foreign workers do 'bad work', that she had told the girl not to come, and that the girl came to Dubai without telling her; she said her employer later told her the girl had reportedly been killed and she passed the news home.

headline_en: Bangladeshi young man dies after falling from a building in the United Arab Emirates
summary_en: Sourav Majhi (23) of Naria, Shariatpur died after falling while trying to jump to a neighbouring building to escape a police raid on a building in 'Rolla city' in the UAE on a Sunday (about 14 January 2024). He had gone to the UAE in 2021 and worked as a painter in Sharjah before recently leaving that job. His family, who say his visa was valid, ask the government to bring the body home quickly; the UNO says they will contact the mission.

A doctor at a local hospital declared him dead. The family got the news on Tuesday 16 January 2024.

Sourav Majhi went to the UAE in 2021 and worked as a painter in Sharjah; a short time before his death he left that job and moved from Sharjah to Rolla. His cousin Jamil Ahsan said his visa was still valid and the family does not understand why he ran away from Sharjah to another town.

facts.statement: The family asked the government to bring Sourav Majhi's body home quickly. summary_en: Reporting Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's question hour in parliament on Wednesday 18 November 2026, the article covers traffic, reserves, loan recovery and other domestic topics. headline_en: Malaysia-bound workers must pay Tk 8,000 for the health test
summary_en: In a press release on Saturday 31 October 2026 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment fixed the health test fee for general workers going to Malaysia at Tk 8,000 per person, with nothing extra allowed. Medical centres will not work under any particular recruiting agency, selected workers may use any approved centre, the MiGRAMS slip is free, and a worker who switches agency must have the test report passed on. Overcharging or harassment is to be reported to secretary@probashi.gov.bd.

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has fixed the health test (medical) fee for general workers wishing to go to Malaysia for employment at Tk 8,000 per person; no money beyond this fee may be taken.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 31 October 2026

facts.statement: No medical centre will work under any particular recruiting agency for the Malaysia health test; workers selected to go to Malaysia can have the health test done at any approved medical centre.
The ministry warned Malaysia-bound workers not to contact any broker or middleman for the health test.

If a worker decides to go to Malaysia through a different agency after one recruiting agency has had the medical slip made, the earlier agency must quickly send on the worker's health test report; no objection from the agency that issued the slip will be accepted.
The ministry says no fee has to be paid for the MiGRAMS slip (মাইগ্রামস স্লিপ).
If a medical centre demands more than the fixed Tk 8,000 or causes harassment, delay or other trouble, workers are told to inform the ministry immediately by email at secretary@probashi.gov.bd.
The ministry said medical centres' activities will be regularly monitored and checked and strict legal action will be taken against any centre where irregularities or discrepancies are found.
Medical tests for workers wishing to go to Malaysia start from 31 October (2026), according to a linked headline in the article.

headline_en: Bodies of five Naogaon men identified by DNA test arriving Saturday
summary_en: The bodies of seven Bangladeshis (five from Naogaon, two from Natore) killed in a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh on 9 August 2026 are due in Dhaka on Saturday 31 October 2026 after being identified by DNA testing, nearly three months after the fire. Sixteen Bangladeshi workers died in the fire; nine bodies were sent home on 27 August. Because all flights from Riyadh have been suspended since 10 October, the bodies were taken by road to Jeddah to be flown on Biman.

facts.statement: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers were killed in a fire at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 9 August 2026.

Of the 16 Bangladeshis killed in the Riyadh sofa factory fire, nine bodies were sent home on 27 August 2026; the other seven were identified through DNA testing and their bodies are due home on Saturday 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after the deaths.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; Naogaon Deputy Commissioner citing a ministry letter

facts.statement: The seven DNA-identified dead are: Shahin of Par Naogaon village, Naogaon Sadar; Hasibul Hasan of Dubai village, Minhaj Pramanik of Madhya Boalia village, Masidul Sardar of Madhabpur village and Sagar Ali of Sahanagar village, all in Atrai upazila, Naogaon; and Mohammad Shamim of Dighirpara village and Sharif Hossain of Khajura village, Lalpur upazila, Natore.

A letter from the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment dated Thursday 29 October 2026 said the seven bodies were due at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 8:05 am on Saturday 31 October 2026 on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight; copies went to the deputy commissioners, upazila nirbahi officers and expatriate-welfare offices concerned, and the families were informed.
facts.source_in_article: Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam; Atrai UNO Md. Munizzaman

facts.statement: A letter signed by Counsellor (Labour) Muhammad Rezaye Rabbi said that because all flights from Riyadh have been suspended since 10 October (2026), the bodies were taken by road to King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah, from where a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight would carry them to Dhaka.
facts.source_in_article: Letter signed by Counsellor (Labour) Muhammad Rezaye Rabbi, as reported

facts.statement: According to a linked headline in the article, the Prime Minister expressed grief over the death of the 16 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia and ordered that the bodies be brought home quickly.

headline_en: Lure of residence in Canada: 2 Bangladeshis jailed for physical and sexual abuse
summary_en: On Thursday 22 October 2026 the Saskatoon provincial court in Saskatchewan, Canada sentenced two Canadians of Bangladeshi origin, Mohammad (MD) Masum (45) and Sohel Haider (56), for trafficking a Bangladeshi woman lured with a restaurant job and permanent residence through the temporary foreign worker process. Masum got 14 years for human trafficking and three sexual assaults; Haider got 4 years for human trafficking; both must pay restitution for unpaid wages. The woman was made to work six days a week without a valid work permit, underpaid, had her passport taken and was raped, between 1 August 2022 and 31 March 2023.

facts.statement: On Thursday 22 October 2026 Judge Miguel Martinez of the Saskatoon provincial court, Saskatchewan, Canada, sentenced main accused Mohammad (MD) Masum (45) to 14 years' rigorous imprisonment for human trafficking and three separate sexual assaults (rape), and Sohel Haider (56) to 4 years, the minimum under Canadian law, for human trafficking. Both are Canada residents of Bangladeshi origin.
The court ordered Sohel Haider to pay CAD 5,885.16 and Mohammad Masum to pay CAD 12,268 as the victim's unpaid wages and restitution.

A Bangladeshi woman who had worked about 18 years in a government job in Bangladesh was promised a restaurant job in Canada and permanent residence through the temporary foreign worker (TFW) process. After arriving she was forced to work first at a restaurant run by Sohel Haider in the Gull Lake (গিল লেক) area of Saskatchewan and then at Mohammad Masum's restaurant in the Tisdale area.

The accused did not hold a valid work permit for the woman; telling her the permit papers were being processed, they made her work long hours six days a week and did not pay her properly. Mohammad Masum took her Bangladeshi passport and sexually assaulted her several times by physical force, which the judge explicitly called rape.

Later a different work permit was issued in the name of a restaurant in the town of Elrose; after she arrived there, local Canadian citizens who saw her condition helped her, and with their help she escaped the exploitation and sought legal protection.
The victim's name and identity were not published because of a publication ban ordered by the Canadian court to protect legal confidentiality.

In her victim impact statement the woman said the two men destroyed her life, honour, future, family and career, and that rumours about her at home had damaged her family's standing; she now lives with severe trauma and insecurity.

Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning argued that both accused took extreme advantage of the woman's situation as a newcomer and controlled almost every aspect of her life. (The article's bracketed names here read 'Sohel and Mahfuz', which does not match the convicted Masum; the article is inconsistent.) Judge Martinez said exploitation of newcomers and temporary foreign workers' vulnerability must be firmly suppressed.
facts.source_in_article: Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning; Judge Miguel Martinez

facts.statement: Members of the Bangladeshi community in Canada welcomed the verdict and said everyone should be more careful about coming to Canada on fake visas or by irregular means out of ambition and temptation.
A linked headline in the article refers to a case against 5 people over visa fraud involving 209 Bangladeshis in Canada (no details in this article).

headline_en: Embassy tells Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to stay alert
summary_en: In an urgent notice on Monday 12 October 2026 the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh told Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to stay alert, obey local law and Saudi instructions, and avoid risky and crowded places amid the Middle East situation. It warned that recording, sharing or posting information, photos or videos about the situation is a punishable offence under Saudi law, and gave hotline numbers. After Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, flights were halted at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and one other airport, and several countries issued travel advisories.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, in an urgent notice on Monday 12 October 2026, asked Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia to stay alert, obey local laws and regulations, follow the instructions issued by Saudi authorities, avoid risky and crowded places and take their own safety seriously in the current Middle East situation.

The embassy said that recording, exchanging or publishing on social media any information, photo or video related to the ongoing Middle East situation is a punishable offence under Saudi law; it asked Bangladeshis not to post such photos, videos or sensitive information on Facebook, YouTube, X or any social media, and also not to store them on mobile phones or share them with others.
Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh hotlines given in the notice: labour matters toll-free 8001000125; passport matters toll-free 8001000126; diplomatic wing 8001000124; death-related hotline +966570212180.
After repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, flights were suspended on Monday 12 October 2026 at two Saudi airports including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Japan, Australia and New Zealand issued travel advisories for their citizens about travel to Saudi Arabia after the Houthi attacks on airports.

headline_en: China, India and the United States: Bangladesh's risks in geopolitics
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, a professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam, argues that Bangladesh should build need-based partnerships with India, Japan, South Korea, the EU, the Gulf states, ASEAN, China and the United States rather than choose one camp. Its migration-related content is commentary: Japan's labour shortage is an opportunity only for skilled, language-trained workers; Gulf relations should move to skills partnerships and state bargaining over wages, recruitment cost and job-change rights; and Italy and Malaysia are named as labour-mobility partners. It reports no events.

headline_en: Migration abroad reduces the risk of poverty
summary_en: Research presented at SANEM's annual economists' conference in Dhaka found that Bangladeshi households with a member working abroad face a lower risk of poverty and coped better with Covid-19 and post-Ukraine-war inflation than internal-migrant households. Other papers covered climate-driven internal migration in coastal areas and a Bangladesh Bank study finding no 'Dutch disease' from remittances so far.

facts.statement: A study by Mahtab Uddin, assistant professor of economics at Dhaka University, on the impact of Covid-19 and post Russia-Ukraine war inflation on migrant households found that households with members working abroad are at comparatively lower risk of poverty and withstood the Covid shock well, while internal migrants struggle with economic shocks.
facts.source_in_article: Mahtab Uddin, Dhaka University, at the SANEM annual economists' conference

facts.statement: The study found international migrant households are much less likely than internal migrant households to fall below the poverty line because their income is higher; Mahtab Uddin said remittance works like a shield, so the households can absorb price rises and have better food quality and nutrition security than others.

A Bangladesh Bank study presented by additional director Ripon Roy found that although theory predicts 'Dutch disease' when remittance rises, this tendency has not been seen in Bangladesh so far and rising remittance is not reducing export competitiveness; he said remittance money is not spent only on consumption but accumulates as capital and is invested in education and health, and advised examining how to use it more in productive sectors.
facts.source_in_article: Ripon Roy, additional director, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: A World Bank and BIDS jointly funded survey of 403 coastal households, presented by BIDS senior research fellow Azreen Karim, found (preliminary results) that sudden disasters such as floods or cyclones lead to partial migration (about 40 percent), with able members leaving for work while others stay, whereas slow disasters like river erosion push whole families to migrate; this is internal migration within Bangladesh.

The findings were presented on Sunday 19 April 2026 at BRAC Centre Inn, Mohakhali, Dhaka, on the closing day of the three-day annual economists' conference of the South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM); the session was chaired by Rahnuma Salam Khan, national programme manager of ILO Bangladesh.
