headline_en: Highest remittance in four years came in May
summary_en: Remittances through banking channels reached USD 225 crore (2.25 billion) in May 2024, the highest in about 46 months and the second highest ever, after the central bank raised the official dollar rate by 7 taka to 117 taka. The article gives fiscal-year totals, the rate banks pay exchange houses, and reserve figures, and quotes bankers that hundi and money laundering must be curbed.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 225 crore in remittances through banking channels in May 2024, the highest in about four years (46 months) and the second highest ever; the highest single month was USD 260 crore in July 2020.
In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the official price of the US dollar in one jump by 7 taka, fixing it at 117 taka; the article says the rise in the dollar's price increased remittance inflow.
Banks were buying remittances from foreign exchange houses at rates of up to 118 taka 30 paisa per US dollar.

According to Bangladesh Bank, remittances in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 were USD 2,137 crore, USD 196 crore or 10 percent more than the USD 1,941 crore of the same period a year earlier; the whole previous fiscal year brought USD 2,161 crore.
Expatriates sent USD 204 crore through banking channels in April 2024, against USD 169 crore in the same month a year earlier; remittances usually rise before Eid every year.

Bangladesh Bank's foreign exchange reserves fell to USD 18.72 billion on 29 May 2024, from USD 19.96 billion in April 2024 and USD 21.87 billion at the end of December 2023; the record was USD 48 billion in August 2021.
Bankers said that to raise remittances through banking channels strict action against money laundering and hundi is needed, and that merely raising the dollar price pushes up import costs.

key_quote_bn: সদ্য সমাপ্ত মে মাসে ব্যাংকিং চ্যানেলে মোট ২২৫ কোটি ডলারের প্রবাসী আয় এসেছে, যা প্রায় চার বছরের (৪৬ মাস) মধ্যে সর্বোচ্চ, আর এযাবৎকালে দ্বিতীয় সর্বোচ্চ।

headline_en: Thousands crowd Dhaka airport without air tickets to go to Malaysia
summary_en: On 31 May 2024, the last day Malaysia would admit approved Bangladeshi workers, thousands waited at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport without air tickets after paying recruiting firms five to seven lakh taka each. Named workers had waited two to three days while their agencies stopped answering calls; the airport said extra flights were being arranged.

facts.statement: In March 2024 Malaysia said it would not take workers for the time being, and that those who had already received approval and visas must enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024 (a Friday).
Malaysia's labour market reopened to Bangladeshis in 2022 after being closed for four years over irregularities in sending workers through a ring (syndicate); a ring was then formed again.

Thousands of people crowded Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on 31 May 2024 hoping to fly to Malaysia, many without air tickets, because they had paid recruiting agencies and believed that after that day Malaysia would take no more workers from Bangladesh.

At least 10 more passengers waiting at the airport told Prothom Alo they had paid the firms five to seven lakh taka each to go to Malaysia; some doubted whether the companies would refund the money if they could not go, and they demanded the government act to extend the deadline.

Habibur Rahman of Natore deposited six and a half lakh taka with a firm (not named) to go to Malaysia, raised by mortgaging land and taking a bank loan; company people brought him to the airport three days earlier, he had no ticket as of 5 pm on 31 May 2024, and they stopped answering his calls; someone he sent to the company's office was told to wait.

Rubel Mia of Narsingdi paid six lakh taka to a firm named Ahad Enterprise to go to Malaysia as a construction worker; he had waited two days at Dhaka airport with a brother without getting a ticket, and when he called the company people said they would arrange it.

The executive director of the airport, Kamrul Islam, said there had been heavy pressure of Malaysia-bound passengers for two days and that extra flights were being arranged in addition to regular flights to handle it.
facts.source_in_article: Kamrul Islam, Executive Director, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport

headline_en: Oman is partially reopening visas for Bangladeshis
summary_en: The chairman of Bangladesh Social Club Oman said the Omani government will reopen visas for Bangladeshis in 12 categories, including family, GCC-resident visit, professional, investor and official visas. Oman suspended all visas for Bangladeshis by a Royal Oman Police circular on 31 October 2023, after which travel there fell by more than half.

facts.statement: The Omani government will open visas for Bangladeshis in 12 categories, according to Sirajul Haque, chairman of Bangladesh Social Club Oman; the categories listed include family visa, visit visa for Bangladeshis residing in GCC countries, doctor, engineer, nurse, teacher, accountant and investor visas and all types of official visa (the article lists these nine while saying 12).
facts.source_in_article: Sirajul Haque, Chairman, Bangladesh Social Club Oman

facts.statement: Oman suspended the issue of all types of visa for Bangladeshis on 31 October 2023, announced in a circular issued that day by the Royal Oman Police (ROP); a linked headline in the article attributes the decision to misuse of visas.
facts.source_in_article: Royal Oman Police circular, as reported

facts.statement: After the ban the Bangladesh Embassy in Muscat said in a statement that the ban was for a temporary period.

Since the 31 October 2023 suspension, the number of Bangladeshis going to Oman has fallen by more than 50 percent; the article says the number of Bangladeshi nationals going there 'last September' was 28,201.

headline_en: Proposal to start online classes for Bangladeshi students in Kyrgyzstan
summary_en: After recent incidents in Bishkek (a linked headline refers to attacks on foreigners), Bangladesh's ambassador to Kyrgyzstan, resident in Tashkent, met the Kyrgyz deputy education minister on 22 May 2024 and asked that Bangladeshi students be allowed online classes for the next few months. The deputy minister said government and universities are working on foreign students' safety and that he would consider the request positively.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's ambassador to the Kyrgyz Republic, Mohammad Monirul Islam (resident in Tashkent, Uzbekistan), met Kyrgyz deputy education minister Rasul Avazbek uulu in Bishkek on Wednesday 22 May 2024 and, citing recent incidents in Bishkek, asked him to ensure a safe environment for Bangladeshi students studying at universities in Kyrgyzstan.

The ambassador requested that Bangladeshi students be given the option, according to their needs, of attending classes online for the next few months; the deputy minister assured him he would consider online classes positively.
facts.source_in_article: Ambassador Mohammad Monirul Islam; Deputy Education Minister Rasul Avazbek uulu

facts.statement: The Kyrgyz deputy education minister said that not only government authorities but also university administrations are working sincerely to ensure the safety of foreign students including Bangladeshis; he also expressed interest in concluding a memorandum of understanding on education cooperation with Bangladesh's relevant ministry.
facts.source_in_article: Rasul Avazbek uulu, Deputy Education Minister, Kyrgyzstan

facts.statement: The ambassador discussed academic activities, security, accommodation, transport and food with rectors, vice rectors and deans of universities where Bangladeshi students study, and was told the universities are active in ensuring the students' safety and welfare.
Bangladesh's embassy covering Kyrgyzstan is in Tashkent, Uzbekistan: the ambassador to the Kyrgyz Republic is resident in Tashkent.

Linked headlines inside the article say foreigners were attacked in Kyrgyzstan, Bangladeshi students were in fear, and Pakistan took 140 of its students home (headlines only; no detail in this article).

headline_en: UK will quickly send back illegal Bangladeshis
summary_en: The UK and Bangladesh agreed in London in the week of 17 May 2024, at the first joint working group on home affairs, on a fast-track arrangement to return failed asylum seekers, foreign offenders and visa overstayers to Bangladesh, removing mandatory interviews where evidence is strong. About 11,000 Bangladeshis who entered on student, visit or work visas claimed asylum last year and 95 percent were refused.

facts.statement: The United Kingdom made a new agreement with Bangladesh under which people whose asylum claims have been rejected, foreign criminals and people whose visas have expired will be returned to Bangladesh by a 'fast-track' process.
The UK-Bangladesh agreement eases returns by allowing people to be sent back without a mandatory interview in cases where there is strong evidence for removing them.

About 11,000 Bangladeshis who came to the UK on student, visit or work visas applied for asylum last year in order to stay permanently; UK immigration authorities rejected 95 percent of these applications, and the rejected applicants will now be returned under the new agreement.

The agreement was reached at the first UK-Bangladesh joint working group on home affairs, held in London; the group also committed to continuing to facilitate legal migration through existing visa routes, tackling illegal migration, stronger information sharing and understanding each other's approaches to serious organised crime.
UK minister for illegal migration Michael Tomlinson said speeding up removals is an important part of the plan to stop people coming and staying illegally, and called Bangladesh a valued partner.
facts.source_in_article: Michael Tomlinson, UK Minister for Illegal Migration

headline_en: Jordan to take women workers, with medical care and air fare provided
summary_en: BOESL published a notice to recruit 150 women machine operators for Sidney Apparels LLC, a textile company in Jordan, by walk-in interview on 15 March 2024 at the Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Mohila TTC in Mirpur. Basic pay is BDT 19,184 a month on a three-year renewable contract with free accommodation, food, primary medical care and air fare; selected workers pay only a BDT 1,000 medical fee and BDT 220 fingerprint fee.

facts.statement: Through the state company Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), 150 women workers are to be recruited as machine operators for Sidney Apparels LLC (শিডনি অ্যাপারেলস এলএলসি), a textile/garment company in Jordan, by direct interview.

Eligibility for the BOESL Jordan machine-operator recruitment: experience in the relevant work and age between 20 and 35; priority for Sudan-returned workers on the basis of qualification and skill in the work, and for certificate holders trained in the garments trade at BMET-run technical training centres. Anyone with a case against them in Bangladesh or Jordan is ineligible.
The monthly basic salary for women machine operators at Sidney Apparels LLC in Jordan via BOESL is BDT 19,184; duty is 8 hours a day, 6 days a week, with overtime available.

The Jordan job contract is for three years and renewable; the employer provides accommodation, food, primary medical care and transport costs, pays the air fare for joining, and pays the return air fare after three years of satisfactory service; other terms follow Jordan's labour law.
Selected workers for the BOESL Jordan recruitment have to pay a medical fee of BDT 1,000 and a fingerprint fee of BDT 220; the notice says there is no other cost.

Interested candidates were to attend the interview at 8 am on 15 March 2024 at the Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Mohila Technical Training Centre, Mirpur (Dhaka), bringing: four passport-size colour photographs, the original passport, one colour and four black-and-white photocopies of the passport's photo page, current office ID card or attendance card, and educational/experience certificates if any.
For information on the BOESL Jordan recruitment the notice gives telephone numbers 02-48319125 and 02-48317515.

headline_en: Bodies of five Naogaon men killed in Saudi Arabia fire return home after three months
summary_en: The bodies of seven Bangladeshi workers, five from Naogaon and two from Natore, arrived in Dhaka on 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh on 9 August 2026 killed 16 Bangladeshis; these seven had to be identified by DNA testing. Families describe loans of BDT 5.7 to 7 lakh taken to migrate, one worker went a year without an iqama, and the Atrai UNO said each family will get BDT 35,000 for burial now and a BDT 3 lakh grant after three months.

facts.statement: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers were killed in a fire at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 9 August (2026).

Of the 16 Bangladeshis killed in the Riyadh sofa factory fire, nine bodies were sent home on 27 August; the remaining seven, whose bodies were disfigured by burning, were identified by DNA testing and reached Bangladesh on 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after the fire.

The flight carrying the seven bodies, a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight, landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at about 8:30 am on Saturday 31 October 2026; after the necessary airport procedures, officials of the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry handed the bodies to relatives, who took them to Naogaon and Natore.

The seven identified by DNA were, from Naogaon: Md. Shahin of Par Naogaon, Naogaon municipality; Hasibul Hasan of Dubai village, Atrai upazila; Minhaz Pramanik of Moddhoboalia village, Atrai; Masidul Sardar of Madhabpur village; and Sagor Ali of Sadhonnagar village; and from Naldanga upazila, Natore: Mohammad Shamim of Dighirpar village and Sabbir Hossain of Khajura village.
The Atrai upazila nirbahi officer said 11 people from Atrai upazila (Naogaon) died in the Saudi fire; seven of their bodies came in the first round on 27 August and four in this round.
The Atrai UNO said each family of the dead will for now be given BDT 35,000 for burial of the body, and after three months each affected family will be given a grant of BDT 3 lakh.

Shahin (printed both as শাহিন and শাহীন) of Par Naogaon, a father of two and his mother's only child, went to Saudi Arabia in April 2026 on borrowed money; his mother Nargis Begum said he took a loan of BDT 5 lakh 70 thousand from a samity (সমিতি, a society; not further identified) to go. He found work and was killed in the factory fire three months after arriving.
facts.source_in_article: Nargis Begum, mother of Shahin; article

facts.statement: Akkas Pramanik said he sent his son Minhaz Pramanik of Moddhoboalia, Atrai, to Saudi Arabia a year ago by borrowing seven lakh taka, through a broker ring.

Minhaz Pramanik, who went to Saudi Arabia through a broker ring, did not get an iqama (residence permit) even in one year; he got work at a sofa factory in Riyadh four months before his death and had sent some money home after that. His father is now worried about how to repay the loan.

headline_en: Investing in technical education will change the economy
summary_en: An opinion piece by a Satkhira polytechnic instructor arguing that Bangladesh should invest in technical education so that migrant workers go abroad with training and recognised certificates and earn more. It cites the skill mix of Bangladeshis who went abroad in 2025 and the under-used network of technical institutions.

facts.statement: According to 2025 figures cited in a Prothom Alo opinion piece, about 43 percent of Bangladeshis going abroad were low-skilled and 34 percent semi-skilled, i.e. roughly seven in ten.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: A Prothom Alo opinion piece of 12 Oct 2026 says Bangladesh's annual remittance has crossed USD 30 billion and that Bangladesh is one of the world's largest remittance-receiving countries.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer says a worker who goes abroad without the necessary training and a recognised certificate generally stays in the low-skilled or semi-skilled category, and that sending the same people with better training, technical skills and internationally recognised certificates would raise earnings without raising the number of migrants.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: Bangladesh has about 12,932 institutions at various levels offering technical education and training; of the 3,440 vocational institutions approved by the Technical Education Board, 621 did not admit a single student in the last five years (as stated in a 12 Oct 2026 opinion piece).
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer cites the dual training systems of Germany and South Korea, where industry is a direct partner in training and students gain workplace experience (often as apprentices) alongside classroom study, as a model for Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: The writer says demand for technology-skilled workers is rising in textiles, construction, agro-processing, IT, tourism, hospitality and services, and that many countries face a shortage of skilled technical manpower, which he calls an opportunity for Bangladesh if polytechnics update curricula.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Md. Mamun Hasan, instructor at Satkhira Government Polytechnic Institute

facts.statement: Humayun Kabir said the Bangladesh-Saudi relationship earlier depended mainly on sending workers and on remittance, and is now being made more modern and multi-dimensional with cooperation in energy, technology, investment and other sectors.

facts.statement: In the context of attacks by Yemen's armed Houthi group, Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh is ready to give any help Saudi Arabia asks for to protect Makkah and Madinah; asked whether there was a plan to send Bangladeshi troops, he repeated that Bangladesh is ready to give any necessary help if asked. headline_en: Haal Fashion lifestyle guideline: what an immigration officer can and cannot ask you, and what to do if harassed
summary_en: A legal explainer, prompted by three unmarried women being stopped at Dhaka airport on 8 August while travelling to Nepal, on what Bangladeshi immigration officers may check and ask at departure and what they may not. It lists the documents a departing traveller needs (including BMET clearance for those going for work), cites constitutional rights to leave and return, and sets out how and where to complain about harassment, including a 24-hour airport immigration hotline.

facts.statement: Three unmarried Bangladeshi women with valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets for Nepal were stopped from travelling at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 8 August; they alleged that immigration police phoned their guardians to ask about their travel and profession and made 'indecent' remarks about their clothes, financial means and personal matters. One said an immigration police member told her unmarried girls cannot go abroad alone.
facts.source_in_article: the three women, in statements to police

facts.statement: Immigration in Bangladesh is not governed by a single law but by a combination including the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013 (and its 2023 amendment), the Foreigners Act 1946, the Citizenship Act 1951, the Bangladesh Passport Order 1973 and travel rules. The Ministry of Home Affairs has overall responsibility; the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) issues passports, processes visas and runs immigration services.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi immigration officer may examine passport, visa, ticket and other required papers of departing and arriving passengers; ask about the purpose of travel, length of stay and other information and verify it; and detect, detain and take legal action against users of forged papers. Officers may also verify risks of human trafficking, forged documents, a criminal leaving or a legal ban, and question a passenger on reasonable suspicion based on facts, law and professional standards.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: According to the writer, whether a traveller is unmarried, why she is travelling alone, where her husband is, who her guardian is or whether the guardian knows are not relevant questions for an immigration officer; security checks are not the same as intrusion into private life or moral policing.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: To travel abroad legally from Bangladesh a passport and visa are needed; the passport must have at least 6 months' validity and the destination visa must be correct and valid. The traveller needs the airline boarding pass from check-in and a completed departure immigration form.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Additional papers at departure from Bangladesh: an employee needs an official ID card and an NOC (no-objection certificate); a businessperson a trade licence; a student a student ID or a leave/permission letter from the college or university; a person going for work needs BMET clearance (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training); other specific travel categories need their relevant papers.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: An immigration officer in Bangladesh may ask why a citizen is going abroad, the destination, where and with whom they will stay or whether there is a hotel booking, and the travel plan; and may ask to see a return flight ticket and proof of enough foreign currency, cash, an international credit or debit card, or a bank solvency certificate/statement.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: The writer states that if a citizen has a valid passport, valid visa, correct air ticket, hotel reservation, a lawful purpose and other travel papers in order, stopping their travel abroad is illegal. The Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court has held that no citizen's lawful foreign travel can be blocked without a court ban on travel; a criminal case alone is not enough, and even a convicted person on bail pending appeal may travel if there is no court ban. The same rule applies regardless of marital status, religion, caste or sex.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Constitutional provisions cited: Article 27 (equality before law), Article 28 (no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equal rights of women and men in state and public life), Articles 31 and 32 (protection of law; life and personal liberty), and Article 36 (right to move freely, to leave Bangladesh and to re-enter, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest). Restricting a person's freedom by executive order alone without legal backing would be unconstitutional.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: If harassed at immigration or an airport in Bangladesh: complain immediately, in writing and orally, to the senior authority or the Superintendent of Police; stay calm without arguing and note the officer's name, rank or badge number, the time and the counter number; keep specific proof or documents if possible. The matter can be reported at once to the airport's complaint-settlement officer, the shift in-charge, the duty officer or the officer-in-charge (OC) of that immigration post.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: The airport immigration 24-hour hotline number in Bangladesh, as printed, is 01320007588.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: Other complaint routes for immigration harassment in Bangladesh: Special Branch (police) Immigration, the Bangladesh Police portal or the relevant control number; a written complaint with specific details to the airport or Special Branch Immigration; the police immigration online complaint page; an application to the office of the executive magistrate present at the airport; and the national Grievance Redress System (GRS) online platform for dissatisfaction with a government service.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

facts.statement: If none of the complaint routes gives a remedy, a writ can be filed in the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court; a complaint must first have been lodged with the proper authority before filing the writ.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, an advocate of the Bangladesh Supreme Court (name not printed)

headline_en: Higher study in New Zealand: 24 qualifications make you eligible for the post-study work visa
summary_en: New Zealand is widening eligibility for its post-study work visa for certain graduates from 16 November 2026 and introducing a six-month Short-Term Graduate Work Visa for those who do not qualify. Immigration New Zealand has published a 2026 list of 24 approved qualifications, from Level 4 certificates to Level 7 graduate diplomas, in engineering, construction, education and agriculture, with work limited to jobs directly related to the study.

facts.statement: From 16 November 2026 New Zealand is expanding post-study work visa eligibility for specified graduates.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Alongside the expansion, New Zealand will introduce a new six-month 'Short-Term Graduate Work Visa' for those who are not eligible for the post-study work visa.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Immigration New Zealand has published a list of 24 approved educational qualifications for post-study work visa eligibility for 2026, ranging from Level 4 certificates to Level 7 graduate diplomas, covering graduates in engineering, construction, education and agriculture.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

facts.statement: Under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF), students who complete a non-degree course at Level 7 or below may only work in jobs directly related to their study; the job after qualifying must be in the relevant field.
facts.source_in_article: the article (Prothom Alo report on Immigration New Zealand's announcement)

summary_en: An opinion column on the 81st UN General Assembly session, presided over by Bangladesh's foreign minister Khalilur Rahman, arguing what Bangladesh should press for: Rohingya repatriation, a smooth LDC graduation, trade ties and migration. On migration, the writer says Bangladesh should move the discussion beyond remittance to migrants' rights, recruitment costs, wage theft, skills recognition and reintegration.

facts.statement: Writing about the 81st UN General Assembly, Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah argues Bangladesh's position in international migration talks often stops at remittance, and should move to migrants' rights, excessive recruitment costs, wage theft, recognition of skills, portability of social protection, safe migration routes and reintegration of returning migrants.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam

facts.statement: The writer says labour demand in many European and East Asian countries is changing because of artificial intelligence, automation and demographic change, and Bangladesh needs market-driven 'skills diplomacy' - partnerships on skills, not just sending people.

facts.statement: Background stated in the column: Khalilur Rahman, Bangladesh's foreign minister, was elected President of the 81st UN General Assembly on 2 June with 99 votes against 91 for Cyprus's candidate; Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office on 17 February 2026; Bangladesh is scheduled to leave the least-developed-country list on 24 November 2026 but has asked for a longer preparation period.

headline_en: Killed in Saudi Arabia fire: joint funeral for seven in Atrai
summary_en: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers died in a fire at a sofa factory in Manfuha, Riyadh on 9 August 2026. Saudi authorities identified nine by fingerprint; their bodies reached Dhaka on 27 August and were buried on 28 August in Naogaon (seven from Atrai), Rajshahi and Natore, while seven remain unidentified and DNA testing is under way. Families describe the debts taken to send the men, and one victim sent through brokers had no iqama for his first three years.

facts.statement: On 9 August (2026) a fire at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia killed 16 Bangladeshi workers.

After the Riyadh sofa factory fire, Saudi authorities identified nine of the 16 Bangladeshi dead by fingerprint testing; seven were still unidentified as of 28 August 2026, and DNA testing was being used to try to identify them.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report; Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam

facts.statement: The bodies of the nine identified victims of the Riyadh fire arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at about 4:30 pm on Thursday 27 August 2026. (The article's opening sentence says eight identified bodies were buried, but it lists nine: seven from Atrai, one from Bagmara and one from Naldanga.)

Seven victims from Atrai upazila, Naogaon had a joint funeral at 10 am on Friday 28 August 2026 at Molla Azad Memorial Government College ground: Md. Farid (Udonpoi village), Rubel Pramanik, Kalimuddin Islam, Mohon Ali and his younger brother Sumon Ali (Gandagohali village), Sohel Rana (Dubai village) and Abdul Jalil Sarkar (Parkasunda village).

Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam said the process of identifying the remaining six Naogaon residents killed in the Riyadh fire and bringing their bodies home was under way, with identification being attempted by DNA test. Among the unidentified is Minhaj of Madhyaboali village, Atrai, whose mother Parul Bibi appealed to the government to bring his body quickly.
facts.source_in_article: Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam; Parul Bibi

facts.statement: Naldanga (Natore) acting UNO Shamim Hossain said that, besides Rabiul Islam, two others from Khajura union died in the same Riyadh fire - Shamim Hossain (35), son of Zakir Ali of Dighirpar village, and Sabbir Hossain, son of Golam Rabbani of Sripurpara - and their bodies had not yet been identified, so could not be brought home.

Rabiul Islam (28) of Naldanga, Natore was sent to Saudi Arabia five years before his death in August 2026 with a loan of BDT 5 lakh, according to his father Ashraful Islam; part of the loan was repaid from his remittances and the rest remains unpaid.
Rabiul Islam went to Saudi Arabia through a broker ring and did not get an iqama (residence permit) for the first three years, so he could not work regularly or earn much, his father said.

Shyamal Uddin Majhi (46) of Marugram Dangapara village, Jhikra union, Bagmara, Rajshahi, a father of three daughters, went to Saudi Arabia eight years earlier on borrowed money and died in the Riyadh fire; his coffin was opened in the presence of police at about 10:30 am on 28 August 2026 and the family is worried about repaying his debts. A related headline in the article says he had been due to return home that week after 8 years.

Former Jhikra union chairman and BNP leader Saiduzzaman thanked the government for bringing Shyamal Uddin's body home quickly and demanded government financial assistance for the family; the article does not report any assistance having been paid.

headline_en: Prime Minister's Malaysia visit: a new horizon of partnership on the East Asian model
summary_en: An opinion column on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's June 2026 visit to Malaysia arguing the two countries should move from the cheap, unskilled 'manpower export' model damaged by middlemen and syndicates to a skills- and knowledge-based partnership. It proposes post-study work rights for Bangladeshi students, sending technicians to Malaysia's semiconductor industry, and notes that the joint statement included a Bangladeshi proposal for a 'Talent Cooperation Framework'.

facts.statement: The writer says the old 'manpower export' model between Bangladesh and Malaysia - Bangladesh supplying cheap unskilled labour - has damaged both countries' image through middlemen and syndicates.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: According to the column, Bangladeshi students are the second-largest source of international-student tuition income for Malaysian universities; a large share of the top 2 percent most-cited foreign researchers in Malaysia are Bangladeshi academics; and Bangladesh ranks second in capital invested under Malaysia's MM2H scheme.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer says his own move from the UK to Malaysia was eased by the Malaysian government's 'Residence Pass-Talent' scheme, and that Bangladesh has no equivalent scheme to attract talent home.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer proposes a 'Graduate Plus' initiative giving merit-based post-study work rights to Bangladeshi students in Malaysia, and a special agreement to place Bangladeshi engineers and polytechnic graduates in Malaysia's chip-packaging and semiconductor industry: a state-funded pilot of 300 people leading to 30,000 technicians over 10 years, which he estimates could earn about USD 10 billion (the article prints 'BDT 18 thousand crore'). These are the writer's proposals, not decisions.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The column says Malaysia's technology and data-centre sector has a gap of about 60,000 skilled engineers that Bangladeshi IT and engineering graduates could help fill.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: According to the column, the joint statement after the Putrajaya meeting of the two prime ministers shows agreement on linking Malaysia's semiconductor packaging industry with Bangladesh's IT sector, and Bangladesh's Prime Minister proposed a bilateral 'Talent Cooperation Framework' to skill engineering graduates.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: The writer attended an early-June 2026 event of the Dhaka University Alumni Association Malaysia (DUAM) in Kuala Lumpur and says young Bangladeshi entrepreneurs in AI and big data serve high-level public and private clients in Malaysia, but no Bangladeshi state initiative supports them.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

facts.statement: Malaysia was the first foreign visit of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman after the February 2026 election; Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim had visited Dhaka in late 2024 and Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus later visited Malaysia, but the writer says those visits stayed at protocol and paper MoUs.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, M Niaz Asadullah, economics professor at Dhaka University and formerly at Universiti Malaya

headline_en: Bangladesh and Malaysia sign one MoU, exchange two documents
summary_en: On 22 June 2026 Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim at Perdana Putra, Putrajaya. A cultural MoU was signed and documents on counter-terrorism cooperation and investment were exchanged. The talks gave weight to reopening Malaysia's labour market to Bangladeshi workers and to regularising Bangladeshis who had become irregular and renewing work permits; the article reports discussion, not an agreed outcome, on these.

facts.statement: At the Bangladesh-Malaysia prime ministers' talks in Putrajaya on 22 June 2026, reopening the Malaysian labour market for recruitment of Bangladeshi workers was among the issues given importance; the article reports it as a topic of discussion and does not report a decision.

The 22 June 2026 Bangladesh-Malaysia talks also covered regularisation of Bangladeshi nationals who had become irregular ('illegal') for various reasons and renewal of work permits; the article does not report a decision.

After the 22 June 2026 talks, an MoU on culture was signed in the presence of both prime ministers, and the two foreign ministers exchanged a document on cooperation in counter-terrorism research and capacity building and a bilateral document on investment. No labour MoU is reported as signed.

Other topics at the talks: greater access for Bangladeshi mangoes, fruit and vegetables to the Malaysian market, Bangladesh's application to become an ASEAN Sectoral Dialogue Partner, Bangladesh's inclusion in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, the Rohingya issue, and cooperation at the UN and other multilateral forums.

The Bangladesh delegation at the talks included Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, among others. Tarique Rahman arrived in Kuala Lumpur at 8:45 pm local time on Sunday 21 June 2026; it was his first state visit since taking office on 17 February.

headline_en: Krishi Bank now top in remittance; Islami Bank drops to second place
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data for the first 13 days of June 2026 show Bangladesh Krishi Bank overtaking Islami Bank as the top remittance-receiving bank, after Bangladesh Bank dissolved Islami Bank's board and took over the bank amid customer protests and panic. Overall remittance was not affected. Islami Bank waived charges for old customers and its acting MD apologised to remittance customers, though cheque clearing and ATMs were not yet fully working.

facts.statement: In the first 13 days of June 2026, Bangladesh Krishi Bank received the most remittance of any bank, USD 23 crore 40 lakh (২৩ কোটি ৪০ লাখ ডলার), followed by Islami Bank with USD 21 crore 30 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Total remittance to Bangladesh in the first 15 days of June 2026 was USD 162 crore, against USD 148 crore in the same period the previous year; the Islami Bank crisis had not yet affected overall remittance.

facts.statement: On Sunday night (about 14 June 2026) Bangladesh Bank dissolved the board of Islami Bank and took charge of the bank, after sustained protests by a group of customers, heated debate in parliament and customer panic; many customers closed accounts and many expatriates turned away from the bank. headline_en: The risks created by the controversy over postal ballots
summary_en: An opinion column on expatriate postal voting after viral videos showed many postal ballots with Bahrain addresses being counted in one house, with similar videos from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait; the Election Commission is investigating. It explains how expatriate voting works (registration in the 'Postal Vote BD' app, ballot posted to the voter's foreign address and posted back), why shared addresses are common among migrant workers, the risk from third-party 'centres' filling in the app, and compares the Philippines, Mexico and Sri Lanka.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi expatriate voting is postal, not in-person voting at embassies: the voter registers/enrols in the Election Commission's official 'Postal Vote BD' app (which is for registration and ballot tracking), the ballot is posted to the voter's address abroad, and the voter marks it and posts it back to Bangladesh. The Commission's documents do not make the embassy a mandatory intermediary.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The Election Commission warns that the address entered in the 'Postal Vote BD' app must be the address where the voter currently lives, with road, building and block/area written clearly and an accurate postal/ZIP code.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Prothom Alo reported on 13 January 2026 that a video had spread showing many postal ballots bearing Bahrain addresses being counted in one house, with a request heard in the video not to spread it on Facebook; journalist Zulkarnain Saer then posted two more videos showing similar incidents in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, with migrant workers angry that some ballots were found with other people. Experts confirmed the videos were not fake or AI-made, and the Election Commission is investigating.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The writer notes that in labour-receiving countries, especially in the Middle East, many workers share one house, flat or camp so one address serves many people; in Malaysia many Bangladeshi workers are irregular and lack a permanent address, valid tenancy agreement or regular postal access, so a colleague's or acquaintance's address is used as a 'common address'.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Because many migrant workers have little education and struggle to write an address in English or understand postal codes, informal 'centres' or third parties in Bangladesh fill in online applications or the voting app for them; the writer warns this concentrates personal data, addresses and the whole voting process in a few hands. He does not report a proven fraud.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The writer warns that suspicion of rigging in expatriate voting could break bonds among workers abroad and increase conflict, and that employing countries might reconsider taking workers from Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: Comparisons cited: the Philippines passed its overseas absentee voting law (Republic Act 9189) in 2003, amended by Republic Act 10590 in 2013, with voting generally through embassies/consulates and low turnout; Mexico's National Electoral Institute (INE) registers voters abroad and uses postal, remote and in some cases consular voting, where postal delivery and address problems limited participation; Sri Lanka has not yet decided on expatriate voting.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

headline_en: 174 Bangladeshis arrested in Malaysia
summary_en: Malaysia's Immigration Department arrested 468 foreigners, including 174 Bangladeshis, in raids on 20 November 2025 in Cameron Highlands, Pahang. The raids covered commercial areas, construction sites and vegetable farms; those arrested are accused of holding expired passports, having no travel documents and other immigration offences, and some showed temporary work permits that appeared fake. From the start of 2025 to 18 November, 83,994 foreigners were detained across Malaysia.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Immigration Department arrested 468 foreigners, including 174 Bangladeshis, in several raids in Cameron Highlands, a tourist area in Pahang state, Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: The Cameron Highlands raids ran from 11 am to 2 pm on Thursday 20 November 2025 in four areas, covering commercial zones, building construction sites and vegetable farms; 547 Immigration Department members and officers took part and a Bernama reporter was present.
During the Cameron Highlands raids most of the foreigners were busy packaging vegetables; they did not notice the authorities' arrival and had no chance to flee.
The Cameron Highlands raids in Malaysia were planned a month in advance on the basis of various complaints from local residents.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: In the Cameron Highlands operation the details of a total of 1,886 foreigners were checked, of whom 468 were arrested.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Those arrested in Cameron Highlands, Malaysia were accused of holding expired passports, having no travel documents and other breaches of immigration law; some showed temporary work permits that appeared to be fake.

Nationalities of the 468 arrested in Cameron Highlands: 175 from Myanmar, 174 from Bangladesh, 67 from Indonesia, 20 from Nepal, 16 from Pakistan, 11 from India, and one each from the Philippines, Thailand, Sri Lanka, China and Colombia. They were 388 men, 76 women and 4 children.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Of those arrested in Cameron Highlands, people aged 20 to 54 will be sent to detention centres in Kelantan, Perak and Selangor, Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: Malaysia's immigration chief said intelligence showed Cameron Highlands has become an attractive work hub for foreigners, with arrivals rising notably in recent years, worrying local residents; foreigners like working there because it is hilly and far from cities, and local business owners often prefer to hire them.
facts.source_in_article: Zakaria Shaaban, Director General of Malaysia's Immigration Department

facts.statement: According to Malaysia's Immigration Department statistics, 83,994 foreigners were detained across Malaysia from the beginning of 2025 to 18 November 2025 as part of controlling illegal immigration.

headline_en: Remittances of USD 2.43 billion in 29 days
summary_en: Expatriate Bangladeshis sent USD 2,432 million in the first 29 days of October 2025, about 10 percent more than the same period a year earlier, Bangladesh Bank said. July to October 2025 remittances totalled USD 10,018 million, up 14.50 percent, and gross reserves again passed USD 32 billion.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshis sent USD 243 crore 20 lakh (2,432 million) in remittances in the first 29 days of October 2025; in the same period of the previous year it was USD 220 crore 80 lakh, an increase of about 10 percent.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank assistant spokesperson Mohammad Shahriar Siddiqui

facts.statement: On 29 October 2025 alone, USD 9 crore 30 lakh in remittances came to Bangladesh.
In the first four months (July to October) of fiscal year 2025-26, total remittances to Bangladesh were USD 1,001 crore 80 lakh, 14.50 percent more than the same period of the previous year.
Monthly remittances to Bangladesh in 2025: September USD 268 crore 58 lakh, August USD 242 crore 18 lakh, July USD 247 crore 80 lakh.
In fiscal year 2024-25 Bangladesh received more than USD 30 billion in remittances, about USD 6.5 billion or 27 percent more than in fiscal year 2023-24.
With good remittance inflow, Bangladesh Bank's gross foreign exchange reserves again exceeded USD 32 billion (3,200 crore dollars).

headline_en: The South Korea dream: protests in Bangladesh and Vietnam's success
summary_en: An opinion piece by a Bangladeshi EPS worker in South Korea comparing Vietnamese and Bangladeshi workers and arguing that infighting among Bangladeshi workers in Korea and protests by EPS candidates in front of BOESEL discourage Korean employers and officials. He says passing the lottery and language test does not guarantee going to Korea, that a Korean circular for Bangladesh may come in one to two months, and that about 40,000 Bangladeshi EPS workers have gone to Korea.

facts.statement: In the EPS (Employment Permit System) process for South Korea, passing the lottery and the language proficiency test does not guarantee going to Korea; neither the government nor BOESEL gives such a guarantee, and the writer calls it an uncertain and long process that depends partly on luck.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says he has seen many times with his own eyes that factionalism, quarrels and fights among Bangladeshi workers in South Korea are discouraging Korean owners from hiring Bangladeshi workers; although they know Bangladeshis as hard-working, some behaviour makes them give visas to workers from other countries.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The recent protest by EPS workers in front of BOESEL in Bangladesh is not viewed well by South Korean officials and damages Bangladesh's image; a senior Korean official is quoted as saying 'Our country needs workers without complaints, not protesters.'
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club, quoting an unnamed senior Korean official

facts.statement: The writer says a Korean circular (EPS recruitment notice) for Bangladesh is likely within the next one to two months from late August 2025, and claims that if no Korean circular comes, Bangladesh's EPS system will be shut down.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says about 40,000 Bangladeshi EPS workers have gone to South Korea, and that Bangladeshi workers are going to South Korea every month.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says Vietnamese workers accept living 7-8 to a room, do not stop work for fasting or other religious reasons, work together without division by religion or region and readily eat Korean food, which makes them more reliable to Korean employers; he says Bangladeshi workers tend to live alone or with few people, religious observance sometimes interrupts work continuity, and many are unwilling to take on anyone not from their own district or village.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

facts.statement: The writer says Korean owners generally want a calm and cooperative work environment, and advises Bangladeshi EPS candidates to focus on making themselves qualified rather than protesting, so that others' future chances of going to Korea are not blocked.
facts.source_in_article: the writer, Asim Bikash Barua, Vice Chairman of Korea-Bangla Press Club

headline_en: Bangladeshi teenage girl rescued in Hyderabad; details of India-Bangladesh human trafficking ring emerging
summary_en: Police in Hyderabad, India rescued a Bangladeshi teenage girl who had been trafficked and forced into prostitution, the fourth such rescue of a Bangladeshi woman in the city. Officials describe how agents lure poor women and girls with job and good-pay promises, bring them illegally across the border by land or water, make local identity papers and send them to various Indian cities.

facts.statement: Police in Hyderabad, India rescued a teenage girl who had been trafficked from Bangladesh and forced into prostitution; this was the fourth incident of a Bangladeshi woman being rescued in Hyderabad, with rescues made from brothels in Khairatabad, Chaderghat and Bandlaguda.

According to a law-enforcement official in India, women trafficked from Bangladesh enter India illegally by land or water with the help of agents at the border; the ringleaders in India and Bangladesh have a very strong network and arrange money for brokers and others.

Trafficked women are brought to India with the lure of a job and the promise of good pay: agents find helpless women or teenage girls in extremely poor areas of Bangladesh, persuade them to come with the promise of a better livelihood, and after arrival local identity documents are made for them and they are sent to different cities.
A police officer in India said men, women and children enter India illegally from Bangladesh because of poverty and earn a living presenting themselves as Bengali until they are caught.
A study run by India's Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) found that 2.7 percent of women who are victims of commercial sexual exploitation in India are Bangladeshi citizens.

Women trafficked from Bangladesh are sold to brokers in Indian cities including Kolkata, Delhi, Hyderabad and Mumbai; in Hyderabad the ringleaders operate actively in Attapur, Bandlaguda, Chintalmet, Himayatsagar Road and Champapet.

Police have been rescuing women trapped in mafia-controlled brothels in Hyderabad since the early 2000s; women are brought into the sex trade there not only from Bangladesh but also from Uzbekistan, Russia, Ukraine, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

headline_en: Studying in Malaysia: scholarships, part-time job opportunities, apply with 3.5 in SSC/HSC
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students on higher study in Malaysia: admission requirements, top public universities, tuition ranges, intake windows, application and student-visa documents, the EMGS online visa process (VAL in 14 working days, then e-visa in 48 hours), steps after arrival, living costs, part-time work limits, scholarships and the post-study Employment Pass.

facts.statement: Malaysia has more than 200,000 foreign students, students from more than 140 countries study there each year, and Bangladesh ranks near the top by number of foreign students.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: General admission requirements for foreign students at Malaysian universities: at least 12 years of schooling for a bachelor's; a minimum CGPA of 3.50 out of 5 in SSC/HSC/O-level/A-level for bachelor's programmes; a bachelor's degree with at least CGPA 2.5 out of 4 for a master's; IELTS 6.5 (may vary by programme and university); some programmes may also need GRE or GMAT scores.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article names Malaysia's public universities as the best for low-cost higher education, led by Universiti Malaya (UM), Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM), Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM), International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Popular subjects for higher study in Malaysia listed by the article: MBA; bachelor's and master's in computer science, data science, medicine and health care, and banking and finance.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Depending on university and programme, a 3.5 to 4 year bachelor's degree in Malaysia may cost MYR 9,600 to MYR 137,500, and a 1 to 2 year master's programme may cost MYR 7,500 to MYR 12,700 (figures as printed).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Malaysian universities usually take applications in two windows: one opens in June each year with a deadline through September, and one opens in November with a deadline through February.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Basic documents for a Malaysian university application (varies by university): completed application form, high school certificate (for bachelor's), bachelor's certificate (for master's), passport-size photo, valid passport, motivation letter, English proficiency certificate (IELTS or TOEFL), and proof of application fee payment where applicable.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Documents for a Malaysia student visa application: one passport-size photo with white background (35/45 mm); the first pages of a passport with 18 months' validity (photo and personal details) plus any visa-stamped pages; acceptance/offer letter from the Malaysian university; medical report; copies of all academic records with certificates; a personal bond of MYR 750; English proficiency certificate (IELTS/TOEFL).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: A Malaysia student visa requires a personal bond of MYR 750, which is refunded at the end of the student's studies at the institution on condition that no provision of Malaysia's immigration law was violated.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Additional documents for the Malaysia student visa: an approval letter from the Malaysian university; a cover letter issued by the university stating the student's application to study there; proof of sufficient funds for study and living costs; and a pre-VAL medical report from the student's home country.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The pre-VAL (pre Visa Approval Letter) medical screening can be done in the student's home country or, if the student prefers, at a registered clinic after arriving in Malaysia; applicants to public universities must contact their own institution for pre-VAL medical screening instructions.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Bangladeshi students must apply for a student visa before coming to Malaysia; the application can be started online through EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services), or made through a representative of the chosen university or an EMGS agent.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services) is described as part of Malaysia's Ministry of Higher Education that runs all international-student operations and works as a one-stop centre for foreign students at public and private higher education institutions.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: A visa processing fee must be paid for the Malaysia student visa; the amount varies by university and programme (no figure given).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The Visa Approval Letter (VAL) for Malaysia is issued 14 working days after the application is submitted, and students can check the application status while it is processed; Bangladeshi students then need an e-visa at the time of entry to Malaysia, which the article says can be obtained within 48 hours.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: After arriving in Malaysia a student must have a medical screening at any EMGS-registered clinic within the first seven days, arrange housing, and contact the institution and EMGS to confirm academic documents are in order.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: After arrival the student collects from the university a Student Pass (a sticker placed in the passport) and an i-Kad (printed as 'আই-ক্যাড'; the identity card for foreign students in Malaysia, which confirms the legality of their stay).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article says living in Malaysia (housing, food, transport, medical, mobile and internet, bank account) may cost about USD 170 to 180 in total; the period (e.g. per month) is not stated.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Foreign students in Malaysia are allowed part-time work of at most 20 hours, during semester breaks or weekend holidays, subject to the validity of their Student Pass; applications for part-time work must be made through the student's own institution.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: The article advises students in Malaysia to look for work on campus first: university libraries, cafes or office reception desks often offer jobs that fit alongside study.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: Support for foreign students in Malaysia includes loans, tuition fee waivers and education funds; popular scholarships named are the Malaysian Government Scholarship, Malaysia Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan, and the Malaysian International Scholarship, and many universities have their own scholarships, grants and tuition waivers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

facts.statement: To work in Malaysia after study a foreign student must first secure a job; the employer then takes full responsibility for the work permit, also known as the Employment Pass, valid for a minimum of 2 years and a maximum of 5 years; the passport should have at least 18 months' validity when applying for the work permit.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo education report (source credited: UNB)

headline_en: How to stop an artificial crisis in the dollar market
summary_en: A column on Bangladesh Bank's move to a market-based exchange rate and the role of remittance 'aggregators' (large money-transfer firms that collect remittances from small exchange houses). It says aggregators cut dollar sales after banks agreed not to pay above BDT 122.50, that they distort source-country remittance statistics, and gives remittance and exchange-rate figures.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank recently decided to leave the dollar exchange rate fully to the market to meet IMF loan conditions; at the start, bank treasury officials decided nobody would buy remittance dollars above BDT 122.50, and the central bank reportedly gave similar advice.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst, citing people concerned

facts.statement: After the exchange rate was left to the market, aggregator firms in the Middle East and Far East reduced their sales of remittance dollars and Bangladeshi banks could not buy as many dollars from them as expected; they are suspected of holding dollars to create an artificial crisis.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst, citing newspaper reports

facts.statement: Aggregators are large money-transfer companies that collect remittances or cross-border payment money from small exchange houses in different countries; over a few years they have come to control Bangladesh's remittance market, and banks are reportedly forced to buy expatriates' money at the dollar rate these firms set.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: In the first 10 months of fiscal year 2024-25 Bangladesh received USD 2,536 crore (25.36 billion) in remittances, 28 percent more than the same period of the previous fiscal year.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: Five to seven years ago Bangladesh's remittance market depended on small money exchanges with which banks had contracts; now small exchanges give dollars to aggregators, who bargain and sell to Bangladeshi banks at higher prices. Many aggregators are US-based.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: The columnist says it is alleged that the United States appears as the top source of Bangladesh's remittances largely because aggregators' money is recorded under the country that owns the aggregator; a large part of remittance shown as from the US is collected in the Middle East and elsewhere, and similarly much is shown as from the UK and the UAE, so source-country remittance statistics are unreliable.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: After the exchange rate was fully left to the market, the dollar traded at a maximum of BDT 126 in the kerb (retail) market and a maximum of BDT 123 at banks; before that the rate had been fluctuating by 30-50 paisa per dollar.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: The columnist alleges that six banks owned by S Alam acted like a cartel or aggregator in the Middle East and Far East: collecting foreign currency from expatriates, keeping it abroad for laundering or under-invoicing, giving workers advance loans before they went abroad and buying foreign currency from them at higher prices; he says this has stopped and so remittances are rising.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Mamun Rashid, banker and economic analyst

facts.statement: The columnist argues that diplomatic operations in Riyadh, Dubai, Muscat and Doha must be urgently expanded to give better services to about 8 million (80 lakh) expatriate workers, that Gulf diplomatic posts could be consolidated for effectiveness, and that app-based consular services are needed.
facts.source_in_article: the columnist Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, professor of Development Studies, Dhaka University

facts.statement: The columnist says expatriate workers' suffering begins with a corrupt migration process, harassment in the name of visas, and false job and salary promises, and that solving this should start in Dhaka.

facts.statement: The columnist states that about 12 million (1 crore 20 lakh) Bangladeshis live abroad, that Bangladesh's annual trade is about USD 120 billion, and that large numbers of migrants work in Malaysia and Singapore.

headline_en: The lure that put 20 teenagers and young men in a Myanmar jail for two years
summary_en: Twenty Bangladeshi teenagers and young men from Teknaf and Ukhiya, lured by brokers with promises of well-paid jobs in Malaysia, set off by the illegal sea route without telling their families, were detained in Myanmar in June 2023 and served 22 months in prison for illegal entry. They were brought back from Yangon on the navy ship BNS Samudra Avijan, arriving in Chattogram on 15 April 2025, and were handed to their families.

facts.statement: Brokers lured teenagers and young men, some aged 16 and some nearly 18, from the Teknaf and Ukhiya areas of Cox's Bazar district with the dream of well-paid jobs and a better life in Malaysia; they set off on the illegal, dangerous sea route without telling their families and were detained on reaching Myanmar.
The Bangladeshi teenagers and young men were detained by Myanmar law-enforcement in June 2023 on charges of illegal entry and served 22 months in prison in Myanmar.

20 Bangladeshi citizens left MITT port in Yangon, Myanmar on Sunday 13 April 2025 on the Bangladesh Navy ship BNS Samudra Avijan and reached BNS Issa Khan sea jetty in Chattogram on the morning of Tuesday 15 April 2025; in the evening they were taken by bus to Chattogram Circuit House and handed over to waiting family members at about 6:30 pm.

After the detainees' Bangladeshi citizenship was verified, the government began talks with the Myanmar authorities and the Bangladesh Embassy then arranged their repatriation; the families had submitted papers to the government a year earlier to bring them back.
None of the 20 had told their families about the journey to Malaysia; relatives learned about a month later that they had been detained.

facts.statement: Chattogram Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Md. Kamruzzaman said the youths were brought back to Bangladesh after their information was verified and were handed over to the custody of their families.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman, Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), Chattogram

facts.statement: EU Ambassador and Head of Delegation to Bangladesh Michael Miller said that if skilled workers are produced according to demand, Bangladeshis will be able to migrate to Europe for work, and that safe migration would benefit both the EU and Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Michael Miller, EU Ambassador to Bangladesh

Mohammad Shahin, Joint Secretary (Development wing) of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, said the government is working through various initiatives to make people going abroad skilled, and that skilled labour migration makes the migration process safe.

headline_en: 2.5 percent incentive will also apply to compensation money due to expatriates
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank decided on 12 September 2024 that compensation received from employers or insurers for expatriates who die or are injured abroad will get the existing 2.5 percent remittance incentive if brought home through legal channels, effective from the date of the directive. The article also gives the history of the incentive, remittance figures, Wage Earners' Welfare Board data on bodies returned, and the board's BDT 35,000 burial grant.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank decided that compensation money received from the employing organisation or an insurance company for expatriates who died or were physically injured while working abroad will receive incentive (cash assistance) at the existing rate when it comes to Bangladesh through legal channels; all scheduled banks' managing directors and chief executives were informed. The decision followed a direction from the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare.

Conditions for the incentive on compensation money: the source of the money sent from abroad as compensation must be confirmed, and the money must be converted into taka as soon as it arrives in Bangladesh through legal channels.

The incentive on compensation money applies only from the issue of the directive; expatriates who died or were injured and whose compensation was received before the new decision do not get the incentive.
The government currently gives a 2.5 percent incentive on remittances; banks earlier gave extra incentive on top, but now give no additional incentive beyond the government's.
The government first announced a 2 percent incentive (cash assistance) on remittances on 1 July 2019; from 1 January 2022 it was raised from 2 percent to 2.5 percent.
After the 2 percent incentive was introduced, money sent through the banking channel rose to USD 1,820 crore in fiscal year 2019-20, about 13 percent more than in 2018-19.
Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 222 crore in August 2024 and USD 191 crore in July 2024, a rise of about 16.25 percent from July to August.

According to Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, 18,166 bodies of expatriates arrived in Bangladesh in the five years 2018 to 2022; of these, 3,698 died from road accidents, workplace accidents, burns, falls from buildings and electric shock, the most being road accidents with 2,649 deaths, which people concerned think happen while travelling to and from work.
According to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, 3,691 bodies of expatriates arrived in Bangladesh in fiscal year 2018-19 and 4,107 in fiscal year 2022-23.
The Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives BDT 35,000 in cash assistance for the burial of each expatriate's body that arrives in Bangladesh; in addition the worker's family gets life insurance benefit.
If there is a compensation claim abroad for a deceased Bangladeshi worker, it is recovered through the embassy, and the embassy also takes steps to recover any unpaid dues of the dead worker.
