headline_en: Execution of two Bangladeshis in Makkah: Bangladesh did not know beforehand, letter sent to Saudi Arabia seeking information
summary_en: Bangladesh learned only from media that two Bangladeshis, named as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter, were executed in Saudi Arabia for 'immoral' acts in a mosque area in Makkah; the Saudi Press Agency confirmed it on Wednesday 14 October 2026. The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday 15 October asking for details. The sentence was a discretionary 'taazir' punishment under Shariah, upheld by a higher judicial authority and carried out by royal order.

facts.statement: The Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the Saudi interior ministry, confirmed on Wednesday (14 October 2026) that death sentences were carried out on two Bangladeshi nationals for 'immoral' acts in a mosque area in Makkah; those executed are reported to be Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi Press Agency; Prothom Alo sources

facts.statement: According to Gulf News, Saudi security forces arrested the two Bangladeshis on the allegation of engaging in immoral and indecent acts in a mosque in Makkah; after preliminary investigation they were charged and sent to court, which sentenced them to death under 'taazir', the judge's discretionary punishment under Shariah law, considering the violation of the mosque's sanctity and the circumstances; a higher judicial authority upheld the verdict and a royal order directed that it be carried out.
facts.source_in_article: Gulf News, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Saudi interior ministry said in a statement that it stands firm on protecting the security of the holy mosques and enforcing Shariah law against violators of religious sanctity, and warned that repetition of such crimes in holy places will face severe punishment.

A source at the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah said Saudi authorities did not formally inform Bangladesh before carrying out the executions; Bangladesh learned from media reports, and on Thursday 15 October 2026 the Jeddah consulate sent a letter to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting details.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah source; Foreign Ministry sources in Dhaka

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; under its Article 36, when a national is arrested abroad the detaining country must, at the prisoner's request, inform that person's consulate without delay and allow consular assistance. It is not yet clear whether the two prisoners asked for the consulate to be informed.

Unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial of the two Bangladeshis had been going on for several months in a Jeddah court and two distinguished Bangladeshi citizens helped as interpreters during it. Foreign Ministry officials, speaking anonymously, said it is not expected that Saudi authorities detained and executed them very quickly, and called it mysterious that no one contacted the mission on their behalf.
facts.source_in_article: unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia; unnamed Foreign Ministry officials

facts.statement: No information was yet available on the type and duration of the two executed Bangladeshis' stay in Saudi Arabia or on whether any legal assistance or appeal was used in the trial.

headline_en: Where is the law or rule that an unmarried woman cannot go abroad
summary_en: Three adult women with valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets were stopped at Bangladesh airport immigration on their way to visit Nepal, allegedly because they were unmarried and travelling on their own. After a complaint to the additional inspector general of police got no response they filed a writ, and on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule. Sakia Haque of Travelettes of Bangladesh argues no Bangladeshi law bars unmarried women from travelling abroad.

facts.statement: Three adult women travelling to Nepal as tourists allege that Bangladesh airport immigration stopped them despite valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets: officers asked whether their families knew, told them to phone home (which they did), and asked why they were going on their own while unmarried.
facts.source_in_article: the three women, as reported by Prothom Alo and Sakia Haque

facts.statement: The three women complained to the additional inspector general of police asking for an investigation and action; getting no response they filed a writ, and on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule asking why stopping the three women from travelling abroad should not be declared to be without lawful authority.

Article 36 of Bangladesh's Constitution recognises a citizen's right to leave and re-enter Bangladesh, subject to reasonable restrictions set by law; Article 28 provides for equal rights of women and men and non-discrimination by the state on grounds of sex.
facts.source_in_article: Sakia Haque, co-founder, Travelettes of Bangladesh

facts.statement: Under the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 no one can leave the country without a valid passport or travel document, and a passport can be refused, restricted or cancelled on specific legal grounds; the writer says it contains no separate prohibition on 'unmarried women'.
facts.source_in_article: Sakia Haque, co-founder, Travelettes of Bangladesh

facts.statement: The writer says women leaving Bangladesh have for years faced irrelevant immigration questions such as 'Are you married?', 'Your husband let you go alone?' and 'Where do you get so much money?'; a 'gender equity' component she and Manoshi Saha worked on in immigration police training some years ago has, she has heard, been discontinued.

people_cases.what_happened: Stopped at Bangladesh airport immigration despite valid passport, visa/entry permission and tickets; asked whether family knew and made to phone home.
people_cases.outcome: Filed a writ; High Court issued a rule on 29 September 2026

headline_en: Bribe-taking video on Facebook, election officer transferred
summary_en: A Bahrain-based expatriate filmed himself paying a bribe to the Goalanda upazila election officer in Rajbari for a new national ID card and posted it on Facebook; the officer was transferred to Jhenaidah on 16 Sep 2026 while an inquiry continues. The article reports allegations that a broker ring working through local computer shops takes BDT 5,000 to over half a lakh per NID job, and quotes an unnamed person who paid BDT 50,000 for a voter ID to go abroad urgently.

facts.statement: On 10 Sep 2026 Bahrain expatriate Russell Molla of Ujanchar, Goalanda upazila, Rajbari went to the Goalanda Upazila Election Office for a new voter ID (NID) card; upazila election officer Khabirul Alam demanded a BDT 5,000 bribe for the work and, after much pleading, Russell paid BDT 2,000.

Russell Molla, a Bahrain expatriate ill with a brain tumour, said the Goalanda election officer made him come back to the office for three to four days on various excuses and issued his national ID card only after he paid; he secretly filmed the payment and posted it on Facebook.

After the bribe video spread on social media, Goalanda upazila election officer Khabirul Alam was show-caused by the district election officer (reply due in three working days, submitted 15 Sep 2026) and then transferred to the Jhenaidah District Election Office by a notification signed on 16 Sep 2026 by Election Commission Secretariat assistant secretary Mohammad Shahidur Rahman; further action may follow after the inquiry.
facts.source_in_article: Rajbari district election officer (name printed both as Sek Mohammad Jalalur Rahman and Sek Muhammad Jalal Uddin)

facts.statement: It is alleged that several local computer shopkeepers in Goalanda, Rajbari are part of a broker ring: money handed to them reaches the election officer at once, and new NID cards, corrections of name spelling and corrections of father's and mother's names then get done very easily. The alleged bribe per job ranges from a minimum of BDT 5,000 to more than half a lakh taka.

An unnamed person said he paid BDT 50,000 to get a voter ID made at the Goalanda Upazila Election Office because he needed to go abroad urgently, and that nobody in that office does any work without money.
Khabirul Alam told Prothom Alo that an inquiry against him is under way and he cannot comment.

headline_en: How much economic and diplomatic gain if Bangladesh joins the Mecca alliance
summary_en: An opinion column by a Shahjalal University professor on the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan joint defence pact signed in Mecca on 7 Aug 2026 and whether Bangladesh should join. It argues the biggest potential benefit is the Saudi labour market, citing BMET figures for 2025, but says such gains need separate labour agreements, skills programmes and effective consular management.

facts.statement: According to the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), about 1,117,000 (11 lakh 17 thousand) Bangladeshis went abroad for employment in 2025, of whom more than 752,000 (7 lakh 52 thousand) went to Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: BMET data, cited by the columnist from BSS (2026)

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca on 7 Aug 2026 (the 'Mecca Pact'); at the first committee meeting in Istanbul on 31 Aug 2026 it was named the 'Mecca Defence Alliance', with a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and a Pakistani representative as first secretary general for three years.
facts.source_in_article: Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan, as cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Bangladesh's participation in the Mecca Defence Alliance is not decided: Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman told parliament the government would consider it positively if members want to include Bangladesh, State Minister Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh sees no risk in joining, and no formal invitation or membership terms have been publicly confirmed.

The columnist argues closer political ties with Saudi Arabia could let Bangladesh press Riyadh on opening new sectors for skilled workers, transparency in recruitment, preventing contract breaches, ensuring wages and working conditions and more legal aid for expatriate workers, but that joining a defence framework will not guarantee these; separate labour agreements, skills development programmes and effective consular management are needed.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Md Shahabul Haque, professor, Political Studies, SUST Sylhet

headline_en: Highly educated young people fight for a single peon's job
summary_en: An opinion column by a Prothom Alo editorial assistant on youth unemployment in Bangladesh, using two reports of graduates competing for low-grade government posts. It says young people pay BDT 20-25 lakh on 'body contract' to cross the Mediterranean and drown, die from Ukrainian drones, and that 8-9 lakh must go abroad each year, many by selling homesteads and borrowing at high interest through brokers.

facts.statement: The columnist writes that Bangladeshi young people are drowning while trying to cross the Mediterranean on 'body contract' deals costing BDT 20-25 lakh, and that young men are dying one after another from Ukrainian drone strikes.

According to the columnist, 22-23 lakh young people join Bangladesh's labour market each year, at most 12-13 lakh find work in the country (about 3 lakh of them in decently paid government and private jobs), and 8-9 lakh young people have to go abroad each year in search of work.

The columnist writes that those who can go abroad legally are the lucky ones; a large share sell their homestead, borrow at high interest and go through brokers, and many who go by illegal routes are forced into a slave-like life. He adds that spending on education abroad is now almost equal to the higher-education budget.
The 2022 census counted about 4 crore 59 lakh people aged 15-29 in Bangladesh, about 28 percent of the population.

In Pabna, 17 of those appointed to 18 office-assistant (grade 20, formerly MLSS/peon, class-eight qualification) posts advertised on 25 Oct 2025 were highly educated; and 1,234,409 people applied for 312 third-class (grade 16, HSC-level) posts at the Department of Social Services, 3,956 per post.

headline_en: Masud Uddin Chowdhury on four-day remand in ACC case
summary_en: A Dhaka court on 21 Jun 2026 granted four days' remand of former MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury in an Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) case alleging embezzlement of over BDT 119 crore in the name of sending workers to Malaysia. The remand petition says the government-set fee was BDT 78,990 but he and others, appointed as agents through abuse of official power, illegally collected BDT 119 crore 32 lakh 70 thousand from workers and laundered it.

facts.statement: According to the ACC's remand petition, the government-fixed fee for sending a worker to Malaysia was BDT 78,990.

On Sunday 21 Jun 2026 special judge Md Sabbir Foyez of the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court granted four days' remand (seven sought by investigating officer ACC assistant director Abul Kalam Azad) of former MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury in an ACC case over alleged embezzlement of more than BDT 119 crore in the name of sending workers to Malaysia.

The ACC alleges that Masud Uddin Chowdhury and associated persons, in collusion and by abusing government power, got themselves appointed as agents for sending workers to Malaysia and illegally collected BDT 119 crore 32 lakh 70 thousand from workers, which was then laundered through illegal transfer, conversion and transactions; the case is under the Penal Code, the Money Laundering Prevention Act and the Prevention of Corruption Act.

Masud Uddin Chowdhury was arrested in the Baridhara area of Dhaka on 23 Mar 2026, has been taken on remand several times in various cases (including a human trafficking case, per a linked headline) and has been in jail since.

Masud Uddin Chowdhury was GOC of the army's 9th Division in 2007 and a key figure in the 1/11 changeover, became High Commissioner to Australia in 2008, later ran restaurants and other businesses in Dhaka, and was Jatiya Party MP for Feni-3 (Sonagazi-Daganbhuiyan) in 2018 and 2024.

headline_en: The 3 proposals from UK universities to stop visa fraud
summary_en: The Russell Group of 24 leading UK universities called for targeted, risk-based action against student visa fraud rather than blanket restrictions, after the UK government announced a stricter compliance regime for universities sponsoring student visas. It proposed giving universities access to UKVI fraud data, considering penalties harsher than the current 10-year re-entry ban, and a direct fraud-reporting channel, and listed checks members already make on applicants' qualifications, English test results and financial documents.

facts.statement: The current penalty for a fraudulent UK student visa application is a 10-year re-entry ban; the Russell Group has proposed that the UK consider harsher punishment than this.
The UK government recently announced a stricter compliance regime for universities that sponsor student visas; the article gives no details of the measures.

Russell Group universities say they already apply these checks to international applicants: an extra approval step before issuing the CAS (Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies), mandatory second-person review of applications, verifying academic qualifications directly with the awarding institution, verifying English language test results with the test provider, and checking financial documents through banks and third-party verification.

The Russell Group's other two proposals are to give universities direct access to UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) data on forged documents, regional trends and recruitment agents' conduct, and to open a direct fraud-reporting channel between universities and UKVI with clear rules for sharing information on suspect applicants.

Russell Group chief executive Professor Libby Hackett said attempts to get student visas by fraud and false information undermine trust in the whole system and put genuine students' opportunities at risk; the group says the vast majority of international applicants are genuine and most international students leave the UK within five years of arrival, and it opposes blanket restrictions.

headline_en: 'I heard after my son died that he had gone to war; had I known I would not have let him go to Russia'
summary_en: Abdur Rahim (30) of Fulbaria, Mymensingh went to Russia on 7 Dec 2024 for about BDT 5 lakh as a welder, later took BDT 3 lakh more from his family for a supposed power-plant job, and in fact joined the Russian army through a broker on a promise of high pay. After a month's training he joined on 1 May 2026 and was killed by a drone the next day, his first day at the front, together with Riyad Rashid of Kishoreganj; campmate Limon Dutta of Narsingdi was injured. The family wants the broker tried and the body returned.

facts.statement: Abdur Rahim (30) of Putijana Namapara village, Putijana union, Fulbaria, Mymensingh went to Russia on 7 Dec 2024 spending about BDT 5 lakh; the family understood he was doing welding work there.
Three months before his death Abdur Rahim took a further BDT 3 lakh from his family saying it was for a new job at a power plant in Russia; it later emerged he was in Russian army training.

Abdur Rahim told his younger brother that the 'new company' would pay BDT 2 lakh a month and that all problems would be solved in two months; in the month before his death he sent home BDT 1 lakh 40 thousand, which surprised the family. After reaching Russia he had earlier sent money only irregularly.

Abdur Rahim's mother said he went to Russia for welding work, and a broker then took him into the army with a promise of good pay; he told his parents he had taken a power-plant job and did not say it was the army. For a month after joining the 'new job' he did not speak directly with his parents, citing network problems, but stayed in touch with two younger brothers on WhatsApp.

After one month of Russian army training Abdur Rahim joined duty on 1 May 2026 and was killed in a drone strike the next day, his first day taking part in the Ukraine war; Riyad Rashid, a young man from Kishoreganj, was killed with him and campmate Limon Dutta of Narsingdi was injured in the same attack. The family got the news on the evening of Monday 11 May 2026.

facts.statement: The family learned of the death because Limon Dutta, a friend in the same Russian army camp, contacted the family of Riyad Rashid by Facebook Messenger and said Rahim had also been killed; Rahim's family confirmed it through Riyad's family and Limon Dutta.

Local MP Kamrul Hasan, who visited the home with UNO Shahidul Islam and Fulbaria OC Rashedul Hasan on 12 May 2026, said he had spoken with the ministry concerned, that there is a process for bringing a body home and the family has been told to apply accordingly; the UNO promised help to bring the body quickly, humanitarian aid, and awareness work against broker rings.
facts.source_in_article: MP Kamrul Hasan; UNO Shahidul Islam

facts.statement: Abdur Rahim had earlier gone to Singapore in 2015 with money from loans and mortgaging land and worked there as a welder for seven years before returning to Bangladesh.

headline_en: What are the new challenges of building public trust and stability
summary_en: An opinion column by a North South University academic arguing that Bangladesh needs professional strategic, risk and crisis communication in three sensitive areas: energy, migration and the macroeconomy. On migration it says the state's contact with migrant workers has been limited to recruitment, paperwork and formal praise, and proposes a 24-hour crisis platform, location-based SMS alerts, verified safe-area information and clear emergency-help instructions for expatriate workers.

facts.statement: The columnist recommends that the Bangladesh government set up, for expatriate workers, a separate 24-hour crisis platform, location-based SMS alerts, verified information on safe areas and clear instructions on getting emergency help, saying this would leave expatriates less panicked, less cheated and less likely to return home chaotically. These are proposals, not existing services.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Rizwan-ul-Alam, associate professor and chair, Media, Communication and Journalism, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist warns that when tension rises in a region an information vacuum becomes very dangerous and is quickly filled by broker rings, rumour-spreading groups and opportunists, so risk and crisis communication to migrants must be direct, digital and continuous.

The columnist says the state's communication with migrant workers has mostly been limited to recruitment, paperwork and formal praise, which is no longer enough amid regional conflict, labour-market uncertainty and growing rumours; expatriates must be assured, with visible arrangements, that the government has contingency plans, diplomatic contact, emergency assistance and security measures ready in a crisis.

headline_en: 'Swarms of missiles and drones fly over our heads'
summary_en: Rashedul Hasan, chief engineer of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) ship Banglar Joyjatra, describes to Prothom Alo how its 31 Bangladeshi seafarers have lived through the US-Israel war on Iran while stuck in the Persian Gulf. The ship was at Jebel Ali port when the war began, finished unloading on 11 March 2026, tried to leave through the Strait of Hormuz on 12 March and was turned back to the Sharjah anchorage by the UAE coast guard.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) ship Banglar Joyjatra, with 31 seafarers on board, arrived at Jebel Ali port (UAE) on 27 February 2026 carrying steel coils from Qatar; news of the attack on Iran came at dawn the next day, and the ship had been in the Persian Gulf since before the US-Israel conflict around Iran began.
facts.source_in_article: Rashedul Hasan, chief engineer of Banglar Joyjatra

facts.date: about 1 March 2026 (the night after the war began)
facts.statement: On the night after the war began, at about 1:30 am, a loud blast shook the area around the Banglar Joyjatra at Jebel Ali; the crew started an extra generator, readied the emergency fire pump, gave instructions by walkie-talkie and all took shelter in the ship's most protected room. A control room of a nearby oil depot had been hit and was on fire, with two tugboats trying to put it out.

In the following days the seafarers on the Banglar Joyjatra went to the ship's safe room whenever a warning message arrived on their mobile phones; they saw swarms of missiles and drones from Iran heading towards Dubai, many destroyed in the air and some hitting. A missile also struck one terminal of Jebel Ali port, but no ship was there so major damage was avoided.

BSC managing director Commodore Mahmudul Malek contacted the Banglar Joyjatra repeatedly, and the Ministry of Shipping and the Bangladesh embassy in the UAE checked on the crew regularly; the crew had no opportunity to leave the ship, so they stayed aboard and tightened precautions.

Unloading of the Banglar Joyjatra at Jebel Ali port finished on 11 March 2026 after being disrupted for several days for security reasons; maximum alert was declared on the ship and a separate emergency action plan was made. The ship had been scheduled to go on to Kuwait, but because of the war it was decided to bring it back safely out of the risky area.

On 12 March 2026 the Banglar Joyjatra sailed for the Strait of Hormuz, the only exit from the Persian Gulf. About 66 nautical miles from the entrance it radioed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) authority and got no reply; missiles were seen in the strait area and six ships were attacked while crossing the strait that day. A UAE coast guard patrol then told the ship not to proceed for safety reasons, and it returned to the Sharjah anchorage, where missiles and drones from Iran were again seen passing overhead.

Asked on WhatsApp whether he is still afraid, Rashedul Hasan said the crew has got used to the sound of missiles and drones; at first they were frightened and two seafarers used to cry, but now everyone is braver and is fighting 'a war to keep morale up'.

Rashedul Hasan grew up in Madhabdi, Narsingdi, is a cadet of the 47th batch of Bangladesh Marine Academy, became a chief engineer at BSC in 2024 and is currently the youngest chief engineer in the BSC fleet.

headline_en: How much influence do British Bangladeshi voters have on Bangladesh's election
summary_en: An Al Jazeera feature from East London, published in translation ahead of Bangladesh's 12 February 2026 election, looks at expatriate Bangladeshis voting for the first time by postal ballot. Only about 32,000 registered in the UK against roughly 645,000 Bangladeshis in England and Wales, while Saudi Arabia had over 239,000 and Qatar about 76,000 registered. People describe a complicated process (NID card, biometric registration at the High Commission with long queues, then a mobile app), limited publicity and missed deadlines.

facts.statement: For the national election of 12 February 2026, Bangladeshis living abroad got the right to vote for the first time: the Election Commission brought expatriate voters under registration and they vote by postal ballot.

In practice the expatriate vote is only for Bangladeshi citizens who hold a national identity card (NID); many British Bangladeshis, especially those born in the UK, have no citizenship documents and are left out.

To vote from the UK an expatriate needs a national ID card, biometric registration (done at the High Commission, with long queues), and then a further digital step through a mobile app; Khaled Noor said this is quite complicated for many, especially elderly voters.
facts.source_in_article: Khaled Noor, barrister and political analyst, former local councillor, Tower Hamlets

facts.statement: About 32,000 (more than 32,000) Bangladeshi citizens in the UK registered as postal voters, against about 645,000 people in England and Wales who identified as Bangladeshi or British Bangladeshi in the 2021 census.
According to the Election Commission, more than 239,000 expatriate Bangladeshi voters registered in Saudi Arabia and about 76,000 in Qatar, compared with 32,000 in the UK.

About 35 percent of residents of Tower Hamlets alone are Bangladeshi; there are also large numbers of Bangladeshis in Newham and in Barking and Dagenham, and East London is the most densely Bangladeshi area.

Expatriates in East London complained of limited publicity by the authorities; some learned about postal voting late. One person applied for an NID a few days before the deadline but the card arrived after registration closed; an elderly man said 'everything is in the app now, whom do I ask if there is a problem?'. The Bangladesh High Commission in London did not comment when contacted.
facts.source_in_article: expatriates interviewed; Moshahid Ali, editor of weekly Bangla Sanglap

facts.statement: Khaled Noor said people in the UK who are eligible to vote but lack permanent or secure immigration status are wary of speaking about the election because they do not want attention on themselves.

Khaled Noor explained the gap in registration: expatriates in Gulf countries are usually single men whose families are in Bangladesh and who have limited political and social rights there, so they stay tied to Bangladesh, whereas many Bangladeshis in the UK and US live permanently with families, careers and children.

Bangladeshis have lived in Britain for over 100 years; large-scale migration began in the mid-20th century, when in the 1950s and 1960s economic hardship in then East Pakistan and UK labour shortages drew Bengali-speaking men, mostly from Sylhet, to London and Birmingham; the 1971 war brought another wave, followed by family reunion.
Tower Hamlets councillors Sabina Khan and Ohid Ahmed were among several British-Bangladeshi politicians who entered the contest in Bangladesh's election, which caused debate.

headline_en: Remove the disease, not the patient
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial condemns the long-running practice in Middle Eastern countries of quickly sending Bangladeshi workers home without any treatment once they are found HIV-positive. It notes that an HIV-negative certificate is mandatory before going abroad but there is no practical health training, and that returnees get free medicine but very limited counselling, mental health or livelihood support. It calls for mandatory pre-departure health education, raising HIV-based expulsion in bilateral talks, and a separate support structure for returnees.

facts.date: ongoing for many years (as of February 2026)
facts.statement: According to a Prothom Alo report cited in the editorial, Bangladeshi workers found HIV-positive in Middle Eastern countries are hurriedly sent back to Bangladesh without any medical treatment or treatment plan; the practice has gone on for many years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing Prothom Alo's own report

facts.statement: Many Middle Eastern countries still keep a policy of expelling migrant workers solely because of HIV, although the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization have repeatedly said that expelling someone only because of HIV is discriminatory.
An HIV-negative certificate is mandatory before a Bangladeshi worker goes abroad, but there is no practical training on reducing risk, safe behaviour or sexual health.

Workers who return to Bangladesh with HIV are given medicine free of charge, but counselling, mental health support and livelihood rehabilitation arrangements are very limited; many fear telling even their families because of sudden loss of work and income and social stigma.

The editorial calls for mandatory health education in simple language for workers before going abroad, for the issue of ending HIV-based expulsion to be raised strongly in bilateral talks with destination countries, and for a separate structure of treatment plus mental health support and rehabilitation for returning affected workers.
The editorial states that HIV does not spread through air or ordinary social contact, and that a person with HIV who is under treatment can live and work normally.

headline_en: Bangladesh determined to build skilled manpower to meet future challenges: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: Speaking at the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh on Monday 26 January 2026, Expatriates' Welfare adviser Professor Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh is certifying 60,000 workers a month for the Saudi market under the Skill Verification Programme (SVP) agreement with Saudi Takamol. He also cited the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Ordinance 2025, ratification of ten ILO fundamental conventions, and the recently signed Bangladesh-Saudi worker recruitment agreement.

facts.statement: As a result of the Skill Verification Programme (SVP) agreement with Saudi Takamol, Bangladesh is now giving skill certificates in various occupations to 60,000 workers every month in line with Saudi labour market demand.
facts.source_in_article: Professor Asif Nazrul, adviser, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, at the Global Labour Market Conference in Riyadh

facts.statement: A worker recruitment agreement between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia was recently signed; Asif Nazrul hoped it will play an important role in safe migration.

The 'Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025' has been issued; according to Asif Nazrul it will make forming trade unions easier, remove gender-based wage discrimination and ban blacklisting of workers.

Asif Nazrul said Bangladesh has ratified ten fundamental ILO conventions (described as within South Asia) and reaffirmed its commitment to fairness, welfare and accountability in the labour market, and that the government has taken various steps to meet growing global demand for skilled manpower.

headline_en: Wages fall when too many workers go to one country
summary_en: A theoretical research paper presented at a Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) seminar in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Thursday 11 December 2025 argued that when too many workers go to one country an oversupply of labour forms and migrant workers' average wage eventually falls, a risk avoided by sending skilled workers in varied sectors rather than only low-skilled ones. The paper, by Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed of Southern Illinois University, modelled the effects of oil price rises on remittances and migrant workers.

facts.statement: A theoretical research paper presented at a BIDS seminar on 11 December 2025 said that when workers go to a particular country in large numbers, an excess supply of labour is created there and the average wage of migrant workers eventually falls; sending skilled workers in various sectors instead of only low-skilled workers removes this risk.
facts.source_in_article: theoretical research paper by Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed, Southern Illinois University, presented at BIDS

facts.statement: According to the paper, right after oil prices rise, production and working hours rise in the Middle East and other oil-rich countries, earnings of migrant workers in the related sectors increase, existing migrants work more because of higher wages and overtime, and in the first round remittance flows rise significantly.
facts.source_in_article: Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed

facts.statement: The paper shows that when oil prices rise, host (oil-producing) countries gain, with GDP and labour demand rising, while home (labour-exporting) countries like Bangladesh face long-term contraction in production, consumption and spending because costlier imported fuel raises production costs; the living standard of both domestic workers and new aspiring migrants falls.
facts.source_in_article: Professor A K M Mahbub Morshed

facts.statement: The research was titled (in translation) 'The effect of world oil price rises on remittances and migrant workers of small-economy countries'; the seminar was held by BIDS at Agargaon, Dhaka, and chaired by BIDS research director Mohammad Yunus.

headline_en: How the country's first 'Digital Island' sank
summary_en: Maheshkhali in Cox's Bazar was declared Bangladesh's first 'Digital Island' in 2017 under an IOM-funded project whose stated aims included preventing unsafe migration and human trafficking by sea. The project worked for about two and a half years, then collapsed for lack of oversight: 19 km of optical fibre was stolen, equipment was ruined or stolen, and distance-learning, telemedicine and e-commerce services stopped. The Department of Social Services, which took it over, has neither staff nor budget to restart it.

facts.statement: The 'Digital Island' project was launched in 2017 in Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar (about 400,000 residents) with aims that included improving living standards, expanding education and business and preventing unsafe migration; it was implemented jointly by Korea Telecom, the Bangladesh government's ICT Division and Bangladesh Computer Council with financial support from the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM), at a cost of BDT 22 crore 35 lakh 81 thousand.

Under the Maheshkhali Digital Island project, law enforcement agencies had taken an initiative to use high-speed internet to run operations at sea to stop human trafficking and arms and drug smuggling, in order to ensure safe migration.

The Digital Island project ran properly for the first two and a half years and then stalled; 19 km of optical fibre for the internet link was stolen, laptops, computers and projectors were ruined, and distance learning, telemedicine and e-commerce activities stopped. Internet at Adinath Government Primary School was cut in December 2019, and the ICT centre run by the Maheshkhali social services office was burgled on 13 October 2020.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's field visit; local teachers and officials

facts.statement: The project's ICT Training Centre was inaugurated on 25 January 2018 and handed to the Maheshkhali upazila Department of Social Services, which was to keep the project running but has not managed to in the last five and a half years; the Maheshkhali social services office has only two officers.

Md. Sofi Uddin, assistant director of the Department of Social Services, Cox's Bazar office, said the whole project collapsed during the Covid pandemic, restarting it would need everything including the optical fibre to be installed anew with a large budget the department does not have, and that for now they have moved to reopen the training centre and written to the director general for an allocation. The UNO, Md. Hedayet Ullah, said the computer training centre is to be reopened with the help of a private development organisation.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Sofi Uddin; UNO Md. Hedayet Ullah

The three possible exchange notes between Bangladesh and Malaysia are on the halal ecosystem, the two countries' foreign service academies, and cooperation in the higher education sector.

Touhid Hossain, energy adviser Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan, national security adviser Khalilur Rahman, special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi and BIDA executive chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun.

Bangladesh has long been trying to become a 'sectoral dialogue partner' of ASEAN, and Malaysia's prime minister is the current ASEAN chair, so Dhaka hopes for a positive result; Anwar Ibrahim visited Bangladesh 'last October', the first head of government to visit after the interim government took office on 8 August 2024.

headline_en: What is in the NCP's 24-point 'Second Republic' manifesto
summary_en: National Citizen Party (NCP) convener Nahid Islam announced a 24-point 'Manifesto for a New Bangladesh' at the Central Shaheed Minar on Sunday 3 August 2025. Most points concern the constitution, justice, governance, health, education and the economy, but point 15 pledges training and certification for exporting skilled manpower, point 18 pledges recognition and legal protection for migrant workers, and point 22 sets out pledges on expatriates' voting rights, harassment-free embassy and airport services, body repatriation, an emergency fund and reintegration. These are party promises, not government measures.

facts.statement: On 3 August 2025 the National Citizen Party (NCP) convener Nahid Islam announced a 24-point manifesto at a rally at the Central Shaheed Minar; point 22 is titled 'Dignity and rights of expatriate Bangladeshis'. These are a political party's pledges.

NCP manifesto point 22 pledges that if an expatriate worker dies the party will arrange for the body to be brought home without harassment and give the family all kinds of support, and that it will work to ensure expatriate workers' healthcare and overall welfare.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 22 pledges voting rights for expatriates, harassment-free service at embassies and airports, an emergency assistance fund, safe investment at home and digital government services for expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 22 pledges rehabilitation and dignified employment arrangements for expatriates who return home or fall into crisis, firm steps to prevent human trafficking and protect the interests and human rights of Bangladeshi citizens abroad, and creating scope for expatriates to take part directly in state policy-making.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: The NCP manifesto refers to 'more than one and a half crore' expatriates who it says played an outstanding role in the July mass uprising, and pledges state recognition of that contribution.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 15 pledges special emphasis on IT, healthcare, nursing, management, logistics, hospitality and engineering for exporting skilled manpower abroad, with enough training centres to teach sector- and country-specific skills and languages.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 15 pledges to widen training and certification in technical trades for skilled manpower export and to take joint initiatives with foreign certification bodies to bring them to international standard.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: The NCP manifesto states that Bangladesh has about 30 lakh unemployed people, two of every three of them young.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 18 pledges recognition and legal protection for all workers, explicitly including migrant, domestic, agricultural, transport, informal and self-employed workers, and a 'permanent labour commission'.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

headline_en: Three detained in Malaysia on suspicion of militancy have returned and are being questioned: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said on Friday 4 July 2025 that three of the Bangladeshi workers arrested in Malaysia over alleged militant links have already returned and are being questioned, and all who return will be questioned and tried if evidence is found. Earlier that day Malaysia's police chief Khalid Ismail said 36 Bangladeshis were detained for spreading Islamic State ideology and raising funds among workers: 5 charged, 15 to be deported, 16 still in custody.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Inspector-General of Police Khalid Ismail told a press conference in Kuala Lumpur on Friday 4 July 2025 that 36 Bangladeshi nationals had been detained for alleged militant links; of them 5 have been charged with being members of a terrorist organisation, 15 will be sent back to Bangladesh, and 16 remain in police custody under investigation.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail, via Reuters

facts.statement: The Malaysian police chief said authorities had broken up a ring of Bangladeshi workers that used social media and online messaging platforms to spread Islamic State (IS) ideology among workers, recruited other Bangladeshi workers and collected funds; the detained workers sent money to the IS group in Syria and Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail, citing intelligence, via Reuters

facts.statement: Khalid Ismail said 100 to 150 people are believed to be involved in the ring; those with a low level of involvement will be sent back to their own country, those deeply involved will be dealt with under Malaysian law, and operations to catch suspects will continue.

Adviser Asif Nazrul said on the night of Friday 4 July 2025 that three of those arrested in Malaysia had already returned to Bangladesh and were being questioned; everyone detained on this allegation who returns will be questioned, and if evidence of militant involvement is found, by Bangladesh itself or from Malaysian authorities, they will be put on trial.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said Malaysia is a friendly state where 'several lakh' Bangladeshis work, that such allegations against a few are very embarrassing and a concern for both countries, and that Bangladesh is in contact with Malaysia at a high level and will take a tough stand against militancy.
The article says Malaysia relies heavily on foreign manpower for factories, plantations/farming and construction, and that thousands of Bangladeshi nationals go there for work every year.

headline_en: Travel ban on 12 people including Nizam Hazari and Meher Afroz Chumki
summary_en: On Sunday 25 May 2025 Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Md. Zakir Hossain, on separate Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) applications, banned 12 people from travelling abroad. Ten of them are linked to the ACC's inquiry into charging more than the government-fixed amount for manpower export to Malaysia and laundering money abroad, including former MP Nizam Uddin Hazari and owners or managing directors of several recruiting firms. The other two, former state minister Meher Afroz Chumki and her husband, face an unrelated illegal-wealth case.

facts.statement: On 25 May 2025 Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Md. Zakir Hossain imposed a foreign travel ban on 10 people connected with the Malaysian labour market, after the ACC told the court it is inquiring into allegations of collecting money in excess of the government-fixed amount for manpower export to Malaysia and laundering money abroad, and had learned that these 10 were trying to flee abroad.
facts.source_in_article: ACC submission to court; court order

(The wording does not make clear which firm M Amirul Islam, Nasir Uddin Ahmed and Khondaker Shawkat Hossain belong to.)

In a separate matter the same court banned former state minister Meher Afroz Chumki and her husband Mohammad Masudur Rahman, former chief executive of Bangladesh Petroleum and Lubricants, from travelling abroad until investigation ends in an ACC case alleging BDT 2 crore 31 lakh of wealth beyond known income; this case is not about migration.

headline_en: Four kg of gold recovered by burning the clothes of two Bangladeshis returning from Dubai
summary_en: Two Sylhet men working in Dubai, Mohammad Shajahan and Alim, were arrested on 25 April 2025 at Dhaka and Sylhet airports wearing underwear and vests coated with gold, from which customs recovered more than four kg by burning the garments. Shajahan, who needed gallbladder surgery, had been offered his travel costs by a man named Ziaur Rahman in return for carrying 'valuables'. Both are in jail under the Special Powers Act and police are trying to identify the ring behind Ziaur.

facts.statement: On 25 April 2025 customs arrested Dubai returnee Shajahan at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, and Alim the same day at Osmani International Airport, Sylhet; more than four kg of gold was recovered by burning the clothes they were wearing, and both are in jail in a case under the Special Powers Act.

The gold was hidden as a coating inside garments: in a fifth-floor room of a multi-storey building in the Deira area of Dubai, where four or five other men from Sylhet were already present, Ziaur Rahman gave Shajahan and Alim three pairs of underwear and three vests each to wear, photographed them, and told them to land very carefully because 'their man' at the airport would find them on arrival.
facts.source_in_article: Investigators, citing interrogation; Airport police inspector Rafiqul Islam

facts.statement: Recruitment of the carriers: Shajahan was found to have gallstones, learned that surgery in a Dubai hospital would cost more than BDT 2 lakh, and decided to have it done in Bangladesh; Ziaur Rahman of Gowainghat, Sylhet then offered to pay his travel costs to and from Bangladesh if he carried Ziaur's 'valuable goods', saying he would be told what it was when he left. Shajahan and Alim sent passport photos and their own photos to Ziaur's WhatsApp number and Ziaur bought their air tickets.

Both men flew from Dubai on the same flight (printed as 'Bangladesh Airlines'), which landed at Sylhet after 10 am, where Alim got off and was arrested by customs on prior information; he named Shajahan, who was arrested with intelligence-agency help when the aircraft landed at Dhaka at about 11:15 am.

Customs recovered 2 kg 417 g of gold from Shajahan's garments, which were cut into pieces and burned for 8 hours, after which the gold was separated from the ash; the complainant customs officer said it took about 24 hours in all to separate the gold after his arrest (the article gives both 8 hours and about 24 hours). Gold dust was recovered from Alim's clothes in the same way.
facts.source_in_article: Customs assistant revenue officer Baki Billah (name spelled two ways in the article)

facts.statement: Airport police station questioned Shajahan on seven days' remand from 26 April to 2 May 2025 in the Special Powers Act case; investigating officer Inspector Rafiqul Islam called Ziaur Rahman one of the ringleaders of gold smuggling and said conversations and messages with Ziaur found on Shajahan's phone are being checked to identify the ringleaders.
facts.source_in_article: Airport police station inspector Rafiqul Islam

facts.statement: Mohammad Shajahan, 38, of Dewar village, Gowainghat, Sylhet went to Dubai four years earlier and sent his monthly earnings home; Alim, from the same area, also went to Dubai for work.

headline_en: Religious affairs ministry asks people not to perform Hajj without a permit
summary_en: In a government handout on Friday 2 May 2025 Bangladesh's religious affairs ministry asked Bangladeshis at home and in Saudi Arabia not to perform Hajj without a permit, not to stay in Makkah or the holy sites on visit visas during the Hajj season, and not to sponsor, transport or house violators. It sets out the Saudi rules for 29 April to 10 June 2025: fines up to SAR 20,000 for pilgrims without a permit, up to SAR 100,000 for helpers, vehicle confiscation, deportation and a 10-year entry ban.

facts.statement: Under new rules issued by the Saudi government for the 2025 Hajj, entry into Makkah is prohibited without a valid permit from the relevant authority to work in the holy sites, proof of residence (iqama) registered in Makkah, and an officially issued Hajj permit.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh government handout (Ministry of Religious Affairs), citing Saudi rules

facts.statement: The Saudi government said the rule is in force from 1 Zilqad (29 April) to 14 Zilhajj (10 June) 2025: in this period no one may enter or stay in Makkah city or the surrounding holy sites without Hajj permission, and people who entered Saudi Arabia on visit visas will be under the highest level of surveillance.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi government, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia's interior ministry said anyone who tries to perform Hajj without a Hajj permit will be fined up to 20,000 Saudi riyals; anyone who helps faces a fine of up to 100,000 Saudi riyals, and if the offence is proved the helper's own vehicle will be confiscated by court order.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi interior ministry, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: The Saudi government said any foreign national who overstays or tries to perform Hajj without valid permission will be expelled from the country and barred from entering Saudi Arabia for the next 10 years.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi government, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: Bangladesh's Ministry of Religious Affairs instructed Bangladeshis not to stay in Makkah or Saudi Arabia's holy sites on a visit visa during the current Hajj season, and asked Bangladeshis in Bangladesh and in Saudi Arabia not to perform Hajj without a Hajj permit.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Religious Affairs, government handout of 2 May 2025

facts.statement: The ministry asked Bangladeshis to refrain from sponsoring visit-visa holders who break Hajj rules, transporting them, helping them enter the restricted Hajj area, or arranging accommodation for them in hotels or homes.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Religious Affairs, government handout of 2 May 2025

facts.statement: Religious affairs adviser A F M Khalid Hossain said about 35 lakh Bangladeshis are working in Saudi Arabia and the highest remittance comes from Saudi Arabia, and that everyone should refrain from acts that would harm relations between the two countries.
facts.source_in_article: Religious affairs adviser A F M Khalid Hossain, in the government handout

headline_en: Satisfaction with immigration and many other services at Shahjalal airport, but dissatisfaction too
summary_en: A field report from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on Saturday 8 March 2025. Returning and departing migrants said immigration now takes minutes rather than a long wait, luggage arrives quickly, and the Probashi Lounge opened on 11 November offers a good environment and cheaper food. Complaints remain: the 24 e-gates installed two and a half years ago mostly do not work, Wi-Fi is unreliable, and immigration police say they are short of staff, work on equipment from 2014 and have faulty passport readers and document detectors.

facts.statement: The interim government opened a 'Probashi Lounge' for the country's migrant workers at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 11 November (2024). On 8 March 2025 the reporter saw 15-20 passengers there, talking with relatives, eating food bought from the adjacent shop and charging mobile phones.

A worker at the Probashi Lounge food shop, Provati, said arrangements have been made so expatriates can buy food at low cost; Kuwait-based Alif Hossain said the lounge environment is much better than elsewhere in the airport and the food comparatively cheaper.
facts.source_in_article: Food shop worker Provati; expatriate Alif Hossain

facts.statement: Rayhan, a construction worker in Abu Dhabi since 2012, said that when he returned on 24 September he completed immigration and got his luggage within 15 minutes, and that on Saturday 8 March 2025 the whole departure immigration process at Shahjalal airport took about 10 minutes, whereas earlier it took a long time.

Alif Hossain of Bancharampur, Brahmanbaria, who has lived in Kuwait since 1996 and travels every three months, said he finished immigration at Shahjalal airport in one minute on Saturday 8 March 2025.

Sharmin Shiri, who arrived from the United States on the night after 1 March 2025, said immigration took 10-15 minutes and luggage came quickly, but she could not use the Wi-Fi; passengers from Singapore who landed at 5:30 pm on 2 March said they finished immigration and had their luggage before iftar.
On average 150 flights take off and land at Hazrat Shahjalal airport per day, and police complete immigration (arrival and departure) for an average of 28,650 passengers a day.

From 1 December to the afternoon of Saturday 8 March 2025, Shahjalal airport immigration police processed arrival immigration for 1,337,856 passengers of 204 countries and departure immigration for 1,469,695 passengers of 199 countries.

From 'last September' to Saturday 8 March 2025 the immigration police Document Analysis Centre detected 46 fake visas, 5 residency cards, 4 fake/tampered passports and 30 impostors (people using another person's passport details with their own photo).

Besides processing outbound passengers, immigration police detain passengers on the 'stop list' (people with a ban or objection on leaving the country), seize forged travel documents, issue visas on arrival and collect fines for expired visas.

Shahjalal airport has 12 e-gates each at arrival and departure (24) plus two VIP e-gates, 26 in total; they were launched two and a half years ago and were supposed to complete an e-passport holder's immigration automatically in 18 seconds, but the reporter found most gates not working and most passengers reluctant to use them.
facts.source_in_article: Staff on duty at the e-gates; reporter's observation

facts.statement: Two passengers said the e-gates are effectively useless: after passport data is verified at the e-gate, the passenger still has to complete immigration through the same process as everyone else.

Immigration police at Shahjalal airport have 48 counters at arrival and 42 at departure; more than 500 police work in four shifts around the clock, 125-130 per shift. They worked three shifts before and moved to four shifts after 5 August (2024), but a staff shortage remains.

The computer equipment used for the immigration software system dates from 2014 and no longer works properly; the passport readers mostly cannot read a passport in one go and sometimes need 7-8 attempts, wasting passengers' time.

An immigration police officer said each shift was given 10 'document and bank note detectors' about two months earlier, but most have already become unusable, which makes it hard to detect fake passports or visas.

Special Branch chief Md. Golam Rasul said visa on arrival will from now on be given online with payment made on reaching the airport, and that within one to two months payment by card from abroad will also be possible, as part of automating the whole process.

SB Special Superintendent of Police (Immigration Operations) A K M Akhtaruzzaman said automation is being prioritised so passengers do not wait long and the aim is to make immigration paperless; desk officers' duty allocation and some other functions have already been automated.
facts.source_in_article: SB Special SP (Immigration Operations) A K M Akhtaruzzaman

facts.statement: In January and February (2025) 18,151 Chinese nationals arrived in Bangladesh and 18,308 left; immigration police say 99 percent of them understand no language other than Chinese, so officers need language training.
Immigration police say they have no food arrangement inside the airport and must buy food at high prices, lack enough transport, and desk officers' chairs are not ergonomic.

headline_en: Career opportunities in Ireland for Bangladeshi doctors and nurses; three exams
summary_en: A feature by Syed Atiqur Rob explains why few Bangladeshi doctors and almost no Bangladeshi nurses work in Ireland despite Ireland's heavy reliance on foreign health workers. It sets out the registration steps (IMC registration, PRES exam or PLAB/MRCP alternative, IELTS/OET), the barriers (degree recognition, no government agreement, no sponsorship channel or recruiters), pay ranges, and what the writer says Bangladesh should do.

facts.statement: According to 2023 figures cited in the article, about 40 percent of all doctors working in Ireland are foreign.
According to 2023 figures cited in the article, about 51.8 percent of Ireland's nursing workforce was trained abroad.

The Irish Medical Council (IMC) recognises (the article says 'easily recognises') medical degrees from India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Egypt, but recognition is hard to get for Bangladeshi degrees, so Bangladeshi doctors face extra exams that are time-consuming and costly.

Ireland's nursing board (NMBI) recognises nurses from the Philippines, India and Nigeria because it has formal agreements with those countries; there is no such agreement with Bangladesh, so Bangladeshi nurses who apply face various complications.

The article says Bangladeshi doctors in Ireland are very few and Bangladeshi nurses almost non-existent; most Bangladeshi doctors working in Ireland come there from various Middle Eastern countries. Thousands of health workers from India, Pakistan, the Philippines, Egypt, Sudan and Nigeria work in Ireland.
Step 1 for a Bangladeshi doctor to work in Ireland: register with the Irish Medical Council (IMC); registration depends on the doctor's experience and educational qualifications.
Step 2: if the medical degree is not recognised, the doctor must sit PRES (Pre-Registration Examination System), which includes a written exam, a clinical skills exam and a supervised internship.

Alternative route: a doctor who has passed PLAB or MRCP can get IMC registration without the PRES exam. To work as a specialist, CESR (Certificate of Eligibility for Specialist Registration) or an equivalent qualification is required.
Even after passing PRES, a language test (IELTS or OET) is mandatory for IMC registration. Doctors and nurses need at least IELTS 7.0 or OET grade 'B' to work in Ireland.
The article says the Philippines, India, Nigeria and Sudan have formal health-worker supply agreements with Ireland, so their doctors and nurses are approved easily; Bangladesh has no such agreement.

Applying directly to an Irish hospital requires sponsorship, which the article says is quite hard for Bangladeshis to get. India and other countries have specific recruitment agencies that connect with Irish hospitals; there is nothing like that for Bangladeshis.
The article says demand in Ireland for specialist doctors is very high, especially in anaesthesia, cardiology, neurology and surgery.

Ireland runs a special employment programme called the 'Critical Skills Employment Permit' through which certain professionals easily get work permission; the writer says that if Bangladesh could be included in it, entry for doctors and nurses would be easier.

Pay in Ireland as stated in the article: an entry-level doctor can earn about 50,000 to 60,000 euros a year; specialist doctors 120,000 to 200,000 euros; consultant-level doctors can earn more than 210,000 euros.
Nurses' pay in Ireland as stated in the article: about 30,000 euros a year at entry level, and can exceed 55,000 euros at senior level.

The writer recommends that the Bangladesh government negotiate degree recognition with the IMC and NMBI, sign a formal government-level health-worker supply agreement with Ireland, set up government IELTS/OET training centres (private ones exist), introduce English-medium teaching in medical colleges and nursing institutes, form reliable public or private recruitment bodies linked to Irish hospitals, train specialists, and seek easier visa facilities.

headline_en: Dollar price suddenly up in the open market for two reasons
summary_en: In about a week to ten days before 19 December 2024 the open-market dollar rate in Dhaka rose by at least 4 taka, and the rate banks pay for remittance dollars passed 124 taka. Bankers attribute it to December travel demand and banks buying remittance dollars at higher rates to settle import bills, and call the rise temporary.

facts.statement: In Dhaka's open (kerb) market the dollar was being bought at 126.70 taka and sold at 127.50 taka; only 10 days earlier it was bought at 122.50 taka and sold at 123 taka.

The price of remittance dollars (what banks pay for expatriate income) rose above 124 taka per dollar, because banks were buying remittance dollars at higher prices to meet travel demand and to settle import liabilities.
Banks were still selling the US dollar at 120 taka, and the rate on credit cards and other cards was kept at 120 taka, while the open-market rate was higher.

Bankers said the rise in the dollar price was temporary and that the price would return to its earlier level in January (2025). The two stated causes: sharply higher dollar demand from outbound travellers in December, and banks paying more for remittance dollars to settle import bills.

facts.statement: According to a World Bank report cited in the article, expatriates sent USD 21.8 billion in remittances to Bangladesh in 2020, of which 73% came from the Gulf / Middle East. facts.statement: Researcher Md. Abu Bakar Siddique is quoted as saying that lack of language skills once caused little problem at work, but now foreign companies give priority to workers who know Arabic.

The writer says that in Saudi Arabia most Bangladeshis are seen doing low-level work because of weak Arabic, while Indian and Pakistani workers skilled in Arabic are seen being appointed to various official/office jobs; India patronises Arabic officially and Pakistan trains its citizens in Arabic.
facts.source_in_article: Tajul Islam Kawsar, King Saud University, Riyadh (article author)

facts.statement: From field work in Saudi Arabia the writer reports that Bangladeshis who open a baqala (small grocery shop) or other small businesses have to keep a Sudanese or Egyptian employee to handle daily correspondence, communication and legal formalities, paying them a large sum, which the writer says would be saved if the owner knew Arabic well.

This is a proposal, not an existing course.

headline_en: Various events in Paris on AEBA's twelfth anniversary
summary_en: At its twelfth-anniversary event at its Paris headquarters on Saturday 7 December 2024, the All European Bangladesh Association (AEBA) put a set of demands (described as seven points) to Bangladesh's interim government on expatriates' rights and services.

facts.statement: The All European Bangladesh Association (AEBA), at its 12th anniversary event at its Paris headquarters, demanded of the interim government: easier issuance of visas for all EU countries from Dhaka; making every Bangladesh embassy, high commission and consulate abroad free of brokers with the highest service standard; national identity/voter ID cards for expatriates; online voting from their countries of residence; reserved parliamentary seats for expatriates; expatriate representation in the Expatriates' Welfare ministry and other relevant ministries; the right to contest elections despite dual citizenship; a government initiative from Dhaka to regularise irregular Bangladeshis abroad; and strong steps to cut migration cost and Biman Bangladesh Airlines ticket prices.
The AEBA event was chaired by AEBA president Joynul Abedin and conducted by secretary general Kazi Enayet Ullah.

headline_en: Chief Adviser seeks Singapore's help to bring back laundered money
summary_en: On 10 November 2024 Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus asked Singapore's High Commissioner Derek Loh for help in recovering money laundered from Bangladesh and in cutting the cost of recruiting Bangladeshi workers. The envoy responded positively and advised Bangladesh to digitalise its overseas recruitment system.

facts.statement: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus urged Singapore to work with Dhaka to significantly reduce the cost of recruiting workers from Bangladesh, saying the interim government wants to cut migration costs so expatriates can send more money to their families, and proposed building 'a model framework' with Singapore for reducing recruitment cost.

Singapore's High Commissioner to Bangladesh Derek Loh gave assurance of help on recruitment cost, said Singapore is also keen to stop illegal money transactions in the recruitment process, and advised Bangladesh to digitalise its overseas recruitment system to reduce the risk of human trafficking and worker exploitation.

Yunus told the envoy that large amounts of money had been laundered from Bangladesh to many countries including Singapore and asked for Singapore's full cooperation to bring it back; the envoy promised cooperation.

headline_en: How much longer will drivers wait
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial on the BRTA driving-licence backlog says workers going abroad as drivers suffer most because they cannot leave without the smart-card licence, and some pay brokers heavily. It reports about 625,000 licences stuck at BRTA, the dispute with card supplier Madras Printers, and the interim government's decision to issue PVC cards to new applicants.

facts.statement: The editorial says outbound workers (drivers) are suffering most from the BRTA licence backlog because they cannot go abroad without the driving-licence smart card.
One driver bound for abroad applied for a licence through a broker paying 13,000 taka and had been waiting two months.

Fuzayel Ahmed, owner of a visa-processing service firm in Paltan, Dhaka, told Prothom Alo that many of his clients wait for licences and that some obtained a licence through brokers by spending 50,000 taka.
facts.source_in_article: Fuzayel Ahmed, owner of a visa-processing firm in Paltan

facts.statement: According to Prothom Alo reporting, about 625,000 (6.25 lakh) people's driving licences were stuck at BRTA. BRTA gives the applicant an application-acknowledgement paper instead of the licence, which drivers show to avoid police harassment on the road.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo news report cited in editorial

facts.statement: The interim government decided to drop the driving-licence smart card system and issue ordinary plastic polyvinyl chloride (PVC) cards. BRTA sources say PVC cards go to new applicants while old applicants get the earlier (smart) card; the PVC card can be printed quickly and will carry a QR code to verify the licence.

Card supplier Madras Printers says it cannot supply cards because BRTA is not paying its bills; BRTA says it cannot give licences because Madras Printers is not supplying cards. Under the contract the supplier was to deliver 4 million (40 lakh) cards by July 2026 but had delivered only 2 million (20 lakh) so far.

A 2021 Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) survey found 83.1 percent of households faced corruption when getting a driving licence and 83.7 percent took the service through brokers or other intermediaries.

headline_en: Thailand's e-visa for Bangladeshis to start early next year
summary_en: Thailand told Bangladesh's ambassador on 24 October 2024 that it would launch an e-visa service for Bangladeshis in early 2025. The Thai official also described the five-year Destination Thailand (DT) visa for medical travellers, warned about fake documents submitted through agents, and announced visa-free travel for official passport holders from 19 December 2024.

facts.statement: The Thai government said it would start an e-visa service for Bangladeshis in early 2025, letting Bangladeshi nationals apply for and receive a visa online from home. Thailand has already started e-visa service at 69 embassies worldwide.
facts.source_in_article: Thai Foreign Ministry consular department DG Worawoot Pongprapapant (ওরাউত পংপ্রাপাপান্ত), per a press release of 27 Oct 2024

facts.statement: The Thai official advised Bangladeshi passport holders who want to come to Thailand for medical treatment to apply for the DT (Destination Thailand) visa through the Thai Embassy in Dhaka. The DT visa is given for five years, allows a stay of up to six months at a time, lets one caregiver accompany the patient, and does not require a recommendation letter from the Bangladesh Embassy in Bangkok.
facts.source_in_article: Thai Foreign Ministry consular department DG Worawoot Pongprapapant (ওরাউত পংপ্রাপাপান্ত), per a press release of 27 Oct 2024

facts.statement: The Thai official urged Bangladeshi applicants who submit papers through agents to verify the documents' authenticity, otherwise there may be a fine; he warned that a person whose visa application documents contain forged or false information can be blacklisted.
facts.source_in_article: Thai Foreign Ministry consular department DG Worawoot Pongprapapant (ওরাউত পংপ্রাপাপান্ত), per a press release of 27 Oct 2024

facts.statement: An agreement signed in April 2024 allowing official passport holders of Bangladesh and Thailand to travel to each other's country visa-free takes effect on 19 December 2024; diplomatic passport holders have had this facility since 2018.

headline_en: 65 Bangladeshis return home from Lebanon
summary_en: On 23 October 2024 a second group of 65 Bangladeshis, including 2 newborns, returned to Dhaka from war-hit Lebanon, bringing the total to 119. A third group of 31 was due the next day via Jeddah; 1,800 Bangladeshis had registered to return, with repatriation coordinated in partnership with IOM.

facts.statement: A second batch of 65 Bangladeshis from Lebanon, including 2 newborns, landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 5:34 pm on Wednesday 23 October 2024 on a commercial flight of Saudi Arabia, bringing the total returned from Lebanon to 119.
The first batch from Lebanon, 54 expatriate Bangladeshis including 7 children, returned on 21 October 2024.

A third batch of 31 Bangladeshis was to leave Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport for Jeddah on the morning of 24 October 2024 (Lebanon time) and reach Dhaka around 1 am after Thursday midnight.
A total of 1,800 Bangladeshis registered to return home from Lebanon; each of them is to be brought back in phases.
Repatriation of Bangladeshis affected by the conflict in Lebanon is being coordinated in partnership with IOM (International Organization for Migration).

summary_en: Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain said on 17 October 2024 that the government was trying to bring back Bangladeshis who want to leave war-hit Lebanon, at government cost, with first flights expected on 20 and 22 October. About 1,800 of an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 Bangladeshis there had registered; about 90 percent of them were irregular, and the government was arranging waiver of exit-clearance fines.

facts.statement: The number of Bangladeshis in Lebanon is 70,000 to 100,000; about 1,800 of them registered to return home because of the war.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain, speaking to journalists at the Foreign Ministry on 17 October 2024

facts.statement: The Foreign Adviser said 53 people were expected to arrive in Dhaka on the first flight on 20 October 2024 and 58 on 22 October 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain, speaking to journalists at the Foreign Ministry on 17 October 2024

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshis in Lebanon do not want to return: they spent a lot of money to go and, not knowing what they would do back home, want to stay despite the danger.

facts.source_in_article: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain, speaking to journalists at the Foreign Ministry on 17 October 2024

facts.statement: IOM is working to bring back 200 people on a chartered flight; the government is arranging flights for the others; those willing to return are being brought at government expense. About 50 people a day can come.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain, speaking to journalists at the Foreign Ministry on 17 October 2024

facts.statement: Because more than 50 seats cannot be obtained on flights from Beirut, and bringing everyone by air is not assured, the government was considering taking people by sea to Turkey's Mersin port and then flying them home, although this is very costly.
