headline_en: Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit: the 10 mistakes that get applications refused
summary_en: An explainer on Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), an open work permit of up to three years for graduates of Canadian institutions, listing ten reasons applications are refused after recent IRCC rule changes. It covers eligible programmes (CIP list), full-time status, the 24-hour off-campus work limit, in-Canada study, language scores, the 180-day deadline, documents, passport validity, temporary intent and inadmissibility.

facts.statement: Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) is an open work permit that lets graduates of Canadian educational institutions work for any employer in Canada; depending on the length of study it can be valid for up to three years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: Since 2024 only programmes on the IRCC-approved Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) list are eligible for the PGWP. Recently 119 new fields were added and 178 programmes removed, effective from the start of 2026. Diploma and certificate students in particular must confirm their programme's CIP code; changing programme midway means eligibility must be re-checked under the new code.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: For the PGWP a student must keep full-time enrolment throughout the study period; part-time is allowed only in the final semester, and part-time study at other times can make the application ineligible.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: International students in Canada may currently work off-campus up to 24 hours a week while classes are in session; working without authorisation can cancel student status and lead to PGWP refusal.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: Online study from outside Canada counted towards PGWP eligibility during Covid, but this no longer applies to programmes that started after September 2024; study must now be completed while present in Canada.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: From 1 November 2024 proof of language proficiency is mandatory for the PGWP: minimum CLB 5 for college graduates and CLB 7 for bachelor's, master's or PhD graduates; test results more than two years old are not accepted.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP application must be submitted within 180 days of receiving proof of programme completion; after the deadline the application is generally refused.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: The PGWP is applied for online. Required documents: proof of programme completion (degree, diploma or transcript), proof of full-time enrolment, language test results, proof of an eligible programme and, if required, medical exam results. Incomplete applications are refused.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP cannot be valid beyond the passport's expiry; if the passport expires earlier the work permit is issued for a shorter time, so it is better to renew the passport before applying.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A PGWP applicant must show they will leave Canada when the permit ends (temporary intent), even if they may later wish to settle; family ties, property or proof of a job in the home country help.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

facts.statement: A person can be found inadmissible to Canada for medical problems, insufficient financial means, a criminal record, security risk or giving false information; even a family member's inadmissibility can affect the application.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo higher-education explainer, citing IRCC rules

headline_en: Expatriate Bangladeshis are getting the consulate's hotline service in Jeddah
summary_en: The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah runs a toll-free hotline (8002440051), launched in April 2019 under a ministry-ILO agreement and now funded by the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, which has received more than 200,000 calls. It operates 8 am to 9 pm local time except weekly and other holidays. Users praise the free service, though one caller complained operators could not check e-passport delivery status for him.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah's toll-free hotline number is 8002440051 (as printed); expatriates can call free of charge for immediate service every day from 8 am to 9 pm local (Saudi) time, except weekly and other holidays.

The Jeddah consulate hotline was launched in April 2019 as a pilot, in addition to the consulate's regular telephone lines, under an agreement between the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and the International Labour Organization (ILO); it is now run as a toll-free line funded by the Wage Earners' Welfare Board.

Since launch the Jeddah consulate hotline has received more than two lakh (200,000) calls; most callers were given information on the spot and the rest were connected to the relevant section of the consulate. Callers' names, mobile numbers and the place they called from are entered in a register.

Through the Labour Welfare Wing, expatriates seeking special exit and domestic workers call the Jeddah consulate hotline from Jeddah and from areas outside Jeddah to get service (as worded in the article).
More than 10 lakh (1 million) expatriate Bangladeshis work in Jeddah and the western region of Saudi Arabia, which is served by the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah.
A Bangladeshi working in Taif, Abul Hossain, said he got information about his passport by calling the Jeddah consulate hotline.

A Bangladeshi working in Bisha, Dulal, said he got through to the Jeddah consulate hotline only after several tries; after submitting an e-passport application he called to ask whether the passport had arrived and was told the hotline has no server (access) and that he should check online himself, which he said less-educated workers do not know how to do. He asked that operators check and tell callers.
A Bangladeshi domestic worker in Makkah, Dilruba, called the Jeddah consulate hotline about her problem and said no money was deducted from her phone for the call.

headline_en: Man gets life imprisonment in Faridpur 15 years after human trafficking case
summary_en: On 30 September 2025 the Faridpur Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal sentenced Md. facts.statement: On Tuesday 30 September 2025 Judge Shamima Parvin of the Faridpur Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal sentenced Md. headline_en: Rajbari's Azad, who went to Iraq to restore his family's fortunes, is murdered there
summary_en: Azad Ali Khan (47), a clothing trader and tailor from Goalanda, Rajbari, went to Iraq on 24 June 2025 through his cousin Babul Khan, an Iraq-based expatriate, after paying BDT 725,000. He was left at a hotel in Baghdad without the promised job, later took work in a house, was not paid for over three months, and was killed by the house owner on 12 September 2025 after a pay dispute; his dismembered body was found in a drain on 18 September. The house owner surrendered to police and confessed.

facts.statement: Azad Ali Khan (47) of Goalanda, Rajbari spent BDT 725,000 (7 lakh 25 thousand taka), raised through borrowing, to go to Iraq on 24 June 2025 through his cousin Babul Khan, a Bangladeshi living in Iraq.
facts.source_in_article: Azad's relatives and his wife Sharmin Begum

facts.statement: Azad Ali Khan was promised a well-paid job in Iraq, but after arriving at Kazumia (কাজুমিয়া) in Baghdad his cousin Babul Khan, who had taken him there, left him at a hotel and went away; he got no job and stayed unemployed.
After a few days in the Baghdad hotel Azad Ali Khan took work in a private house; after more than three months of work the house owner had not paid his wages, which led to a dispute.

On 12 September 2025, during an argument over unpaid wages, the house owner (described by a relative as his kafil) killed Azad Ali Khan in Baghdad, cut the body into three pieces according to the cousin Babul, and dumped it in a nearby drain.
facts.source_in_article: Azad's relatives; brother-in-law Anwar Hossain quoting Babul Khan

facts.statement: Six days after the killing, on Thursday 18 September 2025, cleaners smelled the body in the drain and told police, who recovered the dismembered body; the house owner then surrendered at the police station himself and confessed to killing Azad.
In about four months in Iraq Azad Ali Khan was able to send home only BDT 60,000 in total, his wife said, because he could not get work.

After reporting the death by phone at about 2 am, the cousin Babul Khan, who had taken Azad to Iraq, could not be reached properly by the family; the family said they did not know what to do next. The wife last spoke to Azad on the night of 11 September, when he said he was not well.
facts.source_in_article: wife Sharmin Begum and brother-in-law Anwar Hossain

headline_en: Every expatriate's life is a novel
summary_en: A first-person 'Dur Porobash' reader column by a Bangladeshi doctor on training at a Paris hospital describes the lives of Bangladeshis he met there. One waited 12 years in Europe for a residence card without visiting home; another reached Paris via Libya and a Mediterranean boat to Italy and has worked 14 hours a day at a kebab shop for seven years; a third paid BDT 10 lakh to reach Cyprus and another BDT 10 lakh to reach Paris and is jobless, selling roasted corn for 5 to 10 euros profit a day.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi named Azad in Paris came to Europe on a programme and stayed on, applied for permanent status and expected a residence card ('sthayikoron card') in two or three years, but waited more than 12 years; he said that leaving Europe without the card would mean he could not come back, so he did not visit Bangladesh for 12 years. He received the card about 15 days before the column was written and was going home.

Giasuddin from Sylhet reached Paris via Libya: in Libya the smuggler ('adam bepari') kept him confined in one room for a month with one piece of bread and one cup of water a day, then sent him across the Mediterranean towards Italy.

On Giasuddin's Mediterranean crossing from Libya, 80 people were put on one plastic boat at night and one of the passengers was made the boatman; the trip was supposed to reach Italy after one day but the boatman lost the way and after two days no land was seen. A cargo ship found them adrift and handed them to the Italian coastguard. Three other boats left with them and Giasuddin later learned that one sank at sea.

Giasuddin has worked for seven years at a kebab shop in Paris grilling about 300 chickens a day over wood fire, working 14 hours a day (leaving at 8 am and returning at midnight), and sends almost his whole monthly pay to Bangladesh.
Giasuddin did not visit Bangladesh for seven years while waiting for a residence card; about a month before the column he was given status in Paris for one year and planned to go home in September.
A Bangladeshi man selling roasted corn beside a Paris metro station said he spent BDT 10 lakh to go to Cyprus, worked there two years and sent some money home, then lost his job.
The same man, unable to do anything in Cyprus, paid another BDT 10 lakh to come to Paris; seven months after arriving he had no job.

The jobless Bangladeshi in Paris said his room rent is 150 euros and food costs about 100 euros (the article does not state the period); he sells roasted corn on a fellow Bangladeshi's advice and makes 5 to 10 euros profit a day, sends nothing home, and says fellow Bangladeshis no longer help him.

The columnist writes that his plan to stay in a hotel for a few days in Paris and then look for a rented room would have been 'a big mistake', as he understood after arriving; he was housed through a Bangladeshi contact arranged before travel.

The columnist says expatriates often do not get the benefit of the money they send: relatives take it, and when they return in old age they find the property registered in others' names and nothing in their own.

headline_en: How students going abroad can get certificates attested online
summary_en: An explainer (source: UNB) on the government's online attestation service for educational certificates and transcripts for people going abroad, available on the MyGov platform, which the article says started on 'last 1 October' so applicants no longer need to go to the Ministry of Education. It walks through registration, profile verification with NID or birth registration, finding the service, filling the form, uploading scans, paying any fee, tracking, and downloading the attested document.

facts.date: since 1 October (article published 3 July 2025 says 'last 1 October'; year not stated)
facts.statement: The Bangladesh government runs an online service for attesting educational certificates and academic transcripts for people going abroad; applicants no longer have to go to the Ministry of Education for attestation.

For online attestation of education documents on MyGov, the only identity document needed is the national ID (NID) or an online-registered birth registration certificate; documents must be scanned beforehand and saved as JPEG, JPG or PNG files of no more than 1 MB each.

Step 1 of online attestation: open an account on the MyGov platform with name and mobile number or email address and set a password; then verify the profile immediately with NID or birth registration number and birth year. One NID can verify only one MyGov account.

On the MyGov homepage the first listed service is 'বিদেশগামী নাগরিকদের সার্টিফিকেট সত্যায়ন' (certificate attestation for citizens going abroad); clicking it shows separate application options for each type of document, and a specific document can also be found through the homepage search box, including by voice command.

Each MyGov attestation application option lists the documents needed, upload rules, the application fee, how to fill the online form and the processing time; these differ by document type, some services are free and others carry a set fee, payable by online banking, card or mobile payment gateway.

In the MyGov attestation form, fields marked with a red star are mandatory and others may be left blank; a plus (+) button adds multiple pages or files; a partly filled application can be saved as a draft and resumed later from the 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' (service management) option after logging in with mobile number or email and password.

Documents can be uploaded to the MyGov account once, right after account verification, and are then attached automatically to later applications; an applicant cannot go to the next step until attachments have fully uploaded.

After final submission each MyGov attestation application gets a unique tracking number; its status can be checked from the 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' option and the personal dashboard. After the set number of working days the attested document appears on the dashboard and can be downloaded.

headline_en: Balance of payments improves on the back of exports and remittances
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show the overall balance of payments deficit fell to USD 66 crore at the end of July to April of fiscal year 2024-25, helped by strong growth in goods exports and remittances. Remittances in July to April were USD 2,454 crore, 28 percent higher than a year earlier, and reserves rose.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh in July to April of fiscal year 2024-25 were USD 2,454 crore, 28 percent more than in the same period of the previous fiscal year.
After April, a record amount of remittances also came in May 2025, according to economists and Bangladesh Bank officials.

On 29 May 2025 Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves were USD 25.80 billion by Bangladesh Bank's own method and USD 2,057 crore by the IMF's BPM6 method; a year earlier the BPM6 figure was USD 1,872 crore, so usable reserves rose USD 185 crore in a year.

Bangladesh's overall balance of payments deficit fell to USD 66 crore at the end of July to April of FY2024-25, from USD 107 crore a month earlier and USD 557 crore at end April of the previous fiscal year; the current account deficit fell to USD 139 crore, from USD 661 crore for all of FY2023-24.
In May 2025 the dollar exchange rate in Bangladesh was left to the market; officials said it stayed stable because supply was good.

headline_en: After a year in a Saudi ICU, Rajshahi's Jabbar opens his eyes once brought home
summary_en: Abdul Jabbar Sardar (45) of Tanore, Rajshahi, who went to Saudi Arabia in January 2018 for BDT 7 lakh, was badly injured in a road accident on 10 May 2024 and lay in a Saudi hospital ICU for over a year. After his wife applied in writing to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board in January 2025 and the Board wrote to the embassy, he was flown home unconscious on 23 May 2025 and is now in Rajshahi Medical College Hospital. The Board says the family can apply for treatment assistance of up to BDT 1.5 lakh if he is a registered worker.

facts.statement: Abdul Jabbar Sardar, a farmer from Hiranandapur village, Tanore, Rajshahi, raised BDT 7 lakh through borrowing and went to Saudi Arabia on 16 January 2018.

On landing at the airport in Saudi Arabia Jabbar was put to work as a cleaner; he understood that the brokers had 'sold' him as an airport cleaner. After three years he was sent away from the airport job empty-handed.
After three years of airport cleaning work in Saudi Arabia Abdul Jabbar Sardar was dismissed with nothing in hand; he later got work at another establishment through a man from his home area.

Abdul Jabbar Sardar was seriously injured in a road accident in Saudi Arabia on 10 May 2024; Saudi law enforcement rescued him and admitted him to a local hospital, where he remained in the ICU for more than a year; a tracheostomy tube was inserted there.
facts.source_in_article: wife Adori Khatun; Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal, ICU in-charge, Rajshahi Medical College Hospital

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board has a programme to bring a migrant worker back to Bangladesh by contacting the embassy, on an application from the worker or the worker's family.

summary_en: A 35-second viral video shows a man hanging from and falling off a moving train near Nasratpur station, Adamdighi, Bogura on Sunday 18 May 2025. headline_en: Fees for English-medium exams can be sent abroad through exam centres: Bangladesh Bank
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank issued an order on Monday 21 April 2025 allowing banks to remit abroad, without its prior approval, fees for O Level, A Level and AS Level exams held in Bangladesh and for tests such as TOEFL and SAT. Authorised exam centres may collect the admission and exam fees in taka and banks remit against invoices.

facts.statement: Under a Bangladesh Bank order issued on 21 April 2025, authorised exam centres may collect admission and exam-related fees in taka for O Level, A Level/AS Level and tests such as TOEFL and SAT, and the fees can be sent abroad through the centres; the centres must be duly approved by the foreign authority concerned.

Banks in Bangladesh can now remit fees for TOEFL, SAT and similar tests and for secondary/higher-secondary equivalent foreign exams held in Bangladesh without Bangladesh Bank's approval, which was previously required; banks remit on the basis of an invoice and a detailed statement, and must take a declaration and undertaking from the exam centre before the remittance.

headline_en: Air ticket bookings cannot be held for more than three days
summary_en: The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism has issued ten directives, gazetted on 18 February 2025, to curb abnormal rises in air ticket prices. Airlines may not hold a booking for more than three days (72 hours) without issuing the ticket in the passenger's name with passport details, group-booked blocked tickets must be sold within seven days, all tickets must be sold online with the price shown, and Biman and others were told to act to cut fares for migrant workers going to the Middle East and Malaysia.

facts.statement: No airline in Bangladesh may hold an air ticket booking for more than three days (72 hours): a booked ticket must be issued in the passenger's name within three days, the booking must be made with the passenger's name, passport number and passport photocopy, and a booking not ticketed within three days must be cancelled automatically.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism directive

facts.statement: Tickets that airlines and travel agencies had blocked through group booking before the directive must be sold in the names of specific passengers within seven days, failing which they are cancelled automatically within the following three days.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism

facts.statement: For group bookings the actual sale price of each ticket must be reported to the civil aviation ministry at the time of sale and the ministry will publish it on its website; all air tickets must be sold online, with the price shown online and on the ticket.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism directive

facts.statement: If a travel agency stockpiles more tickets than demand and sells them through other agents so that prices rise, the original travel agency's registration certificate will be cancelled or suspended.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism directive

facts.statement: The civil aviation ministry directed Biman Bangladesh Airlines and others concerned to take the necessary steps to reduce ticket fares for migrant workers going abroad, including to the Middle East and Malaysia; no fare figure is given.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism directive

headline_en: Service seekers allege they are sent back repeatedly and forced to use brokers
summary_en: An inquiry committee of the Department of Immigration and Passports heard 15 to 16 complainants at Rajshahi Circuit House on Monday 17 February 2025 about bribe-taking at the Rajshahi Regional Passport Office. Complainants described being turned back over invented errors until they paid BDT 2,000 to BDT 20,000 through intermediaries, with Ansar members said to fix everything; the deputy director, Rozy Khondoker, declined to comment before the inquiry report.

facts.statement: At Rajshahi Regional Passport Office, complainants told an inquiry that applicants with correct papers are shown false errors and sent back repeatedly until they go to a broker; Ansar members there 'solve all problems', and those who pay a bribe through a broker are served first while the queue stays where it is. One complainant claimed 98 percent of people have to pay bribes there.
facts.source_in_article: a complainant (social worker) before the inquiry committee

facts.statement: A woman told the inquiry her passport form at Rajshahi Regional Passport Office was rejected for an error at the start and the deputy director gave no solution; she paid a BDT 2,000 bribe through an intermediary, was sent straight to the photo room, and the same form was accepted.
facts.source_in_article: a woman complainant before the inquiry committee

facts.statement: The nephew of a Rajshahi city BNP leader said his uncle, who has a court case against him, submitted the court's permission with the passport application, but the file was held for three months by the deputy director; after a BDT 20,000 bribe paid through an intermediary the passport was issued within 15 days.
facts.source_in_article: nephew of a Rajshahi city BNP leader, before the inquiry committee

facts.statement: A pharmacy owner in Rajshahi city told the inquiry he paid a BDT 2,000 bribe through an intermediary, after which his passport was corrected.

facts.statement: The Department of Immigration and Passports formed an inquiry committee after victims held a human chain on 20 November against corruption at Rajshahi passport office and deputy director Rozy Khondoker filed a police complaint against protesters; on 17 February 2025, from 11 am to 5 pm at Rajshahi Circuit House, director A K M Mazharul Islam and assistant director Moinul Hossain took written and oral statements from 15 to 16 complainants and will submit a report.

headline_en: Government issues 10 directives to control air ticket prices
summary_en: On Tuesday 11 February 2025 the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism issued a circular with ten directives, effective immediately, to stop abnormal rises in air ticket prices. They cover named bookings with passport copies, automatic cancellation after 72 hours, release of blocked group tickets, online sale with printed prices, tariff filing, a ban on selling above approved fares and through unregistered agencies, and special fares for outbound workers.

facts.statement: Directive 1: any ticket reservation in Bangladesh, including group bookings, must have the passenger's name, passport number and passport photocopy attached; if the ticket is not issued in that passenger's name within three days of booking it is cancelled automatically after 72 hours.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directive 2: tickets blocked by airlines or travel agencies through group booking up to the date of the circular must be sold with passenger name, passport number and passport copy within seven days; otherwise the airline cancels them automatically within the next three days.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directives 3 and 4: for group bookings the real ticket price must be reported to the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism as soon as the ticket is sold and will be published on a website; all air tickets must be available for sale online and the price must be stated online and on the ticket.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directives 5 and 6: airlines and travel agencies must follow tariff filing under the Civil Aviation Rules 1984 and publish the tariff approved by the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB/Bebichak) on a website; no airline or travel agency may sell a ticket above the CAAB-approved fare, and travel agencies must give the passenger the ticket at the airline-set price and a sales receipt.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directive 7: if a travel agency hoards extra tickets without need and sells them through other agents so that the price rises, its registration certificate will be suspended or cancelled.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directives 8 and 9: airlines operating flights in Bangladesh and travel agencies are to arrange special air fares for workers going abroad, and Biman Bangladesh Airlines, all airlines and the Board of Airlines Representatives (BAR) are to take the necessary steps within seven days to reduce ticket fares for migrant workers to the Middle East, Malaysia and elsewhere; no fare amount is stated.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

facts.statement: Directive 10: ticket sales through travel agencies not registered under the Bangladesh Travel Agency (Registration and Control) Act 2013 must be stopped.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism circular

headline_en: Demand for jobs for expatriates harmed over the mass uprising
summary_en: At a press conference at the National Press Club on Friday 7 February 2025, returnees under the banner 'expatriates from the United Arab Emirates and elsewhere' made six demands, including jobs and a trust like the July Shaheed Smriti Foundation for expatriates who were arrested and sent back after protesting abroad in support of the July-August 2024 movement. They alleged that the then consul general in the UAE passed protesters' details to Emirati law enforcement. The article recalls that the UAE jailed 57 Bangladeshis for protesting and later pardoned them and 75 more.

facts.statement: A court in the United Arab Emirates sentenced 57 Bangladeshis to prison terms of various lengths for demonstrating in the UAE in solidarity with Bangladesh's quota reform movement; the UAE government later pardoned them after efforts by Bangladesh's interim government.
Towards the end of November 2024 the UAE government pardoned a further 75 detained Bangladeshi expatriates.

Returnees alleged that some people handed the addresses and passport numbers of Bangladeshis who protested in the UAE and other countries to the consular office, that the then Consul General in the UAE, B M Jamal, sent the information to that country's law enforcement, that Awami League leaders prepared lists of protesters and critics, and that expatriates in the UAE were arrested on that basis; they demanded those responsible be identified and tried.

summary_en: Opening the integrated online attestation system (first step of implementing the Apostille Convention 1961) on Wednesday 29 January 2025, Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said 60,000 Bangladeshi passports are stuck in Italy because of doubts about the credibility of documents. He also spoke of manpower shortages at missions, citing Qatar, said a decision has been made to increase mission staff, and of the image cost of Bangladeshis being the largest group among those drowning in the Mediterranean.

facts.statement: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said 60,000 Bangladeshi passports are stuck in Italy because of doubts over the credibility of documents; he said every case has some problem, for example a Bangladeshi broker obtained an approval from a company there that in reality is in no position to employ the person.

The Foreign Adviser said Bangladesh missions abroad are short of staff, citing Qatar: a mission that has to distribute 300 passports cannot provide other services, and even a person sent as a night guard is made to stamp passports; a decision has been taken to increase mission manpower.

The Foreign Adviser said passport services need to be digitised so that people do not have to come to the mission, and the passport reaches the applicant once correct documents are submitted; this was stated as an aim, not an existing service.
The Foreign Adviser said that Bangladeshis are the largest number among those who drown trying to cross the Mediterranean, and that this damages the country's image.

headline_en: Integrated online attestation system inaugurated
summary_en: On Wednesday 29 January 2025 the Foreign Adviser inaugurated an integrated online attestation system under the Apostille Convention 1961 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Students and professionals going abroad apply on the MyGov portal; the issuing authority, the controlling ministry and then the foreign ministry attest online and an e-Apostille certificate is downloaded, removing the need for attestation at foreign embassies in Dhaka, which charge BDT 3,000 to 20,000 per page. Documents attested this way will currently be accepted in 117 countries.

facts.statement: Bangladesh inaugurated an integrated online attestation system on 29 January 2025 to replace manual attestation of certificates for students, professionals and others going or living abroad; attestation is done under the Apostille Convention 1961, to which Bangladesh has acceded, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues an Apostille certificate as the attestation of a public document.
facts.source_in_article: the article; inauguration by Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain

facts.statement: The Apostille Convention 1961 currently has 127 party countries, but documents attested from Bangladesh will at present be accepted in 117 countries.
With an Apostille certificate, applicants will not need attestation from foreign embassies or, after travelling, from authorities in the destination country.

Under the manual system, academic certificates and other documents had to be attested by the issuing body, several authorities and the ministry concerned, then the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, then the foreign embassy in Dhaka, and after travel by the destination country's foreign ministry and authorities; for countries with no embassy in Dhaka, applicants had to travel to the neighbouring country whose embassy is concurrently accredited to Bangladesh.

Foreign embassies in Dhaka charge a service fee of BDT 3,000 to BDT 20,000 per page to attest a document; once the apostille programme is implemented this embassy fee will not be needed, saving Bangladeshi citizens an estimated BDT 500 to 700 crore a year.

To get an e-Apostille, students and professionals going abroad apply online on the MyGov portal (printed as মাইগভডটজিওভি); the issuing authority verifies and attests the document and sends it to its controlling ministry, which counter-attests and sends it online to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which counter-attests under the convention and issues an e-Apostille certificate online.

When the Ministry of Foreign Affairs completes attestation, a notification goes to the applicant's registered mobile number, and the applicant downloads the e-Apostille certificate by clicking the 'Download' button on the personal dashboard of the MyGov portal.

During manual attestation of hard copies at government offices, applicants stand in long queues and fall into the hands of brokers, and forged seals and signatures are used; the article says the apostille programme is expected to remove brokers/middlemen and forged attestation.

headline_en: How students going abroad can get certificates attested online
summary_en: A step-by-step explainer on the government's online attestation of educational certificates for people going abroad, run through the MyGov platform (www.mygov.bd) since 1 October 2024. It covers the documents and file formats needed, account registration and profile verification, finding the right application, fees and payment, uploading, tracking and downloading the attested document.

facts.statement: Bangladesh started an electronic (online) system for attesting educational certificates and academic transcripts for people applying to or going to study abroad on 1 October (2024); applicants no longer have to go to the Ministry of Education for attestation of these documents.
For attestation of education-related documents on MyGov, the applicant needs only a National ID (NID) or an online-registered birth registration certificate.

Because the whole MyGov attestation process is online, soft copies of the documents must be scanned in advance; scanned files must be saved in JPEG, JPG or PNG format and each file must be within 1 MB.
The online attestation of certificates for people going abroad is done on the MyGov platform, www.mygov.bd.
Step 1 on MyGov (www.mygov.bd): open an account by giving a name and a mobile number or email address, then set a password; this completes initial registration.

Step 2 on MyGov: after the account is opened a personal profile is created, which must be verified immediately with the NID or birth registration number or year of birth. One NID can verify only one MyGov account.

On the MyGov homepage the first listed service is 'বিদেশগামী নাগরিকদের সার্টিফিকেট সত্যায়ন' (certificate attestation for citizens going abroad); clicking it opens a page with separate application options for attesting each kind of document relevant to going abroad, from which students pick the attestations their foreign institution has asked for. A specific document can also be found through the homepage search box, including by voice command; the wanted application appears at the top of the results.

Each MyGov attestation application option lists what documents are needed, upload rules, the application fee, how to fill in the online form and the processing time; these differ by document type, and processing time is not the same for all documents.
On MyGov some attestation services are free and some carry a set application fee (amounts not given in the article); fees can be paid by online banking, card and mobile payment gateways.
In the MyGov application form, fields marked with a red star are mandatory and the others may be left blank; where applicable a plus (+) button allows adding multiple pages or files.

A MyGov application need not be completed in one sitting: it can be saved as a draft and resumed later by logging in with the mobile number or email and password and going to the 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' (service management) option.

The applicant cannot move to the next step on MyGov until attachments are fully uploaded. Instead of uploading at each application, all documents can be uploaded to the account right after account verification; relevant ones are then attached automatically when separate applications are submitted.

After final submission each MyGov application gets a unique tracking number; with it the latest status can be seen under 'সেবা ব্যবস্থাপনা' (service management) and on the applicant's personal dashboard.
After the specified number of working days, the successfully attested document appears on the applicant's MyGov dashboard and can be downloaded immediately.
The article advises verifying the MyGov profile first so the whole attestation process runs without interruption, and notes that one NID can verify only one account.

headline_en: The many sorrows of the expatriate
summary_en: A reader's essay from the UAE describing the hardships of Bangladeshi workers abroad: long separation from family, hard labour, financial pressure, isolation, discrimination, and difficulty resettling after return. It gives no figures and calls on the government to pay attention to migrants' mental health and financial security.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi expatriate writer in the UAE says most Bangladeshi workers in Middle Eastern countries get to go home no more than once a year, and many cannot return for ten to twelve years at a stretch.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says most Bangladeshi migrant workers are in hard manual work abroad such as construction, transport, services or agriculture, working from morning to evening in extreme heat or cold and sending money home at the end of the month.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says that after paying for house building, children's education, bank loan repayment and other family costs, many expatriates cannot keep any savings for themselves and are themselves under financial pressure.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says isolation and lack of direct contact with family leave many expatriates depressed, and that they sometimes need mental health care and counselling which they cannot easily get.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says workplace discrimination, racist behaviour, legal complications and visa problems are common for expatriates, that language or citizenship problems stop them securing their rights, and that in the Middle East in particular many expatriates are denied fair pay even after hard labour.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The essay says returning expatriates need a lot of money to rebuild life in Bangladesh, often cannot reintegrate into work, lose their earnings when they fail to invest them properly, and often get no government support when repaying bank loans or trying to start a business.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

facts.statement: The writer calls for special attention to expatriates' mental health and financial security so they can build a proper life after returning, and for a more responsible role from the state and government.
facts.source_in_article: Reader's essay by Md. Tofael Ahmed, writing from the United Arab Emirates

headline_en: How remittance fighters can be given VIP status
summary_en: An opinion column arguing that Bangladesh neglects remittance senders and proposing a tiered 'Wage Earners Elite Club' card with airport, travel, insurance and social-security benefits, plus a government remittance app. It cites export and remittance figures and the 6 percent incentive on formal-channel remittances. All measures are the writer's proposals, not decisions.

facts.statement: The columnist says Bangladesh's exports in the last fiscal year were about USD 47 billion; assuming about 50 percent value addition, net foreign-currency earnings from exports were about USD 23 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The columnist estimates that, judging by the current trend, remittances this year could be between USD 27 and 30 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says remittances sent through official channels receive only a 6 percent incentive, which the writer calls inadequate.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says that to remit formally expatriates must go to banks and licensed remittance houses, and describes an unskilled worker in Dubai who, rather than go through an exchange house's complicated and bureaucratic process, phones a hundi operator, agrees an exchange rate and gets money to his family, bypassing formal channels entirely.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The columnist says remittance senders are often treated badly and are not given due respect at airports or at foreign embassies.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: The column says the Chief Adviser recently said remittance fighters should be treated as VIPs.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): a government 'Wage Earners Elite Club' listing expatriates in Platinum, Gold, Silver and Bronze tiers according to remittances sent in the previous year, each tier with separate benefits.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): separate immigration and check-in counters for Elite Club members, government-paid airport transport on arrival and departure (private car or bus pick-up and drop by category), and dedicated airport lounge access for Platinum, Gold and Silver cardholders.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): Platinum and Gold cardholders treated as Commercially Important Persons (CIP), honoured with crests at national events and invited to government events; and free round-trip tickets to Bangladesh (business or economy class by category) depending on remittance amount.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): a remittance app for expatriates linked to banks and remittance houses at home and abroad (sending via bank account, mobile wallet or remittance house), showing real-time exchange rates and all fees before the transaction, with biometric login, two-factor security, AML and KYC compliance, real-time tracking by push notification, SMS and email, multiple languages and 24/7 live-chat support.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Proposal (not a decision): promote the app through embassy roadshows and seminars, print, electronic and social media, testimonials and emails via employers and embassies; and use the app's Net Promoter Score and in-app surveys to rate immigration-related services (e.g. visa tracking, residency permit renewal), airport meet-and-greet services and the conduct and performance of embassy staff.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

facts.statement: Long-term proposals (not decisions): annual renewal and re-grading of Elite Club cards on the previous year's remittance amount and consistency, with extra benefits such as free return tickets for top performers; life insurance and health care for cardholders' families up to a limit and school priority for their children; customer-service training for embassy and airport staff; and a social safety net of pension schemes, education scholarships for children and government housing loans.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion column by Masud Khan, Chairman, Unilever Consumer Care

headline_en: Higher education in Ireland: application method, costs, scholarships and facilities
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students to studying in Ireland: entry requirements, universities, admission cycle and documents, the long-stay Type D study visa (submitted via the Irish embassy in New Delhi), fees, processing time, tuition and living costs, scholarships, part-time work rules and post-study work permits.

facts.statement: For undergraduate programmes in Ireland, generally at least 75 percent marks in the higher secondary certificate examination are needed; for postgraduate study the usual condition is a bachelor's degree in the same subject with at least 60 percent. Master's and PhD programmes need a bachelor's in the same or a relevant subject; PhD applicants must show publications and MBA applicants professional experience.
Irish universities check English proficiency through test scores such as IELTS, TOEFL or PTE.

QS world rankings cited by the article: Trinity College Dublin 81, University College Dublin 171, University of Galway 289, University College Cork 292, University of Limerick 426, Dublin City University 436.

Institutions the article lists as top choices in Ireland for international students: American College Dublin, University College Dublin, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin City University, University of Limerick, University College Cork, Maynooth University, Queen's University Belfast, National University of Ireland Galway / University of Galway. Courses named as most important: business analytics, investment banking and finance, data science, medicine science, business management and administration, computer science and IT, medicine and health science, hospitality and tourism management.

Undergraduate admission at Irish universities generally starts in September, with some universities also taking a January intake; postgraduate admission starts at the end of August or in September and ends in May. Applications are made by opening an account on each university's own website and uploading scanned documents; status is shown in the account.

University application checklist for Ireland: completed application form, all previous academic documents and marksheets, passport-size photo, copies of passport and national ID, IELTS certificate, application fee receipt, letter of recommendation; for postgraduate also publications, a personal essay or writing sample and reference letters. Programmes may ask for more.
Application fees at Irish universities vary, generally EUR 45 to 90. After checking documents the university sends an offer letter, which is later used for the visa.

Bangladeshi students going to study in Ireland apply for the long-stay Type D visa, which allows a stay of more than 90 days. The application is made online; the portal keeps the applicant's information for 30 days during the process; the completed form is printed, signed and submitted with documents to the embassy.

Irish student visa documents listed: 2 passport-size photos; passport valid at least 12 months after the date of arrival in Ireland; previous passports if any; statement of purpose; offer letter from the Irish institution; proof of tuition fee payment (EUR 6,000 is the minimum to be shown at immigration, though some institutions may require the full fee); previous academic certificates; English proficiency certificate; proof of work experience where applicable; a personal bank statement of at least EUR 10,000; signed letter and national ID copy of any sponsor; completed financial summary form; private medical insurance of at least EUR 25,000 each for accident and illness; police clearance certificate.
The Irish study-visa financial summary form is at https://www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/IRL-study-visa-financial-summary.docx.
All documents for the Irish student visa must be originals, and any document in Bangla must be supplied with a full English translation.

To submit the Irish visa application, the applicant first takes an appointment at the visa application centre and receives a confirmation email with the date; on that date they attend in person to give biometrics (fingerprints, photo). The embassy address printed is C-17, Malcha Marg, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi, Delhi-110021, India.
For an Irish visa the visa facilitation service charge is INR 3,518 per applicant; the visa fee is INR 5,300 for single entry and INR 9,000 for multiple entry.

An Irish study visa takes 30 working days to 2 calendar months, sometimes longer; the article advises applying 6 to 8 weeks before the travel date. Once decided, the visa and original documents are returned by courier.

Study costs in Ireland as given: public universities EUR 14,000 to 21,000; private institutions EUR 12,000 to 14,000; Institutes of Technology (IoT) EUR 10,000 to 12,500. The article also gives annual costs of EUR 9,850 to 25,500 for bachelor's and EUR 9,500 to 34,500 for master's and doctoral degrees. Medicine and health science is the most expensive subject.

Monthly living costs in Ireland as given: EUR 550 to 1,000 on average in most cities; EUR 1,500 to 1,800 in big cities such as Dublin; EUR 860 to 1,400 in Cork; EUR 800 to 1,100 in smaller cities such as Galway.

Scholarships listed for Ireland: Irish Government International Education Scholarship (up to EUR 10,000 per level, bachelor's, master's or PhD); Higher Education Authority international scholarship (tuition plus EUR 10,000 stipend); Erasmus Mundus (full tuition and monthly allowance for master's); Go Overseas full tuition scholarship; Enterprise Ireland's Education Ireland scholarship (EUR 3,000 to 5,000).

University scholarships listed: UCD Global Excellence Scholarship up to EUR 10,000; University of Limerick International Education Scholarship EUR 3,000; Dublin City University International Scholarship EUR 2,000 to 7,000; National University of Ireland Galway International Student Scholarship up to EUR 5,000; Maynooth University International Master's Scholarship EUR 2,000; Dublin Institute of Technology Centenary Scholarship Programme EUR 10,000.

The article says students in Ireland holding immigration Stamp 2 are covered by a permission to work that stays valid as long as Stamp 2 is valid; they need a Personal Public Service (PPS) number, which the article says is obtained through being hired for a job. Work is allowed 20 hours a week, and full time during winter and summer holidays.
The article says the minimum pay for part-time jobs in Ireland is EUR 733 a month, or about BDT 93,190.

After graduating, a work permit is needed for full-time work in Ireland; fresh graduates mainly use the General Employment Permit or the Critical Skills Employment Permit. Both initially allow up to two years of work, take 28 days to process and allow 40 hours of work a week. The General permit can be renewed for a further three years and not after that; the Critical Skills permit can be renewed every two years. Either can be applied for at least 12 weeks (3 months) before the first day of work.
The article notes that higher education costs in Ireland are somewhat higher than in other EU member states, and that English is the only language needed for study, scholarships and jobs.

headline_en: Expatriates want VIP status for remittance fighters

They also protested the budget's duty on mobile phones and demanded pensions, health insurance, free repatriation of bodies and interest-free loans.

headline_en: 'I learned yesterday how hard it is for a father to carry his son's body'
summary_en: Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) of Debgram, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria, whose Malaysia flight arranged through a broker was cancelled on Friday 31 May 2024, fell from a train door into the Meghna river at Bhairab on the way home and died; his body was recovered about 44 hours later. The family had paid BDT 6.5 lakh a year earlier to broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village and his Malaysia-based brother, who have since fled their home.

facts.statement: Tanvir Mia alias Sohel (22) of Debgram village, Akhaura upazila, Brahmanbaria, was returning home with his father on the Upakul Express intercity train on Friday afternoon 31 May 2024 after his Malaysia flight was cancelled when he fell from the train door into the Meghna river while crossing the Bhairab rail bridge in Kishoreganj; his body was recovered about 44 hours later on Sunday 2 June 2024 around midday and buried that evening.

Tanvir's family paid BDT 6.5 lakh (sare chhoy lakh taka) one year before June 2024 to send him to Malaysia through broker Alamgir Hossain of Noyadil village, Akhaura, and Alamgir's Malaysia-based brother.

Broker Alamgir Hossain first gave Tanvir a flight date of 19 January 2024, which was cancelled; a second flight was to be on the morning or midday of Friday 31 May 2024 and its cancellation was announced after the family had travelled to Dhaka. A sub-headline quotes the family that the brokers gave dates two or three times and did not keep their word.
The family trusted the broker because three days earlier he had taken 30 people (to Malaysia); many others were due to go with Tanvir on the cancelled 31 May 2024 flight.
Tanvir's father Meraj Mia sold 130 decimals (shotok) of land to send his son abroad and for his own business.
Father Meraj Mia said the people through whom he tried to send his son to Malaysia made no enquiry after the death and have fled their home; he does not know where they are.

headline_en: Crowds at the airport to go to Malaysia
summary_en: A photo caption from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 31 May 2024, the deadline for approved Bangladeshi workers to enter Malaysia. It recaps that Malaysia's market reopened in 2022 after four years, a syndicate formed again, and in March 2024 Malaysia said it would take no more workers for now; many could not get air tickets.

facts.statement: Malaysia's labour market reopened for Bangladeshis in 2022 after being closed for four years over irregularities in sending workers through a syndicate; a syndicate was formed again afterwards.
In March 2024 Malaysia said it would not take any more workers for the time being.
Workers who had already received approval and visas had to enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024 (a Friday).

For several days before 31 May 2024, on recruiting agencies' assurances, people from around Bangladesh came to Dhaka to go to Malaysia and crowded Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport every day; many could not get air tickets and were left in uncertainty.

headline_en: Critical patient takes three days just to get from Sandwip to Chattogram
summary_en: Cyclone Remal stopped Sandwip-Chattogram sea crossings for three days from Saturday 25 May 2024, stranding a critically injured boy, a pregnant woman and passengers bound abroad whose visas or tickets were about to expire. On Tuesday 28 May a single speedboat was run by special arrangement for critical patients and foreign-bound passengers.

facts.statement: When Cyclone Remal shut Sandwip-Chattogram sea transport from Saturday (25 May 2024), passengers bound abroad whose visas or tickets were about to expire were stuck on Sandwip island for about three days.

On Tuesday 28 May 2024, at the request of the Sandwip Upazila Nirbahi Officer, one speedboat carried only critical patients and foreign-bound passengers across from Gachhua Amir Mohammad Ghat by special arrangement; Md. Akbar Hossain of Santoshpur union said his flight was that Tuesday evening and he had no option but to cross.

Sandwip UNO Rigyan Chakma said boat movement must stay closed while cautionary signal no. 3 is in force regardless of the actual sea state, while crossings continue when there is no signal even if the sea is very rough; the 28 May 2024 speedboat was requested as a special case for people in distress.

headline_en: Recommendation to give expatriates a special smart card to raise remittances through legal channels
summary_en: On 24 April 2024 the parliamentary standing committee on the finance ministry recommended non-financial incentives alongside the existing financial incentive to boost remittances through banking channels. It recommended a special smart card for remitters and their families giving priority at government hospitals, service offices and with law enforcement, plus smooth airport immigration and customs clearance.

facts.statement: At its meeting in the Jatiya Sangsad building on Wednesday 24 April 2024, the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Finance recommended (a recommendation, not a decision) giving non-financial incentives in addition to the ongoing financial incentive to speed up remittances through legal banking channels, including a special smart card for remittance senders and their family members.

The committee recommended that expatriates' parents, spouses and children get special priority at government hospitals, government service offices and, for protection, with law enforcement agencies, and advised giving hassle-free immigration and customs clearance at airports.

The committee advised using a smart app to raise remittances and taking the necessary steps to issue national ID cards and birth registration certificates to expatriates so they can send money without obstruction.

The meeting was chaired by committee chairman A H M Mustafa Kamal; members and State Minister for Finance Waseqa Ayesha Khan, M A Mannan, A K Abdul Momen, Ahmed Firoz Kabir, A K M Selim Osman and Runu Reza attended.

headline_en: Higher education in Malaysia: costs and facilities
summary_en: A guide for Bangladeshi students to studying in Malaysia: entry requirements, top public universities, tuition costs, intake periods, university and student-visa documents, the EMGS online visa process (VAL in 14 working days, e-visa in 48 hours), what to do on arrival, living costs, part-time work limits, scholarships and the post-study Employment Pass.

facts.statement: The article says Malaysia has more than 2 lakh (200,000) foreign students so far, that Bangladesh ranks high by number of foreign students there, and that students from more than 140 countries study there each year.

General requirements for foreign students at Malaysian universities: at least 12 years of schooling for a bachelor's; a minimum CGPA of 3.50 out of 5 in SSC/HSC/O-level/A-level for bachelor's programmes; a bachelor's degree with a minimum CGPA of 2.5 out of 4 for master's; IELTS 6.5 (varies by programme and university); some programmes also need GRE or GMAT.

The article says Malaysia's public universities are best for low-cost higher education, topped by Universiti Malaya (UM), Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM), Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM), International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM); popular subjects are MBA, computer science, data science, medicine and health care, and banking and finance.

Depending on university and programme, a 3.5 to 4 year bachelor's in Malaysia can cost MYR 9,600 to 137,500 and a 1 to 2 year master's MYR 7,500 to 12,700; the article gives 1 ringgit as equal to 23 taka.
Malaysian universities generally take applications in two windows: one opening in June each year with a deadline up to September, and one in November with a deadline up to February.

Basic documents for a Malaysian university application: completed application form, high school certificate (for bachelor's), bachelor's certificate (for master's), passport-size photo, valid passport, motivation letter, English proficiency certificate (IELTS or TOEFL), and proof of application fee payment where applicable; requirements differ by university.

Documents for a Malaysian student visa: one passport-size photo on white background (35/45 mm); the first pages of a passport with 18 months' validity (photo and personal details) and any pages with visa stamps; acceptance/offer letter from the Malaysian university; medical report; copies of all academic records with certificates; a personal bond of MYR 750, refunded at the end of study on condition that the student has not broken Malaysian immigration law; English proficiency certificate (IELTS/TOEFL).

Additional documents for a Malaysian student visa: an approval letter from the Malaysian university; a cover letter issued by the university mentioning the student's application to study there; proof of sufficient funds for tuition and living costs; and a pre-VAL (pre Visa Approval Letter) medical report issued in the student's home country, although the student may instead do the pre-VAL medical screening at a registered clinic after arriving in Malaysia. Applicants to public universities must contact their institution for pre-VAL medical instructions.

Bangladeshi students must apply for a student visa before coming to Malaysia; the application can be started online through EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services), or made through a representative of the chosen university or an EMGS agent. The article describes EMGS as part of Malaysia's Ministry of Higher Education and a one-stop centre for international students at public and private institutions.
The applicant pays a visa processing fee for the Malaysian student visa, which varies by university and programme (no amount given).

The Visa Approval Letter (VAL) for Malaysia is issued 14 working days after the application is submitted, and status can be checked meanwhile. Bangladeshi students also need an e-visa to enter Malaysia, which the article says can be obtained within 48 hours.

After arriving in Malaysia: within the first seven days do medical screening at any EMGS-registered clinic; in the first month arrange housing, check with the institution and EMGS that academic documents are in order, and collect from the university the Student Pass (a sticker in the passport) and the i-Kad (the foreign student identity card that confirms legal stay in Malaysia).
The article says accommodation, food, transport, medical, phone and internet and bank account in Malaysia together may cost about USD 170 to 180 (the period is not stated in the article).

Foreign students in Malaysia are allowed at most 20 hours of part-time work, counted across semester breaks or weekend holidays, tied to the validity of the Student Pass; applications for part-time work must be made through the student's own institution. The article advises looking for work on campus (library, cafe, office reception).

Scholarships named for Malaysia: Malaysian government scholarship, Malaysia Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan, and Malaysian International Scholarship; many universities also have their own scholarships, grants and tuition waivers, and loans, tuition waivers and education funds exist.

After study, a foreign graduate must first secure a job in Malaysia; the employer then handles the work permit, also called the Employment Pass, valid for a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 5 years. The passport should have at least 18 months' validity when applying for the work permit.

headline_en: Accused allegedly snatched from police after attack in Faridpur
summary_en: On Friday 1 March 2024 in Majhardia village, Saltha, Faridpur, Md. Turap Molla (45), a warrant-listed accused in a human trafficking and murder case, escaped after police arrested him; locals say relatives attacked police and snatched him, which police deny. A local leader says he is the main accused over a man taken to Libya on a promise of Italy, tortured and killed.

facts.statement: According to local Swechchhasebak League leader Md. Faruk Hossain, on 12 February 2023 a man named Nur Alam of Majhardia village, Saltha, Faridpur was taken to Libya on the promise of being sent to Italy, tortured and killed (the article's wording attaches the date 12 February 2023 to the incident).
facts.source_in_article: Md. Faruk Hossain, local Swechchhasebak League leader

facts.statement: Md. Turap Molla (45) of Majhardia village, Majhardia union, Saltha, Faridpur, described by a local leader as a manpower broker ('adam byabsayi'), is the main accused in the human trafficking and murder case over Nur Alam's death, and a court has issued an arrest warrant against him.

On Friday 1 March 2024 around Jumma prayers, a Saltha police team led by ASI Nazmul Hossain arrested Turap Molla in front of the Eidgah mosque in Majhardia west para; locals and the UP chairman Md. Afsar Uddin Matubbar say his brothers, nephews and relatives then snatched him from police, while ASI Nazmul Hossain says there was no attack: family members pushed Turap down and he ran away.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Faruk Hossain; UP chairman Md. Afsar Uddin Matubbar; ASI Nazmul Hossain

facts.statement: Faridpur Assistant Superintendent of Police (Nagarkanda Circle) Md. Asaduzzaman said several police teams were in the field to catch Turap Molla and he hoped to arrest him quickly.
The case illustrates the route in which a person from Faridpur is promised Italy but is taken to Libya and tortured there.

headline_en: 63 Bangladeshis in Malaysia surviving on mashed potato and lentils
summary_en: At least 63 young men from Gangni upazila, Meherpur, who went to Malaysia in November 2023 have been confined for three months in a three-storey building in Kuala Lumpur without work, with passports taken and visas mostly expired. Each paid BDT 4 to 5 lakh to three related local brokers working with an unnamed Dhaka travel agency in Banani; the district administration advised families to file cases but none agreed.

facts.statement: At least 63 young men from four villages of Kazipur union and Mohammadpur village of Motmura union, Gangni upazila, Meherpur, who went to Malaysia for labour work in November 2023, said on 11 February 2024 that they had been held for three months on the ground and first floors of a three-storey building in Kuala Lumpur with no work, not allowed outside, and living on two meals a day of mashed potato and lentils.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: On landing in Malaysia, agency people took the workers by vehicle to a building and took away all their passports; they were promised work within one month (elsewhere: within 40 days of arrival) but three months passed without any job.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Suruj Ali and Awal of Sahebnagar village and Abdullah of Mohammadpur village (Gangni, Meherpur), who are cousins, took BDT 4 to 5 lakh from each of the men to take them to Malaysia for labour jobs.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Meherpur men were promised construction labour jobs in Malaysia at a monthly salary of BDT 45,000 to 50,000 within 40 days of arrival; none received any work.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The victims say 54 of them were taken on 6 November 2023 to an agency's office on Road 4, Banani, Dhaka, stayed there several days, and were flown from Dhaka airport to Malaysia on one flight at about 6 pm on 11 November 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The confined men said almost all of their visas had expired; they live crammed into a few rooms; potatoes, lentils and rice are delivered morning and night by Chinese and Malaysian nationals who do not talk, threaten them when they ask about work and tell them to contact those who sent them from Bangladesh. Many have become mentally and physically ill and said they might be driven to suicide.
facts.source_in_article: Stranded workers, by WhatsApp to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Kazipur union ward 1 UP member Faruk Hossain said more than a hundred people from Kazipur and nearby areas went to Malaysia hoping for good work, arranged by a travel agency in Dhaka, and none of them got work.
facts.source_in_article: Faruk Hossain, UP member, Kazipur union ward 1

facts.statement: Abdullah of Mohammadpur village told Prothom Alo by phone that 'some trouble happened in Malaysia' so work could not be given, that everyone would get work within the month (he hoped by 28 February 2024), and that those who do not get work would be brought home after getting visas affixed; he did not answer whether they would get their money back. He said he is a computer operator at the Dhaka travel agency. Main broker Suruj Ali's phone was switched off.

headline_en: Current monetary policy not enough to control inflation
summary_en: At an ICAB roundtable on the January-June 2024 monetary policy, economists and business leaders said the policy will do little to control inflation because the exchange rate is not stable. Several speakers touched on remittances: they cushion rural inflation, remitters get a different dollar rate from exporters, and remittance inflows have fallen. One speaker said students going abroad struggle to buy dollars, often outside banks.

facts.statement: Former state minister for planning Shamsul Alam said on 31 January 2024 at an ICAB roundtable that remittances arriving through both formal and informal channels are keeping the impact of inflation in rural Bangladesh less severe than it would otherwise be.
facts.source_in_article: Shamsul Alam, former state minister for planning

facts.statement: CPD honorary fellow Mostafizur Rahman said in January 2024 that exporters are given one dollar rate while people bringing in remittances are given another rate, which he said has already created discrimination; he argued a 'shock therapy' on the exchange rate would raise both exports and remittance inflows.

DCCI president Ashraf Ahmed said in January 2024 that dollar inflows, including good remittance inflows, were one of the drivers of Bangladesh's growth in recent years, but remittances have now fallen a lot.
facts.source_in_article: Ashraf Ahmed, president, Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry

facts.statement: BUILD CEO Ferdaus Ara Begum said in January 2024 that four different exchange rates are seen in the market, and that people going abroad to study have to struggle to buy dollars, in many cases from outside the banks, adding extra pressure on their parents.
facts.source_in_article: Ferdaus Ara Begum, CEO, Business Initiative Leading Development (BUILD)

facts.statement: Ferdaus Ara Begum of BUILD said in January 2024 that although manpower export (sending workers abroad) is doing well, foreign currency is not coming in to the same extent.
Former ICAB president Jamaluddin Ahmed said in January 2024 that Bangladesh has about 250 authorised money changers but more than 700 businesses are operating in the currency exchange market.

headline_en: Canada's two-year cap to cut foreign students by 35 percent; what Bangladeshis should do
summary_en: On 22 January 2024 Canada announced a two-year cap on international student entry, limiting approvals to 360,000 per year, about 35 percent fewer than in 2023, citing a housing crisis. Provinces will set quotas per institution; some provinces may see about 50 percent fewer foreign students, and spouse open work permits are limited to spouses of master's, PhD and postdoc students. The article gives advice to Bangladeshi students on choosing provinces and institutions.

facts.statement: On Monday 22 January 2024 Canada announced a two-year cap on the entry of international students; the immigration ministry said the government decided to approve at most 360,000 students in 2024, about 35 percent fewer than the number admitted in 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Canada's immigration ministry statement; Immigration Minister Marc Miller

facts.statement: Canada said that during the two-year cap period announced in January 2024, issuing work permits to some postgraduate students will be stopped.

Immigration Minister Marc Miller said in January 2024 the cap is not permanent: it will run for the next two years, at 360,000 students per year, and was taken because of Canada's growing housing crisis.

Under the 2024 cap, the federal government in Ottawa will tell each of Canada's 10 provinces and 3 territories its number of foreign students after counting current students; the provinces will then sit with their colleges and universities to set a number for each institution. As of 23 January 2024 the per-province numbers had not been fixed.
Marc Miller said in January 2024 that in some provinces the number of foreign students will fall by about 50 percent under the cap.
Students already studying in Canada whose visa expires before they finish their studies will not fall under the 2024 cap.
Canada has taken steps to reduce foreign students at newly sprung-up small private colleges, which face allegations of low-quality education while bringing in students from around the world.

From the January 2024 announcement, only spouses of students at master's level and above (such as PhD and postdoctoral students) will get an open work permit in Canada; other students' spouses will not be given work permits.

The article advises Bangladeshi students to choose institutions carefully because competition will be high at institutions in Ontario and British Columbia, so they can try provinces other than these two.
The article advises Bangladeshi students to research before choosing a Canadian institution and to pick reputable ones.

The article advises Bangladeshi students who want to stay in Canada after study to finish their studies on time and then start working on a work permit; chasing work instead of studying will make it quite hard to stay on in Canada.

headline_en: Why Bangladesh's growth prospects are shrinking
summary_en: An opinion column by economic analyst Mamun Rashid argues that Bangladesh's growth slowdown to around 4 percent is structural, citing a narrow base (garments and remittances), weak investment climate, weak banks, poor human capital and corruption. On remittances, it says most Bangladeshi migrant workers are unskilled, earn much less per head than workers from competitor countries, and their earnings go mostly to family consumption and land or flats.

facts.statement: Economic analyst Mamun Rashid wrote in a November 2026 Prothom Alo column that remittances are the second pillar of Bangladesh's foreign currency earnings after garments (which bring over 80 percent of export income), a concentration that leaves the economy exposed to external shocks.

Mamun Rashid wrote in November 2026 that because most Bangladeshi migrant workers are unskilled, their per-head income is much lower than that of workers from competitor countries, and most of the remittance income is spent on family consumption and unproductive things like land and flats rather than long-term productive capital.
Mamun Rashid wrote in November 2026 that Bangladesh's growth is now around 4 percent, and that a stable remittance flow is still one of the country's strengths.

headline_en: Let foreign relations serve our own interests, on our own terms
summary_en: An opinion piece by Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah (University of Brunei Darussalam) argues Bangladesh should pursue strategic autonomy among India, China and the United States and diversify partners. In passing it says relations with Southeast Asia and the Gulf must go beyond sending workers, that migrant workers' fair wages, safety and legal protection should be central in Gulf bilateral talks, and suggests skilled employment and worker protection cooperation with Malaysia.

facts.statement: Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah wrote in a November 2026 Prothom Alo opinion piece that Bangladesh needs a specific programme with Malaysia on skilled employment and worker protection, and that relations with Southeast Asia should go beyond sending workers and official visits.
facts.source_in_article: A K M Ahsan Ullah, professor, international security and migration, University of Brunei Darussalam

facts.statement: A K M Ahsan Ullah wrote in November 2026 that relations with the Gulf countries should go beyond sending workers and buying energy, and that economic cooperation will be meaningful only when migrant workers' fair wages, safety and legal protection become central topics of bilateral talks.

A K M Ahsan Ullah suggested in November 2026 that Bangladesh can build issue-based alliances with like-minded countries on migrants' rights, climate compensation, refugee burden-sharing and ocean resources.
