headline_en: Studying in Taiwan: part-time jobs and scholarships, IELTS or TOEFL score needed
summary_en: A study-abroad guide (sourced to UNB News) on higher education in Taiwan for Bangladeshis: eligibility, English requirements, intakes, documents, the resident visa process via the Taipei Economic and Cultural Center in New Delhi (no Taiwan mission in Bangladesh), visa and authentication fees, scholarships, study and living costs, part-time work rules (20 hours a week with ARC and work permit), and the route to jobs and permanent residence.

facts.statement: Eligibility for study in Taiwan: undergraduate needs a pass in higher secondary or equivalent diploma; master's needs a bachelor's degree; doctoral needs a master's degree.

Learning Mandarin or Chinese is not required for bachelor's, master's or doctoral study in Taiwan, as there are English-taught courses; English proficiency needed is IELTS 5.5 to 6 or TOEFL iBT 71 to 80. Learning Mandarin is important for cheaper study options and scholarships.

Taiwanese universities admit in September (fall) and February (spring); fall has the most course choices. Applications are online through each institution's own application platform; deadlines and conditions must be checked on the university websites.

Documents for admission to a Taiwanese university: higher secondary or equivalent diploma certificate, academic transcript, online application form, passport-size photo, national ID card, passport, IELTS or TOEFL score, application fee (varies by university; some accept applications free), several recommendation letters, proof of financial solvency, study plan, statement of purpose, and a research proposal for PhD.
Bangladeshi students going to Taiwan for higher study must apply for a resident visa, which allows stay of more than 180 days (6 months) and is valid for 1 year; it can be renewed after one year.

Taiwan resident visa application: enter details at https://visawebapp.boca.gov.tw and upload scanned documents; after submitting, download and print the application, making sure it carries a barcode, and sign it in the marked place.

For Bangladeshi passport holders the key document for a Taiwan resident visa is a guarantee letter from a person living in Taiwan inviting the applicant. The applicant downloads the Letter of Guarantee form (from the rocaiwan.org website, link printed in the article) and sends it to the inviter, who fills, scans and e-mails it back and keeps the original. TECC (Taipei Economic and Cultural Center) then gives the applicant a visa number, which the applicant passes to the inviter; the inviter then submits the original guarantee letter to Taiwan's BOCA (Bureau of Consular Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs). After the consular office verifies it and informs TECC, the visa is issued. Guarantee verification takes at least seven working days.

Documents for a Taiwan student resident visa: signed online visa application form; request letter stating purpose, type and length of study; two recent passport photos on white background (3.4 x 4.5 cm); valid passport with more than six months' validity and at least two blank pages; admission offer letter from a Taiwanese university; photocopies of latest degree certificate and transcripts (originals to show at the counter; must be translated into English); guarantee letter; health certificate issued within three months; proof of finances (sponsor's income tax return and last three months' bank statements, covering at least six continuous months of living costs); scholarship certificate stating period and amount if any; study plan; language certificate if applicable; police criminal record certificate if applicable. These documents must be authenticated by an ROC (Republic of China) foreign mission.
Taiwan has no embassy in Bangladesh; visa documents are submitted and the interview held at the Taiwan consular office in India: 34, Paschimi Marg, Vasant Vihar, New Delhi-110057, India.

At the Taiwan office in New Delhi, documents are taken, fingerprints and photo are recorded for biometric registration, visa fees are collected and an ICR (Invoice cum Receipt) is given, which must be brought when collecting the passport with visa. Resident visa processing takes a total of eight working days; original documents are returned after processing.

Document authentication fees for a Taiwan visa: 400 NTD (1,498 taka) per original and 200 NTD (749 taka) per copy, ready after two working days; for same-day (one day), 600 NTD (2,246 taka) per original and 300 NTD (1,123 taka) per copy (article uses 1 NTD = 3.74 taka).

Taiwan resident visa fee: single entry 2.2 thousand NTD or 5.7 thousand Indian rupees (about 8,137 taka); multiple entry 4.4 thousand NTD or 11.4 thousand rupees (16,275 taka) (article uses 1 rupee = 1.43 taka).

Taiwan scholarships: Taiwan Scholarship Program gives a monthly stipend of 25,000 NTD (93,582 taka); Taiwan ICDF Scholarship gives 12,000 NTD (44,920 taka) a month for undergraduates, about 18,000 NTD (67,379 taka) for master's and 20,000 NTD (74,866 taka) for PhD; Huayu Enrichment Scholarship gives 25,000 NTD (93,582 taka) a month.

Study costs in Taiwan: undergraduate about 53.2 thousand to 84 thousand NTD a year (about 199,142 to 314,435 taka); master's 33 thousand to 168 thousand NTD a year (123,527 to 628,870 taka); PhD tuition 96 thousand to 2 lakh NTD a year (359,354 to 748,654 taka).

Living costs in Taiwan: foreign students spend on average 3,000 NTD (11,230 taka) a month on groceries; eating out at a local market costs at least 60 NTD (225 taka); city bus monthly pass 500 NTD (1,872 taka); Taipei Metro MRT monthly fare 700 NTD (2,621 taka); a one-bedroom apartment outside the city centre about 12,000 NTD (44,920 taka) a month; utilities 2,000 NTD (7,487 taka) a month.

International students in Taiwan may work up to 20 hours a week during the semester, but need two things: an Alien Resident Certificate (ARC) card, the foreign student ID and proof of legal residence, which students should apply for first on arrival; and a work permit applied for from the Workforce Development Agency, usually valid for one semester or six months and to be re-applied for before it expires.

Part-time jobs for students in Taiwan include restaurant work and sales assistant (non-academic) and research or teaching assistant, translator and language teaching at a cram school (academic); they pay 120 to 400 NTD (450 to 1,498 taka) an hour.
After at least five continuous years in Taiwan a person can apply for permanent residence, with no criminal record in that period, skills in a specific job, and a contribution to national prosperity.
A fresh graduate in Taiwan may stay an extra six months after graduation to find a job or start a business, and can apply for a further six-month extension if more time is needed.

Average annual salary for full-time jobs in Taiwan is about 1 lakh to 6.7 lakh NTD (about 374,327 to 2,507,991 taka); jobs include doctor, pharmacist, nurse, marketing manager, salesperson, electrical, mechanical and civil engineer.

headline_en: 26 more Bangladeshis return from UAE after pardon
summary_en: 26 more Bangladeshis jailed in the UAE for protesting in support of the anti-discrimination student movement returned home on 13 September 2024 on an IndiGo flight after a pardon. The UAE had arrested and jailed 57 Bangladeshis in July; President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan pardoned all 57 at Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's request, and 31 had already returned in three batches. BRAC Migration Programme is giving transport and other support and will work with the Wage Earners' Welfare Board on reintegration.

facts.statement: In July 2024 the UAE government arrested 57 Bangladeshis for protesting in the UAE in support of the anti-discrimination student movement and sentenced them to jail terms of various lengths.

At Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus's request, UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan ordered a pardon for the 57 Bangladeshis and their jail sentences were withdrawn; 31 returned home in three batches, and the remaining 26 returned on Friday 13 September 2024 at 3:05 pm on an IndiGo Airlines flight.

BRAC Migration Programme, through the Probashi Kallyan (expatriate welfare) desk, is giving the 26 returnees from the UAE necessary support including transport costs; the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's Wage Earners' Welfare Board and BRAC will work on their economic and social reintegration, providing psychosocial and economic support according to their needs.

summary_en: On Eid ul-Azha (17 June 2024), the article reports that nearly 4.75 lakh workers went to Malaysia in a year and a half, spending on average more than 5 lakh taka each, and some got no job. A worker from Shibchar who paid 4.9 lakh taka has had no work for three months. Many Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia get no leave on Eid, work long shifts, and are not even given time for Eid prayers.

facts.statement: In about a year and a half up to June 2024, nearly 4.75 lakh (পৌনে পাঁচ লাখ) Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia, spending on average more than 5 lakh taka each; some of them did not get jobs. Several lakh more Bangladeshi workers were already in Malaysia.

Md. Rajib of Shibchar, Madaripur, went to Malaysia about three months before 17 June 2024 after spending 4 lakh 90 thousand taka, but had not got a job; he was staying with an uncle (খালু) in Kuala Lumpur for food and lodging and could not send any money home.

Migrants say a large share of workers in Malaysia get no holiday even on Eid day and go to work instead of Eid prayers. Md. Raihan Kashem, in Malaysia for six to seven years and working at a supershop in Malacca, said he gets no leave on Eid and is not given time even to pray, in any year.

In the Facebook group 'Malaysia Kajer Khobor' (মালয়েশিয়া কাজের খবর), migrant Iftekhar Ahmed wrote he was going to duty on Eid day, working 10 am to 10 pm, and was refused a single day off; another migrant, Md. Ashraful Ahmed, replied that he works 6 am to 8 pm.

facts.statement: As of 19 March 2024, 23 Bangladeshi sailors were held hostage by pirates in Somalia together with a Bangladeshi ship; Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said the government was using various strategies to free the sailors safely and also free the ship.

Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on 19 March 2024 that not everything about the hostage sailors could be disclosed, asked media to report carefully, and declined to comment on a Reuters report about the hijacked Bangladeshi ship.

Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on 19 March 2024 that during his recent bilateral visit to the UAE and in a meeting with UAE ambassador Abdulla Ali Abdulla Khasif Almudi in Dhaka, Bangladesh discussed making it easier to transfer an "akama" (permission to work) from one employer to another in the UAE.

headline_en: Facebook romance: woman in trouble after giving over 1 crore taka
summary_en: A man from Narail, Benojir Hossain (40), posing on Facebook as "Shahid Hasan", a US-based Bangladeshi-born pilot, promised to marry a divorced bank officer and take her to the USA, and took 1 crore 9 lakh taka from her for passport, visa and other pretexts. CTTC arrested him after she filed a case at Wari police station in November 2023; she later settled with him for 60 lakh taka because of debt pressure, and he got bail.

facts.statement: Benojir Hossain (40) of Narail, Bangladesh, sent a Facebook friend request under the name "Shahid Hasan", claimed to be a pilot and Bangladeshi-born US citizen living in New York, gathered the woman's personal details over Messenger, told an emotional story of being an orphan, proposed marriage and promised to take her to the USA.

The fraudster asked for money repeatedly for passport, visa and other pretexts to take the woman to America; she sold 37 bhori of gold jewellery, cashed savings certificates, took a bank loan, borrowed from relatives and sent money to 13 mobile financial service numbers he gave.
A divorced woman bank officer paid 1 crore 9 lakh taka to the fraudster who promised to marry her and take her to the USA, according to the CTTC report submitted to court.
When the woman went to the Khulna address he had given and found no "Shahid Hasan" there, the fraudster threatened to leak private videos on social media.

The woman filed a case at Wari police station, Dhaka, in November 2023; the Dhaka Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit arrested Benojir in Narail soon after; investigating officer SI Md. Sumon of the CTTC Cyber Terrorism Investigation division said the taking of the money was verified.

In a compromise petition filed in court on 28 January 2024, the victim said she had received money from the accused and did not object to his bail; she told Prothom Alo she settled for 60 lakh taka because she could not repay bank and personal debts; the court then granted bail.

summary_en: On 8 October 2026 Malaysia's Immigration Department (JIM) raided premises in Taman Datuk Ahmad Razali and detained 20 people, including 11 Bangladeshis, over foreign worker quota fraud. The syndicate allegedly used an "A-to-B" method: company A got approval and brought workers on PLKS temporary employment passes, then supplied them for profit to company B. 265 Bangladeshi passports were seized; profit per worker was estimated at RM 3,800 to 5,000.

facts.statement: On Thursday 8 October 2026, from 7:30 am, Malaysia's Immigration Department (JIM) intelligence and special operations division from Putrajaya headquarters, with two divisions of the Inland Revenue Board (IRB), raided premises in Taman Datuk Ahmad Razali and detained 20 people aged 23 to 47, including 11 Bangladeshis, for alleged involvement in foreign-worker quota fraud.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: Those detained in the 8 October 2026 Malaysian raid were two Bangladeshi men believed to be owner and manager of the business, 6 local women staff, and 12 foreign customers: 9 Bangladeshi men and 3 Indonesian women.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: In the raid the team seized 265 Bangladeshi, 63 Indonesian, 12 Pakistani and 1 Indian passports, and RM 6,700 believed to be money paid by customers.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: The syndicate used an "A-to-B" method: a company (employer A) got approval to bring foreign workers and brought them under the PLKS temporary employment pass, but the workers were then supplied for profit to another company (employer B) instead of working for the original employer; the syndicate is also suspected of submitting false company information to obtain foreign-worker quota approvals.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: Further investigation found that foreign workers brought into Malaysia did not work for the companies that applied for the quota, but worked independently at other companies.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: The syndicate is believed to have made a profit of RM 3,800 to RM 5,000 for each worker brought to Malaysia; the companies understated profits to evade tax and did not file personal income returns from 2020 to 2023.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

facts.statement: Malaysia's Immigration Department said it will keep taking strict action against all illegal activity, including those who plan, run and profit from misuse of foreign-worker quotas; the raid was based on public tip-offs and the department's own intelligence.
facts.source_in_article: JIM Director General Datuk Zakaria Shaaban

headline_en: Six years in Canada: US will not return Bangladeshi detained at border
summary_en: Mahin Shahriar, a Bangladeshi-origin refugee claimant living in Canada since 2019, accidentally crossed into the US on 12 May 2025 while following a friend's directions near Montreal and is held by ICE in Buffalo. ICE is ready to return him to Canada but the Canada Border Services Agency has not approved his entry; his lawyer Wasim Ahmed has sought an urgent Federal Court hearing. His first asylum claim had been rejected because it was filed through a fraudulent immigration consultant.

facts.statement: On 12 May 2025 Mahin Shahriar, a Bangladeshi-origin refugee claimant in Canada, followed a friend's phone directions to an address near Montreal very close to the border, unknowingly crossed into the US, reported to border guards, and was detained; as of October 2025 he was in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in Buffalo.
ICE was ready to send Mahin Shahriar back to Canada, but the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) did not approve his entry; ICE cannot deport him to Bangladesh because he has no travel document.
CBSA said by email that it does not comment on individuals detained abroad and that each entry decision is made case by case.

Under the Safe Third Country Agreement, there is a rule that an asylum claimant linked to Canada detained in the US is to be returned to Canada within 14 days; Shahriar's lawyer believes he should be taken back under it.
US immigration authorities acknowledged that Mahin Shahriar could face torture if sent back to Bangladesh.
Mahin Shahriar's first asylum application in Canada was rejected because it was filed through a fraudulent immigration consultant; his lawyer says this and the stress led to his breakdown.

Lawyer Wasim Ahmed applied for an urgent hearing at the Federal Court to compel Canada to take Shahriar back on humanitarian grounds, noting he has lived in Canada since 2019, his mother has refugee status and his sister is a full-time student there.

headline_en: Bangladeshi youth burned in Iraq dies; uncertainty over getting body back due to Middle East conflict
summary_en: Mohammad Ali (25) of Bhola Sadar, who went to Iraq in 2020 and worked at a company in Baghdad, was burned in a generator room fire at work on 15 June 2025 and died in hospital on Wednesday 18 June. The employer has no objection to sending the body home or burying it in Iraq, but flights from Iraq were suspended because of the Iran-Israel conflict and legal processes will take time. Bhola's DC said no ministry letter had arrived yet.

facts.statement: On 15 June 2025 Mohammad Ali (25), son of Saleh Ahmed of East Bapta Cheuakhali village, Bapta union, Bhola Sadar upazila, was seriously burned in a fire/generator explosion in the generator room of his workplace in Baghdad, Iraq; he died in a Baghdad hospital on Wednesday 18 June 2025 and his family learned on Thursday 19 June.
The employer told Ali's family it had no objection to sending the body to Bangladesh, and the family could also choose burial in Iraq.
Because of the Iran-Israel conflict, flights from Iraq were suspended for the time being in June 2025, making repatriation of Ali's body uncertain; completing legal procedures would also take time.
Bhola Deputy Commissioner Azad Jahan said no letter on the case had come from the ministry yet, perhaps would after offices reopen, and then the administration would contact the family and act.
Ali went to Iraq in 2020; he last visited home in November 2024 and had borrowed money from the company owner to build a house in Bangladesh; his income supported a 9-member family.

facts.statement: The Chinese Government Scholarship for the 2027-28 academic year is open to Bangladeshi students under the Type 'A' category through the Chinese embassy in Bangladesh, for bachelor's, master's, PhD and general and senior research or training (scholar) programmes.

To apply for the Chinese Government Scholarship, register on the official Chinese Government Scholarship website and apply online; choose 'Type-A' as the programme type and use agency number '0501'; then enter personal information, education, preferred university and subject, upload required documents and submit; interviews or other selection steps may be required as the authority instructs. headline_en: Germany makes the visa process easier for Bangladeshi students
summary_en: The German embassy in Dhaka is introducing the digital Consular Services Portal (Auslandsportal) for bachelor's and master's student visa applications from 1 January 2027, to cut long appointment waits. Applicants will fill forms and upload documents online before attending, with preliminary document checks through VFS. Those already on the old appointment waiting list must open an account on the new portal and apply again.

facts.statement: From 1 January 2027, the German embassy in Dhaka will take bachelor's and master's student visa applications through the digital 'Consular Services Portal' (Auslandsportal), where students fill in the application, submit documents and check the latest status online.

Under the new German student visa system (from 1 January 2027), applicants fill in the form and upload required documents online before appearing in person at the embassy, and can have their application documents preliminarily checked through VFS; on the appointment day, biometric data collection, visa fee payment and document verification are expected to be done faster.

Once the new Consular Services Portal starts, applicants already on the old German student visa appointment waiting list must apply again: students who registered under the old system must open an account on the new portal and apply afresh.

Under the old German embassy appointment system in Dhaka, students had to wait a long time for visa appointments; the embassy expects the new portal to reduce the waiting time, though it said re-applying may cause temporary inconvenience for those who had waited long.
Application process, required documents and detailed instructions for German student visas are on the new Consular Services Portal (Auslandsportal) and the German embassy's official website.

headline_en: 'Italy-bound thinking' a main cause of poor exam results
summary_en: In Rajoir upazila of Madaripur, where many families have members in Italy, no student at any of the seven colleges got GPA-5 in the 2026 HSC and the pass rate fell to 37.11%. Teachers and education people blame irregular attendance and boys' focus on going to Italy. The district employment and manpower office says 960 people went to Italy officially from Madaripur between June 2015 and October 2026, while a private organisation says over one lakh went irregularly to Italy and Europe from Madaripur in 15 years, over 70,000 of them from Rajoir.

facts.statement: From June 2015 to October 2026, 960 people went to Italy from Madaripur district through official (government-recorded) channels.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Abdul Jalil Mia, Assistant Director, Madaripur District Employment and Manpower Office (DEMO)

facts.statement: According to a private organisation (not named), over the last 15 years more than one lakh people from various upazilas of Madaripur went irregularly (illegally) to Italy and other European countries, of whom more than 70,000 young men from Rajoir upazila went to Italy.
A village in Ishibpur union of Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, is known as 'Italy village' (ইতালি গ্রাম); several thousand young men from this village alone have gone to Italy irregularly.

In Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, many families have a member in Italy; most boys become keen to go to Italy after passing SSC and lose interest in college studies, which education people say is one main reason for the poor 2026 HSC results.

In the 2026 HSC exam, 1,172 students sat from Rajoir upazila's 7 colleges and 435 passed (37.11%); no student got GPA-5; Rajoir Government Degree College's pass rate was 25.27%. In 2025 the upazila pass rate was 40.55% with six GPA-5s; in 2022 68.65% (62 GPA-5), 2023 59.12% (9), 2024 67.44% (26).

Sukdeb Chandra Banik, acting principal of Lundi Government Degree College, Rajoir, said boys in the area are always busy trying to go to Italy and pay no attention to studies, and girls also marry Italy-based expatriate men when they can; 80% of the college's students are girls.

Alik Kumar Dhar, headteacher of Government Rajoir Gopalganj KJS Pilot Model Institution and College, said boys rarely come to college and think 'what is the use of studying? The boy next door went to Italy and is earning lakhs of taka.'

headline_en: Bangladesh writes to Saudi Arabia seeking answers to 6 questions on two executions
summary_en: Bangladeshi nationals Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter were executed in the Makkah region on 14 October 2026 as a discretionary (ta'zir) punishment. On 19 October Bangladesh's Consul General in Jeddah handed a note to the Saudi foreign ministry asking six questions: the offence, the attested verdict, the method of execution, where the bodies are, and whether they had lawyers or sought legal aid. Saudi Arabia's prisoner list had named them without their sentences, so Bangladesh could not give consular help; Saudi had not replied.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi nationals Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter were executed in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia on 14 October 2026; the death sentence was carried out as a judge's discretionary punishment (বিচারকের স্বেচ্ছাধীন শাস্তি).

On 19 October 2026 Bangladesh's Consul General in Jeddah, Md. Sakhawat Hossain, met Saudi foreign ministry Director General Farid bin Saad Al Sehri and handed over a diplomatic note (addressed to the Makkah branch of the Saudi foreign ministry) asking six questions about the two executions: the type and nature of the offence, when and where it happened and when they were arrested; an attested copy of the verdict; how the sentence was carried out (public beheading by sword or another method); where the bodies are and whether they will be sent to Bangladesh or were buried in Saudi Arabia; whether lawyers were appointed for them during investigation and trial; and whether either sought legal aid.

Neither Dhaka nor the Bangladesh mission in Jeddah had detailed information about the execution process for the two Bangladeshis, and the mission was not sure whether they had legal representation at trial.

Saudi authorities regularly give Bangladesh lists of jailed and convicted Bangladeshis; the September 2026 list named the two later executed, one charged with 'adultery' and the other with an 'ICT' (information technology) offence, but did not give their sentences, so Bangladesh could not provide consular service without knowing of the death sentences.

According to the Saudi Interior Ministry statement, the two Bangladeshis were punished for violating sanctity by engaging in immoral acts in a mosque complex in Makkah; how this matches the charges on the prisoner list is unclear.

Diplomatic sources said that had the mission known of the death sentences it could have acted to protect the two; in such cases legal aid, appeals and high-level diplomatic intervention are usually attempted.

Foreign State Minister Humayun Kabir told journalists in Dhaka that executing on such charges was disappointing; according to information from Saudi Arabia the sentence was carried out in October 2026 after trial in a lower court and appeal court.

On 30 September 2026 Saudi Arabia sent a list of about 2,500 prisoners which said 22 Bangladeshis, including the two later executed, had been sentenced but did not specify what punishment each received; Bangladesh has written to Saudi Arabia seeking specific information about those 20 others.
As of 23 October 2026 Saudi authorities had not replied to Bangladesh's diplomatic note on the two executions.

headline_en: Visa fraud for 209 Bangladeshis in Canada: case against 5 people
summary_en: On 22 October 2026 the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) announced charges against five people running a visit-visa fraud ring that filed 243 temporary resident visa applications for 209 Bangladeshi nationals using fake Canadian hosts, invitation letters and forged documents. Four accused appeared in court in Quebec; one, believed to be in Bangladesh, faces an arrest warrant. CBSA warned that false information can bring the applicant a 5-year ban even if an agent prepared the application.

facts.statement: On 22 October 2026 the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) announced it had laid charges against five people who ran an organised visit-visa fraud ring using forged Canadian visit visa documents and false information. Four accused were brought before a court in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield (printed 'প্ররভ্যালিফিল্ড'), Quebec: Russell Mirza (রাসেল মির্জা) and Mohammad Aminul Islam of Montreal, Md. Mudassar Alam Bhuiyan of Toronto, and Md. Rakibul Hasan, believed to be in Bangladesh, for whom an arrest warrant was issued; one more associate was found to be involved.

The ring submitted 243 temporary resident visa (TRV, visit visa) applications in the names of 209 Bangladeshi nationals, showing Canadian citizens as fake hosts with invitation letters and using forged documents and false information to obtain visit visas.

The investigation began after a CBSA joint control and inspection operation with local police and fire service at a residential building in Mercier, Quebec on 3 July 2024 found signs of immigration-law violations among residents; a formal investigation started in August 2024. On 3 June 2025 CBSA anti-fraud officers executed search warrants at four locations in Quebec and Ontario, seizing many computers, digital devices and documents; investigators focused on 79 of the visa applications to build the case.

Charges in the Canadian visit-visa fraud case were laid under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA): sections 117(1) and 117(3) (organising illegal entry into Canada through conspiracy), 126 and 128(a) (knowingly helping create false information and conceal facts in immigration applications), and 131 (knowingly inducing or aiding violation of Canadian immigration law).

CBSA warned that fake bank statements, fake invitation letters or false information must never be used for a Canadian visa; even if an agent or third party prepares the application, the main applicant can face serious immigration penalties including a 5-year ban for misrepresentation.

headline_en: 59 foreigners executed in Saudi Arabia in first 6 months of this year, including Bangladeshis
summary_en: The European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR) recorded at least 108 executions in Saudi Arabia in the first half of 2026, 59 of them foreigners (including Bangladeshis) from 17 countries; 71 were for drug offences. The recent execution of two Bangladeshis in Makkah is not in that count, and how many Bangladeshis were executed in the half-year is not known. ESOHR documents lack of interpreters and legal aid for foreign prisoners on death row.

facts.statement: In the first six months of 2026 the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR) recorded at least 108 executions in Saudi Arabia, including Bangladeshis and nationals of other countries; 59 were foreigners (about 54%) and 49 Saudis (46%). How many Bangladeshis were executed in that period is not known.

Nationalities of those executed in Saudi Arabia in H1 2026 (17 countries) included Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Sudan, Yemen, Syria, Jordan, Somalia, Egypt, Nigeria, Benin, Iraq, Kuwait, Kenya, Uganda and Afghanistan.

Of the 108 executions in Saudi Arabia in H1 2026: 71 for drug-related offences (66%; elsewhere given as 65.7%), 25 for murder (23%), 9 for political and security cases (8%; also given as about 8.3%), 3 for other offences (3%); 83 (76.8%) were for crimes not involving killing; 84 (77.7%) were ta'zir (judge's discretionary) sentences.
Of the 71 drug-related executions in Saudi Arabia in H1 2026, 49 (45.3% of all executions) were of foreign nationals, most from Ethiopia, Pakistan, Sudan and Yemen.
Drug offences were the largest single cause of executions in Saudi Arabia in the first half of 2026 (71 of 108), and most executions (83 of 108) were for crimes not involving killing.
For 91 of the 108 Saudi executions in H1 2026 (84.2%), ESOHR or other organisations could not learn of or document the case before the execution, showing a continued lack of transparency.
Two Bangladeshi nationals convicted of 'immoral acts' in a mosque in Makkah were recently executed; they are not included in ESOHR's first-half 2026 count.

ESOHR documented violations in death-row cases of foreign prisoners in Saudi Arabia: no professional interpreter, no legal aid, defendants not understanding the judicial process, and no effective chance to defend themselves. Prisoners said death-row inmates were recently isolated for a short time, cut off from the outside world, and then suddenly taken for execution.
ESOHR says many people remain on death row in Saudi prisons, including 58 Ethiopians in Khamis Mushait prison, five Ethiopians and five Somalis in Najran prison, and eight Egyptians in Tabuk prison.
Under King Salman bin Abdulaziz and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, total executions reached 2,000 by the first half of 2026, a record compared with any previous reign.

headline_en: Dhaka asks why punishment details were omitted though the two were on the prisoner list
summary_en: On 19 October 2026 Bangladesh's Consul General in Jeddah asked Saudi foreign ministry DG Farid bin Saad Al Sehri why the 30 September prisoner list named Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter without saying they had been sentenced to death; the Saudi official gave no satisfactory answer, and Bangladesh sent another diplomatic note. The two, from Brahmanbaria and Tangail, went to Saudi Arabia in late 2022 and worked as cleaners for Al Majal company; they were arrested in August 2023, sentenced by a lower court, upheld by a 13-judge appeal panel, and executed on 14 October. A mission message says 306 Bangladeshis are held in western Saudi prisons on moral-misconduct cases.

facts.statement: On Monday 19 October 2026 in Jeddah, Bangladesh Consul General Md. Sakhawat Hossain asked Saudi foreign ministry Director General Farid bin Saad Al Sehri why the regular prisoner list named Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter but omitted their sentences; the Saudi official could not give a satisfactory answer. Bangladesh gave a further diplomatic note the same day asking for case details, the steps taken during the trial, and whether they had any chance to defend themselves after conviction.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Ministry officials; Sakhawat Hossain confirmed the meeting

facts.statement: On 14 October 2026 the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the Saudi Interior Ministry, reported the execution of the two Bangladeshis. On 15 October the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah sent a diplomatic note to the Saudi foreign ministry seeking details, and on 18 October the note was given again to the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka.

According to the Saudi side, the two Bangladeshis were arrested in August 2023, first sentenced by a lower court, then a 13-judge appeal court panel upheld the death sentences, which were carried out in separate cells for men and women.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi officials, as reported by Dhaka officials

facts.statement: Nazrul Islam (home district Brahmanbaria) and Sweety Akter (Tangail) went to Saudi Arabia in late 2022 and joined Al Majal company (আল মাজাল কোম্পানি) as cleaning workers; they were colleagues at the same company.

Nazrul Islam was detained on 1 August 2023 and Sweety Akter on 2 August 2023. The 30 September 2026 list said Nazrul, held in Jeddah correctional facility, was convicted of a cyber crime / information technology offence, without stating when or what sentence; Sweety Akter was listed in Jeddah women's prison for adultery, with no sentence details.
facts.source_in_article: diplomats in Dhaka, Riyadh and Jeddah; government documents

facts.statement: The Bangladeshi diplomat told the Saudi side that if the Jeddah mission had known from the list that the two had been sentenced to death, it could have acted to protect them.

A Bangladesh mission message sent from Jeddah to Dhaka on 18 October 2026 said no Bangladeshi had previously been sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia for cyber or adultery offences; 306 Bangladeshis are held in prisons in western Saudi Arabia on various moral-misconduct cases, of whom 147 have been sentenced to terms from a minimum of one month to a maximum of 15 years in prison.
In three other cyber-crime cases in Makkah, three Bangladeshis were sentenced to between six months and five years in prison.

Foreign State Minister Humayun Kabir told journalists at the Foreign Ministry on 19 October 2026 that the execution on these charges was disappointing and that there had been a lapse in information exchange and diplomatic communication; Bangladesh had asked Saudi authorities for a detailed explanation.

headline_en: From Ferdous to Imran and Akshay: stars in citizenship and visa controversies in India
summary_en: A round-up of film stars caught in Indian citizenship, visa or OCI-card controversies. Two Bangladeshi actors were made to leave India in 2019: Ferdous Ahmed, whose business visa was cancelled after he joined a Trinamool election campaign, and Gazi Abdun Noor, who had overstayed his visa by about nine months. Bollywood actor Imran Khan was told to leave by 28 October for joining a protest.

facts.statement: In 2019 Bangladeshi actor Ferdous Ahmed, who was staying in India on a business visa, joined a road show and campaign for Trinamool Congress candidate Kanaiyalal Agarwal in Raiganj during the Lok Sabha election; after a BJP complaint to the Election Commission, India's Home Ministry cancelled his business visa and served him a notice to leave India; reports say he was also blacklisted. He returned to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: media reports cited by the article

facts.statement: In 2019 Bangladeshi actor Gazi Abdun Noor was served notice to leave India by the Home Ministry after being seen campaigning for Trinamool candidate Saugata Roy in Dum Dum; reports say his visa had expired on 6 July 2018 but he stayed about 9 more months, which officials treated as a visa violation; he was told to return to Bangladesh and apply for a new visa.
facts.source_in_article: media reports cited by the article

facts.statement: India does not allow dual citizenship; an OCI (Overseas Citizenship of India) card gives foreign nationals some special benefits including residence in India but is not equal to Indian citizenship.

Mumbai police detained Bollywood actor Imran Khan (not an Indian citizen) after he joined a protest at August Kranti Maidan, and served him notice to leave India by 28 October, alleging he violated immigration law provisions by taking part as a non-citizen; his lawyer said he would challenge it in the Bombay High Court, arguing the rules do not bar OCI card holders from protests.

facts.statement: The 'Study Abroad Fair 2026', organised by Prothom Alo and the British Council with Eastern Bank PLC as banking partner, was held at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre, Dhaka, on Friday 16 and Saturday 17 October 2026, 10 am to 8 pm, offering information on higher education abroad, admission processes, scholarships and application advice; the online fair on the website ran until 25 October 2026.

More than 40 education consultancies took part in the Study Abroad Fair 2026, including AHZ (MH Global Group), BD Expert Education Consultancy, Banglay IELTS, BSC, CHS Education, Dream Study International, Dreambaz, Education Hub, Executive Study, Education Connect Global, Education At, Future ED, Faith Overseas Limited, Go Zayan, Growth Academy Global, Fantasy Global Education, H&H Global Education, Campus Group, H&I Council, International Education Counselling Centre (IECC) Limited, Lumos Global, LVS Global Education Consultancy, Maximus Education and Migration, Mentors, Maps Edu, Brit Academy, Pinnacle Consultancy Group, PFEC Global, Sheba Consultancy, Schengen Edu Limited, Study Solutions, 10 Minute School, UniGlobal, Visa Express, Wisdom and Wems Education and Migration.

Visitors at the Study Abroad Fair 2026 said they could not find a good consultancy; Minhaj Hossain, who works at a research organisation, said he wants to take his family with him while studying abroad and return after the degree; final-year student Raisa Meherin said going abroad to study is harder now than before.

headline_en: UK universities limiting admission of Bangladeshi students
summary_en: British universities are withdrawing offers to students from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria and others to avoid losing sponsor licences after the Home Office halved the maximum acceptable visa refusal rate under the Basic Compliance Assessment from 1 June 2026. The Financial Times reported that the visa application withdrawal rate (as the article words it) for Bangladeshi students rose from 7.1% to 23.5% in the first half of 2026. Prothom Alo found at least 42 UK institutions restricting Bangladeshi admissions, 20 specifically for Sylhet-region students; a consultant said about 20 of his students lost sponsorship after being called for UKVI interviews.

facts.statement: According to a Financial Times analysis of Home Office data (reported 10 October 2026), in the first six months of 2026 the rate the article calls the UK student 'visa application withdrawal rate' (ভিসা আবেদন প্রত্যাহারের হার; the article's opening otherwise speaks of visa refusals) was 40.9% for Pakistani students (3% a year earlier), 23.5% for Bangladeshi students (up from 7.1%), 22.7% for Nigerians (up from 4.5%), and 10.5% for all countries combined (up from 2.3%). Bangladesh ranked second.
facts.source_in_article: Financial Times, citing Home Office data

facts.statement: From 1 June 2026 UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) applies a stricter 'Basic Compliance Assessment' to universities: the maximum acceptable international student visa refusal rate is cut from below 10% to below 5%; the minimum rate of visa holders completing enrolment is raised from 90% to 95%; the minimum course completion rate, currently 85%, becomes 90% from June 2027. Under a new red, amber and green rating, failing institutions may have to take corrective action and serious or repeated failure risks loss of sponsor licence.

Prothom Alo reviewed two lists based on the experience of agencies recruiting international students for the UK and found at least 42 British universities, campuses and institutions with full, regional or course-based admission restrictions for Bangladeshi students: 22 have stopped or limited admission from various regions of Bangladesh and 20 have separate restrictions specifically on students from the Sylhet region; some restrict only certain courses or campuses.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo review of agency lists

facts.statement: UK institutions listed as limiting or stopping Bangladeshi admissions include Middlesex University, Keele University, De Montfort University, University of East London, University of Roehampton, University of Sunderland, Coventry University and University of Bradford. Those with separate restrictions on Sylhet-region students include University of Chester, University of Wolverhampton, Canterbury Christ Church University, University of Brighton, Cardiff Metropolitan University, Oxford Brookes University and University of Portsmouth.
facts.source_in_article: agency lists reviewed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Professor Steven McGuire, Deputy Vice-Chancellor of the University of East Anglia, told the Financial Times his institution has begun withdrawing offers to students from several countries because visa refusals rose.

For the September 2026 intake, many students who applied for UK visas were called for interviews by UKVI; when the university was told of the interview it reassessed the application and withdrew the admission sponsorship (CAS). About 20 students of Global Admission were affected, and the consultant claimed several hundred Bangladeshi students faced the same problem in the September intake.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Mustafizur Rahman, Senior Recruitment Consultant, Global Admission

facts.statement: Because of the Home Office's new compliance system, UK universities are checking students' eligibility, language ability and financial capacity much more strictly than before.

Higher tuition fees, depreciation of the taka against the pound, and higher accommodation and visa costs in the UK are putting heavy financial pressure on Bangladeshi students, and many are choosing countries other than the UK.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Mabrur Ahmed, International Student Adviser (Sylhet region), Global Admission

facts.statement: The Home Office says that although international students contribute positively to the UK economy, universities must select students more responsibly to protect the credibility and order of the immigration system.

headline_en: Special courts will be set up for expatriates: Law Minister
summary_en: At RMMRU's 30th anniversary event in Dhaka on 13 October 2026, Law Minister Md. Asaduzzaman said migrants facing harassment can get primary legal aid from the government by calling a hotline, and that special courts for expatriates are being set up at divisional level to hear only migrants' cases. He described long bathroom queues and early starts he saw among workers on a recent visit to Dubai and said Bangladeshi workers earn much less than workers from other countries.

facts.statement: Law Minister Md. Asaduzzaman said on 13 October 2026 that expatriates facing various kinds of harassment can get primary legal aid from the government by calling a hotline (the number was not given in the article).

The Law Minister said special courts (প্রবাসী আদালত) are being set up to resolve expatriates' legal problems; setting them up at divisional level is under process, expatriates' cases will be heard only in these courts, and he hoped it would be implemented soon.

The Law Minister said that on a visit to Dubai a few days earlier he saw workers' inhuman toil: long queues for the bathroom in the morning, leaving for work well before the scheduled time, and calling family after returning from a full day's work; he said Bangladeshi workers are paid much less than workers from other countries despite such hard work.

The statements were made at the 30th anniversary of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU) and 'Sonar Manush Sommilon 2026' at a Dhaka hotel, chaired by RMMRU adviser C R Abrar; President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was due to attend the closing on 14 October.

facts.statement: Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, the Prime Minister's adviser on finance and planning, said in Bangkok on Friday 9 October 2026 that linking Bangladesh's large workforce to labour markets in the Middle East and Gulf countries has created opportunities to increase overseas employment and remittances.

headline_en: 'Five, it has to be five, that's VP Nur's order': Jubo Odhikar president expelled after phone call leaks
summary_en: An audio recording spread on social media on 5 October 2026 in which Lakshmipur district Jubo Odhikar Parishad president Faruk Hossain is heard demanding money from a person wanting to go abroad for passport work, visa, police clearance and BMET card; a party source said he demanded BDT 5 lakh. He was expelled the same night. Expatriates' Welfare State Minister Nurul Haque Nur said police were asked to take legal action; Faruk claims the audio was AI-altered and that he asked BDT 5,000 for a passport.

facts.statement: In an audio recording that spread on social media on 5 October 2026, Faruk Hossain, president of Lakshmipur district Jubo Odhikar Parishad, is heard demanding money from a person wanting to go abroad as initial costs for passport work, visa, police clearance and the BMET card, saying 'five, it has to be five, this is VP Nur's order'; a party source said he demanded BDT 5 lakh (five lakh taka) for these.

On the night of Monday 5 October 2026, Jubo Odhikar Parishad expelled Faruk Hossain and relieved him of all organisational duties, in a notice signed by central office secretary Naim Hossain on the orders of central president Nadim Hasan and general secretary Muntajul Islam; Muntajul said the decision followed preliminary verification of the audio.

Expatriates' Welfare State Minister and Gono Odhikar Parishad president Nurul Haque Nur posted on Facebook that nobody can get away with extortion using his name, and that besides the expulsion the Lakshmipur Superintendent of Police had been asked to take legal action against the accused.

Faruk Hossain denied the allegation, claiming a local group used AI to edit his voice; he said a younger acquaintance named Sakib from his area asked him to arrange a passport and he asked BDT 5,000, which was distorted into five lakh taka.

headline_en: Bangladeshi youth killed in Houthi attack on Aramco facility in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: Md. Sajib Hossain, 26, from Brahmanpara, Cumilla, was killed on 4 October 2026 when a missile or drone fired by Yemen's Houthis hit an Aramco facility in the Al Khurais area of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. The Foreign Ministry condemned the attack; the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh contacted his family and employer and is coordinating with Saudi authorities to repatriate the body. His father and brother, also in Saudi Arabia, will lead the repatriation.

headline_en: Children bought and sold in the name of adoption; bargaining on Facebook
summary_en: A Prothom Alo investigation of 39 public Facebook groups (12 August to 16 September 2026) found babies offered and sought for money in the name of adoption, outside law and oversight, and a Jatrabari company brokering adoptions for a fee. Some posters sought babies to take to Italy or Australia. Bangladesh has no general civil adoption law; the 2026 Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Act treats adoption for dishonest purposes as exploitation. The article is mainly about domestic child sales.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's 2026 Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Act (মানব পাচার ও অভিবাসী চোরাচালান প্রতিরোধ ও দমন আইন, ২০২৬) includes adoption for a 'dishonest purpose' as exploitation; sections 372 and 373 of the 1860 Penal Code provide strict punishment for selling, buying or transferring a child for illegal or immoral use.

In Facebook adoption groups reviewed by Prothom Alo in August-September 2026, one woman wrote she would make a deal with a woman five-six months pregnant, pay the caesarean cost and take the baby to Italy; another sought a three-four-month-old girl to take to Australia.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo review of Facebook posts

facts.statement: Bangladesh has no general (civil) adoption law; family laws are religion-based and Muslim family law has no adoption provision. Lawyers say Hindus, Buddhists and Christians can adopt religiously, and anyone can obtain legal guardianship of a child through the family court; under the Children Act 2013, alternative care of disadvantaged children can be transferred through the Child Welfare Board.

Abdul Alim of Kushtia said he was cheated three times in Facebook adoption groups: a woman showed a baby on a WhatsApp video call and asked BDT 10,000 in advance for travel costs; after he sent it via bKash, the Facebook group vanished and all numbers including WhatsApp were blocked.

Al-Bokhari Caregiving Services Limited, Jatrabari, Dhaka (managing director Md. Abdul Ahad) advertised at Dhaka Medical College Hospital to take babies for adoption; its form sets a BDT 35,000 fee from the adopting side (Ahad asked BDT 50,000 verbally), total costs come to nearly BDT 2 lakh, an affidavit agreement is made at a computer shop, and the company does nothing about court guardianship; Ahad said they also provide surrogacy services in India.

DMP Detective Branch Joint Commissioner Syed Harun-or-Rashid said running such child-sale activity on Facebook is a crime whatever the purpose, but the social media monitoring team has not yet brought anyone to book for selling children through adoption groups.

headline_en: Jobs after studying abroad: how to spot fake recruitment and visa sponsorship traps
summary_en: An education-section explainer warns international students looking for jobs after finishing studies abroad about fake job ads, fraudulent recruiters and paid 'guaranteed' visa sponsorship offers. It gives checks: verify the post on the company's own careers page, treat requests for money as a red flag, verify the recruiter's link to the company, and do not hand over passport, bank or immigration documents before verifying.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026), citing education-sector people: a job ad seen on LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp is not by itself proof that the job is real; international students who finish studies abroad should check whether the same post appears on the company's own website and careers page, and whether the duties and application process match.
facts.source_in_article: education-related people quoted by the article

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): a demand for money in exchange for a job or visa sponsorship abroad is a major warning sign; in a normal recruitment process the company, not the job seeker, pays the recruiter.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): if a fee is requested in a job process abroad, the student should verify why it is charged, to whom it is paid and whether it is necessary; if in doubt, consult the university's career service or the international student support team.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): fraudsters targeting international graduates promise '100 percent guaranteed visa', 'guaranteed sponsorship' or 'guaranteed work visa' for money; the article says visa sponsorship actually depends on the employer, job type, candidate's qualifications and the country's immigration policy, so paid guaranteed-sponsorship promises are risky to trust without checking.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): when someone contacts a student claiming to represent an established company, check whether they really have a link to that company; using a Gmail or Outlook address is not proof of fraud by itself, but match the company website, official email domain, LinkedIn presence and contact details.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): genuine employers usually have steps such as application, interview, assessment or discussion with HR; an offer of a job within one or two days without detailed discussion or assessment is a warning sign.

Prothom Alo (25 Sep 2026): do not give a copy of your passport, bank account details or immigration documents before verifying the employer's identity and the company's legitimacy; extra checks are needed when there is pressure to decide quickly, a request for advance money, a guaranteed-sponsorship promise, or an offer that comes only through personal contact.

headline_en: Five teens and young men abducted on pretext of an outing, held and tortured by traffickers (Teknaf)
summary_en: Five teenagers and young men from Mithachhari, Ramu, Cox's Bazar were lured on 11 September 2026 with a promised trip to Teknaf's Marine Drive, then blindfolded, held, beaten and ransomed by a human trafficking gang that planned to send them by sea to Indonesia and Malaysia. facts.statement: On the afternoon of 11 Sep 2026, members of a human trafficking gang picked up five teens and young men from Mithachhari area, Ramu upazila (Cox's Bazar) in a CNG auto-rickshaw, saying they would tour Teknaf's Marine Drive and beach; at night in Teknaf they were taken elsewhere on the pretext of staying at Md. Anas alias Munna (21); other gang members fled. Anas and the five victims were handed to Teknaf Model Police Station and a case was filed.

summary_en: An opinion piece by Prof. Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed, convener of the Remittance Fair and president of the Bangladesh USA Chamber of Commerce and Industries, describes four years of trade and remittance fairs in New York with the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce. He says banks at the fair urged expatriates to send money through banks and authorised money transfer firms instead of hundi, and argues that rules of the NGO Affairs Bureau and Bangladesh Bank block expatriates from sending charitable donations to unregistered institutions in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: At the New York Remittance Fair, several large Bangladeshi banks held seminars asking expatriates to send money through banks and authorised money transfer institutions instead of hundi, and presented their special services, incentives and transfer security; some institutions held road shows in parts of New York on sending remittance through legal channels.
facts.source_in_article: Prof. Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed, convener, Remittance Fair (opinion)

facts.statement: The writer says remittance inflow from the United States to Bangladesh has grown significantly in recent years and that at times more foreign currency came from the United States than from some Middle Eastern countries (no figures given).

According to the writer, sending money from abroad to an institution in Bangladesh for charitable work is very difficult: the receiving institution is told to register as an NGO with the NGO Affairs Bureau, and that registration is hard to get because of delays and approval complexity; he names the NGO Affairs Bureau, the national security agency and Bangladesh Bank as sources of complexity.

The writer says a New York pharmacist friend, Liakat, wanted to donate USD 50,000 to the Sylhet kidney hospital (Kidney Foundation) during COVID, but it could not be sent because the foundation was not registered with the NGO Affairs Bureau; after about eight years as a charity hospital it still had not obtained registration, so donations from abroad cannot go directly to the hospital's bank account for free dialysis.

The writer urges the Bangladesh Bank governor and finance authorities not to limit expatriates' foreign currency transfers to individuals or NGO Affairs Bureau-registered bodies, and to let social organisations registered with the Ministry of Social Welfare, schools, colleges, universities, hospitals, cultural and environmental bodies and charities receive foreign donations legally under audit and reporting obligations.

The writer says this year's trade and remittance fair by the Bangladesh USA Chamber of Commerce and Industries with the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce was to be held on 17 Sep 2026 in New York City, with the New York governor expected as chief guest and senior US Small Business Administration (SBA) representatives attending.

The 2025 New York Remittance Fair's chief guest was Kelly Loeffler, head of the Small Business Administration under the Trump administration; leaders of Bangladeshi NRB business chambers from the UK, Italy, Poland and Canada attended for the first time.
The writer proposes that every expatriate Bangladeshi give at least USD 200 a year to education, health, agriculture, humanitarian aid, road repair or other public-welfare work in Bangladesh.

headline_en: From ration to farmer cards: why one ID now, and what it will contain

headline_en: Higher study abroad: how our young people fall into the push-pull trap (opinion)
summary_en: An opinion piece by Habib Rahman, a doctoral researcher at Curtin University, Australia, describes how international students, including many Bangladeshis across Australian cities, must work multiple jobs (restaurants, cleaning, delivery) to cover high tuition and living costs, so study becomes secondary. He says host countries tighten policies (higher fees, stricter English rules, age and study-gap limits, large proof of funds, rising refusals) when conditions change, and that some unscrupulous Bangladeshi agencies arrange fake bank statements and English certificates and make unrealistic job promises, leaving students with losses of several lakh taka when visas are refused.

facts.statement: The writer says a Sri Lankan student he knew in Perth, Australia, doing a two-year master's, would spend about 1 crore taka in Bangladeshi currency on the degree; the student worked from morning to night in a restaurant and a cleaning company and also delivered food on Uber, and was dismissed by his manager after breaking his hand at work and missing a few days.
facts.source_in_article: Habib Rahman, doctoral researcher, Curtin University (opinion)

facts.statement: The writer says in almost every Australian city a large share of Bangladeshi students have to support themselves through hard labour alongside study, working in restaurants, cleaning companies, ride-sharing or delivery, so that for many the struggle to survive makes study secondary.

The writer says when economic or political conditions change, destination countries in Europe, North America and Australia raise tuition fees, tighten English-language requirements, impose new limits on age and study gaps, demand proof of large financial means, restrict choice of subject, and visa risks rise for citizens of developing or politically unstable countries; visa refusal rates are rising.

The writer says some unscrupulous Bangladeshi agencies exploit students' wish to study abroad with promises of university admission, jobs, visas and an easy life abroad, sometimes preparing fake or staged bank statements, procuring English proficiency certificates, or making unrealistic promises of jobs abroad.

The writer says when a student visa is refused, a student can lose up to several lakh taka in application fees, university fees, agency charges, medical tests, documents, English tests and other costs.

The writer says students with full scholarships or strong finances have an easier time abroad, while others face uncertainty over whether they will keep a visa after study, find a job or be able to settle, amid anti-immigration politics and xenophobia.

headline_en: Bodies of 9 migrants killed in Saudi fire arrive home
summary_en: The bodies of nine of the 16 Bangladeshi workers killed in a 9 August 2026 fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman flight on 27 August 2026 and were received by the expatriates' welfare minister and the foreign state minister. Nine were identified by fingerprints; identification of the remaining six Naogaon victims by DNA is under way before their bodies are returned.

facts.statement: On 9 Aug 2026 a fire at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, killed 16 Bangladeshi workers.

After the 9 Aug 2026 Riyadh factory fire, identification of the 16 dead Bangladeshi workers was done through Saudi authorities; nine were confirmed by fingerprint checks, and the remaining six Naogaon victims were being identified by DNA tests, after which their bodies would be repatriated.

facts.statement: On Thursday 27 Aug 2026 the bodies of nine identified victims of the Riyadh fire arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight around 4:30 pm; they were received by Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury and Foreign State Minister Shama Obaed Islam, with one relative per family present, and were driven home.

Seven of the identified dead were from Atrai upazila, Naogaon (Md. Farid of Udanpoi; Rubel Pramanik, Kalimuddin Islam, brothers Mohon Ali and Sumon Ali of Gondogohali; Sohel Rana of Dubai village; Abdul Jalil Sarkar of Parkasunda); also Rabiul Islam of Mohishdanga, Naldanga, Natore and Shyamal Uddin of Mohishdanga, Bagmara, Rajshahi. A joint janaza for the Atrai seven was set for 10 am Friday 28 Aug 2026 at Atrai Molla Azad Memorial Government College ground, before burial in their villages.

headline_en: 68 data leaks in three years, no accountability or punishment
summary_en: A TechGlobal Institute (TGI) report records at least 68 data breaches in Bangladesh from January 2023 to May 2026 (36 government, 32 private), mostly detected by outsiders. It includes incidents tied to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's database, where passports, NIDs, e-TINs and financial and banking documents were at risk of exposure together, and three attempted intrusions in about six weeks in April and May 2026 into a migrant workers' database holding data on more than 1 million migrant workers.

facts.statement: TechGlobal Institute (TGI) report 'Breached and Unanswered: Bangladesh's Data Breach Epidemic (2023-2026)' says there were three attempted intrusions within about six weeks in April and May 2026 into the database of migrant workers (প্রবাসী শ্রমিকদের তথ্যভান্ডার), which holds data on more than 10 lakh (1 million) migrant workers.

TGI claims that in an incident linked to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's database, there was a risk that migrants' passports, NIDs, e-TINs and financial and banking documents could be exposed together.

TGI recorded at least 68 data breaches in Bangladesh from January 2023 to May 2026: 36 at government and 32 at private bodies; 7 in 2023, 27 in 2024, 14 in 2025 and 20 in January-May 2026 (13 government, 7 private); most were first detected by outside researchers, dark-web monitors or media rather than the institutions.

The Personal Data Protection Act 2026 for the first time requires notification of the relevant authority when a data breach occurs; TGI says broad exemptions for state agencies, delayed implementation and weak accountability remain concerns.

headline_en: 'What use is a house now, when my two boys are gone?' (families of Saudi fire victims left with migration debts)
summary_en: Families in Naogaon of Bangladeshis killed in the 9 August 2026 fire at a sofa factory in Manfuha, Riyadh (16 Bangladeshis dead, 13 from Naogaon) are left with large debts taken to send the workers abroad. Moyna Begum lost two sons whose migration loans now total 8 lakh taka with interest; Rubel Pramanik had gone three months earlier on borrowed money; Shahinur Rahman took a 5.7 lakh taka loan from a samity against his homestead land five months earlier, and his widow fears the samity may take the land.

facts.statement: On Sunday 9 Aug 2026 around 12 noon local time, a fire at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, killed 16 Bangladeshis, 13 of them from Naogaon, including four from Gondogoali village, Atrai upazila alone.

Mohon Pramanik (22) of Gondogoali, Atrai, Naogaon went to Saudi Arabia seven years before his death by mortgaging land and taking a loan of 4 lakh taka from a samity (savings association); with interest the debt has grown to 8 lakh taka, still unpaid when he died in the 9 Aug 2026 Riyadh fire.

Shahinur Rahman of Registripara, Par-Naogaon, Naogaon municipality went to Saudi Arabia about five months before Aug 2026 after taking a loan of 5 lakh 70 thousand taka from a samity, mortgaging homestead land at Par-Boalia, Naogaon Sadar; he was killed in the Riyadh fire before repaying, and his widow fears the samity people may take the homestead land if the loan is not repaid.

Rubel Pramanik of Atrai, Naogaon was sent to Saudi Arabia about three months before Aug 2026 with borrowed money (amount not stated) to repay family debts; he was killed in the 9 Aug 2026 Riyadh factory fire, leaving a daughter born 16 days earlier.
Families of the Riyadh fire victims in Naogaon say that besides waiting for the bodies, their biggest problem is repaying loans taken for the migration and supporting the household.

headline_en: Bangladeshi expatriates: why narrow views develop despite living in liberal societies
summary_en: Opinion column by North South University teacher Mohammad Jalal Uddin Shikder, prompted by a 23 July 2026 incident in which a UK-based Bangladeshi spread a Fenchuganj head teacher's Facebook reel with a negative caption. He asks why some Bangladeshis long settled in Europe or America try to police social behaviour at home, cites diaspora research, and argues that Bangladeshi migration research focuses on labour markets and remittances and neglects identity. He notes that expatriates are now also connected to Bangladesh as voters.

facts.statement: On 23 July 2026, Beauty Rani Pal, head teacher of Pitaitikar Government Primary School in Fenchuganj, Sylhet, posted a Facebook reel; she alleged that a Bangladeshi living in the United Kingdom spread it with a negative caption, triggering wide social-media controversy, after which teachers and others across Bangladesh posted reels with the same song in solidarity (Prothom Alo, 26 July 2026).
facts.source_in_article: Column author citing Prothom Alo report of 26 July 2026

facts.statement: The columnist (Mohammad Jalal Uddin Shikder, North South University) says that Bangladeshis in Europe or America rely on host-country institutions such as state schools, health care, university access, low-interest education and home loans, pensions and other social security, while many maintain their own mosques, cultural organisations, community centres and mother-tongue schools.

The columnist says most migration research in Bangladesh focuses on the labour market and remittances, and very little studies how long residence abroad changes identity and views of the home country; he calls for more research on expatriate identity crisis, the new generation, social media and global events.
The columnist notes that Bangladeshi expatriates now contribute not only to the economy but are also connected to Bangladesh as voters.

headline_en: In Raozan, terrorists are like 'kings'
summary_en: Prothom Alo investigation into political killings and extortion in Raozan, Chattogram: at least 26 murders from 5 August 2024 to June 2026, mostly tied to rival BNP factions, sand-quarry and construction-material control. Among the victims was a returnee from abroad, Manik Abdullah, shot at home on 19 April 2025. Expatriates building houses face extortion: one Noapara expatriate was asked for 25 lakh taka and went back abroad; a BNP notice alleged an Oman-based businessman was asked for 1.5 crore taka and his house burned.

facts.statement: Manik Abdullah, a Jubo Dal activist who had returned from abroad (probashferot), was shot dead at night in his own home at Bhandari Colony, Garibullah Para, Raozan, Chattogram, on 19 April 2025; his family has since left the house. Law enforcers and many locals believe followers of Jubo Dal leader Arafat Mamun were involved; Mamun's associate denies it.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo reporters, locals, law enforcement

facts.statement: In parts of Raozan (Kadalpur and nearby areas), house builders must hire masons and buy bricks, sand and cement from designated people tied to armed groups; bringing outside workers or materials is obstructed, so owners pay above market rates.

Armed men demanded 25 lakh taka from an expatriate in Noapara, Raozan, while he was building a house; he stopped construction and went back abroad, and relatives say he is not returning home for fear for his safety.

A BNP show-cause notice of 5 November 2024 accused local MP Giasuddin Quader Chowdhury of, among other things, demanding 1.5 crore taka from Oman-based expatriate businessman Yasin and burning his house; Giasuddin Quader denies all the allegations.
facts.source_in_article: BNP show-cause notice; Giasuddin Quader Chowdhury's denial to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Prothom Alo counted at least 26 killings in Raozan from 5 August 2024 to June 2026, with over 350 people injured in more than a hundred shootings and clashes; at least 16 killings were linked to political disputes, and six occurred after the BNP government took office in February 2026.

Chattogram district police say associates of Sajjad Ali Khan, a criminal hiding abroad, including Md. Raihan, Mobarak Hossain alias Emon, Md. Kader and Dhama Ilias, are extorting and working as hired killers in Raozan; Superintendent of Police Md. Masud Alam says drones are being used to locate them and checkpoints and patrols have been increased.

Jubo Dal leader Muhammad Jane Alam, who had returned to the Raozan area after 17 years and become active, was shot dead near Olimiar Hat on 5 January 2026; locals also mention a case against him over shooting at an expatriate's house and extortion.

The agencies say the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal route to Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand is the world's deadliest sea route; about 300 Rohingya and Bangladeshi nationals have been reported dead or missing on it so far in 2026.

facts.statement: According to a joint UNHCR-IOM statement issued on 16 July 2026, two boats carrying over 500 passengers, mostly Rohingya including some who came from refugee camps in Bangladesh, left Myanmar's Rakhine State in late June 2026; contact with one boat carrying about 250 people was lost shortly after departure, and another with about 280 people is believed to have sunk near Myanmar's Ayeyarwady coast on 8 July. Deaths are not yet officially confirmed.

Rohingya seeking safety and livelihoods make dangerous sea journeys on small wooden boats hoping to reach Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand; UNHCR and IOM said these voyages were outside the regular season, so sea conditions were more hostile and risky.
According to the UN, about 900 Rohingya refugees died or went missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, making it the deadliest sea route in the world for refugees and migrants.
According to UNHCR and IOM, about 300 Rohingya refugees and Bangladeshi nationals were reported missing or dead in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2026 so far.
In November 2025 a boat carrying Rohingya capsized off Langkawi near the Thailand-Malaysia border; about 12 people were rescued alive.

headline_en: Five-year ban for false information in Canadian visa applications: IRCC takes hard line
summary_en: Canada's immigration authority IRCC recently warned that false information or forged documents at any stage of a visa or immigration application count as misrepresentation under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Consequences include refusal, a ban of at least five years, a permanent fraud record, and for those in Canada, loss of status, removal and possible criminal charges. The applicant is responsible even if an agent or consultant filled in the form.

facts.statement: Under Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), any forgery or alteration in documents such as passports, visas or educational certificates counts as 'misrepresentation'; hiding important information or giving wrong information in an application is the same offence, according to a recent IRCC warning.
facts.source_in_article: IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) warning

facts.statement: IRCC lists the documents most often forged as: passports and travel documents; visas; diplomas, degrees and trade or apprenticeship certificates; birth, marriage, divorce, annulment, separation and death certificates; and police clearance certificates.

IRCC stresses that even if an agent or consultant fills in or submits the application, the applicant bears responsibility for all information in it and cannot shift the blame for false information to a third party.

IRCC says anyone who tries to get a Canadian visa or permanent residence with false information or forged documents may face: immediate refusal of the application; a ban of at least five years from entering Canada or applying again; a permanent record of fraud; and, if already in Canada, cancellation of status and removal, plus possible criminal charges depending on seriousness.

Experts advise people hoping to migrate to Canada not to fall for inducements or follow dishonest agents' advice, and to make sure their own application is truthful; IRCC asks people to visit a Canadian government link (printed as https://bit.ly/3XKMqDC) for details.
Canadian government information link on misrepresentation as printed in the article: https://bit.ly/3XKMqDC.

headline_en: Asylum claims in Canada collapse: asylum via student, visit or work visas no longer as possible as before
summary_en: Asylum claims in Canada by temporary resident visa holders (visit or student visas) fell 84% in two years, from 10,095 in April 2024 to 1,580 in April 2026, according to IRCC data. The article attributes the fall to Bill C-12 (Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act), in force from 26 March 2026, tighter screening of temporary visa applications, and digital portals with strict deadlines. Mismatches between reasons given for the visa and the later asylum claim are treated strictly.

facts.statement: According to IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) data, 10,095 temporary visa holders applied for asylum in Canada in April 2024, against 1,580 in April 2026, an 84% fall in two years.

The 'Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act' (Bill C-12) took effect in Canada on 26 March 2026, making asylum eligibility conditions much stricter; it is a major barrier for people who try to claim asylum long after entering Canada.

Canada now strictly screens asylum claims by people who entered on visit or student visas; any mismatch between the reasons shown when getting the visa and the information given in the later asylum application is treated strictly, so using a visit or student visa as an easy path to permanent residence through asylum has become very difficult.

Canada has introduced digital portals and strict deadlines for asylum processing, and the rate at which ineligible claims are quickly identified and rejected or declared abandoned has risen; temporary visa applications with unclear or suspicious purpose are being refused more often.
New laws proposed on 19 June 2026 are expected by many to further restrict Canada's asylum system.

Canadian immigration experts say the situation is a warning to those who wanted to use asylum merely as an 'easy route' to settle; the government aims to protect only those genuinely facing risk to life.
