headline_en: Bangladeshi youth killed in attack in Iraq buried two and a half months later
summary_en: Md. Shrabon alias Hobi Mia (35) of Bakultala, Munshiganj Sadar, who had worked in Baghdad as an irregular migrant since going to Iraq in 2016, was killed in a missile attack in Baghdad on 14 March 2026. His body reached Dhaka on a Turkish Airlines flight under government arrangement on 29 May 2026, about two and a half months later, with help from local administration and the Bangladesh embassy, and was buried the same day. His widow asked the government for a house on his village land so their two daughters can keep studying.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi worker Md. Shrabon alias Hobi Mia (35), of Bakultala village, Adhara union, Munshiganj Sadar, was killed in a missile attack in Baghdad, Iraq, on 14 March 2026.
Md. Shrabon went to Iraq in 2016 and had worked for several years in Baghdad as an irregular (undocumented) migrant; he had not come home in about 10 years.
Shrabon's family learned of his 14 March 2026 death in Baghdad on 16 March, when a co-worker phoned his wife Khadija Akter.

Shrabon's body was flown to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 5:15 am on 29 May 2026 on a Turkish Airlines flight under government management, and handed to the family after all legal procedures; this was about two and a half months after his death.
The return of Shrabon's body from Iraq was arranged with the cooperation of Munshiganj local administration and the Bangladesh embassy, even though he was working in Iraq irregularly.

In his last phone call with his wife on 13 March 2026, Shrabon described a terrifying situation of missile attacks all around in Baghdad and said he would come home when the war ended and not go abroad again.

Shrabon's widow Khadija Akter, who has two daughters (Habiba Akter, 16, and Nafiza Akter, 10), said the family has no means and asked for the government to build a house on his village land so the girls can continue their studies.

headline_en: Bangladeshis in Spain get direct police clearance service
summary_en: A special Home Ministry team led by Deputy Secretary Kazi Arifur Rahman gave Bangladeshi migrants in Spain police clearance certificates directly, for the first time in any European country. About 600 people were served in Barcelona from 9 to 11 May 2026, and the service was extended to the Madrid embassy on 14, 17, 18 and 19 May. Speakers said police clearance is an essential document for Spain's amnesty to regularise about 500,000 undocumented migrants.

facts.statement: A special delegation of Bangladesh's Ministry of Home Affairs, led by Deputy Secretary Kazi Arifur Rahman, gave police clearance certificates directly to Bangladeshi migrants in Spain; in the first phase in Barcelona, from 9 to 11 May 2026, about six hundred-plus (ছয় শতাধিক) expatriates received the service.
According to related sources, this was the first time the Bangladesh government provided police clearance directly in any European country.

In Barcelona the police clearance service ran daily from 10 am to 5 pm in a hall room in the Josep Tarradellas (জোসেফ তারাদিয়া) area; for new online applicants, the certificate was handed over on the spot after their information was verified.
The Home Ministry team in Spain also corrected errors in old police clearance certificates and settled long-stuck offline applications quickly by having them re-filed as new online applications.

The special police clearance service, which started on 9 May and was to run until 13 May across Barcelona and Madrid, was extended due to heavy demand; under the new decision it was to be given in the hall room of the Bangladesh Embassy in Madrid on 14, 17, 18 and 19 May 2026.

Spain's government recently announced an amnesty ('general pardon') to regularise about five lakh (500,000) undocumented migrants in the country, and a police clearance certificate is an essential document for it.
facts.source_in_article: speakers at a Spain BNP thanksgiving meeting in Barcelona, 9 May 2026

facts.statement: People involved said the special police clearance service saved Bangladeshi migrants in Spain time and money, and speakers said getting it on time made it easier for thousands of Bangladeshis to become legal.
Bangladesh's ambassador to Spain, Masudur Rahman, was chief guest at a short thanksgiving meeting held by Spain BNP in Barcelona on 9 May 2026 for the police clearance service.

headline_en: Demand to post police officers at some embassies abroad
summary_en: At a Police Week 2026 event at Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's office on 11 May 2026, senior police officers asked for police officers to be posted as liaison officers and legal attachés at Bangladesh embassies in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Dubai, Italy, Singapore and Malaysia, to help expatriates quickly and to recover laundered money via Interpol. They also asked for police to be posted again at the Department of Immigration and Passports. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said work is under way to deliver police clearance certificates and online GDs faster and ordered that past complaints of harassment over police clearance must not recur.

facts.statement: At a Police Week 2026 event at the Prime Minister's office on 11 May 2026, a senior Police Headquarters officer told PM Tarique Rahman that very large numbers of Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Dubai, Italy, Singapore and Malaysia, and asked that police officers be posted to Bangladesh embassies there as liaison officers and legal attachés so expatriates' problems can get immediate help.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said work is under way to provide citizen services such as police clearance certificates and online GDs (general diaries) quickly, and ordered police to ensure that the complaints of harassment over police clearance seen in the past do not come again.
The Home Minister said a new decision assigns joint operations in border and coastal areas: BGB, river police and Coast Guard in border areas, and the Navy at sea.

The Home Minister said integrated laws and institutions are urgently needed against money laundering, digital fraud and telecom-based crime, proposed a separate cyber crime unit in Bangladesh Police, and said a high-level committee is drafting a new law on cyber crime, false information and propaganda.
Police HQ spokesman AIG (Media and PR) A H M Shahadat Hossain said the PM listened to the police demands and the Home Minister assured that some needs would be met.

headline_en: Father's only wish: that US law enforcement finds Bristi's body
summary_en: Bangladeshi PhD student Nahida Sultana Bristi, murdered in Florida, had still not been found by US police as of 26 April 2026; her father asked US law enforcement to find her body and send it to Bangladesh. She had gone to the University of South Florida on a full scholarship on 25 August 2025. Madaripur's deputy commissioner said the family must submit an application, which the district will forward to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry to arrange bringing the body home once police find it. Fellow student Jamil Ahmed Limon's body was found on Friday 24 April and his roommate Hisham Saleh Abugharbeh (26), a US citizen, was arrested.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshi PhD students at the University of South Florida (USF) in Tampa, Florida, Jamil Ahmed Limon (geography, environmental science and policy) and Nahida Sultana Bristi (chemical engineering), went missing from 17 April 2026; both were last seen on campus on the Thursday before.

US police recovered Jamil's mutilated body from the Howard Frankland Bridge in Tampa, Florida, as announced by the Hillsborough local law enforcement agency at a press conference; Bristi's body had not been found as of 26 April 2026, though police found a body part at Limon's residence believed to be hers, without confirming.
facts.source_in_article: Hillsborough law enforcement; Bristi's father Jahir Uddin Akon

facts.statement: Local police arrested Hisham Saleh Abugharbeh, a 26-year-old US citizen who shared a room with Jamil, at his family home, over the disappearance of the two Bangladeshi students.

Bristi's father said the Bangladesh embassy in the US, Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Florida police and the Bangladeshi community in the US were keeping regular contact with the family and promised help to find the body and ensure the killers' maximum punishment.

Nahida Sultana Bristi, of Char Gobindapur, Khoajpur union, Madaripur Sadar (family living in Mirpur, Dhaka), left Dhaka for the US on 25 August 2025 after getting a full scholarship for a PhD at the University of South Florida; she had a BSc in chemistry and chemical engineering from Noakhali Science and Technology University and had enrolled in a master's at BUET before leaving.

headline_en: 2025 was the deadliest year for Rohingya sea journeys: UNHCR
summary_en: UNHCR says about 900 Rohingya refugees went missing or died in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, the deadliest year on record for sea journeys in South and South-East Asia; one in seven of the 6,500-plus who attempted the crossing died or went missing. Overcrowded, unseaworthy boats usually leave Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh or Rakhine in Myanmar for Indonesia or Malaysia. A boat that left Bangladesh on 26 March 2026 sank with about 250 missing; only 9 were rescued near the Andaman Islands on 9 April.

facts.statement: About 900 Rohingya refugees went missing or died in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, the deadliest year in the history of sea journeys in South and South-East Asia.
More than 6,500 Rohingya tried to cross the sea in 2025, and one in every seven died or went missing; UNHCR says this route has the highest death rate of all refugee sea routes in the world.
More than 2,800 Rohingya had taken the dangerous sea journey in 2026 up to 13 April; in recent years more than half of those crossing have been women and children.

Overloaded, unseaworthy boats carrying Rohingya usually set off from Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh or Rakhine State in Myanmar bound for Indonesia or Malaysia, despite risks of trafficking, abuse and death at sea.

An overloaded boat that left Bangladesh by sea on 26 March 2026 sank in rough seas in the Andaman Sea; about 250 people went missing and only 9 were rescued alive near the Andaman Islands on 9 April 2026; UNHCR is giving the survivors medical and mental health care.

There are more than 13 lakh Rohingya refugees in the region, 12 lakh of them sheltered in Bangladesh; the 2025 joint humanitarian response received only 53 percent of the required funds, and lack of funds, insecurity in camps and no education or jobs push Rohingya onto the sea route.

Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; Bangladeshi students handle education-related visa work through the Bangladesh embassy in Uzbekistan. Kyrgyzstan has no embassy in Bangladesh; Kyrgyz visa work is done through the Kyrgyz embassy in New Delhi, India.

headline_en: Bangladeshi Tanim charms Qatar with his voice
summary_en: Tanim Hasan, a young hafiz from Pakundia, Kishoreganj, who came to Qatar in 2025 and has worked for eight months as a food-delivery bike rider, went viral after a Kenyan colleague posted his Quran recitation on TikTok on 20 February 2026. The CEO of delivery app company Snoonu sent him 5,000 Qatari riyals (over 1.5 lakh taka) and promised him an office job and an imam post, plus Umrah. He lives in the Sanaiya industrial area, Street 13.

facts.statement: Tanim Hasan, a Bangladeshi from Narandi union, Pakundia, Kishoreganj, came to Qatar in 2025 for a living and has worked for the past eight months as a bike rider for a food-delivery company; he lives in the Sanaiya industrial area, number 13.

After Tanim Hasan's Quran recitation video went viral in February 2026, Hamad Mubarak Al-Hajri, CEO of the delivery app company Snoonu (printed 'সুনুনো/সুনুনু'), sent him more than 1.5 lakh Bangladeshi taka (5,000 Qatari riyals) as a gift and promised a job at the company's office, an arrangement to serve as a mosque imam, and to take him on Umrah.
Prothom Alo's 'Dur Porobash' diaspora section takes stories, videos and photos from readers abroad at email dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: 'Save me, son... it hurts so much': no ICU could be found for him either
summary_en: Md Jahangir Alam (40) of Baliadanga, Satkhira, who went to Malaysia in 2018 through a broker at great expense, fell seriously ill there, was ruined by brokers in the name of treatment and returned on 17 February 2026. He died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital on 19 February without getting an ICU bed. His family mortgaged land and sold cattle to pay his treatment in Malaysia and in Dhaka. The article mainly covers the ICU shortage at DMCH.

facts.statement: Md Jahangir Alam (40) of Satkhira, who had gone to Malaysia in 2018, fell seriously ill there (acute necrotising pancreatitis, with no bowel movement for about a month and unable to eat), returned to Bangladesh on 17 February 2026, was taken round several Dhaka hospitals and admitted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital that night, and died there on the afternoon of 19 February 2026 without getting an ICU bed.
facts.source_in_article: DMC student Alfaz Hossain; son Afzal Hossain

facts.statement: Jahangir Alam went to Malaysia in 2018 through a broker (dalal) after spending a lot of money; the amount is not given.
In Malaysia, sick Bangladeshi worker Jahangir Alam was ruined by brokers in the name of treatment: he spent money but did not get proper treatment.

Jahangir Alam could not send money home regularly from Malaysia; his family mortgaged land and sold cattle to cover his treatment costs in Malaysia and his hospital costs after returning to Bangladesh in February 2026.

Dhaka Medical College Hospital has 2,600 beds but over 4,000 admitted patients, 140 ICU beds in 8 ICUs, and a waiting list of over 40 patients per ICU bed; a senior official says at least 400 ICU beds are needed. Private-hospital ICU costs are beyond low- and middle-income families (one Dhanmondi private hospital quoted 50,000-60,000 taka per day in a 2023 case).
facts.source_in_article: Unnamed senior DMCH official; Prothom Alo 2023 report

headline_en: Elder brother had to leave for Saudi Arabia leaving his younger brother's body behind
summary_en: On Monday 23 February 2026 at about 6 am, a microbus taking Mehedi Hasan (25) of Brahmanpara, Cumilla, to Dhaka airport for his 1:20 pm flight to Saudi Arabia hit a stopped truck at Malikhil, Daudkandi, on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway, killing his brother Ibrahim Khalil (14) and the driver-owner Md Shahin (40). headline_en: BG 387, my experience
summary_en: A reader's account of a Biman Bangladesh flight from Kuala Lumpur to Dhaka on 1 January (New Year's Day), full mostly of migrant workers going home on short leave, which was diverted to Yangon because fog closed Dhaka, Chattogram and Sylhet airports. Passengers were kept in the hot plane for about three hours without updates, tempers rose, and the pilot said fuel could not be bought by card because Myanmar is under sanctions, so the Bangladesh mission brought cash. The trip took 12 hours.

facts.statement: On 1 January (English New Year's Day; the article is published 10 February 2026), a Biman Bangladesh Kuala Lumpur-Dhaka flight departing at 6:45 am (numbered BG 286 in the text, BG 387 in the headline), carrying mostly Bangladeshi migrant workers going home, could not land at Dhaka, Chattogram or Sylhet because of fog and diverted to Yangon, Myanmar, after about three hours of flying; the normal KL-Dhaka flight time is 3 hours 40 minutes.

On the diverted Biman flight, passengers were kept about three hours in the plane at Yangon with weak air-conditioning, little food and no updates from crew or pilot until passengers went to the pilot; the pilot then said fuel could not be bought by debit/credit card because Myanmar is under sanctions, so the Bangladesh mission was bringing cash to buy fuel. Passengers were then given pink dummy tickets and allowed to rest at gate 11 of Yangon airport for about an hour; the whole trip to Dhaka took 12 hours.

Many of the migrant workers on the flight had travelled overnight by bus from far away to reach Kuala Lumpur airport on very short leave; during the delay one worker filmed a vlog walking through the plane urging other workers not to send remittances in protest at their suffering.
The writer describes the Bangladeshi workers from Malaysia on the flight as living in inhuman conditions and doing 16-hour duties.
Prothom Alo's 'Nagorik Songbad' reader section takes stories at email ns@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: Those going abroad rely on the 'minus' market
summary_en: People leaving Bangladesh for cold countries such as Russia, Germany, Finland, Italy, Canada, the US and Romania buy cold-weather 'minus products' in Dhaka, mainly on the fifth floor of Anexco Tower next to Bangabazar (40-42 shops), and also at New Market, Nurjahan Market, Uttara-Baridhara outlets and Rafah Fashion on Green Road, Farmgate. The article gives prices for jackets, thermals, shoes, gloves and other items. A Finland-based worker says the gear suits indoor use but outdoor gear must be bought abroad.

facts.statement: Shubhash Chandra (28) of Araihazar, Narayanganj, enrolled in a master's programme at a university in Russia and flew on 22 January 2026; his uncle in Saratov told him to prepare for daytime temperatures of minus 2-3°C and night temperatures of minus 13-14°C, so he bought a 'minus' jacket, gloves, shoes and trousers in Dhaka before leaving.

In Dhaka, cold-weather clothing for people going to cold countries ('minus products') is sold year-round on the fifth floor of Anexco Tower next to Bangabazar, in 40-42 shops (moved there after the Bangabazar fire), and also at New Market, Nurjahan Market, outlets in Uttara-Baridhara, and Rafah Fashion on Green Road, Farmgate, which sells full sets and can make sets to suit the destination's temperature.

Prices at Dhaka's 'minus' market (Anexco Tower) in early 2026: jackets 2,000-12,000 taka depending on quality; thermal inner 500-1,000 taka; waterproof trousers 1,000-1,200 taka; sherpa hoodie 1,000-1,300 taka; shoes 2,000-4,000 taka; socks 150 taka; waterproof gloves 400-700 taka; cap 400 taka.

A seller at KS Winter Fashion, Anexco Tower, said a North Face jacket costs 70,000-80,000 taka abroad, while a similar jacket sells for 5,000-6,000 taka at his shop; goods come from buying houses and Chattogram factories, including cancelled-shipment stock and fresh orders.
facts.source_in_article: Md Redwan (30), seller at KS Winter Fashion; Aminul Islam, Ashraf Garments

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi working in Finland said the clothing from Dhaka's 'minus' market is fine for wearing at home but not much use outdoors; outdoor gear has to be bought after arriving there.

headline_en: Rangpur division: no one keeps promises, the interim government didn't either
summary_en: An opinion column on Rangpur division's neglect in development spending. It says about 250 recruiting agencies got new licences in the past 16 months but Rangpur division got not even four or five, for failing conditions. It also reports that the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sought 50 acres from BEZA for a 'skills processing zone', and that three Japanese companies were ready, with an MoU, to set up a car-driving training track on 30 acres to take 10,000 drivers a year, but got no land after at least five meetings.

facts.statement: About 250 recruiting agencies received new licences in the 16 months before January 2026; fewer than four or five of them were in Rangpur division, which officials said was because applicants there could not meet the conditions.

Over the six months to January 2026 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment held several meetings with BEZA (Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority) seeking 50 acres for a 'skills processing zone' where institutions from around the world would invest in nursing training institutes, pre-fab housing, 6G welding and other sectors, with Singapore-standard training centres.

Zia Hasan, economist and policy adviser to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, wrote on Facebook that three Japanese companies were ready with money, technology and set-up to build a car-driving training track needing 30 acres, would take 10,000 drivers a year, had an MoU ready and could set up within three months of getting land; with 30 acres they would have trained and taken 30,000 workers including language training within 6 months.

headline_en: Russia forcing Bangladeshis into the Ukraine war with job promises
summary_en: An Associated Press investigation, reported by Prothom Alo, found Bangladeshi migrant workers were lured to Russia with false promises of civilian jobs and forced to fight in the Ukraine war. Three who escaped said they were made to sign Russian-language papers that turned out to be military contracts, trained in drone warfare, evacuation and heavy weapons, and forced into front-line tasks under threat of 10 years' prison and beatings. Victims said they saw hundreds of Bangladeshis with Russian forces.

facts.statement: A labour broker persuaded Maksudur Rahman to leave his home town in Bangladesh for Russia with a promise of work as a janitor; within a few weeks of reaching Moscow he was on the front line of the Ukraine war.

Three Bangladeshis who escaped the Russian army told AP that on arrival in Russia they were forced to sign papers written in Russian that turned out to be military contracts, then taken to an army training camp for basic training in drone warfare, evacuating wounded and heavy weapons.
When Maksudur Rahman protested, a Russian commander told him through a translation app: 'Your agent sent you here. We bought you.'

The three escaped Bangladeshis said they were forced against their will into very dangerous front-line work: advancing ahead of Russian troops, carrying supplies, evacuating wounded soldiers and recovering bodies of the dead. Families of three more missing Bangladeshis said their relatives described similar experiences before going missing.
Bangladeshis forced to fight for Russia were threatened with 10 years' imprisonment and beaten if they refused to work; Maksudur Rahman escaped and returned home after seven months.

It is not clear how many Bangladeshis have been tricked this way, but victims told AP they saw hundreds of Bangladeshis with Russian forces in Ukraine. Russia's defence and foreign ministries and the Bangladesh government did not answer AP's questions.

AP reviewed travel papers, Russian military contracts, medical and police reports and photos of war injuries as evidence of the Bangladeshis' participation in the Ukraine war; officials and rights activists say Russia has used the same tactic on citizens of India, Nepal and other South Asian and African countries.

headline_en: Who will be hit by this Trump decision
summary_en: The US is suspending immigrant-visa processing for citizens of 75 countries including Bangladesh from 21 January 2026, for people seeking to live permanently in the US; tourist, business, temporary and other non-immigrant visas are not affected. Applicants can still apply but no immigrant visa will be approved or issued during the suspension, which has no set end date; dual nationals applying on a passport of an unlisted country are exempt. The article also lists other Trump restrictions, including the USD 100,000 H-1B fee.

facts.statement: From 21 January 2026 the United States suspends immigrant-visa processing for citizens of 75 countries including Bangladesh; it applies only to people who want to live permanently in the US, and tourists and short-term visa holders are not covered.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department, via Prothom Alo

facts.statement: During the US immigrant-visa suspension (from 21 January 2026), citizens of the listed countries including Bangladesh can still submit immigrant-visa applications, but no immigrant visa will be approved or issued; the US has given no date for lifting it.
A dual national who applies for a US immigrant visa using a valid passport of a country not on the suspension list is exempt from the January 2026 suspension.
The January 2026 US immigrant-visa suspension does not apply to non-immigrant, temporary, tourist or business visas.

The US State Department told consulates to stop processing immigrant visas for the 75 listed countries, following a November 2025 order to tighten screening of prospective immigrants who could become a financial burden; during the pause it will re-evaluate procedures so that foreigners who might take public welfare funds and benefits cannot enter.

Other South Asian countries on the January 2026 US immigrant-visa suspension list with Bangladesh are Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bhutan and Nepal; the 75-country list also includes Myanmar, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Thailand, Cambodia, Russia, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Brazil, Colombia and others.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department list via Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In September 2025 the US raised the H-1B visa application fee, used by US companies to hire foreign workers, to USD 100,000 at once.

US restrictions in 2025: a full travel ban on 12 countries in June 2025 (Afghanistan, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Haiti, Iran, Libya, Myanmar, Somalia, Sudan, Yemen), extended after November 2025 to six more (Palestine, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, South Sudan, Syria); a FY2026 refugee cap of 7,500; and a pause on asylum applications and on citizenship and green-card processing for citizens of the first-banned countries.

headline_en: Lives ruined in the cycle of debt
summary_en: Prothom Alo looked at 24 indebted lower-middle-class families in five upazilas of Rajshahi (Bagha, Charghat, Paba, Mohanpur, Tanore) who took loans from several microcredit NGOs at once; some borrowed for family needs including sending a son abroad. Eight unnatural deaths of indebted people were reported in Rajshahi between 16 April and 23 September of the previous year. One farmer in Bagha took a 3 lakh taka loan partly to send his son abroad; the son fell into the hands of a broker ring and came back, and the father is now in hiding driving a rickshaw.

facts.statement: Of 24 indebted families Prothom Alo examined in Rajshahi's Bagha, Charghat, Paba, Mohanpur and Tanore upazilas (article published January 2026), every family had borrowed from several places at once; besides business and crop loans, some had borrowed for family needs such as a child's wedding, sending a son abroad and medical treatment.

Belayet Pramanik (40) of Majhpara Bausa village, Bagha upazila, Rajshahi, took a 3 lakh taka loan about 10 months before the report (published January 2026), used it to grow onions and to send his son abroad; the son fell into the hands of a broker ring (dalal chakra) and came back.

After his son's failed migration and losses on onions, Belayet Pramanik of Bagha, Rajshahi took loans from three more organisations, bringing his weekly instalments to 11,860 taka; unable to pay, he left home four or five months before the January 2026 report and now drives a rickshaw elsewhere, paying only what he can.

Between 16 April and 23 September of the year before the January 2026 report, eight unnatural deaths of indebted people, including four members of one family, were reported in Rajshahi; police and families said four were suicides, and one man killed his wife and two children and then himself.

Afzal Hossain, director of the Rajshahi NGO Rural Under Privileged and Landless Farmers Organisation (RULFAO), said microcredit NGO staff give 'target loans' to meet targets without feasibility checks and without checking how many other NGOs the borrower already owes.

Jahangir Alam, assistant director (HR and admin) of Shapla Gram Unnayan Sangstha, a Rajshahi lender, said that once the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) work is complete a borrower's ID card can be used to check whether they have loans at any other organisation or bank; he said young officers often lend in a hurry to meet targets and borrowers also hide information.

Foreign adviser Touhid Hossain said village youths go from Bangladesh to Kenya on tourist visas though they cannot actually afford to go to Kenya or Turkey, and that until this is stopped people will keep dying in the Mediterranean.

headline_en: 9 million people in the UK, including those of Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian origin, could lose citizenship
summary_en: A report published by UK groups Runnymede Trust and Reprieve on Thursday (11 December 2025) says about 9 million people, about 13% of the UK population, could legally be stripped of British citizenship by the home secretary. Under current law citizenship can be removed if the government thinks a person is eligible for another country's citizenship, even if they never lived there. People with ties to Pakistan, Bangladesh, Somalia, Nigeria, North Africa and the Middle East are most at risk.

facts.statement: Under current UK law a British citizen's citizenship can be revoked if the government believes they are eligible for another country's citizenship, even if they have never lived in that country or do not consider themselves its citizen, according to a Runnymede Trust and Reprieve report published in December 2025.

The Runnymede Trust and Reprieve report (published Thursday, about 11 December 2025) says about 9 million people in the UK, about 13% of the population, could legally lose citizenship under the home secretary's power; those with links to Pakistan, Bangladesh, Somalia, Nigeria, North Africa and the Middle East are most at risk.

Per the Reprieve and Runnymede analysis, three in five people from non-white groups are at risk of losing British citizenship against one in 20 white Britons, a 12 times higher risk; about 984,000 people of Indian origin, 679,000 of Pakistani origin and 3.3 million Asian Britons including Bangladeshis are among the most potentially affected.

The best-known UK citizenship-revocation case is Shamima Begum, UK-born, whose citizenship was revoked on the claim that she was a Bangladeshi citizen, which the Bangladesh government denied; she had left the UK as a teenager to join IS and the UK rejected her application to return.

The report came as Conservative and Reform UK politicians talk of plans that could remove hundreds of thousands of people legally living in the UK; the UK Home Office had not commented at the time of writing.

headline_en: Fellowship in America: apply with English proficiency
summary_en: Applications are open for the fully funded Fulbright Visiting Scholar Program 2026-27 in the US, for Bangladeshi professionals, university teachers and researchers with 10 or more years of experience to do research or teach for one academic year. Candidates need a PhD or equivalent professional degree and English proficiency; the programme starts next September. The deadline is stated as 20 December 2026, 11:59 am Bangladesh time.

facts.statement: The US Fulbright Visiting Scholar Program 2026-27, announced on the US Embassy Dhaka Facebook page (reported November 2025), gives fully funded grants for one academic year of research or teaching at a US institution to experienced Bangladeshi government and private professionals, university teachers, and researchers at research institutions with 10 or more years of professional experience.

Fulbright Visiting Scholar applicants must hold a PhD or equivalent professional degree, submit a research and teaching proposal in their field, and have English proficiency for professional work at a US university; the exchange starts in September of next year (2026 per November 2025 article).

Fulbright Visiting Scholar 2026-27 proposals are invited in all education-related fields, with priority to university administration and curriculum, distance learning, education technology, public health, biology, pharmacy, climate change and disaster management, urban planning and international relations; some short-term grants are also given for needs assessment, faculty development exchanges and curriculum or material design.

Fulbright Visiting Scholar benefits include return airfare, teaching and related academic fees, a monthly stipend for room, lodging and incidentals, a book allowance, health and accident insurance, and travel and excess baggage allowances.

To apply for the Fulbright Visiting Scholar Program, create a login account on the online application form; full instructions and application details are at https://bd.usembassy.gov/call-for-applications-for-the-2026-27-fulbright-visiting-scholar-program/.
For more information on the Fulbright Visiting Scholar Program, contact dhakausexchanges@state.gov.

The article gives the Fulbright Visiting Scholar 2026-27 application deadline as 'next year 20 December, 2026', by 11:59 am Bangladesh time (as printed in a November 2025 article; the year may be an error).

Over the past 50 years about 200-plus Bangladeshis have taken part in the Fulbright Visiting Scholar exchange, including academics, researchers, senior government officials and development professionals.

headline_en: How to get a work visa in Australia after finishing studies
summary_en: An explainer on Australia's Temporary Graduate visa, which lets international students who complete a degree in Australia stay two to three years to work, study further or travel, depending on the degree. It lists eligibility conditions, durations by degree and a base application fee of AUD 2,300. Indian students get extra duration under the AI-ECTA trade agreement; the article says students of other countries also get the visa.

facts.statement: Australia's Temporary Graduate visa lets international students who complete higher education in Australia stay for a set time to work, study further or travel; holders can live and work two to three years depending on the degree, but it does not guarantee a job and they must find work themselves.

Temporary Graduate visa durations in Australia: bachelor's (including honours) two years; master's (coursework or extended) two years; master's (research) three years; doctoral (PhD) three years; graduate diploma holders usually two years, which may vary with personal circumstances.

To apply for Australia's Temporary Graduate visa the applicant must hold a valid student visa and have completed a degree from an approved Australian institution, meet health and character requirements, hold adequate health insurance, and repay any debts to the Australian government; family members can be included in the same application or apply separately later.

The base application fee for Australia's Temporary Graduate visa is AUD 2,300, with possible extra costs for health examination, police certificate and biometrics; processing time varies with completeness of the application and document checks.

Indian students get additional, longer Temporary Graduate visa periods under the Australia-India Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (AI-ECTA); the article says students from other countries also get this work visa opportunity.

headline_en: Canada's new immigration plan: chance for temporary residents to become permanent
summary_en: Canada's 2025 federal budget, tabled on 4 November 2025 by Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal minority government, plans to give permanent residence to up to 33,000 temporary work-permit holders in 2026 and 2027. The 2026 temporary resident intake target is cut to 385,000 (about 43% below 673,650 in 2025), with international students cut to 155,000 and temporary foreign workers to 230,000. The permanent resident target for 2026 stays at 380,000.

facts.statement: Canada's 2025 federal budget, presented to parliament on 4 November 2025 by Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal minority government, plans to grant permanent residence (PR) to up to 33,000 foreign workers holding temporary work permits in 2026 and 2027.

Canada's 2026 target for admitting temporary residents is 385,000, about 43% lower than 673,650 in 2025; within it, international students are cut almost by half to 155,000 and temporary foreign workers by 37% to 230,000.
Canada's 2026 permanent resident target stays at 380,000, 64% in economic immigration: 239,800 economic class, 84,000 family reunification and 56,200 refugee and humanitarian.
The Canadian government said its plan will give special priority to rural and remote regions hurt by labour shortages and tariff changes.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in September 2025 that the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) must be restructured to match real labour demand in specific sectors and regions; the 2025 budget gives no separate figure, but more work permits are expected to be issued under the International Mobility Program.

From January to August 2025 only 42% of the targeted temporary foreign workers and 29% of the targeted international students arrived in Canada, so the government says the lower targets do not mean a sudden stop to entries.

summary_en: Miki Watanabe, founder of Japan's Watami Group, told Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus in Dhaka on Saturday (25 October 2025) that he plans a driving school in Bangladesh to train large numbers of drivers for jobs in Japan, and is looking for a 12,000 square metre site. Watanabe already runs a language training academy in Monohardi, Narsingdi that plans to train and place at least 3,000 Bangladeshis; 52 workers have already gone to Japan for construction and agriculture. Yunus asked for more Japanese language test sittings, currently only twice a year.

facts.statement: Miki Watanabe, Japanese entrepreneur and politician and founder of Watami Group, announced at a meeting with Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus at state guest house Jamuna, Dhaka, on Saturday (25 October 2025) a plan to set up a driving school in Bangladesh to recruit large numbers of trained drivers for jobs in Japan; he said they are looking for a 12,000 square metre site and that demand for skilled drivers in Japan is very high.

Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus immediately instructed officials to identify suitable land on the outskirts of Dhaka for Watami Group's driving school, and expressed interest in another training centre in or near Dhaka so Japanese companies need not travel to Monohardi, Narsingdi.
During Chief Adviser Yunus's visit to Japan in May 2025, Japanese entrepreneurs signed an agreement to recruit 100,000 workers from Bangladesh over the next five years.

Watami Group founder Miki Watanabe has set up a language training academy in Monohardi, Narsingdi district, planning to train and recruit at least 3,000 Bangladeshis; batches currently have 40 students each and will be scaled up gradually.
Miki Watanabe said 52 workers trained through his Monohardi, Narsingdi academy have already gone to Japan to work in construction and agriculture.
Chief Adviser Yunus called for more Japanese language proficiency test sittings in Bangladesh, saying the test is currently held only twice a year, which is not enough for growing demand.

Yunus said teaching Japanese culture, etiquette and behaviour should be an essential part of training so Bangladeshis understand Japan and are properly prepared before going; he urged Watami Group to expand training in service, nursing, construction and agriculture, where skilled workers can earn well in Japan, and Watanabe said they want to do this too.
facts.source_in_article: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, Miki Watanabe

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has a newly formed Japan Cell that facilitates cooperation between Japanese investors and Bangladeshi institutions, praised by the Chief Adviser.

headline_en: Is Bangladesh ready for expatriate voting?
summary_en: An opinion column (10 Oct 2025) argues that Bangladesh is rushing into expatriate (probashi) voting. It reports the Election Commission plan to pilot voting by Bangladeshis abroad in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the UAE and the UK through embassy booths after online registration, gives estimates of Bangladeshi populations in those countries, and lists risks such as registration and verification problems, vote-buying under the kafala sponsorship system, and the lack of a specific law.

facts.statement: As of October 2025, Bangladesh's Election Commission (EC) has said it plans to start expatriate voting on a pilot basis in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.
facts.source_in_article: Election Commission, as reported in the column

facts.statement: Under the EC plan reported in October 2025, in the first phase voting would be at booths in Bangladesh embassies: voters would first register online, and on the set day would vote after their passport and NID (national ID) are verified.
facts.source_in_article: Election Commission plan, as reported in the column

facts.statement: As of October 2025, no detailed announcement had been made on foreign government approval, security protocols or server set-up for expatriate voting; the columnists note the election schedule (tofshil) is to be announced in December.
The column states there are about 25 lakh (2.5 million) Bangladeshi expatriates in Saudi Arabia.
The column states there are about 12 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in Malaysia.
The column states there are about 10 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in the United Arab Emirates.
The column states there are about 5 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in the United Kingdom.
The column gives the number of Bangladeshis living in various countries as about 1 crore 30 lakh (13 million); a subheading elsewhere in the article refers to 'one and a half crore' expatriates.
According to the column, expatriates sent USD 7.59 billion in remittances in the first three months of 2025, and Bangladesh is the sixth largest remittance-receiving country in the world.
About 13 crore NIDs have been issued in Bangladesh, but there is no updated database tracking whether holders live abroad, according to the column.
The columnists say the biggest obstacle at the registration stage is duplication and verification, because passport, NID and birth registration are held in three separate systems.

The columnists warn that in the Middle East, where workers are under the sponsor or 'kafala' system, creating conditions for expatriates to vote freely will be harder; experts from Sri Lanka and the Philippines have warned that many expatriate voters at one address raise risks of vote-buying, coercion, or influence through politically appointed mission officials.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists; Sri Lankan and Philippine experts

facts.statement: Bangladesh has not yet passed a clear law on expatriate voting; under Article 122 of the Constitution voting rights depend on citizenship, but the legal position of those permanently settled abroad is unclear, the column says. The columnists propose a separate 'Probashi Vote Ain 2025' (Expatriate Voting Act 2025) with strict penalties for fake registration or undue influence.

Unanswered questions listed by the column: whether people who register abroad will stay on the voter list at home, what happens to people who gave up their Bangladeshi passport abroad but still have a voter number, and how a voter abroad will know and vote for the candidates in their own constituency under the current symbol-based paper ballot system.

Comparisons given by the column: in India, of 1.2 lakh registered overseas voters only 2,958 voted in the 2024 election because they must return home to vote; in the Philippines fewer than 15% of over 10 million overseas citizens register and only 20% of those vote; in Pennsylvania (USA) ballots of more than 4,000 overseas voters were challenged.

The columnists recommend embassy/consulate in-person voting (which they say most of the UK Bangladeshi community favours), strict verification with annual renewal, a simple online registration system, an independent oversight committee with international observers, and voter education for expatriates.

headline_en: Denmark tightens rules: international students' rights to work and bring family limited
summary_en: Denmark's Ministry of Immigration and Integration announced in an 18 September (2025) notice stricter rules for non-EU (third-country) students, aimed particularly at students from Bangladesh and Nepal who it says used student visas as a backdoor into the labour market. Measures include stricter academic requirements, document checks, review of past residence permits for fraud, limits on bringing family, cutting the post-study work permit from three years to one, higher tuition and monitoring of agents. The article also gives statistics on family accompaniment, dropout and pass rates of Bangladeshi students.

facts.statement: Denmark's Ministry of Immigration and Integration said in a notice on 18 September that university admission rules for third-country (non-EU) students will be made stricter, and that it will now be 'much harder for those without the necessary qualifications to study at Danish universities'; the measure targets in particular students from Bangladesh and Nepal entering the labour market through student visas.

facts.statement: Between 2022 and 2024, 74% of Nepali students, 58% of Bangladeshi students and 23% of Indian students brought family members to Denmark, compared with only 1% of Chinese and 2% of US students.

A survey by Aarhus University found one-third of Bangladeshi students were considered 'not study-oriented'; Bangladeshi first-year dropout was 13% against 4% for other international students, and Bangladeshi exam pass rates were 55-65% against 90% for students from other countries.

headline_en: 66 people including women and children rescued while being trafficked to Malaysia
summary_en: A joint Coast Guard and Navy operation on 18 September 2025 rescued 66 people, 44 of them women and children and most of them Rohingya, gathered in a hideout in the deep hills of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf (Cox's Bazar) for trafficking to Malaysia. Some were lured with promises of a better life in Malaysia, others abducted and held for ransom; 15-20 traffickers escaped.

facts.statement: On Thursday 18 September 2025, between 6 pm and 10 pm, a joint Coast Guard and Navy operation rescued 66 people gathered for trafficking to Malaysia from a hideout in the deep hills of Kachchhopia area, Baharchhara union, Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar; 44 of them were women and children, and most were Rohingya.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard; Lt Cdr Siam-ul-Haque, Coast Guard HQ media officer

facts.statement: Traffickers, helped by an organised broker (dalal) ring, gathered people at a hill hideout in Teknaf: some were lured with promises of a better life in Malaysia and others were abducted and held hostage while ransom was sought (September 2025).

During the 18 September 2025 Teknaf raid, 15 to 20 members of the trafficking gang escaped; the Coast Guard said efforts are under way to identify and arrest them, a case is being prepared at Teknaf police station, and the 66 rescued will be handed to relatives after identity checks.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard; Lt Cdr Siam-ul-Haque, Coast Guard HQ media officer

facts.statement: So far in 2025 (as of 19 September), 62 human traffickers have been arrested and 77 people rescued in Teknaf, according to law enforcement sources.
Human trafficking incidents occur more in the winter season, according to law enforcement sources cited for Teknaf.

headline_en: Alleged attempt to traffic three girls in Netrokona; two including a Chinese national detained
summary_en: Police detained Chinese national Li Oi Hao (32) and his associate Faridul Islam (34) of Kurigram in Kendua, Netrokona on 15 September 2025 on suspicion of human trafficking and rescued three girls. Li had married a 17-year-old garment worker on 1 September, promising to take her to China and to give her family 1 lakh taka; a friend of his married another 17-year-old on 14 September. Police found photos, voter IDs, passports and payment records of many girls on Faridul's phone.

facts.statement: At dawn on Monday 15 September 2025, police detained Chinese national Li Oi Hao (লি ওই হাও, 32) and his associate Faridul Islam (34), son of Abdul Hanif Mia of Sukhdeb Paschim Para, Rajarhat, Kurigram, in Kamalpur area of Kendua municipality, Netrokona, on suspicion of human trafficking, rescued three girls and seized a microbus.
facts.source_in_article: Netrokona Superintendent of Police Mirza Saem Mahmud; local residents and police

facts.statement: Method described: a Chinese man married a 17-year-old girl from Kamalpur, Kendua (a garment factory worker in Dhaka) on 1 September 2025 with a Bangladeshi associate's help, said he would take her to China on 20 September, and promised her family 1 lakh taka; a Chinese friend of his married a 17-year-old from Gopi Nadi, Melandaha, Jamalpur in Dhaka on 14 September, also saying he would take her to China; a 19-year-old from Gogda, Kendua was also promised a trip to China.

On the evening of 14 September 2025, local people in Kendua, suspicious of the two men, asked for their passport numbers and legal papers for staying in Bangladesh; when they could not show them, locals informed the Madan temporary army camp and Kendua police, who detained them the next dawn.

The Netrokona SP said Faridul Islam claimed to be a garment worker, but his phone held photos, voter IDs, passports and money-transaction records of many girls from various parts of Bangladesh; the ring is believed to have been involved in trafficking for a long time, targeting women from simple, poor rural families through brokers with various lures to traffic them to China. Investigation and legal action are under way.

headline_en: Attempt to grab Italy-based migrant's house in Keraniganj by claiming the land, vandalism
summary_en: Liton Howlader (45), who has lived in Italy for 17 years, returned to Keraniganj to save a house he built on land bought four years earlier, after a group led by alleged land grabber Alamgir Hossain claimed the land after 5 August 2024, evicted tenants on 31 August 2025 and began demolishing the house. A court case is pending with a hearing on 1 October; police say they received a written complaint.

facts.statement: Italy-based migrant Liton Howlader (45) of Kulchar, Shakta union, Keraniganj says that on the morning of 31 August 2025 Alamgir Hossain (36), Shahadat, Shahin and 30-35 others armed with local weapons forcibly entered his six-room semi-pucca house on 5.75 decimals of land in Madhyerchar mouza (Keraniganj Model police station area), attacked and evicted tenants, beat his younger brother Rafiqul and began demolishing the house despite a pending court case.

Liton Howlader, in Italy for 17 years, bought the land four years earlier with valid papers and pays land tax; after the 5 August (2024) political change, alleged land grabbers claimed it. His family filed a written complaint at Keraniganj Model police station and later a court case, with the next hearing on 1 October (2025). He returned from Italy about four days before his 8 September 2025 press conference and says he has received death threats.

Alamgir Hossain, who lives in Lalbagh, Dhaka, is accused of buying disputed land, occupying it and reselling it; he claims he bought land in the same plot (dag) and has valid papers, but could not explain why he made the claim only after 5 August.
Keraniganj Model police station officer-in-charge Monirul Haque said the station received a written complaint about the Italy-based migrant's land and would take necessary action after inquiry.

headline_en: 30 more Bangladeshis sent back from the United States
summary_en: Thirty Bangladeshis (29 men, one woman) deported from the US for living without valid documents landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, around 12:15 am on the night of Thursday 4 September 2025. They were handcuffed on the plane; SB says 187 Bangladeshis have been returned so far amid Trump's second-term crackdown.

facts.statement: Thirty Bangladeshis (29 men and one woman) deported from the United States for living without valid documents arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on a plane that landed around 12:15 am on the night of Thursday 4 September 2025.

Since Donald Trump began his second term as US president and stepped up operations against undocumented migrants, 187 Bangladeshis in total have been sent back as of 5 September 2025, according to SB sources.
Bangladesh foreign ministry officials say only people who have lost their legal battles in the US are being sent back, and the ministry is informed in advance about those being deported.
The 30 Bangladeshis were put on the plane in handcuffs in the US and kept handcuffed on board; the handcuffs were removed after landing in Dhaka, they told law enforcement.

headline_en: Why is the price of the dream abroad so high?
summary_en: A short reader opinion piece says migrant workers going to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia or other Middle East countries often borrow several lakh taka because of legal and illegal broker chains, face lower pay and harsh conditions than promised, and suffer stress, illness, accidents and suicide, leaving families with debt. It calls for worker safety, transparent recruitment and debt-free migration.

facts.statement: Because of legal and illegal broker (dalal) chains, a worker going to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia or another Middle East country often has to borrow several lakh taka, raising it by selling land, taking high-interest loans or using all savings, according to the opinion piece.
The piece says brokers promise large salaries but many workers in reality face low wages, excessive work and inhuman conditions, sometimes without proper food, housing or healthcare.

The piece says fear of not repaying debt, humiliation abroad, physical labour and mental distress make many ill; some die in workplace accidents and some take their own lives, leaving families with debt for many years.
Readers can send stories to Prothom Alo's Durporobash section at email dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: BSF to get 5,000 bodycams for the Bangladesh border
summary_en: India's Border Security Force (BSF) is being given about 5,000 body cameras, in two phases, for the India-Bangladesh border, to record evidence of sending back undocumented Bangladeshis and of attacks on BSF members, according to Indian security sources quoted by PTI (July 2025). Biometric equipment is also being supplied to some border posts to take fingerprints and eye scans of undocumented Bangladeshis and send them to the foreigners registration office.

facts.statement: India's Border Security Force (BSF) is being given about 5,000 body-worn video cameras, sent in two phases, for members on duty on the India-Bangladesh border, to record scenes and evidence when undocumented Bangladeshis are sent back and to monitor attacks on BSF members.

Special biometric equipment is being given to certain BSF border posts on the 4,096 km India-Bangladesh border; with it, fingerprints and eye scans of undocumented Bangladeshis will be taken and sent to the foreigners registration office (বিদেশি নিবন্ধন দপ্তর).

India's Union Home Ministry approved the two BSF headquarters proposals (bodycams and biometric devices) after a 'coordinated review' of the security situation in areas bordering Bangladesh, taken in the changed situation after the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on 5 August 2024.

The bodycams work day and night and can record about 12 to 14 hours of video continuously; they are to record incidents when BSF sends back undocumented Bangladeshis or confronts smugglers of drugs, cattle and fake Indian currency, human traffickers and infiltrators.

Bangladesh and its border force BGB have complained in various bilateral forums that the Indian side uses excessive force and unfair treatment against Bangladeshi citizens; BSF has repeatedly said it uses non-lethal or lethal weapons only as a last resort to protect soldiers' lives.

headline_en: Returnees from abroad can bring one phone a year without duty
summary_en: On 2 July 2025 Bangladesh's National Board of Revenue (NBR) amended the baggage rules so a returning passenger can bring one new mobile phone duty-free once a year, and migrants with a BMET card who stayed abroad at least six months can bring two. Duty-free gold jewellery up to 100 grams and silver jewellery up to 200 grams once a year are allowed, and a gold bar up to 10 tola once a year on duty of 5,000 taka per tola. Baggage declaration can be made online but must be submitted before leaving the customs hall.

facts.statement: Under an NBR directive issued Wednesday 2 July 2025, a passenger returning from abroad can bring one new mobile phone once a year without paying any duty (previously the baggage rules allowed one new phone on payment of duty).

Under the 2 July 2025 NBR directive, expatriates who hold a Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) card and have stayed abroad for at least six months can bring two new mobile phones a year duty-free.
Under the 2 July 2025 NBR directive, a returning passenger can bring at most 100 grams of gold jewellery once a year without duty, and 200 grams of silver jewellery.
Under the new baggage rules, a passenger can bring one gold bar of at most 10 tola weight once a year by paying duty of 5,000 taka per tola.

NBR issued the new baggage rules, the Non-Tourist Passenger Baggage Rules 2025 (অপর্যটক যাত্রী ব্যাগেজ বিধিমালা, ২০২৫), on 2 June 2025; the article says they took effect from Wednesday 2 July 2025, with amendments to make them more passenger-friendly based on views of stakeholders and field offices.

From 2 July 2025 all passengers arriving from abroad can fill in the baggage declaration form online, but submitting the baggage declaration before leaving the customs hall or area is mandatory, to prevent misuse of the facilities.

headline_en: 250 Bangladeshis register to return home from Iran
summary_en: As of 24 June 2025, 250 Bangladeshis had registered with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran to return home amid the Iran-Israel conflict; 90 of them were to be brought back overland via Pakistan (Mirjaveh to Taftan), then flown from Karachi via Dubai to Dhaka. The foreign ministry said about 2,000 Bangladeshis are in Iran, about 400 in Tehran, 672 listed with the embassy including 66 students, and gave hotline numbers.

facts.statement: As of 24 June 2025, 250 Bangladeshis had registered to return home from Iran; of them 90 were to be brought back through the Pakistan land border.
Initially women and children, along with people who had gone to Iran for medical treatment, were planned to be repatriated first, according to foreign ministry sources (June 2025).

Repatriation plan (June 2025): Bangladeshis registered with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran would be taken overland from Mirjaveh (মারজাভেহ) in Iran across the Taftan border in Pakistan's Balochistan province, then flown from Karachi with a transit in Dubai to Dhaka; other routes besides Karachi-Dubai were also being considered, and start of travel depended on the situation on the ground.

Dhaka had given Islamabad the details of about 90 Bangladeshis so they could cross from Iran into Pakistan easily; a senior government official said the top level of government had approved bringing Bangladeshis back from Iran via Pakistan.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs; senior government official

facts.statement: About 2,000 Bangladeshis were living in Iran, about 400 of them in Tehran; 672 Bangladeshis were listed (registered) in Iran, of whom 66 were students.
The foreign ministry urged all Bangladeshis in Iran wanting to return home to register quickly with the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran, giving name, address and necessary information.
Hotlines for Bangladeshis in Iran (June 2025): Bangladesh Embassy, Tehran +989908577368 and +989122065745; Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Dhaka +8801712012847.

headline_en: Wife 'flees' leaving Italy expat's body at hospital
summary_en: Halim Khan (45), an Italy-based migrant from Nagargoaldi village, Rajoir, Madaripur, was found dead at Rajoir upazila health complex on 24 June 2025 after his second wife and in-laws left his body there. Relatives allege he was beaten and strangled after he returned from Italy and demanded back about 60 lakh taka he had sent his father-in-law and a motorcycle bought in his brother-in-law's name; the wife denies it and police called the death suspicious.

facts.statement: Italy-based migrant Halim Khan (45) of Nagargoaldi village, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, was allegedly called to his in-laws' house on the night of Monday 23 June 2025 and beaten and strangled to death; on the morning of 24 June his wife and mother-in-law took him to Rajoir upazila health complex and fled leaving the body after he was declared dead.

Relatives say Halim Khan, while abroad (in Italy), gave his second wife Reshma Begum's father about 60 lakh taka at various times; his brother said all of Halim's earnings from 9 years were with Reshma Begum, and money he sent to buy a motorcycle for himself before returning was used to buy one in his brother-in-law's name. After returning he demanded the money and motorcycle back, leading to quarrels.

Rajoir police OC Mohammad Masud Khan said the body was recovered from the hospital and sent to the morgue of the 250-bed Madaripur district hospital; he called the incident suspicious and said police had begun investigating. Reshma Begum denied the allegation, saying he was brought to hospital ill.

headline_en: Bring citizens back safely (editorial)
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial (19 June 2025) urging the government to evacuate Bangladeshis from Iran during the Iran-Israel conflict. It reports the acting foreign secretary's figures (about 400 in Tehran, about 100 in contact), notes more than 2,000 Bangladeshis live in Iran including fishermen and others without papers and some in detention centres, and says air links are closed and land routes to Turkey or Pakistan are risky and costly.

facts.statement: Acting foreign secretary Ruhul Alam Siddique told a Dhaka press conference on Tuesday (17 June 2025) that about 400 Bangladeshis were in Tehran and about 100 had contacted the embassy; work had begun to move them to safety.
facts.source_in_article: Acting foreign secretary Ruhul Alam Siddique

facts.statement: More than 2,000 Bangladeshis live in Iran, some sources say more; a notable number have married Iranians and settled permanently.

Bangladeshis in Iran who live by fishing in sea areas and small jobs are the most vulnerable; many lack legal papers; some Bangladeshis are held in Iranian detention centres; some are professionals in media and health care.
In June 2025 all air links between Iran and the outside world were closed, making leaving Iran difficult; land routes to Turkey or Pakistan might be possible but are very risky and costly.

Process began to move 40 Bangladesh embassy staff in Tehran including diplomats to safe places; on Monday night ambassador Manzurul Karim Khan Chowdhury and family left the official residence. BBC Bangla reported one Bangladeshi diplomat's residence was heavily damaged in an Israeli attack.

Al Jazeera reported China, South Korea and Pakistan were already evacuating their citizens from Iran; the editorial says Bangladesh should seek help from the UN, international bodies and friendly states and should evacuate citizens whether or not they have legal papers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial citing Al Jazeera

headline_en: Canada's tightening: illegal US-Canada border crossings by Bangladeshis and Indians falling, Ottawa claims
summary_en: Canadian government documents say stricter visa policies for travellers from Mexico, India and Bangladesh cut illegal crossings from Canada into the US, and more than 2,000 Indian and Bangladeshi nationals were stopped from boarding Canada-bound flights after re-checks for visa fraud from March 2024. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) recommended about 11,050 passengers not be boarded in 2024, including 493 Bangladeshis (475 suspected of fraud). The writer, a Canada-based journalist, says many who came on visit visas with fake papers after COVID-19 crossed into the US or claimed asylum in Canada.

facts.statement: Since March 2024, re-checking of visa fraud cases led to more than 2,000 Indian and Bangladeshi nationals being prevented from boarding flights to Canada, according to a Global Affairs Canada document dated 15 January (2025).

Global Affairs Canada documents say that, owing to improved visa screening from June 2024, illegal crossings into the United States (from Canada) fell 84 percent by November 2024, and Canada's refusal rate for new visa applications reached 63 percent.

The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) said it recommended not boarding about 11,050 passengers with suspicious travel documents in 2024, including 3,250 Indian nationals (3,104 suspected of fraud) and 493 Bangladeshi nationals (475 suspected of fraud).
Canadian government documents say stricter visa policies for travellers from Mexico, India and Bangladesh reduced illegal crossings from Canada into the US.

The writer says that after COVID-19, Canada issued large numbers of visit visas to boost its economy, and lakhs of people from Bangladesh, India and elsewhere obtained Canadian visit visas using fake documents; many crossed illegally into the US and a large share claimed political asylum in Canada, with those asylum cases still pending in Canadian courts.

summary_en: Israel's missile strike on Monday 16 June 2025 on the IRIB building in Tehran, which houses Radio Tehran, killed three people, but the eight Bangladeshis working in its Bangla section were unharmed, the acting foreign secretary said on 17 June. Foreign ministry officials gave a breakdown of more than 2,000 Bangladeshis in Iran, including about 800 working illegally for over 10 years and 300 to 500 always present in transit waiting to be trafficked elsewhere.

facts.statement: Israel struck the state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) building in Tehran with missiles on Monday 16 June 2025; three were killed and several injured, but eight Bangladeshis working in the Bangla section of Radio Tehran who were present were unharmed.
facts.source_in_article: Acting foreign secretary Ruhul Alam Siddique, press conference 17 June 2025

facts.statement: More than 2,000 Bangladeshis were in Iran (June 2025); in Tehran about 400, including about 40 at the embassy (ambassador, 2 officers, 5 staff and families), 27 people linked to Radio Tehran's 8 Bangladeshis with families, 10 to 12 students and about 10 professionals.

About 600 Bangladeshis elsewhere in Iran have lived there more than 30 years, married and settled; about 200 students study at various institutions; about 800 more Bangladeshis have worked illegally in various sectors in Iran for over 10 years.
As a transit country for human trafficking, Iran always has 300 to 500 Bangladeshis waiting to be trafficked to other countries, according to foreign ministry officials (June 2025).

headline_en: Boat out of fuel was leaking through a cracked hull; what passengers said
summary_en: On 16 June 2025 a speedboat of Sandwip Marine Service left Guptachhara ghat, Sandwip, for Kumira despite a ban on sailing in rough weather, after pressure from passengers including some travelling abroad who would miss their flights if they could not reach Chattogram. Passengers say the boat ran out of fuel and took in water; all 27 reached shore at Akilpur, Sitakunda. The company denies running out of fuel but says it sailed under pressure from passengers going abroad; BIWTA blamed owner and driver.

facts.statement: On Monday 16 June 2025, with no boats allowed on the Sandwip-Kumira route due to bad weather, passengers including some bound abroad who would miss their flights if they could not reach Chattogram pressed a speedboat to leave Guptachhara ferry ghat, Sandwip, after 11:30 am.

Passengers said the speedboat (owned by Sandwip Marine Service) repeatedly stalled, ran out of fuel near the first buoy from the Kumira end (about 4 km / 2.8 nautical miles from Kumira ghat per a BIWTA official), and took in knee-high water through a cracked hull; all 27 passengers (including 3 children and 1 woman; one passenger said 25 to 27) reached shore at Akilpur, Sitakunda, a little before 2 pm.

headline_en: Bangladesh embassy in Tehran at risk; decision to move everyone quickly
summary_en: A 16 June 2025 report from the Bangladesh Embassy in Tehran said the embassy is within about 1 km of Tehran University's nuclear research facility and other sensitive sites targeted by Israel, and the government decided to move all mission staff to safety, possibly moving embassy operations to a third country. About 2,000 Bangladeshis in Iran were reportedly fairly safe, most having left Tehran; 28 due to fly home on 13 June were stranded by flight suspension. The embassy set up emergency hotlines (with WhatsApp).

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy building in Tehran is within about one kilometre of at least two sensitive facilities including Tehran University's Research Institute for Nuclear Medicine (first nuclear research centre), targeted by Israeli attacks since Friday 13 June 2025, and close to one of Tehran's two main IT centres; the mission reported diplomats' and staff families needed to move 30-40 km outside the city.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Embassy Tehran report to foreign ministry, 16 June 2025

facts.statement: After the report, an immediate decision was made to move everyone at the mission including diplomats to safe places; officials said finding suitable safe housing outside Tehran was difficult and moving the embassy's work to a third country was being considered if needed.
About 2,000 Bangladeshis in Iran were reported fairly safe as of 16 June 2025, almost all of them having moved outside Tehran; an official said Israel had announced Tehran should be evacuated.
28 Bangladeshis who were due to return home on 13 June 2025 were stranded in Iran because flights stopped; the foreign ministry learned that more than a hundred Bangladeshis in all were in Tehran.

Bangladeshis in Tehran include about 40 at the embassy (ambassador, two officers, five staff and families), 27 linked to the eight Bangladeshis at Radio Tehran with families, about 10 to 12 students and about 10 professionals.

About 600 Bangladeshis in several places in Iran have lived there over 30 years and settled through marriage; about 800 more have stayed illegally for over 10 years working in various sectors; about 200 students study in Iran; and 300 to 500 Bangladeshis are always in Iran as a human-trafficking transit country waiting to be trafficked onward.
In a special notice on Sunday 15 June 2025 the Bangladesh Embassy in Iran set up an emergency hotline for Bangladeshis living in Iran: +989908577368 and +989122065745 (including WhatsApp).

headline_en: Returnee Shah Alam, successful at chui jhal farming, says 'I won't go abroad again'
summary_en: Shah Alam (45) of Niamatpur village, Sirajganj Sadar, returned after about 12 years in Saudi Arabia and in 2022 began commercial chui jhal (a spice vine) farming with help from local NGO National Development Programme (NDP) under a PKSF high-value spice demonstration. He says he spent 1.17 lakh taka and sold 7.37 lakh taka worth this year, and urges young people to farm at home instead of going abroad.

facts.statement: Returnee Shah Alam (45), son of Shukur Ali of Niamatpur village, Shialkol union, Sirajganj Sadar, spent about 12 years in Saudi Arabia, then on 30 August 2022 leased 33 decimals of land beside his home for 3 years for 60,000 taka to start chui jhal cultivation.

Shah Alam started with support from local NGO National Development Programme (NDP), which implements high-value spice crop demonstrations under the integrated agriculture unit of Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF).

Shah Alam says he has spent 1,17,000 taka on chui jhal since starting and this year (2025) sold 7,37,000 taka worth in two phases; wholesalers from Khulna and elsewhere buy from his field. He plans two more bighas of chui jhal and has started papaya on three bighas.

Per the district Department of Agricultural Extension, raw chui jhal sells for 700 to 1,500 taka per kg and dried for 1,500 to 3,000 taka; one hectare of bush chui jhal can yield about 2 to 2.5 metric tons a year.
Shah Alam, addressing unemployed youth, said he will not go abroad again and wants to farm at home, and that farmers and young people could profit from chui jhal, which has demand at home and abroad.

headline_en: Unconscious husband finally brought back from abroad; wife in another fight to make him well
summary_en: Abdul Jabbar Sardar (45) of Hiranandapur, Tanore, Rajshahi went to Saudi Arabia on 16 January 2018 after borrowing 7 lakh taka; brokers 'sold' him as an airport cleaner who worked three years unpaid and was then turned out with nothing. Undocumented, he later worked at an Indian-owned tile factory, was badly injured in a road accident on 10 May 2024 and spent a year in ICU; his wife's appeals to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board failed, but the Tanore UNO reached the embassy and he was flown home unconscious in May 2025 and admitted to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital ICU.

facts.statement: Abdul Jabbar Sardar went to Saudi Arabia as a worker on 16 January 2018; on landing he was put to work as a cleaner and later realised brokers had 'sold' him as an airport 'cleaner'; for three years he worked cleaning at the airport without pay and was then sent away from the airport empty-handed.
Abdul Jabbar Sardar raised 7 lakh taka by borrowing to go to Saudi Arabia in 2018; the loan had still not been repaid as of May 2025.
Thinking Saudi police would send him home if caught, Jabbar surrendered to police himself; police took his fingerprints and released him again, and he was left with no money for food.
A man from Mondumala, Tanore, Rajshahi named Moazzem, whom Jabbar met by chance, got him a job at a tile factory owned by an Indian national, where he worked without papers.
On 10 May 2024 Jabbar was seriously injured in a road accident in Saudi Arabia; Saudi law enforcement took him to a local hospital and he was in ICU for about a year.

About three months after the accident, the people Adori Khatun dealt with (via the Indian employer) asked for 70 lakh taka to send Jabbar home because he had no papers; later they asked her to pay 19,000 taka for the air fare, which she could not raise.
On the Indian company owner's advice, Adori Khatun applied through the Wage Earners' Welfare Board in Dhaka for her husband's return, but it did not work.

Adori Khatun waited 22 days at the Tanore Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) office without being let in; after she cried out, a police member took her inside; the UNO tried to contact the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, got through after 15 days, and connected her to them by phone.

On 13 May 2025 Adori was called and told to keep a bed ready at the hospital where the patient would be admitted in Dhaka, and was told a doctor and nurse would accompany him and hand him over at the hospital and that some money would be given; on arrival in Dhaka they gave no money, did not go to the hospital and left the patient at the airport.

After return, seven hours at a private hospital in Dhaka cost 70,000 taka; Adori then hired a vehicle with oxygen for 25,000 taka and on Saturday (24 May 2025) brought him to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital, where an ICU bed was available only from Sunday (article gives both 25 May and 26 May).

Rajshahi Medical College Hospital ICU in-charge Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal said Jabbar had become skeletal after a year in ICU abroad, needs much nutrition and a head operation, after which he might regain consciousness; his son was being trained to feed him before moving him to the general ward.
facts.source_in_article: Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal, ICU in-charge, RMCH

facts.statement: Adori Khatun says the family is indebted, has no means even to eat, let alone pay for treatment, and lives on loans.
