headline_en: Three exams for Bangladeshi doctors and nurses to build careers in Ireland
summary_en: A contributor in Ireland explains that Ireland's health system relies heavily on foreign doctors and nurses, but Bangladeshis are few because the Irish Medical Council (IMC) and nursing board (NMBI) do not readily recognise Bangladeshi degrees, there is no government supply agreement, sponsorship is hard to get, and IELTS 7.0 or OET B is required. Doctors generally go through IMC registration, the PRES exam if the degree is unrecognised, or an alternative via PLAB or MRCP. Salaries are given, and he recommends government action.

facts.statement: As of 2023 about 40 percent of all doctors working in Ireland were foreign, and about 51.8 percent of Ireland's nursing workforce were trained abroad.

The Irish Medical Council (IMC) readily recognises medical degrees from India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Egypt, but recognition is hard for Bangladeshi degrees, so Bangladeshi doctors face extra exams that are time-consuming and costly.

Ireland's nursing board (NMBI) recognises nurses from the Philippines, India and Nigeria because of formal agreements; with no such agreement with Bangladesh, Bangladeshi nurses face various complications when applying.

Bangladeshi doctors usually go through three main steps to work in Ireland: (1) registration with the Irish Medical Council (IMC), depending on experience and qualifications; (2) the PRES (Pre-Registration Examination System) exam if the degree is not recognised, which includes a written exam, a clinical skills exam and a supervised internship; (3) an alternative route: doctors who have passed PLAB or MRCP can get IMC registration without PRES.

To work as a specialist in Ireland a doctor needs CESR (Certificate of Eligibility for Specialist Registration) or equivalent; even after passing PRES, a language test (IELTS or OET) is mandatory for IMC registration.
Doctors and nurses working in Ireland must score at least 7.0 in IELTS or grade 'B' in OET.

Applying directly to Irish hospitals requires sponsorship, which is hard for Bangladeshis to get; India and some other countries have dedicated recruitment agencies linking with hospitals, but there is nothing similar for Bangladeshis.
Ireland has formal health-worker supply agreements with the Philippines, India, Nigeria and Sudan; Bangladesh has no such agreement.

Thousands of health workers from India, Pakistan, Philippines, Egypt, Sudan and Nigeria work in Ireland, but Bangladeshi doctors are very few and Bangladeshi nurses almost none; most Bangladeshi doctors working in Ireland came from various Middle Eastern countries.
Ireland runs a 'Critical Skills Employment Permit' programme through which certain professionals get work permission easily; the writer suggests Bangladesh seek inclusion for doctors and nurses.
Demand in Ireland is high for specialist doctors, especially in anaesthesia, cardiology, neurology and surgery.

In Ireland an entry-level doctor can earn about 50,000 to 60,000 euros a year, specialists 120,000 to 200,000 euros, and consultants more than 210,000 euros; nurses start at about 30,000 euros a year at entry level and can exceed 55,000 euros at senior level.

The writer recommends Bangladesh negotiate recognition with IMC and NMBI, sign a formal health-worker supply agreement with Ireland, set up government IELTS/OET training and English-medium teaching in medical and nursing colleges, and create reliable recruitment agencies linking with Irish hospitals.

He also urged investment in technical education, social protection and labour law reform.

facts.statement: ILO country director in Bangladesh Tuomo Poutiainen said on 19 May 2025 that workers going abroad from Bangladesh often have no guarantee of work, there is lack of transparency in sending them abroad, and far too much money is taken from them.

Poutiainen said that if a skilled workforce can be built, people going abroad will be more aware of these issues (job guarantees, opaque process, excess costs); he urged government attention to investment in technical education.

Poutiainen, ILO country director in Bangladesh since 4 June 2018, was to leave on 31 May 2025 to become ILO's deputy regional director for Asia and the Pacific; he recommended implementing the Labour Reform Commission's proposals and amending the labour law in workers' interests.

headline_en: Why learn Chinese, where to learn it, what opportunities
summary_en: Md. Kamruzzaman, studying civil engineering at China Three Gorges University on a Chinese government scholarship after learning Chinese at Dhaka University's Confucius Institute, describes why and where to learn Chinese in Bangladesh. Confucius Institutes or classrooms run at Dhaka University, North South University and Shanto-Mariam University; Chinese firms in Bangladesh hire interpreters at 30,000-50,000 taka a month without experience; learning takes about one to two years.

facts.statement: Confucius Institutes or 'Confucius Classrooms' operate at Dhaka University, North South University and Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology, with one being set up at Rajshahi University; limited Chinese courses run at BRAC University, Chittagong University, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Jahangirnagar University and Daffodil International University; Dhaka University offers a bachelor's degree in Chinese. Chinese teachers at Confucius Institutes teach directly in English.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: Some Bangladeshis who studied in China have set up private training centres offering 6-month to 1-year online and offline Chinese courses.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: The writer studies civil engineering at China Three Gorges University on a Chinese government scholarship after learning Chinese at Dhaka University's Confucius Institute; he says Chinese government scholarships are available and Chinese is also valued in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: In Chinese companies in Bangladesh one can work as an interpreter without experience at usually 30,000 to 50,000 taka a month, rising to 1 to 2 lakh taka with experience, with possible promotion to management.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

facts.statement: Chinese is among the hardest languages; mastering it usually takes one to two years (one year with hard work), and the risk of dropping out rises after starting level 3.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Kamruzzaman (writer, Chinese government scholarship student)

headline_en: 34 Bangladeshis sent back from the United States
summary_en: Under the Trump administration's immigration policy the United States deported 34 Bangladeshis between 6 March and 21 April 2025 (46 days), according to immigration police at Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport. They had kept living in the US after losing immigration cases; some had been convicted in various cases. Foreign ministry officials said only people who lost legal battles are being returned, the ministry is told in advance, and more may be sent back.

facts.statement: The United States sent 34 Bangladeshis back to Bangladesh in the 46 days from 6 March 2025 to Monday 21 April 2025, under the immigration policy of President Donald Trump's administration.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka

facts.statement: After Donald Trump took office for a second term, the United States began sending illegal (undocumented) immigrants back to their own countries from February 2025; the deportation of Bangladeshis is part of this.

According to police sources, the Bangladeshis deported from the US in March-April 2025 had continued living in the United States even after losing their immigration cases; those sent back also included people who had been convicted in various cases in the US.

Bangladesh foreign ministry officials said in April 2025 that only people who have lost their legal fight in the United States are being returned, and the Bangladesh foreign ministry is informed in advance about each person being returned.
facts.source_in_article: Officials of the Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Bangladesh foreign ministry officials said in April 2025 that more Bangladeshis may be sent back from the United States in the coming days.
facts.source_in_article: Officials of the Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

headline_en: Qatar migrant returns home in the morning, dies under a train in the evening
summary_en: Abul Basar (48) of Senbagh, Noakhali, who had lived in Qatar for 24 years, returned to Dhaka on 7 April 2025 without telling his family after finding no work in Qatar and suffering depression. After an argument by phone with his wife, who had told him not to come back, he was killed by a train at Chowmuhani railway station that evening; railway police suspect suicide over a family quarrel.

facts.statement: Qatar returnee Abul Basar (48), of Uttar Sahapur village, Kabilpur union, Senbagh upazila, Noakhali, arrived in Dhaka on the morning of Monday 7 April 2025 and died the same evening around 7:30 pm when he lay his head on the rail line at Chowmuhani railway station, Begumganj upazila, Noakhali, and was hit by a train coming from Laksam, Cumilla.

Abul Basar, who had been in Qatar for 24 years, came home in January 2025 for his only daughter's wedding and went back to Qatar, but found no work there and suffered from depression (hotasha), according to his cousin.

When Abul Basar told his wife he had decided to return from Qatar, she told him not to; he then returned without telling anyone in the family, and after a phone argument with her said 'if I don't come, my corpse will go home.'

Chowmuhani railway police outpost recovered Abul Basar's body and sent it to the Noakhali General Hospital morgue for autopsy; police said they initially believe he committed suicide over a family quarrel and an unnatural death case would be filed.
facts.source_in_article: SI Pradip Kumar Majumder, officer in charge, Chowmuhani railway police outpost

headline_en: Joining the LDC list is optional, leaving it is predetermined (interview)
summary_en: Interview with CPD's Mustafizur Rahman on the economy under the interim government, money laundering and LDC graduation on 24 November 2026. On migration-related points he says remittance inflows are the highest ever, credits migrant workers and the interim government's clean image among expatriates for moving people away from hundi, and describes how hundi and a 'vicious circle' around remittance moved laundered money to Dubai, Singapore, Malaysia, the UK, US and Canada. He also cites gold from the UAE far exceeding declared imports.

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman of CPD said in March 2025 that remittance (probashi ay) was coming in well, and that the highest remittance of all time was being received; he said migrant workers deserve major credit for this.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said in March 2025 that the interim government made an important contribution to moving expatriates away from hundi-hawala by stressing that money sent through legal channels serves the country, while through hundi-hawala corrupt people, tax defaulters, loan defaulters and some politicians launder money abroad; he said the government built a clean image among expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: According to the white paper committee on the economy (cited by Mustafizur Rahman), about USD 16 billion was laundered out of Bangladesh during the Hasina government's tenure, about 5% of GDP.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said a vicious circle formed around hundi-hawala and remittance which laundered money from Bangladesh to Dubai, Singapore, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada, where it was kept in bank accounts and used to buy property; many layers were created between sender and receiver so the paper trail is hard to establish.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Citing Prothom Alo, Mustafizur Rahman said gold worth about USD 366.64 crore (about BDT 40,000 crore) came from the United Arab Emirates to Bangladesh in 10 years, but only USD 82 lakh of gold imports were shown in Bangladesh, indicating a nexus between money launderers and gold smugglers.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said in March 2025 that the interim government had clearly decided Bangladesh will graduate from the least developed country (LDC) list on 24 November 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

headline_en: Immigration problems
summary_en: Humorous first-person column from the United States listing ways Bangladeshis harm their own immigration cases: a student whose visa was cancelled after posting on Facebook asking for help finding off-campus restaurant or gas-station work, a student deported after allegedly trying to forcibly kiss a woman at his gas-station job, social media posts promoting switching a visitor visa to asylum, and careless form-filling, including an applicant who wrote a date of death for living parents in an immigration petition. It also describes US hospital billing.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi had his US student visa cancelled because, right after getting it, he posted a Facebook status asking whether any 'elder brother' could help him find restaurant or gas station work in the United States.

According to the columnist, a student in the United States is legally not supposed to work off campus (some institutions allow it); students who do such jobs do it secretly, and authorities pretend not to see unless it is made public, in which case they are forced to act.

A Bangladeshi student in one US state had his student visa cancelled and was sent back to Bangladesh, reportedly for trying to forcibly kiss an unknown woman at the gas station where he worked; his family had spent heavily, possibly selling land, to send him abroad to study, and was ruined.

The columnist warns that some Bangladeshis post on Facebook how to come to the United States on a visitor visa and switch to asylum, and share irregular ('dui nombori') routes; he says if US immigration notices such posts it will become harder for ordinary Bangladeshis to get visas.

The columnist says each of his children was born by C-section in a US hospital; mother and baby were released the same or next day, the bill each time was over USD 50,000 for two days, and he paid USD 6,000 as insurance deductible, with the rest recovered from the insurance company.

According to the columnist, US hospitals do not keep patients even an hour longer than needed because insurers will not pay for unnecessary admission; a low-income vlogger in New York had city insurance and paid nothing out of pocket.

The columnist warns that a Bangladeshi vlogger's video calling US hospitals bad (because a newborn was kept separately for three days, likely for intensive care) could make others avoid taking wives to hospital, risking deaths of mothers or babies.

A woman who applied for US immigration for her parents was told by the embassy that the parents had died in 2002, because a date had been entered in the 'date of death' field of the application; the parents then had to prove they were alive. The columnist warns not to fill in fields that do not apply (leave blank or write 'NA', not the Bangla word 'na').

headline_en: Tripartite agreement signed for online attestation of certificates of students going abroad
summary_en: On 18 February 2025 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the University Grants Commission (UGC) and the a2i (Aspire to Innovate) programme signed an MoU at UGC to attest certificates of students going abroad online using the apostille system through the MyGov platform, with fees paid via the national payment gateway 'ekPay'. The foreign ministry will draft rules for the apostille system, UGC will instruct universities, and the foreign secretary urged extending online attestation to embassies abroad.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 18 February 2025 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the University Grants Commission (UGC) and the Aspire to Innovate (a2i) programme signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding at UGC to make attestation of certificates for students going abroad easier, faster and safer.
Under the February 2025 agreement, students of universities under UGC can pay the certificate attestation fee for applications on the MyGov platform using the national payment gateway 'ekPay' (একপে).
facts.source_in_article: Press release; UGC chairman Prof. S M A Faiz

facts.statement: The foreign ministry, education ministry, a2i of the ICT ministry and UGC will complete attestation of certificates of students from all universities in Bangladesh who want to go abroad through apostille on the MyGov platform; this is for students seeking higher education or jobs abroad and is meant to save time, effort and money.

Under the MoU, the foreign ministry will make the rules, guidelines or policy needed to implement the apostille system and coordinate all parties; UGC will instruct universities to implement it, inform students through universities about paying the attestation management charge, and give universities access to the integrated online attestation management system.
The agreement was signed by a2i project director Md. Mamunur Rashid Bhuiyan, UGC secretary Md. Fakhrul Islam and foreign ministry Director General (Consular and Welfare) Shah Mohammad Tanvir Mansur.

Foreign secretary (East) Muhammad Nazrul Islam said bringing all universities onto one online attestation platform had been very difficult, and urged those concerned to start online certificate attestation at Bangladesh embassies abroad as well.

headline_en: Where are the 20,000 'missing' Indian students who went to Canada
summary_en: Canadian government figures published in March-April 2024 flagged about 50,000 international students as 'no-shows' who got study permits but did not start studying, including about 20,000 Indians (5.4%). Of 11,948 students from Bangladesh in the period, 7.5% did not contact their college or university. Indian media report many work to support themselves, some were cheated by fake colleges, some crossed illegally into the US, and asylum claims by foreign students hit a record in 2024. Working without a work permit is illegal in Canada.

facts.statement: According to Canadian government statistics published in March-April 2024, about 50,000 foreign students at Canadian colleges and universities were marked as 'no-show': they came with study permits but did not start studying.
facts.source_in_article: Canadian government statistics, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Of 11,948 students who went from Bangladesh to study in Canada in the period covered by the March-April 2024 figures, 7.5% did not contact their university or college after arriving in Canada, i.e. did not go there to study.
facts.source_in_article: Canadian government statistics, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: No-show rates in the Canadian figures (published March-April 2024): India about 20,000 students (5.4% of its total), Philippines 2.2%, China 6.4%, Iran 11.6%, Rwanda 48.1%.

Under Canada's International Student Compliance Regime, launched in 2014, educational institutions report twice a year whether students are attending classes in line with their study permit conditions.
In Canada it is not possible to work legally anywhere without a work permit.

Prothom Alo writes that healthcare in Canada is public, so a student working illegally who falls ill must go to public healthcare where police may catch them; it also says Canada is about to take tough action against illegal immigrants.

Indian media report that many Indian students were cheated by fake colleges in Canada: on arrival they found the institutions were fake or lacked facilities. A 24-year-old from Panchkula, Haryana thought he was admitted to a well-known college in Brampton, but the address on the admission letter was a small office with no classrooms; he was told classes were full and to wait, and after weeks realised the college was fake. He had paid INR 4.2 lakh of a 12 lakh 'tuition fee'.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India / Economic Times, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Haryana student dealt with a student agent only by phone; after he paid INR 4 lakh, the agent assured him he could pay the rest of the fee through part-time work without extra loans. He then started working at a local petrol pump.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: According to Economic Times, some Indian students deliberately misused the Canadian student visa system to enter Canada for work, exploiting the policy that tuition fees need not be paid in advance.
facts.source_in_article: Economic Times, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: A 27-year-old from Valsad, Gujarat enrolled in a community college in Canada for INR 7.5 lakh for 2 years, on average three times cheaper than a master's degree in Canada; he said many with places at good colleges have loans of 25 lakh or more. He works two jobs, at a restaurant and night food delivery.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: A 26-year-old from Khammam, Telangana enrolled at a college in Surrey but never attended class; he works full time at a mobile phone shop for USD 7 per hour (as printed). A 25-year-old from Ongole, Andhra Pradesh works as a delivery agent in Toronto.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Indian authorities said some students went to Canada and then entered the United States illegally; Canada has no count of how many. Student organisations say some use Canada as a gateway to enter the US illegally.

According to former federal economist and immigration expert Henry Lotin, most missing Indian students did not cross the border but are working in Canada and trying to settle; the number of foreign students claiming asylum in Canada rose to a record in 2024, and at least 10% of student visa holders were unaccounted for.
facts.source_in_article: Henry Lotin, former federal economist and immigration expert

facts.statement: Henry Lotin proposed requiring foreign students to pay full tuition before coming to Canada to reduce fake applicants. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) has contacted Indian authorities and is investigating the issue.

headline_en: 17 rescued from traffickers' hideout in Teknaf, one held
summary_en: On 25 January 2025 the Bangladesh Navy raided a human traffickers' hideout in the hills of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, rescuing 17 people including women and children (3 Bangladeshis, the rest Rohingya camp residents) held hostage for trafficking by sea to Malaysia, and arrested trafficker Ali Abdullah. The union chairman said syndicates lure Rohingyas with promises of Malaysia, hold them in the hills and demand ransom; about 150 victims were rescued in January 2025 alone.

facts.statement: On the afternoon of Saturday 25 January 2025 the Bangladesh Navy raided a human traffickers' hideout in the hilly area of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar, acting on a tip-off, and rescued 17 women, men and children held hostage to be trafficked by sea to Malaysia; trafficker Ali Abdullah was arrested.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Cdr Afzal Hossain, Bangladesh Navy Teknaf contingent

facts.statement: Of the 17 rescued in Teknaf on 25 January 2025, 3 were Bangladeshi citizens and the rest were residents of Rohingya camps in Ukhia and Teknaf.

Human traffickers operate as syndicates through several points along the coast of Baharchhara union, Teknaf, bringing Rohingyas from camps in Ukhia-Teknaf; they lure them with promises of sending them to Malaysia, hold them captive in the hills and demand ransom.
facts.source_in_article: Amjad Hossain, chairman, Baharchhara union parishad

facts.statement: About 150 or more cheated people were rescued in police, RAB and Navy operations in the Teknaf area in January 2025 alone.
facts.source_in_article: Amjad Hossain, chairman, Baharchhara union parishad

facts.statement: The Navy handed 18 people (17 rescued plus 1 trafficker) to Teknaf Model police station around 7 pm on 25 January 2025; the trafficker was to be sent to Cox's Bazar court on 26 January 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Gias Uddin, OC, Teknaf Model police station

summary_en: On 5 December 2024 the interim government's advisory council approved setting up a Bangladesh High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand. The Cabinet Division said about 10,000 Bangladeshis live in New Zealand and about 1,000 Bangladeshi students study there, and that consular services from Australia (the concurrently accredited mission) cannot always reach them, forcing costly trips to Australia; costs will be met in FY2025-26.

facts.statement: On Thursday 5 December 2024 the interim government's advisory council, chaired by Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus, approved establishing a Bangladesh High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand; all expenses will be met in the next fiscal year (2025-26).
About 10,000 Bangladeshis live in New Zealand and about 1,000 Bangladeshi students study at universities there.

Bangladeshis in New Zealand have been served by the Bangladesh mission in Australia, which is concurrently accredited; proper service from Australia is not always possible, and expatriates face high costs and other difficulties travelling to Australia for consular services.
The Cabinet Division said that once the Wellington high commission is set up, all kinds of consular services will reach Bangladeshis in New Zealand directly, more easily and cheaply.
72 countries, including India and Pakistan, have diplomatic missions in New Zealand; New Zealand ranks 16th on the Human Development Index and 32nd on the global competitiveness index.

headline_en: Preparing to study abroad? Are you making these 5 mistakes
summary_en: Lifestyle feature listing five misconceptions among Bangladeshis planning to study abroad: that IELTS/TOEFL is unnecessary, that shortcuts via agencies or fake certificates work, that one can enrol in one country and move to another, that scholarships cover all costs, and that studying abroad brings citizenship and jobs. Bangladeshi students abroad warn against advertisements promising study abroad for BDT 10 lakh, offer letters from places like Cyprus, and note limits on off-campus work in the US and language needs for jobs in Germany and the Netherlands.

facts.statement: Without IELTS or TOEFL it is almost impossible to go to study in the United States, Canada or various European countries; Atanu Chakraborty (doctoral student, College of Pharmacy, University of Iowa) said the scores matter for admission and also for the visa, as most embassies and visa authorities assess applications based on them, and advised avoiding institutions that invite students abroad without these scores.
facts.source_in_article: Atanu Chakraborty, doctoral student, University of Iowa

facts.statement: Some students believe they can prepare papers in a few weeks, submit fake certificates and get a study visa, or that an agency will do all the paperwork; the article says this is not possible and taking a 'shortcut' carries a high risk of trouble later.

Mohidul Alam (student, New York University) warned not to fall for flashy advertisements such as 'go to study abroad by spending BDT 10 lakh'; he advised verifying information, starting preparation (IELTS/TOEFL, GRE) from after the HSC exam, and emailing foreign universities' admission offices directly rather than always using an agency.
facts.source_in_article: Mohidul Alam, student, New York University

facts.statement: Mohidul Alam said some students reach a foreign country to find no place to live and no work, and that money is needed to cover at least the first few months.

According to the article, under most scholarship and visa conditions students must return home after finishing their studies; opportunities to take citizenship or move to another country are limited, and course or credit transfer is rarely possible.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo; Rounak Saha, PhD student, UNSW

facts.statement: Rounak Saha (PhD student, University of New South Wales, Australia) warned against enrolling in a little-known European country or university planning to move later to another country, and said many come abroad with offer letters from countries including Cyprus and risk losing money and being cheated in various ways.
Most scholarships cover only tuition fees; living, travel and other costs are usually borne by the student, and it is hard to meet all costs without part-time work, which may be limited.
Rounak Saha said opportunities to work off campus are limited in the United States, while Australia offers some opportunity.
Rounak Saha said in countries such as Germany or the Netherlands you need to know the local language to get jobs or part-time work while studying; without it opportunities are very limited.

G M Majidul Islam (student, Central Queensland University) said studying abroad does not guarantee citizenship, which requires separate eligibility and conditions, and that part-time work is bound by many rules; breaking the law can bring fines and other trouble.
facts.source_in_article: G M Majidul Islam, student, Central Queensland University

facts.statement: Anika Tabassum (graduate, Queen Mary University of London) said the work environment abroad is challenging, many fall ill from unprepared exposure to the weather in Europe or America, and students planning to come with family or a spouse should plan carefully.
facts.source_in_article: Anika Tabassum, Queen Mary University of London

headline_en: Trust in '999' restored: over 25 million emergency services in 7 years
summary_en: Feature on Bangladesh's national emergency number 999, its call volumes since 2017 and its collapse and recovery after 5 August 2024. Among example cases, 999 helped a Saudi Arabia-bound migrant, Momin Sheikh, recover a bag holding his passport and air ticket that fell from a train on 27 March, so he could catch his flight. 999 officials say it handles trafficking among other emergencies and is free from any phone.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's National Emergency Service number is 999; anyone anywhere in the country can call it free of charge from any phone; it runs under the Ministry of Home Affairs and links police, fire service and ambulance/health services.

999 was launched on 12 December 2017; according to 999 Police Inspector Anwar Sattar it is used for emergency help in accidents, saving human and animal lives, wildlife rescue, stopping child marriage, fires, lost items, trafficking (pachar) and violence. bKash-related fraud and family land disputes are not emergencies but people still call 999 about them.
facts.source_in_article: Anwar Sattar, Police Inspector, 999 media and public relations section

facts.statement: On 27 March, Saudi Arabia-based migrant Momin Sheikh (45), of the railway colony in Sirajganj Sadar, was standing at the door of the Dhumketu Express from Bangabandhu Bridge East station to Dhaka when his bag with his passport and air ticket fell out of the train. A fellow passenger, Fahim, called 999 saying that without the bag Momin could not board his 2 pm flight to Saudi Arabia that day and could lose his job if he did not join work on time.

After the 999 call about Momin Sheikh's lost passport bag, 999 informed the railway police control room and the Tangail railway police outpost (fari); the outpost found that a woman, Hajera Begum (40), had the bag; she brought it to the Tangail railway police outpost and it was handed back to Momin Sheikh.

From 1 January to 31 October 2024, 999 received 6,635,312 calls; 3,354,497 were given service (50.56%); the remaining 3,280,815 were outside emergency scope and the callers were advised to contact the relevant department.

From launch on 12 December 2017 to 31 October 2024, 999 received 58,488,107 calls, of which 25,350,388 were given service (43.34%); 33,137,719 callers (56.66%) were advised to contact the relevant department. Over seven years 1,933,294 calls sought emergency service: police served 1,606,240, fire service 156,129 and ambulance 170,925.
From 5 August to 15 November 2024, 999 received 2,159,281 calls; 999 currently gets on average 22,000 calls a day and on 29 July 2024 received 48,000 calls; it can take 80 calls at once.

After the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on 5 August 2024, the police-dependent 999 service collapsed because most police were away from work and most calls could not be received; normal service resumed after police returned to stations under the interim government.

headline_en: Bangladeshi students in the US at all-time record, up 26 percent, ranking up 6 places
summary_en: The 2024 Open Doors Report shows over 17,000 Bangladeshi students in US higher education in 2023-24, up 26 percent, moving Bangladesh from 13th to 8th among sending countries. The article gives overall international student numbers and says the US Embassy in Dhaka is holding International Education Week sessions, with a contact email for EducationUSA.

facts.statement: According to the 2024 Open Doors Report on International Educational Exchange, more than 17,000 Bangladeshi students (17,099 in 2023-24) are studying at US higher education institutions, a 26 percent rise over the previous academic year (given as 2022-2023); Bangladesh rose from 13th to 8th place among countries sending international students to the US within one year.
The number of Bangladeshi students in the US rose 250 percent in a decade, from 4,802 in 2013-14 to 17,099 in 2023-24.

The Open Doors Report is published every year by the US State Department's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs and the Institute of International Education, covering international student enrolment at US universities and pre-academic intensive English programmes.

International students in the US reached a record 1,126,690 in 2023-24, 7 percent more than the year before; undergraduate students rose 8 percent to 502,291; participation in graduate-level practical work experience programmes rose 22 percent; community college enrolment rose 13 percent to 59,315.
In 2023 international students contributed more than USD 50 billion to the US economy and supported over 368,000 jobs, according to the US Department of Commerce.

For International Education Week 2024 the US Embassy in Dhaka is holding virtual and in-person sessions on applying to US higher education, academic programmes, funding/scholarships and US government-sponsored exchange programmes; for more information interested people can email EducationUSA-Bangla@state.gov.

headline_en: Because of unemployment, corruption and discrimination, 55% of youth want to go abroad: research
summary_en: The British Council's 'Next Generation Bangladesh 2024' survey of 3,081 people aged 18-35, conducted in November-December 2023, found 42 percent of youth worried about unemployment and 55 percent interested in going abroad. It lists the causes young people give for unemployment and other findings on internet use, gender attitudes and education.

facts.statement: The British Council 'Next Generation Bangladesh 2024' report found that 55 percent of young Bangladeshis are interested in going abroad, which the report links to unemployment causes; 42 percent of youth are worried about unemployment. The report was released at the British Council auditorium, Fuller Road, Dhaka University, on Wednesday (6 November 2024).

The Next Generation Bangladesh 2024 survey was based on interviews with 3,081 people aged 18 to 35 from various backgrounds, conducted in November and December 2023 before the 12th parliamentary election; it was presented by Aibek Iliasov, senior research director, Evaluation and Learning, M&C Saatchi World Services. Researchers could not immediately say what share of youth wanted to go abroad in the 2015 survey.

In the survey, 37 percent of youth named corruption and nepotism as the main cause of unemployment, 20 percent discrimination in hiring, and 18 percent inability to balance family life and work; 44 percent want to start a business within the next year.

66 percent of Bangladeshi youth use the internet regularly (77 percent of young men, 56 percent of young women); education is the top area where youth want progress, with 49 percent citing poor teaching quality, especially teaching and curricula not matched to the modern job market.

headline_en: Hajj cost reduced, packages announced
summary_en: The government finalised Hajj 2025 packages on Wednesday (30 October 2024): two government packages of BDT 478,242 and BDT 575,680 and a private general package of BDT 483,156, with one package about BDT 1 lakh cheaper than 2024. The article gives the Hajj calendar, payment rules, passport validity, and a list of pilgrims' tips, including warnings against middlemen and packages priced below the announced rate.

facts.statement: Hajj may be held in Saudi Arabia on 4 June 2025, subject to moon sighting; 127,198 people from Bangladesh will be able to perform Hajj this time.

Government-managed Hajj 2025 packages: BDT 478,242 (housing within 3 km of Masjid al-Haram) and BDT 575,680 (housing within 1.5 km of Masjid al-Haram); private general package BDT 483,156. Packages were finalised at the Hajj management executive committee meeting at the Secretariat on Wednesday chaired by Religious Affairs Adviser A F M Khalid Hossain.
Hajj 2024 costs were: government general package BDT 578,840, government special package BDT 936,320, private general package BDT 589,800. One 2025 package is BDT 1 lakh cheaper than last year.
The 2024 Hajj packages were calculated at BDT 29.74 per Saudi riyal; the 2025 packages at BDT 32.50 per riyal, so the Saudi-part costs, which must be paid in riyal, will rise for pilgrims.
Hajj 2025 timeline: Hajj agreement with the Saudi government on 13 January 2025; Hajj visas start 19 February 2025; Hajj flights start 29 April 2025.

The full Hajj package money must be paid only into the bank account of the relevant Hajj agency or directly at the agency, and pilgrims must keep the payment receipt; no dealings with middlemen are allowed; women and children must deposit money together with their mahram.
Each pilgrim must pay the sacrifice (qurbani) cost of 1,000 riyal separately; one package provides housing 1.5 km from the outer boundary of the Haram, the other 3 km.
For Hajj 2025, people aged 65 or above can go; pilgrims' passports must be valid until 31 December 2025; those without a passport should make one now matching their national ID card.

Experienced pilgrims advise: check the package length, how long you stay in Saudi Arabia and where; find out under which moallem number the agency has operated in recent years (there are moallems numbered 1 to 115 for South Asian countries, and the distance from Jamarat to the Mina tent depends on the moallem cluster price); get in writing what extra services the moallem gives for extra charges, as this causes disputes in Mina.

Pilgrims are advised to check the type of housing in Makkah and Madinah, its distance from the Kaaba, whether it has a lift, how many share a room and bathroom, whether three meals are given, whether there is a 'fitra' (shifting of house in Makkah) before or after Hajj, and arrangements for food and transport at Mina and Arafat.

To avoid fraud over the sacrifice (qurbani), it is better to buy an Islamic Development Bank (IDB) coupon; otherwise know in advance how you will be sure the sacrifice is done if you or the agency's person buys a goat.

Going on Hajj for less money than the announced package carries a risk of being cheated; never sign an agreement with a middleman, broker (dalal) or so-called moallem; check which agencies have complaints from the Saudi Hajj Ministry.
If possible make your passport yourself; if someone else makes it for you, check that your name and address in the passport are correct.

Prothom Alo has for 16 years published a free Hajj guide, available at www.prothomalo.com/widgets/hajj-guide/hajj_guide.pdf and from Prothom Alo offices in Dhaka and elsewhere; Hajj news is at www.prothomalo.com/religion/islam.

headline_en: 'Everything is finished for me': three Munshiganj workers die after Malaysia factory blast
summary_en: An explosion at a chemical factory in Malaysia on Thursday (10 October 2024) burned three Bangladeshi workers from the same village in Munshiganj, all of whom died. Abdus Salam (24) had gone to Malaysia 1.5 years earlier on BDT 3.5 lakh borrowed at interest, through his maternal uncle Abu Taher, and his mother still owes BDT 2 lakh. Families want the bodies brought home quickly; the Munshiganj DC says contact with the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia is ongoing.

facts.statement: At about 11:30 am on Thursday (10 October 2024) an explosion at a chemical factory in Malaysia burned three Bangladeshi workers over most of their bodies: Abdus Salam (24), his maternal uncle Abu Taher (32) and Jabbar Ali (42), all from Ramzanbeg area, Munshiganj municipality. Jabbar Ali died on Friday (11 October), Abu Taher at dawn on Saturday (12 October) and Salam at about 5 pm on Sunday (13 October) while under treatment.
Jabbar Ali's nephew Khairul Islam said the three burned workers lay on the road for an hour and a half after the blast and that some might have survived if treatment had started in time.
facts.source_in_article: Khairul Islam, nephew of Jabbar Ali

facts.statement: Abdus Salam's mother Taslima Begum said she borrowed BDT 3.5 lakh at interest from various people to send Salam to Malaysia about 1.5 years earlier through her brother Abu Taher; Salam could not work for the first six months and sent some money within a year; she has repaid BDT 1.5 lakh including interest and still owes lenders BDT 2 lakh.
Abu Taher had gone to Malaysia 10 years earlier and worked for the same company for 10 years; because the company was good, he took his nephew Salam there 1.5 years ago.

Munshiganj Deputy Commissioner Fatema Tul Jannat said on 14 October 2024 that contact is ongoing with the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia on how to bring the bodies home quickly, and that the administration is checking on the victims' families. Families demanded the government bring the bodies quickly.

headline_en: Germany's Opportunity Card: students, learn the application process and details
summary_en: Explainer (source: UNB) on Germany's Opportunity Card (Chancenkarte), a residence permit of up to one year for non-EU skilled people to look for work. It sets out the two eligibility routes, the points system (minimum 6 points), benefits, the VIDEX online application, the documents list, the EUR 75 fee at the German Embassy in Dhaka, and processing time of a few weeks to six months.

facts.statement: Germany's Opportunity Card is a residence permit for skilled workers from outside the EU, EEA and Switzerland to enter Germany to look for a job; it is valid for at most one year, within which the holder must find employment, and the applicant must give proof of qualifications for the relevant work.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Opportunity Card route 1: people with professional or academic qualifications fully recognised by Germany, obtained in Germany or from a Germany-recognised institution in their home country.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Opportunity Card route 2 (not yet established skilled workers) requires: an academic degree from a German university or a Germany-recognised university at home, or at least two years of vocational training from a German or Germany-recognised institution; plus German at least CEFR A1 or English at least CEFR B2. The article says IELTS 5.5 to 6.5 and TOEFL iBT 72 to 94 are equivalent to CEFR B2.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Route 2 applicants are scored on points; those with at least 6 points have a better chance of getting the card. Partial recognition of degree/training: 4 points (also given for licensable professions before licensing, but the licence exam must be passed before the residence permit). Qualification in a shortage occupation: 1 point (e.g. mining manager, health service manager, chemist, civil engineer, graphic and multimedia designer, software developer).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Opportunity Card points continued: work experience after the degree of at least 2 years within the last 5 years = 2 points, at least 5 years within the last 7 years = 3 points; German A2 = 1 point, B1 (printed as 'B1-A2') and B2 or above = 3 points, plus 1 extra point for English C1 or above or native speaker; age under 35 = 2 points, 35 to 40 = 1 point; at least six months' legal stay in Germany within the last five years (visit, study or work) = 1 point; if one spouse meets the Opportunity Card conditions, the other gets 1 point.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: The Opportunity Card initially allows up to one year in Germany to look for work; after one year the holder can apply from within Germany to extend it up to two years; holders may seek a job or self-employment, work part-time up to a total of 20 hours a week in one or more jobs, and do job trials of up to two weeks per company.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Application steps: first book an appointment through the online appointment system; then complete the online application on the VIDEX portal; print the completed application and sign it yourself; after booking you get a confirmation email with the date; on that date go to the German Embassy with the application and all documents.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Documents for the Opportunity Card visa include: completed VIDEX form; valid passport issued within the last 10 years with at least two blank pages, plus copies of data page and previous visas; one recent biometric passport photo (not older than six months); signed declaration of consent (https://dhaka.diplo.de/bd-en/service/visa-einreise/-/2669542); vocational or academic certificates with German recognition of equivalence (original plus copy); licence to practise for licensable professions (e.g. medical licence); experience confirmation letters from previous employers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Further documents: motivation letter or statement of purpose covering the kind of work sought in Germany, the period of German study, why Germany among EU countries, companies applied to or interviews, CV and cover letter (in English and also German), proof of funds via a blocked account in Germany of at least EUR 1,027 per month, sufficient funds for a return flight, and an original declaration of commitment if someone else bears the costs; proof of health insurance (travel health insurance for the first three weeks plus a letter from a German health provider, or public German health insurance); proof of accommodation in Germany (written invitation from a host family or hotel booking with full address); for previous legal stay in Germany: rental contract, employment terms, service contract, passport with visas and entry stamps; spouses applying together should attach the marriage certificate.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Recognition of vocational qualifications can be applied for at https://zab.kmk.org/en/app/zeugnisbewertung (prerequisites at https://zab.kmk.org/en/dab); the recognition statement for vocational qualifications costs EUR 150 or BDT 19,766 as printed. For university degrees, proof that the degree and university are listed in the anabin database, or a ZAB (Central Office for Foreign Education) statement of comparability; a pre-check is available at https://zab.kmk.org/en/app/pre-check.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: The Opportunity Card visa application processing fee is EUR 75.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: German Embassy in Dhaka address as printed: Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany, 11 Madani Avenue, Baridhara Diplomatic Enclave, Dhaka-1212.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

facts.statement: Processing of the Opportunity Card application can take from a few weeks up to six months; when the card is ready the German Embassy informs the applicant by email or phone; applying well in advance with up-to-date documents is advised to avoid delays.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo scholarship section, citing UNB

headline_en: Anwar Ibrahim pledges steps to take 18,000 workers
summary_en: On a Friday visit to Dhaka (4 October 2024), Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said his government would immediately attend to the entry of 18,000 Bangladeshi workers in the first phase, subject to all conditions being met, and that workers must not be treated as modern slaves. He also asked Bangladesh not to shelter criminal activity by Bangladeshis in Malaysia. About 800,000 Bangladeshis work in Malaysia.

facts.statement: At a joint press conference with Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus at a Dhaka hotel (InterContinental) on a Friday (about 4 October 2024), Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said his government would immediately give attention to the going of 18,000 Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia in the first phase, subject to all conditions being met, while ensuring a proper working environment.

Anwar Ibrahim said Malaysia needs workers and they cannot be treated as modern slaves, wherever they come from; he also urged Bangladesh to be cautious and not to indulge criminal activities by any Bangladeshi or foreigner living in Malaysia.
About 800,000 (8 lakh) Bangladeshis currently work in Malaysia; about 450,000 (sare char lakh) of them migrated between August 2022 and May 2024.

Anwar Ibrahim stressed quick resolution of problems faced by Malaysian companies in Bangladesh and Bangladeshi companies in Malaysia and said a Joint Commission meeting could be held as soon as possible; it was the first visit to Bangladesh by a Malaysian prime minister in about a decade.

headline_en: No one declared homes or cars abroad in tax files
summary_en: No Bangladeshi taxpayer has declared foreign assets in tax returns since NBR allowed it in 2022, despite reports of politicians' and businesspeople's assets abroad. The article explains the 10(B) asset statement form and why taxpayers avoid declaring, and notes that 3,604 Bangladeshis have settled in Malaysia under its Second Home programme.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's National Board of Revenue (NBR) first allowed declaring foreign assets in income tax files in the 2022 budget; no taxpayer has done so. The same budget allowed bringing back laundered money for one year by paying a set tax rate with no questions asked; no one used it.

In the annual tax return a taxpayer gives income, expenditure and asset information; the asset statement is filed on form 10(B), which is mandatory if assets at home and abroad exceed BDT 50 lakh; column 9 of form 10(B) is for assets held abroad. Bangladesh has more than 10 million TIN holders, of whom more than 3.5 million file returns.

Tax officials say taxpayers avoid declaring foreign assets because of possible double taxation, because assets bought with laundered money could be caught by agencies such as the Anti-Corruption Commission and Bangladesh Bank, and because assets from income earned abroad are safer to show in the foreign tax file and there is no obligation to show them in the Bangladeshi tax file.
So far 3,604 Bangladeshis have settled in Malaysia under the Malaysia 'Second Home' programme; many Bangladeshi businesspeople have also settled in Canada and Singapore through investment programmes.

headline_en: Many Awami League leaders have left the country
summary_en: After the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government, many Awami League leaders and ex-ministers left Bangladesh illegally across the border into India, paying brokers on both sides. The article names border areas used, prices (BDT 50,000 to 25-30 lakh per person), a retired judge robbed by those helping him, and a death at the border.

facts.statement: Families and associates of people who fled say illegal exits to India after 5 August 2024 went mostly through Sylhet, Akhaura (Brahmanbaria), Netrokona and Mymensingh (Haluaghat), the Jashore region, Lalmonirhat and other northern border areas; each person paid brokers (dalal) on both sides of the border from BDT 50,000 up to BDT 25-30 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Families, colleagues of those who left

facts.statement: Retired Appellate Division justice Shamsuddin Chowdhury (Manik) was caught by locals at the Kanaighat border, Sylhet, on 23 August 2024 while fleeing to India; in a video he said he had a BDT 15,000 deal to cross, and that those helping him took the BDT 60-70 lakh he carried and beat him on the other side of the border.

Former Chhatra League general secretary Ishaque Ali Khan (Panna) died on the night of 24 August 2024 while crossing to India through the Dona border at Kanaighat, Sylhet; Meghalaya police said he died of strangulation.

Sources say some people who entered India illegally are using brokers to get Bangladesh exit and Indian entry stamps put in their passports; some are trying to 'manage' Indian immigration to move to other countries, and the former Sylhet mayor Anwaruzzaman Chowdhury is reported to have gone from India to London this way.
Former Additional IGP Naim Ahmed said checkpoints and surveillance should be strengthened and action taken against people involved in human trafficking at the border.

headline_en: 26 Bangladeshis win Commonwealth scholarships this year, welcomed by UK High Commissioner Sarah Cooke
summary_en: 26 Bangladeshis received 2024 Commonwealth Scholarships for master's study at UK universities including Oxford, Cambridge, SOAS, Warwick and Edinburgh. The British Council held a pre-departure briefing at the British High Commissioner's residence on 26 Aug 2024. Since 1960, 1,867 Bangladeshis have received Commonwealth scholarships or fellowships; 105 are currently studying.

facts.statement: In 2024, 26 Bangladeshis received Commonwealth Scholarships for postgraduate (master's) study at UK universities including Oxford University, Cambridge University, SOAS University of London, University of Warwick and University of Edinburgh.
facts.source_in_article: British Council press release; UK High Commissioner Sarah Cooke

facts.statement: The British Council organised a pre-departure briefing session for 2024 Bangladeshi Commonwealth scholars on Monday 26 Aug 2024 at the British High Commissioner's residence in Dhaka, giving essential information and guidance on studying in the UK.

Since the Commonwealth Scholarship programme began in 1960, a total of 1,867 Bangladeshi citizens have received UK-government-funded Commonwealth scholarships or fellowships through the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission (CSC); 105 Bangladeshis are currently studying on Commonwealth scholarships, including the 2023 batch.
Every Commonwealth Scholarship scheme is highly competitive and candidates need an outstanding academic record to succeed.

Subjects of 2024 Bangladeshi Commonwealth scholars include behavioural and economic science, biological chemistry, civil engineering, computational applied mathematics, data and decision analytics, education, electronic and electrical engineering, environmental science, GIS, global health policy, global health science and epidemiology, healthcare management, human rights, international development law and human rights, international relations law, management, medical statistics and health data science, museum studies, public health, public policy, sustainable agriculture and food security, and textiles and apparel.

headline_en: Europe-bound students at risk as Indian visa operations halt
summary_en: A reader piece (Aug 2024) says Bangladeshi students admitted to universities in European countries with no embassy in Bangladesh must take visa interviews in India, but the Indian Visa Application Centre (IVAC) suspended visa operations indefinitely after the July-August 2024 unrest. Students who paid tuition risk cancelled admission if they miss embassy interviews by 15-20 September, and refunds often lose 30-40%. Workers bound for those countries are also affected.

facts.statement: Portugal, Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania, Hungary, Austria and other European countries have no embassy in Bangladesh, so Bangladeshi students going to study there must give their visa interview in neighbouring India.
More than 300 Bangladeshi students go each academic year to study in these European countries (those without embassies in Bangladesh).

In August 2024 the Indian Visa Application Centre (IVAC) in Bangladesh suspended visa operations indefinitely; a week before the 20 Aug 2024 article IVAC announced limited operations on its website but was not accepting any visa forms, only returning previously submitted passports, and most students emailing got no reply.
Students who cannot attend embassy visa interviews (held in India) between 15 and 20 September 2024 risk having their university admission cancelled.

European universities may not refund tuition fees until the student submits a letter from the embassy stating the reason for visa refusal, and even when they refund they usually deduct 30 to 40 percent.
The writer gives an illustrative average tuition payment of 4 lakh taka per student, so 100 students would have paid about 4 crore taka; many are from low or middle income families.

During the July 2024 unrest banks were closed, so many students turned to Bangladeshi expatriates and Bangladeshi students at foreign universities to pay tuition fees on their behalf or to get deadlines extended.
By Aug 2024 most embassies in Bangladesh, including those of the US, UK, Italy, Germany and Denmark, had resumed normal operations.

The writer says workers going to these European countries are also affected: if they cannot travel after getting a company job offer, job opportunities for Bangladeshis there may shrink; recruitment of Bangladeshi workers has become irregular in many countries.

During the July 2024 movement, expatriate Bangladeshis ran a campaign not to send remittances, which spread quickly; a diaspora team was formed to analyse the effect of not sending remittances.
57 Bangladeshis were convicted in the United Arab Emirates over protests linked to the 2024 movement.

The writer says expatriates have long been angry with the state: Bangladesh embassies rarely help them, there is little support from passport-making onwards, no special arrangement for workers in the Middle East, Biman Bangladesh tickets are always more expensive, and the airport shows extreme mismanagement.

headline_en: Offshore banking pays higher profit: how to open an account
summary_en: Bangladeshis living abroad can open foreign-currency offshore (international banking) accounts in Bangladeshi banks from abroad, or a close relative can open one on their behalf. Banks pay up to 8.75% a year, tax-free under the Offshore Banking Act 2024, with no questions on source of funds and full repatriation allowed. About USD 50 million had been deposited, USD 24 million at City Bank alone (printed 22 Jul 2024).

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi living abroad can open a foreign-currency account (offshore banking or international banking account) in a Bangladeshi bank from abroad, or a close relative in Bangladesh can open it on their behalf; Bangladesh Bank allowed this at the end of 2023 amid the dollar crisis.

To open an offshore banking account from abroad, the expatriate applies through the bank's website and submits Bangladeshi citizenship information, proof of residence abroad, a work ID card and a photo; if someone in Bangladesh will operate the account, that person's details must also be submitted.

When a close relative in Bangladesh opens the offshore account on behalf of an expatriate, papers proving the relationship and information on the relative must be submitted, and both must submit ID, photos and other documents; details are found by searching 'offshore banking account' or 'international banking account' on the bank's website.
Banks offering offshore banking accounts to expatriates include The City Bank, BRAC Bank, Dutch-Bangla Bank, Pubali Bank, Eastern Bank and Islami Bank, among others.
Bangladesh Bank sets the maximum profit on offshore banking accounts; banks were paying up to 8.75% a year in July 2024, compared with up to 8% at foreign banks.
Profit earned on offshore banking accounts is fully income-tax-free; by contrast, income from deposits in taka accounts is taxed 15% without a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) and 10% with a TIN.

Under the Offshore Banking Act 2024, no agency questions the source of money deposited in an offshore account, and the depositor can take the full amount with profit back to the country where they live at any time.
About USD 50 million or more had been deposited in offshore banking accounts in Bangladesh by July 2024, of which USD 24 million at The City Bank alone.

Bangladesh Bank's 2024 monetary policy said offshore banking, foreign-currency accounts for returnees and higher remittances would ease pressure on the exchange rate and raise reserves; MDs of several banks travelled abroad to promote international banking accounts to expatriates.

summary_en: Editorial (24 Jul 2024): during the quota-movement unrest and curfew, three airlines cancelled 17 international flights over Friday to Sunday, stranding migrants at Shahjalal airport and nearby hotels at inflated prices. facts.statement: Over Friday, Saturday and Sunday (19-21 Jul 2024), three airlines cancelled 17 international flights from Dhaka; migrants who had spent several times the normal cost to reach Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport were stuck at the airport, unable to fly or return home under curfew, and many stayed in hotels near the Hajj Camp paying several times the normal room rent.

All Saudi Airlines flights were cancelled on 19 and 20 July 2024; 1,200 passengers were booked on four of those flights, and airlines could not say when flights would leave; many workers' visas had only 2 to 7 days left, putting their travel to Saudi Arabia at risk.
facts.source_in_article: Daily Bonik Barta, cited in editorial

facts.statement: Flights to Malaysia and other destinations were similarly disrupted in July 2024.
The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare said it had discussed with the Saudi embassy extending by 15 days the visas of workers whose visas would expire during the flight disruption.

After visiting Shahjalal airport on Monday 22 Jul 2024, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister Muhammad Faruk Khan said efforts were under way to send stranded Saudi-bound migrants to Saudi Arabia on Biman.

Remittances sent legally through TapTap Send arrive instantly in the recipient's bKash account via the banking channel along with the government incentive of 25 taka per 1,000 taka.

A joint TapTap Send and bKash campaign ran from 8 Jul to 30 Sep 2024: each month one recipient of the highest remittance in bKash could get up to 1 lakh taka bonus, and each week the 10 highest recipients got 5,000 taka each.

To qualify for the TapTap Send-bKash bonus, the expatriate had to send at least two remittances of 10,000 taka or more each to the relative's bKash account; a recipient could win the 1 lakh bonus once during the campaign, and weekly bonuses once a month and at most three times in three months; winners received bonuses within 3-4 working days after the week ended.

headline_en: Work while studying abroad: these five countries can be destinations
summary_en: Feature (Jul 2024) based on ApplyBoard's chief experience officer Karun Kandoi, listing Australia, Canada, the UK, Ireland and the US as study destinations with part-time work rights. It gives weekly work-hour limits, post-study work periods and Australia's 2022-23 student visa numbers.

facts.statement: In Australia's 2022-23 financial year, student visas were granted to more than 166,000 of a total 179,000 applications; student visa approval rates rose to a record to fill post-Covid skill and financial gaps.
facts.source_in_article: Feature citing Education.com and India Today

facts.statement: In Australia, student visa holders' work limit was raised from the earlier 20 hours a week to 24 hours a week (after the Covid-era removal of the limit ended).
Australia's 485 Temporary Graduate visa was extended: bachelor's graduates can stay 4 years instead of 2, master's graduates 5 years instead of 3, and doctoral graduates 6 years.

In Canada, international students do not need a work permit for part-time work on or off campus; they can work 20 hours a week during their academic programme and full time during academic breaks, and after graduation can apply for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP).

In the UK, full-time international students may work up to 20 hours a week during studies and during course breaks or as part of academic placements; after graduating, the UK allows work on a graduate work visa for up to two years.

In Ireland, students can work part time up to 20 hours a week during studies and up to 40 hours a week during summer and winter holidays, which requires valid immigration Stamp 2; after graduation international students may work for 12 to 24 months.
In the US, international students on F-1 or M-1 visas get work opportunities under certain conditions, and some institutions offer government-approved on-campus jobs.
A survey cited in the feature says four of every five students are interested in studying in Canada.

headline_en: Women trafficked to India with promises of higher-paid jobs
summary_en: Chattogram police arrested Md. Tarek (34) on 24 Jun 2024 in a case filed by a trafficked woman. The complainant and a friend crossed on 2 June and later escaped.

facts.statement: Jhumu Akter, wife of Md. Tarek, befriended women garment workers in Chattogram factories, especially those who had lost their jobs, and lured them with offers of higher-paid work in beauty parlours in India.
facts.source_in_article: OC Sanjoy Kumar Sinha, Bayezid Bostami police station

facts.statement: The complainant and a friend went with Tarek to Jashore on 29 May 2024; about six kilometres on they saw the India-Bangladesh border barbed-wire fence, were kept in a house beside the border, and on 2 June were taken across the fence to a hotel in Jharkhand state, India.
Women trafficked to Jharkhand, India via the Jashore border were confined in hotels and forced into sex work, and tortured if they refused.

On Monday 24 Jun 2024 police arrested Md. Tarek (34) at Chandranagar, Bayezid Bostami thana, Chattogram, in a trafficking case filed by a victim naming Tarek, his wife Jhumu Akter, associate Anisur Rahman and 3-4 unnamed people; police said Tarek confessed under interrogation.

headline_en: 49 Rohingyas given birth registration in Dhaka North City
summary_en: Dhaka North City Corporation's health department issued birth registrations to 49 Rohingyas, which the Registrar General has suspended in the BDRIS system. Police Special Branch had reported on 26 May 2024 that 102 Rohingyas obtained birth registration illegally through broker rings, dishonest officials and local representatives and then got Bangladeshi passports with false permanent addresses.

facts.statement: Police Special Branch wrote to the Registrar General of Birth and Death Registration on 26 May 2024 that 102 people, Rohingya citizens of Myanmar, had obtained birth registration illegally from various places through broker rings, dishonest officials and staff, and local public representatives, and had then made Bangladeshi passports; the permanent addresses in their passports were found to be false.

On 5 Jun 2024 the Registrar General's office wrote to Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) that 49 Rohingyas' birth registrations issued by DNCC were illegal and had been suspended in the BDRIS system; the registrars and assistants responsible must explain within 5 working days or face legal action.

Of 77 names Prothom Alo obtained from the Special Branch list of 102, 42 got birth registration from DNCC zonal offices: 9 from Zone-2, 17 from Zone-3, 14 from Zone-4, and one each from Zone-5 and Zone-9.

In February 2023 DNCC dismissed birth-death registration assistant Mafruza Sultana (Zone-5) and suspended assistant health officer Azizun Nesa (Zone-3) for birth registration fraud; Azizun Nesa was later reinstated. In April 2023 birth certificates were again issued to a South Korean national and a Rohingya, with no action taken.

headline_en: 5 Bangladeshis released on bail in Spain
summary_en: Five Bangladeshi sailors detained since March 2020 on suspicion of involvement in smuggling drugs from Colombia to Spain on the ship MV Karar were released on conditional bail from Alama (Pontevedra) prison on 24 Apr 2024. The Bangladesh embassy in Madrid said it had pressed Spanish authorities for a speedy hearing.

facts.statement: Spain's coast guard detained five Bangladeshi sailors and 19 other foreign sailors of the ship MV Karar on suspicion of involvement in smuggling drugs from Colombia to Spain; on 20 Mar 2020 the Vigo provincial court ordered them held in interim custody pending further investigation, and the custody was prolonged as the investigation and trial dragged on.

On 24 Apr 2024 the Vigo provincial court released the five Bangladeshis (Alimullah, Mohammad Altaf Hossain, Mohammed Imran Sharif, Md. Ataur Rahman and Mahfuzul Haque) on bail from Alama central prison, Pontevedra, on condition they attend future hearings and do not leave Spain.

The Bangladesh embassy in Spain monitored the case and contacted Spanish ministries several times asking for a speedy hearing and release; the five met Ambassador Mohammad Sarwar Mahmood at the embassy on 4 Jun 2024 and thanked it for consular service.

headline_en: Ambassador in Uzbekistan going to Bishkek to look after Bangladeshis
summary_en: After local mobs attacked foreigners, including Bangladeshi students, in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan from 16 May 2024, Bangladesh sent its ambassador in Uzbekistan to Bishkek. Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the Tashkent embassy covers it. Some students asked to be brought home by charter flight.

facts.statement: From the night of 16 May 2024 local people in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan attacked foreigners, including Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian students, going house to house beating foreigners and vandalising, and entering medical college hostels; there were also allegations of abuse of foreign women students. It followed a 13 May clash between two or three locals and some Egyptian medical university students.

Bangladesh's foreign ministry said on 19 May 2024 that the situation in Bishkek had improved since the night of Saturday 18 May; Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said there was no report of any Bangladeshi student being badly injured and that Bangladesh had conveyed its concern to the Kyrgyz government.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign ministry statement; Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud

facts.statement: Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the Bangladesh embassy in Uzbekistan is responsible for Kyrgyzstan.

On 19 May 2024 Bangladesh's ambassador to Uzbekistan, Mohammad Monirul Islam, said he was trying to go to Kyrgyzstan quickly to meet its foreign and home ministries, and that the embassy was in contact with the students.

Some Bangladeshi students in Kyrgyzstan asked to be returned to Bangladesh by charter flight in May 2024; the ambassador in Uzbekistan said this would be conveyed to the proper authority. No decision was reported.
Several hundred Bangladeshi students, among other Bangladeshis, were in fear in Kyrgyzstan in May 2024.

facts.statement: The Institute of Modern Languages at Dhaka University teaches Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, German, Turkish, Spanish (part-time and long-term), Korean, French, Arabic, Italian and Russian; some private institutions also teach Chinese.
Korean can be learnt in Bangladesh at the Institute of Modern Languages, Dhaka University and at the Bangladesh Korea Technical Training Centre.

German can be learnt in Bangladesh at the Institute of Modern Languages, Dhaka University and at Goethe-Institut Bangladesh, which is recognised by the German embassy.
French can be learnt at Dhaka University's Institute of Modern Languages and Alliance Française; Russian at the Institute of Modern Languages and the Russian Centre of Science and Culture.

headline_en: Bangladeshi women in UK and France suffer after being trolled on TikTok
summary_en: Based on a BBC investigation, Bangladeshi women living in the UK say they have been trolled, harassed and threatened on TikTok, allegedly by Hasan Sayed, a Bangladeshi living in a Paris suburb. Police complaints and platform reports achieved little. One victim's husband, Kamrul Islam, got help via the UK embassy in Paris to file a complaint with the Paris prosecutor, and the UK Information Commissioner's Office told TikTok, YouTube and Facebook to remove videos within seven days.

facts.statement: Several Bangladeshi women in the UK told the BBC that Hasan Sayed (হাসান সায়েদ), a Bangladeshi living in a Paris suburb with thousands of TikTok followers, collected their personal photos and information from social media, put them in troll videos, mocked them in TikTok lives and threatened rape and murder; he did not respond to the BBC's emails and calls.

In February 2023 Kamrul Islam, a Bangladeshi living in Staffordshire, UK, contacted the UK embassy in Paris, which connected him to English-speaking French lawyer Matthieu Croizet (ম্যাথিউ ক্রোইজেত); the lawyer filed a complaint at the Paris public prosecutor's office alleging at least three offences by Hasan Sayed under French law, including violent threats, threats to rape a child and an adult, child pornography and cyberbullying. Case status was unknown and the lawyer said it would take a long time.
facts.source_in_article: Kamrul Islam and lawyer Matthieu Croizet via BBC

facts.statement: In April 2023 Kamrul Islam complained to the UK Information Commissioner's Office, which found the videos concerning and, citing misuse of children's personal data, told TikTok, YouTube and Facebook to remove the videos within seven days; the three platforms said content breaching their community guidelines would be removed and the accounts blocked.

Bangladeshi women victims of TikTok trolling in the UK and France said complaints to police and to the platforms often produced no effective action; TikTok told Kamrul Islam the videos did not breach its community guidelines and police offered no hope.
Lawyer Matthieu Croizet told the BBC that Islamophobia is strong in France and the complaint could stall because the complainant's surname contains 'Islam'.

headline_en: US offering fellowships to Bangladeshi teachers
summary_en: The American Center of the US Embassy in Dhaka was taking applications for the Fulbright Teaching Excellence and Achievement (TEA) programme, a six-week exchange in the US for secondary school teachers in January or September 2025. The article lists benefits including J-1 visa support, eligibility rules, documents and English test requirements.

facts.statement: The Fulbright Teaching Excellence and Achievement (TEA) programme, run by Washington DC-based nonprofit IREX with sponsorship from the US State Department's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs and advertised by the American Center of the US Embassy in Dhaka, is a six-week exchange in the US for Bangladeshi secondary school teachers, held in January or September (spring or autumn) 2025, including a two-week internship at a US secondary school.
The application deadline for the Fulbright TEA fellowship is printed as Saturday 30 March 2025 (as printed in a March 2024 article); finalists are usually informed by the end of September.

Fulbright TEA benefits include J-1 visa support, a pre-departure orientation in Dhaka, round-trip and domestic US airfare, a welcome orientation in Washington DC, programme fees, accommodation (usually shared) and meals, accident and health insurance, travel to the internship school if needed, a book/professional development allowance, a closing seminar, hosting a US teacher for two weeks, and eligibility to apply for post-programme grants.

Fulbright TEA applicants must be current full-time secondary teachers of English, EFL, maths, science, foreign languages, social studies, journalism/communication or special education; hold a bachelor's degree; have at least five years of full-time teaching; have excellent English; know Microsoft Office, Word and Excel; be Bangladeshi citizens living in Bangladesh; hold a valid Bangladeshi passport; and apply online.
Ministry of Education officials, education administrators, full-time teacher trainers, university teachers and private English tutors are not eligible for Fulbright TEA.

Fulbright TEA applicants must submit an Institutional Support and Reference Form (ISRF) completed by a supervisor, a Leave Approval Form (LAF) from https://fulbright.irex.org/, a copy of passport information pages and undergraduate/postgraduate transcripts uploaded in 'Section XV. Supplemental Documents'.

Shortlisted Fulbright TEA candidates must take TOEFL or IELTS, needing a paper-based IELTS score of 6.0 or above or equivalent; candidates with a valid score need not retake; the American Center arranges the tests; shortlisted candidates are interviewed in English.
Fulbright TEA forms and online application: https://fulbright.irex.org/
