headline_en: Long gap no problem: chance to do BA and BSS while living abroad
summary_en: Bangladesh Open University's SSHL school opened admission for its 2024 batch of the Outside Bangladesh (NISH-2) BA and BSS programmes for Bangladeshi migrants or people of Bangladeshi origin in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy, South Korea and the UAE, through the Bangladesh embassy in each country. The article gives the deadline (30 March 2024), eligibility, documents, fees by year (USD 250, 190, 220), process, online classes on weekly holidays and contacts.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Open University (BOU) SSHL school runs an Outside Bangladesh (NISH-2) BA and BSS programme for Bangladeshi migrants or people of Bangladeshi origin working or living in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy, South Korea and the UAE, with admission through the Bangladesh embassy in each country; admission for the 2024 batch ran until 30 March 2024 with classes starting April 2024.
The BOU NISH-2 BA/BSS programme lasts 3 years and 6 semesters of 6 months each; registration stays valid for up to 5 academic years.

To join the BOU NISH-2 BA/BSS, the applicant must have passed HSC/Alim/A-level or equivalent and be a Bangladeshi citizen migrant, or of Bangladeshi origin, in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Italy or South Korea.

Documents needed for the BOU NISH-2 online application: scanned recent photo (300x300 pixel), signature (300x100 pixel), SSC and HSC (or equivalent) certificates and mark sheets, national ID/smart card/birth registration certificate, passport, residence permit card, and proof of admission fee payment.
BOU NISH-2 BA/BSS fees: first year USD 250 (semester 1: 135 + semester 2: 115), second year USD 190 (100 + 90), third year USD 220 (95 + 125); each year's fee is paid at admission to that year.

To apply to BOU NISH-2, pay USD 250 for the first and second semester as instructed on the website or Facebook page of the Bangladesh embassy in the country, fill in the online form, then download and print it and submit it with documents and fee proof to that Bangladesh embassy.

In BOU NISH-2, exams for semesters 1-2, 3-4 and 5-6 are held together in years one, two and three; online tutorial classes (eight per course) and exams are held on the host country's weekly holiday, so students need a device with internet; e-books are used mainly, and free printed books can be obtained by contacting IAPW.

BOU NISH-2 contacts: Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy, South Korea or UAE; Dean, SSHL School, BOU: bousshl2019@bou.ac.bd; International Academic Program Wing (IAPW), BOU: iapw@bou.ac.bd; websites iapw.bou.ac.bd or bou.ac.bd; e-books at ebookbou.edu.bd/ba_bss.php.

headline_en: Experience and impressions of a trip to Germany
summary_en: Travelogue by an Italy-based Bangladeshi (founding president of Europe Bangladesh Press Club) of a short trip to Frankfurt, Germany, in December 2023. It includes remarks that restaurant work is commonly available in Frankfurt with higher pay but higher costs and a housing shortage, that Germany has few migrants because entry is hard and laws strict, and that Bangladeshi students in Germany get permanent residence and citizenship after studying and finding jobs. It gives estimates of Bangladeshis in Italy and Germany.

facts.statement: The writer, an Italy-based Bangladeshi, says that in Frankfurt, Germany, living is expensive and there is a housing shortage, but work is commonly available, especially in the restaurant sector, where Bangladeshi and other migrants work.

According to the writer, pay in Germany (Frankfurt) is much higher than in other European countries, though costs are also much higher; a cappuccino costs 1 euro in Italy but 3 euros 50 cents in Germany.
The writer says Germany has few migrants compared with other European countries because it is not easy to enter and because of strict laws.
Unofficially more than 200,000 Bangladeshis live in Italy; by the count of the Bangladesh Embassy in Rome there are about 160,000, and the number has since risen.
facts.source_in_article: the writer; Bangladesh Embassy in Rome

facts.statement: According to Habib Ullah Bahar, a Germany-based Bangladeshi human rights activist and journalist, there are about 40,000 Bangladeshis in Germany, plus a large number of Bangladeshi students.

According to Habib Ullah Bahar, Bangladeshi students in Germany, after finishing their studies and getting a job, are getting the chance of permanent residence and citizenship; many Bangladeshi students are staying permanently in Germany by this route. Bahar himself was a student and now works as a financial accountant in a private company, living in Mainz.

The writer notes that from Frankfurt's international train station (Hauptbahnhof) one can easily travel to Austria, Switzerland, France and other European countries, so travellers use Germany as a transit point.

Per a statistic cited by the writer, Frankfurt's population in 2024 was about 800,529 (printed as '8 lakh 529'), up from 532,413 in 1950 and up 4,092 in the past year; it hosts migrants from Italy, Turkey, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria and other countries.
facts.source_in_article: a statistic cited by the writer

facts.statement: Bangladesh Open University (BOU) Open School opened admission to its overseas (Bohi-Bangladesh, NISH-2) HSC programme for the 2024-25 session (2024 batch) for Bangladeshi migrants working or living in, or people of Bangladeshi origin in, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, South Korea and Italy, through the Bangladesh embassy in each country. Streams: humanities and business studies.

The online application deadline for BOU's overseas HSC programme (2024 batch) was 20 February 2024; admission is completed at the Bangladesh embassy in the country concerned after applying online and paying the fee.

Online application for BOU's overseas HSC programme is at forms.gle/i5yYws4GyotjtQaDA; contacts: the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy, South Korea or UAE; Dean, Open School, BOU: dean.os@bou.ac.bd; International Academic Program Wing, BOU: iapw@bou.ac.bd; website bou.ac.bd.

Eligibility for BOU's overseas HSC programme: passed SSC/Dakhil/O-level or a government-recognised equivalent, and be a Bangladeshi citizen migrant in Saudi Arabia/Qatar/Kuwait/UAE/South Korea/Italy or of Bangladeshi origin.
BOU overseas HSC programme fees: USD 180 for first-year admission and USD 165 for the second year, each paid at the time of that year's admission.
Registration for BOU's overseas HSC programme lasts a minimum of 2 years and maximum of 5 years; it cannot be completed in under two years, and no student may sit exams after five final examinations.

Documents needed for BOU's overseas HSC programme: one photo, copies of the JSC/JDC/Class 8 or equivalent pass certificate and marksheet, a copy of the passport and a copy of the national ID card (if any).

Registration for BOU's overseas SSC programme lasts a minimum of 2 years and maximum of 5 years; no student may sit exams after five final examinations.

Documents needed for BOU's overseas SSC programme: one photo, copies of the JSC/JDC/Class 8 or equivalent pass certificate and marksheet, a copy of the passport and a copy of the national ID card (if any).

Contacts for BOU's overseas SSC programme: the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy or UAE; Dean, Open School, BOU: dean.os@bou.ac.bd; International Academic Program Wing, BOU: iapw@bou.ac.bd; website bou.ac.bd; e-books at ebookbou.edu.bd/ssc.php.

headline_en: What lies behind youth protests and violence across Italy; Bangladeshi expatriates worried too
summary_en: Youth-led protests over cost of living, housing, education and government policy spread across Italy after violent protests on 17 October 2026, with fresh protests on 24 October in Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Florence and other cities. Many Bangladeshis in Italy run fruit shops, minimarkets and restaurants, and unrest poses a risk of losses; the article found no reliable information that any Bangladeshi-owned shop was attacked or any Bangladeshi was hurt. More protests were announced for 30 October and 20 November.

facts.statement: After violent protests on 17 October 2026, new protests were held on Saturday 24 October 2026 in Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Florence and other Italian cities, with clashes, tear gas and water cannon but less looting than the week before; in Bologna at least 19 protesters were injured, and in Turin about 4,000 marched against militarisation, with 2 arrested and 25 charged.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; local emergency health service for Bologna figure

facts.statement: According to Italy's public security department, 4,292 people were identified over the nationwide protests, violence and looting; 371 were taken to police offices (110 minors and 69 foreign nationals), 9 arrested and 87 charged. Nationalities of the 69 foreigners were not published, so whether any Bangladeshis were among them could not be confirmed.

A significant share of Bangladeshis living in Italy are in fruit shops, minimarkets, restaurants and other small businesses; the reporter says shop closures, fewer customers or disrupted goods transport from unrest risk financial losses, especially for fruit and food businesses.

As of 26 October 2026 there was no reliable information that any Bangladeshi-owned shop in Italy had been directly attacked or that any Bangladeshi was injured in the protests, nor any estimate of Bangladeshi traders' losses, nor of organised Bangladeshi participation.

On 24 October 2026 some shops in Milan closed early and some businesses in Trieste boarded up windows and closed temporarily for fear of violence; soldiers were also deployed for security in central Milan.

Organisers of the anti-militarisation movement in Turin announced another street protest for a general strike on 30 October 2026, and student organisations in Italy and the UK planned action on 20 November 2026 against rising education costs.
Fuel price rises linked to the Middle East conflict raised transport costs in Italy; truck drivers' blockades disrupted goods transport in some areas, with possible effects on food prices.

headline_en: Shops of expatriate Bangladeshis also vandalised and looted in France; traders fearful
summary_en: During cost-of-living protests in France the previous week, several businesses of Bangladeshi expatriates in Paris were vandalised and looted, including one trader's phone-accessories shop with about 90,000 euros of goods. Bangladeshi money-transfer outlet operators, food-delivery workers and undocumented day labourers described fear and police document checks. The article lists French government support for damaged businesses, areas of Paris to avoid on Saturday 24 October 2026, the advice to carry proof of legal status, and the penalty for buying or selling looted goods.

facts.statement: During cost-of-living protests in France the week before 23 October 2026, several businesses of expatriate Bangladeshis in Paris were damaged; according to Paris city authorities, 451 shops in Paris alone were vandalised in the violence of 17 and 18 October (count up to 21 October), and the French government said several thousand businesses were damaged nationwide.

A Bangladeshi expatriate trader in Paris named Hasan said his mobile phone accessories and electronics shop was vandalised and looted during the protests, losing all its goods worth about 90,000 euros.

Bangladeshis running small outlets of money transfer firms such as Ria and MoneyGram in Paris fear attacks if street violence resumes, saying such financial outlets have in the past been looted more during protests.
Monir Hossain, a Bangladeshi food-delivery worker in Paris, said the protest-related standstill made deliveries very difficult and workers constantly fear for their safety.

A Bangladeshi day-wage worker in Paris without regular legal papers said strict police presence and document checks everywhere made it hard to go out to work; the article says risk to undocumented expatriates has increased.

French government support for businesses hit by the violence includes the state covering partial unemployment allowance for workers under certain conditions, deferral of tax and social contribution payments, interest-free loans of up to 50,000 euros, and a special fund for eligible small businesses.

The French Federation of Commerce Associations began collecting information on damaged businesses and arranging help; the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Paris and Ile-de-France is helping damaged businesses prepare insurance papers, compensation claims and administrative support.

For the Saturday 24 October 2026 protests, the French government announced deployment of about 70,000 police and gendarmes nationwide; the Louvre, Musee d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais were closed that day.

Paris authorities advised caution moving around central Paris, especially Bastille, Republique, Nation and Les Halles; those who must go out for work should check public transport updates and police instructions before travelling, avoid protest centres and large crowds unless essential, and foreigners living in France should carry proof of their legal papers.

Under the French penal code, buying, keeping or selling stolen or crime-derived goods (such as goods looted during protests) is a serious offence punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 375,000 euros.

As of 23 October 2026 there was no officially confirmed overall count of damaged Bangladeshi businesses in France; Elan Khan Chowdhury, owner of Union Mart in Paris, said trade had stalled and traders feared for shop security.

On Friday (about 23 October 2026) a shooting in Trappes and La Verriere in western Paris region killed one and injured four; anti-terror authorities were investigating and any link to the protests was unconfirmed.

headline_en: If you want to go abroad for higher education with a low CGPA...
summary_en: Advice piece for students with a low CGPA wanting to study abroad: match universities to results, check minimum requirements, use work experience, research and a strong SOP, and consider foundation, pre-master's or pathway programmes. It says some universities accept proof of English-medium instruction instead of IELTS, but visa and scholarship language rules may differ, and warns against deciding from 'no IELTS / low CGPA' advertisements. Wahid Zaman of consultancy AHZ is quoted.

facts.statement: Students with a low CGPA wanting to study abroad should look for countries, universities and courses matching their results and check minimum entry requirements on the university website; some institutions may relax CGPA requirements or consider alternatives, but admission should not be assumed without meeting minimum requirements.

To offset weak grades, applicants can show relevant work experience, professional training, research, a good portfolio or subject skills, plus a strong statement of purpose (SOP), recommendation letters and a clear future plan.

Many universities require IELTS or TOEFL, but not all; some accept proof that previous study was in English (MOI certificate), an alternative language test, or their own assessment; requirements vary by university and programme.

Wahid Zaman, Country Manager (Bangladesh) of study-abroad consultancy AHZ, advised checking the conditions, tuition fees and progression requirements of pathway or pre-master's programmes, confirming with the university whether an MOI certificate or other test is accepted instead of IELTS, and checking admission and visa requirements separately.

Students who cannot meet direct-entry requirements can look for foundation, pre-master's or pathway programmes that lead to the main course, or conditional admission and preparatory courses at some universities; these are not available in every country, university or level, so eligibility, extra cost, duration and progression conditions should be checked first.

Students should not decide based on advertisements promising admission without IELTS or with low CGPA; they should check the university's recognition, course quality, tuition, scholarship conditions and the language requirement for the visa, because a university accepting an alternative language qualification may still face different visa or scholarship requirements.

headline_en: Australia sharply tightens immigration policy; Bangladeshi students anxious
summary_en: On Thursday 17 September 2026 Australia's Home Affairs and Immigration Minister Tony Burke outlined new visa restrictions: curbing 'visa hopping' by international students, limiting students bringing family, adding a 'no further stay' condition to all tourist visas, stronger removal of overstayers, a lottery for second- and third-year Working Holiday visas, and cutting net migration to 245,000 in 2026-27. Students protested and Bangladeshi students in Sydney voiced fears about their future.

facts.statement: Australian Home Affairs and Immigration Minister Tony Burke said on 17 September 2026 at the National Press Club in Canberra that annual net overseas migration will be cut to 245,000 in financial year 2026-27, with a target of 225,000 a year in later years.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, net migration in the year to March 2026 fell to 292,100, lower than a year earlier and the lowest since mid-2022.

Australia's new policy (announced 17 September 2026) imposes strict restrictions on 'visa hopping', meaning international students enrolling in low-quality courses after finishing higher education or repeatedly changing visas; Bangladeshi students say the chance to move from one course or visa to another is being closed.

Under Australia's new rules, international students' ability to bring family members will no longer be expanded and is being limited; exemptions apply to those already studying in Australia, to applicants from Pacific and Southeast Asian countries, and PhD students can bring their families.
Australia is adding a 'no further stay' condition to all tourist (visitor) visas, which in effect closes the option of going to Australia as a tourist and then applying for another visa there.
Australia is strengthening surveillance and legal measures to make people whose visas have expired leave quickly.

A lottery will be introduced for approval of second- and third-year Working Holiday visas in agriculture and services in Australia; skilled migration will be prioritised in shortage sectors such as construction, healthcare and agriculture.
Australia's new policy gives immigration officers special powers to quickly cancel visas and deport migrants involved in violence against children, family violence and hate crimes.

On 17 September 2026 thousands of international university and high school students boycotted classes and protested in Sydney's Hyde Park, Melbourne and Brisbane against the cuts; universities warned the international education sector could be badly hurt.

A Bangladeshi student living in Denham Court, Sydney, said students paid huge tuition fees to study legally, but frequent rule changes and closing of course/visa switching leave their future very uncertain; a student in Lakemba said temporary-visa holders may face having to return home at any time.

headline_en: CAA in force in West Bengal; Suvendu announces return of 'illegal' Bangladeshis
summary_en: On 20 May 2026 West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari announced the CAA in force in the state, so all who entered India after 31 December 2024 are deemed illegal. State police will arrest and detain infiltrators not covered by the CAA and hand them to the BSF, which will hand them to Bangladesh's BGB ('detect, delete, deport'). Muslims from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan are not covered by the CAA. He also began handing land to the BSF for border fencing.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 20 May 2026 West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari declared India's 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) in effect in West Bengal; as a result everyone who entered India after 31 December 2024 is to be considered illegal.

The CAA covers seven religious communities; Muslims from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan are not covered. After a 2024 amendment, covered people entering by 31 December 2024 (instead of 31 December 2014) are legally treated as citizens, but this does not apply to Muslims from Pakistan, Afghanistan or Bangladesh. Adhikari said police may not harass covered people who arrived by 31 December 2024.

Adhikari said people not covered by the CAA are illegal infiltrators who will be directly arrested and detained by West Bengal state police and handed to India's Border Security Force (BSF), which will arrange their deportation by handing them to Bangladesh's border force BGB ('detect, delete, deport'); the order applies at all police stations along West Bengal's border, and the police chief and home secretary have been informed.

According to Adhikari, the Indian government sent West Bengal a directive on 14 May 2025 (signed by Under Secretary Pratap Singh Rawat) to hand illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators directly to the BSF, which the previous state government did not act on.

India's border with Bangladesh is 4,000 km, 2,200 km of it with West Bengal, of which 1,600 km is fenced and about 600 km is not; West Bengal began handing land to the BSF to secure a first 27 km stretch for fencing.

headline_en: Mother faints on hearing her sons are ill, unaware none of the four is alive
summary_en: Four brothers from Bandarabazar Para, Lalanagar union, Rangunia, Chattogram, all working as drivers in Oman, died together on Wednesday night (13 May 2026), apparently from gas poisoning inside their car; their bodies were found in the car outside a hospital in Muladdah. The eldest had gone to Oman 10-12 years earlier on heavy loans and brought his brothers. Efforts to repatriate the bodies were under way with help from the upazila administration.

facts.statement: Four Bangladeshi brothers, Muhammad Rashed (40), Muhammad Shahed (35), Muhammad Siraj (28) and Muhammad Shahid (24), of Bandarabazar Para, Lalanagar union, Rangunia, Chattogram, died on Wednesday night (13 May 2026) in Oman; they had phoned their mother saying they had difficulty breathing in the car and were going to hospital, and about half an hour after contact was lost their bodies were recovered from the car in front of a hospital in the Muladdah area. Relatives believe gas released inside the car poisoned them.

Muhammad Rashed went to Oman 10-12 years earlier after borrowing heavily, worked as a labourer, then obtained a driving licence and became a driver for a sheikh; he later brought three younger brothers to Oman and arranged the same driver jobs for them, and the family built a two-storey house.
Efforts were under way to bring the four brothers' bodies home from Oman; Rangunia Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Nazmul Hasan said the upazila administration is assisting the repatriation process.
facts.source_in_article: UP member Amir Hossain; UNO Md Nazmul Hasan

headline_en: BSF returns two Bangladeshis who entered India
summary_en: India's Border Security Force (BSF) handed back two Bangladeshi men detained for illegally entering India's Assam state across the Nageshwari border in Kurigram. They were returned at a BGB-BSF flag meeting on the zero line on Monday night (13 April 2026) and passed to Kachakata police station. Their families say they crossed by mistake in bad weather.

facts.statement: On Sunday night (about 12 April 2026) two Bangladeshi men crossed from the North Jhaukuti (Uttar Jhaukuti) border, Choddoghori area, Narayanpur union, Nageshwari upazila, Kurigram, into Takimari area of Dhubri district, Assam state, India; local people there detained them and handed them to India's BSF.

On Monday night (13 April 2026) BSF returned the two detained Bangladeshis to Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) through a BGB-BSF flag meeting held on the zero line of the Nageshwari border, Kurigram; BGB then handed them to Kachakata police station, with family members present.

In the Nageshwari (Kurigram) case of April 2026, the families of the two men informed the Choddoghori BOP (border outpost); BGB then wrote a letter to BSF, and a flag meeting between the two forces was held the next afternoon, after which BSF handed the men to BGB.
The officer-in-charge of Kachakata police station, Arpan Kumar Das, said in April 2026 that the two Bangladeshis returned by BSF would be handed to their families after the necessary legal process.
facts.source_in_article: Arpan Kumar Das, OC, Kachakata police station

headline_en: Mother Hosne Ara wants to see her son's face one last time
summary_en: Mehedi Hasan (21) from Feni, who went to Iraq five months earlier with his father's help, died on Wednesday (about 4 March 2026) along with two other Bangladeshis; the family says from poisoning in iftar food. The family borrowed about 10 lakh taka to send him and wants government help to bring the body home. Feni Sadar UNO said the administration had not been formally informed.

facts.statement: Mehedi Hasan (21) of Debipur village, Sharshadi union, Feni Sadar, died in Iraq on Wednesday (about 4 March 2026); his family claims it was from food poisoning from iftar food, and the Bangladesh Embassy in Baghdad also reported the death in a condolence message.

In Iraq, Mehedi Hasan and two others ate iftar together on Tuesday (about 3 March 2026), fell ill, were taken to a local hospital, got first aid and returned home that night; they ate sehri and went to sleep, and colleagues found all three dead in their room the next afternoon. The other two dead were Mohammad Tarek (45) of Brahmanbaria and his son Md. Sabbir (22).

Mehedi Hasan's family borrowed about 10 lakh taka to send him to Iraq through his father, who has worked in Iraq's Kurdistan region for about eight years; Mehedi went in October of the previous year (2025).
Mehedi Hasan's mother Hosne Ara asked for government help to bring his body home from Iraq in March 2026.

Feni Sadar UNO Sultana Nasrin said in March 2026 that the administration had not been formally told of the death in Iraq and no one from the family had informed them; once informed, necessary help would be given after discussion with the district administration.

Nurul Alam took his younger brother Nurunnabi to Saudi Arabia 10 years ago, and about 11 days before his death arranged for his mother and aunt to go to Saudi Arabia for Umrah; they were still there when he died.
In December 2025 Nurul Alam's father Saleh Ahmad (68) was rushing to send the necessary papers to bring his son's body home from Saudi Arabia; when the body would arrive was still unknown.

Adhunagar union parishad chairman Nazim Uddin said in December 2025 that the union parishad and upazila administration were giving all necessary help to bring Nurul Alam's body home from Saudi Arabia.

headline_en: Bangladesh Bank makes buying air tickets for foreign travel easier
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank issued a directive on Wednesday 19 November 2025 letting Bangladeshi citizens buy any international air ticket themselves, from home, with any internationally usable card, without going to an agency or bank. The previous USD 300 per-transaction limit on foreign-currency card payments no longer applies to air tickets; tickets can be bought within the card's foreign-currency limit and the amount can be refilled.

facts.statement: Under a Bangladesh Bank directive issued on Wednesday 19 November 2025, Bangladeshi citizens can buy any air ticket to an international destination themselves from home with any card used for international transactions, without going to any agency or bank.

Before the 19 November 2025 Bangladesh Bank directive, card users could not buy any good or service costing more than USD 300 in foreign currency in one go; that limit has been lifted for air tickets, which can now be bought at any price within the credit card's foreign-currency limit.

Bangladesh Bank said (November 2025) that after buying an air ticket on an international card, the same amount can be refilled to the card, provided the ticket payment was made entirely through a bank in Bangladesh; banks must keep a separate record of the ticket purchase for each refill.

The November 2025 Bangladesh Bank circular says foreign airlines must deposit ticket-sale income in their foreign-currency accounts with authorised dealer banks in Bangladesh, while locally owned airlines must convert collected money into taka before depositing.

Industry people said in November 2025 that the new Bangladesh Bank rule will let travellers buy tickets easily, ensure competitive prices, reduce the gap between local and foreign ticket prices, and reduce middlemen's influence on tickets to foreign destinations.

headline_en: Documents needed to go abroad for higher education
summary_en: A general checklist of 11 documents needed to study abroad: passport, offer letter, academic certificates and transcripts, language test scores, proof of funds, medical report, visa form and fee, photos, recommendation letters, statement of purpose and letter of motivation. It warns that a wrong or incomplete document can get an application rejected.

facts.statement: A Prothom Alo guide (October 2025) says a student going abroad needs a valid passport that stays valid at least for the length of study, and should renew it before it expires.
The October 2025 guide says the offer letter (admission confirmation from the university applied to) is very important during the student visa process.
The October 2025 guide says students must submit SSC, HSC, bachelor's or master's certificates and mark sheets, officially translated and attested, especially if not in English.
The October 2025 guide says most foreign universities require proof of English such as IELTS, GRE, GMAT, SAT or TOEFL scores, with required scores varying by country and university.
The October 2025 guide says students must prove they can pay tuition and living costs with a bank statement or sponsorship letter; some countries require a set amount shown as a bank deposit.
The October 2025 guide says many countries require a medical report or health certificate for students, and it is especially important for Australia, Canada and New Zealand.

The October 2025 guide warns that wrong information on the visa application form is one of the main reasons for visa delay or refusal, and that any wrong or incomplete document can get the application cancelled.
The October 2025 guide says passport-size photos must follow each country's size, background and format rules, and photo studios will usually take photos to the right size if told the country.
The October 2025 guide says universities usually want two to three recommendation letters from teachers or workplace supervisors, plus a statement of purpose and a letter of motivation.

summary_en: On 25 October 2025 India's BSF handed 31 Bangladeshis to BGB at a flag meeting at the Darshana Joynagar-Gede point, Chuadanga. Most had entered India illegally at different times and were living and working as labourers in Haryana state, where Haryana police detained them. They were passed to Darshana police for verification and return to families.

facts.statement: On Saturday 25 October 2025 at midday, India's BSF handed 31 Bangladeshis (16 men, 10 women, two third-gender people and three children) to BGB through a flag meeting on the zero line at Darshana Joynagar (Chuadanga) and Gede (India) point; BGB Darshana company commander Md. Abu Hasan and BSF Gede company commander Shiv Shankar Singh led the meeting.

According to Lt Col Mohammad Nazmul Hasan, commander of the Chuadanga battalion (6 BGB), the 31 Bangladeshis returned on 25 October 2025 had entered India illegally at different times; most were living and working as labourers in Haryana state, and Haryana police detained them and handed them to BSF.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Mohammad Nazmul Hasan, 6 BGB

facts.statement: The 31 Bangladeshis returned from India via Darshana on 25 October 2025 came from Chuadanga, Narail, Noakhali, Kurigram, Dhaka, Khulna, Satkhira, Cumilla, Mymensingh, Feni, Gopalganj, Moulvibazar, Sherpur and Manikganj.

After the 25 October 2025 return, BGB handed the 31 to Darshana police, who would verify addresses and details; Darshana OC Muhammad Shahid Titumir said they would be kept at Parkrishnapur-Madna union parishad, families informed, and taken home with help from police in their home areas.

headline_en: Seven expatriates from Sandwip killed in road accident in Oman
summary_en: Seven Bangladeshi workers from Sandwip, Chattogram, were killed on 8 October 2025 at about 4 pm Bangladesh time when the vehicle carrying them home after fishing lost control in the Duqm Sidda area of Oman. At least one worked on a fishing boat. Duqm police are investigating.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 8 October 2025 at about 4 pm Bangladesh time, seven Bangladeshi workers from Sandwip upazila, Chattogram (five from Sarikait union, one from Maitbhanga, one from Rahmatpur) were killed in the Duqm Sidda area of Oman when the vehicle carrying them home after fishing at sea lost control.
Md. Siddik, father of Shahab Uddin killed in Oman on 8 October 2025, said his son worked on a fishing boat in Oman and was returning home after several days at sea.
Duqm police in Oman were reported to be investigating the cause of the 8 October 2025 accident that killed seven Bangladeshis.

headline_en: Expatriates in Portugal in trouble over residence permits
summary_en: Portugal's immigration agency AIMA is demanding a declaration from the original house owner as proof of residence, and detailed proof of income scaled to family size, for residence card renewals, leaving Bangladeshis and other migrants unable to renew. A new immigration law tightening family reunification was approved by parliament on 30 September 2025 and takes effect after presidential approval.

facts.statement: In 2025 Portugal's immigration agency AIMA imposed tough conditions for residence permit renewal: proof of residence in the form of a declaration from the original house owner, and detailed proof of income (income declaration, scaled to the number of family members if the family is large).
Migrants in Portugal had for a long time been unable to renew residence cards; in June 2025 AIMA opened an opportunity for renewal, but still demanded a landlord's declaration as proof of residence.
On 30 September 2025 Portugal's parliament approved a new immigration law that tightens family reunification conditions and other matters; it will take effect only after the President's approval.

Bangladeshi expatriate Kamruzzaman, about six years in Portugal, said he had always got and renewed his residence card using an address certificate from the local municipality, but under the new rule his landlord will not give the required certificate, leaving his status uncertain.

facts.statement: Harun Sardar Nur Nabi Sardar (44), a Bangladeshi taxi driver living in Sharjah, UAE, since 2009 whose family lives in Bangladesh, won the 'Big Ticket Abu Dhabi' first prize of 2 crore (20 million) dirhams, about Tk 66.34 crore, announced on Friday 3 October 2025; he bought the ticket on 14 September for a group of 11 people who will share the prize, and he buys a Big Ticket every month.

headline_en: Returnee migrant Lokman succeeds in off-season watermelon farming
summary_en: Lokman Hossain (30) of Charwadel, Chandradwip union, Bauphal, Patuakhali, went abroad in 2018 after graduating and came home in early 2022 because the work was very hard. He now grows off-season hybrid watermelon with mulching on 5 decimals, earning about one lakh taka from a Tk 20,000 outlay; the upazila agriculture officer promised support.

facts.statement: Lokman Hossain (30) of Charwadel village, Chandradwip union, Bauphal, Patuakhali, went abroad for work in 2018 after graduating and returned in early 2022, saying he had to do very hard physical work abroad; he then started farming with his father. The destination country is not named.

Returnee Lokman Hossain says he spent only Tk 20,000 on a previous off-season watermelon crop on 5 decimals of land and sold about one lakh taka worth, and expects about one lakh taka profit in 2025 from the same 5 decimals, using hybrid watermelon with mulching in the rainy season.
Bauphal upazila agriculture officer Md. Milon said in September 2025 that the agriculture department would give returnee farmer Lokman Hossain all kinds of support for off-season watermelon farming.

headline_en: Six detained while crossing into India through Chunarughat border; brokers flee
summary_en: BGB's 55 battalion detained six men from Boail village, Khaliajuri, Netrokona, before dawn on Sunday 21 September 2025 near border pillar 1961/7-S in Chunarughat, Habiganj, as they tried to cross into India through a broker ring for Durga Puja. They had paid brokers Tk 10,000 each; the brokers fled. A case was filed against the six for attempted illegal crossing.

facts.statement: Before dawn on Sunday 21 September 2025, six men from Boail village, Khaliajuri upazila, Netrokona, tried to cross into India near border pillar 1961/7-S in Chunarughat upazila, Habiganj, through a broker ring, and were detained by a 55 BGB patrol.

The six men detained at the Chunarughat border on 21 September 2025 said they each paid Tk 10,000 to a broker ring to be taken across the border into India, to go there for Durga Puja; the brokers fled when BGB caught them.

According to the detainees, as told by 55 BGB commander Lt Col Tanzilur Rahman, Toufiq, Milon and Hakim, members of a human trafficking ring from the Jamburachhara area of Sreemangal, lured them with the promise of reaching India for Tk 10,000 per person.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Tanzilur Rahman, 55 BGB battalion, Habiganj

facts.statement: The six detained at the Chunarughat border on 21 September 2025 were handed to Chunarughat police station that afternoon and a case was filed against them for attempting to cross the border illegally.

headline_en: Claim of 'Graduate Pass' for 10,000 Bangladeshi students is false: Malaysia's higher education minister
summary_en: Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abd Kadir said in a statement on 23 August 2025 that reports of a 'Graduate Pass' giving 10,000 Bangladeshi students in Malaysia work opportunities are false, and that no such agreement was made during Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's visit to Malaysia. He rebuked Kedah state committee chairman Haim Hilman Abdullah, who had claimed this in a TikTok video.

facts.statement: On Saturday 23 August 2025 Malaysia's Higher Education Minister Zambry Abd Kadir said in a statement (reported by The Star) that the spreading report that 10,000 Bangladeshi students studying in Malaysia would be given a 'Graduate Pass' to work is untrue and baseless, and that Malaysia has given no consent to this.
facts.source_in_article: Zambry Abd Kadir, Malaysia Higher Education Minister, via The Star

facts.statement: Malaysia's Higher Education Minister said in August 2025 that no agreement was signed during Bangladesh Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus's recent visit to Malaysia that would oblige Malaysia to give work opportunities to 10,000 Bangladeshi students.

The claim that 10,000 Bangladeshi students would get jobs in Malaysia came from a 2 minute 19 second TikTok video by Haim Hilman Abdullah, chairman of Kedah state's committee on industry and investment, higher education, science, technology and innovation, based on a Bangladeshi newspaper report; Malaysia's minister called it entirely false and irresponsible.

After the hour-long flag meeting in May 2025, BGB formally handed the 24 returnees from India directly to their families with help from local people and public representatives (Naodanga UP chairman Hasen Ali was present).

summary_en: Saiful Islam (28) of East Belagaon, Jayfarnagar union, Juri, Moulvibazar, a poultry-farm worker near Riyadh for about three years, was killed on 20 May 2025 when the goods truck he rode to Riyadh to shop hit a camel on the road and overturned. headline_en: Sylhet migrant killed by co-worker in Middle East, another dies in accident
summary_en: Two migrants from Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, died in the Middle East just after Eid: Sabul Mia (39) died in a road accident in Muscat, Oman, when the driver of their car fell asleep, and Foyzul Haque (55) was stabbed to death at his workplace in Abu Dhabi, UAE, reportedly by two Bangladeshi co-workers who were arrested. Families learned via contacts abroad; Sabul's body was in a morgue with repatriation under discussion, while there was no progress on bringing Foyzul's body home.

facts.statement: Sabul Mia (39), of Hasnaji village, Daulatpur union, Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, died on the morning of Wednesday (about 2 April 2025) in a road accident in the Amla-Ibri (আমলা-ইবরি) area of Muscat, Oman, while he and three others were being driven to work; the driver suddenly fell asleep, the car went out of control and Sabul and two others died on the spot.

Sabul Mia had been working in Oman for about 9 years, had visited Bangladesh twice, returned to Oman last December after about two and a half months of leave, and was due to return home for good in one more year. He leaves a son aged two and a half.
Sabul Mia's family in Bishwanath, Sylhet learned of his death in Oman on Wednesday (about 2 April 2025) through a man from their area who lives in Oman.

As of about 4 April 2025, Sabul Mia's body was kept in the morgue of a local hospital in Muscat, Oman; detailed discussions on bringing the body home were under way and the family hoped it could be brought to Bangladesh within the following week.

Foyzul Haque (55), of Bhurki village, Lamakazi union, Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, was stabbed to death around midday on Tuesday (about 1 April 2025) at his workplace in the Shamkha (শামখা) area of Abu Dhabi, UAE; the family initially learned that two Bangladeshi co-workers stabbed him, and they were arrested by UAE police.
Foyzul Haque's family learned of his death in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday evening (about 2 April 2025) through one of his co-workers, because nobody from their area lives in that country.

As of about 4 April 2025, Foyzul Haque's family said there had been no real progress on bringing his body home from Abu Dhabi, UAE. He had returned to Abu Dhabi about three months earlier after leave in Bangladesh, and leaves a wife, a son and a daughter.

headline_en: Bangladeshi sent back from India over alleged anti-India remarks
summary_en: Indian authorities cancelled the visa of Md. Azadur Rahman of Magura and sent him back to Bangladesh through Changrabandha immigration, Cooch Behar, on 25 March 2025, after he allegedly made offensive remarks about India during a dispute with a taxi driver. Local residents protested after the incident spread on Facebook live; police rescued him, and immigration cancelled his visa after consulting the Kolkata FRRO.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 25 March 2025, Md. Azadur Rahman, from Magura district, Bangladesh, had his Indian visa cancelled and was sent back to Bangladesh from the Changrabandha immigration point in Cooch Behar, West Bengal, accused of making anti-India remarks.
facts.source_in_article: Mekhliganj block police officer Ashish P Subba; Indian media

facts.statement: Azadur Rahman's son studies in Kurseong, Darjeeling, India; Azadur had planned to return to Bangladesh with his son after the son's exams.

According to Indian paper Uttarbanga Sambad citing witnesses, Azadur argued with a driver while hiring a car at the taxi stand near the Changrabandha immigration checkpost, behaved badly with several people and made very offensive comments about India; drivers refused to take him, people streamed it live on Facebook, and residents surrounded and protested against him at Changrabandha VIP crossing. Exactly what he said about India was not known.

Mekhliganj police station rescued Azadur Rahman as the situation heated up, took him to the police station and then brought him back to the Changrabandha immigration checkpost; he admitted his mistake before the crowd but did not answer journalists.

An official of the Changrabandha international immigration office said Azadur Rahman's visa was cancelled after talking with the Kolkata FRRO (Foreigners Regional Registration Office), and he was then sent back to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Indian media quoting a Changrabandha immigration official

headline_en: BSF returns seven Bangladeshis detained at Tetulia border
summary_en: Seven Bangladeshis, including a family of four from Thakurgaon, were detained by India's BSF while crossing the Mahananda river into India through an unfenced stretch of the Kashimganj border, Tetulia, Panchagarh, on 25 February 2025. BSF handed them to BGB at a flag meeting on 26 February; BGB filed a case under the Passport Act and handed them to Tetulia police, who were to produce them in court.

facts.statement: On Tuesday night (25 February 2025), seven Bangladeshis including one woman tried to enter India by crossing the Mahananda river near sub-pillar 6 of main pillar 730 at the Kashimganj border, Banglabandha union, Tetulia upazila, Panchagarh, through an area without barbed-wire fencing.
facts.source_in_article: BGB press release, 18 BGB Battalion Panchagarh

facts.statement: The seven were detained by patrolling members of the Baneshwarjot camp of India's 18 BSF Battalion.

At 6pm on Wednesday 26 February 2025, BSF handed the seven to BGB at a company-commander-level flag meeting near main pillar 730 of the Kashimganj border; that night members of Kashimganj BOP (18 BGB Battalion) handed them to Tetulia Model police station.
BGB filed a case for illegal entry under the Passport Act against the seven returned from India, and police said they would be shown arrested and produced in court on Thursday 27 February 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Tetulia Model police station OC Enayet Kabir

facts.statement: Those arrested were Haren Barman (40) of Uttar Boalia, Ruhia union, Thakurgaon Sadar, his wife Mamata Rani (35), elder son Ajay Kumar Barman (21), a younger son (17), Shushanta Roy (22) of Debiganj area, Ashish Roy (18) of Gareya area, and a 17-year-old boy of Akhanagar area.

headline_en: Saudi-based migrant killed in clash over land dispute in Sylhet
summary_en: Abdul Gafur (45), a migrant worker in Saudi Arabia who had recently come home to Atashon village, Balaganj, Sylhet on leave, was killed on 11 January 2025 in a clash with a rival side over a long-running land dispute; 15 others were injured. facts.statement: Abdul Gafur (45), a Saudi Arabia-based migrant from Atashon village, West Gouripur union, Balaganj upazila, Sylhet, who had recently come home on leave, was killed at midday on Saturday 11 January 2025 in a clash with local weapons between his side and Dilu Mia's side over a long-standing land dispute; 15 others from both sides were injured.
Tension over the old land dispute between Dilu Mia and Abdul Gafur flared up after Gafur came home on leave from Saudi Arabia; the clash began when Gafur's people went near the disputed land.
Balaganj police sent Abdul Gafur's body to the Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College morgue, to be handed to the family after post-mortem, and were conducting raids to bring those involved to justice.

headline_en: Early election in Germany: how hard will it be for Bangladeshi migrants?
summary_en: A Bangladeshi reader writing from Hamburg reports that Germany is heading for an early election, possibly on 23 February 2025, with the far-right AfD polling 18 percent. An AfD campaigner told him the party welcomes migrants with legal work status but wants rules on migration; the writer concludes asylum seekers without work authorisation would find it hard if AfD came to power, while most Bangladeshis in Germany work legally and may not be much affected.

facts.statement: As of December 2024, Germany's early national election could be held on 23 February 2025, according to German parliament sources quoted by news agencies DPA and AFP, after Chancellor Olaf Scholz's coalition broke up when he dismissed FDP finance minister Christian Lindner.
facts.source_in_article: DPA and AFP citing parliament sources

facts.statement: A Der Spiegel election research group poll (as of December 2024) gave CDU 33 percent, the far-right AfD 18 percent, SPD 16 percent, Greens 12 percent and FDP 3 percent support.

Many Bangladeshis and other migrants living in Germany fear that if the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany, founded 2013) comes to power, living in Germany would become harder for migrants and asylum seekers.

An AfD campaigner in Hamburg told the Bangladeshi writer that the party welcomes migrants who have legal work status and wants them to play a bigger role in Germany's future, but wants to bring migrants within a set of rules.

The writer's reading is that if AfD comes to power, it would be truly hard for asylum-seeker migrants without legal work status to stay in Germany, and the party would not support uncontrolled mass migration.
After the fall of the Assad government, the German government had already stopped (processing) applications from Syrian asylum seekers, as of December 2024.
According to the writer, most Bangladeshis currently in Germany work legally, and he did not think an AfD government would cause them much harm.
Prothom Alo's Durporobash (diaspora) section accepts writing, travel stories, videos and photos at dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: Bangladeshi credit card use now highest in the US instead of India
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show that after July 2024 the United States overtook India as the top country for Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad, with about BDT 77 crore spent there in September 2024. Bankers attribute the fall in India (from BDT 92 crore in June to 51 crore) to India restricting visas for Bangladeshis to emergency medical cases since July/August; spending rose in Thailand and Malaysia as alternative travel destinations.

facts.statement: Bankers said that from July 2024 (the article also says after the political change in August) India tightened visas for Bangladeshis and now limits tourist and other visas, apart from emergency medical visas, so Bangladeshi travel to India fell significantly.
In September 2024 Bangladeshis spent about BDT 77 crore by credit card in the United States, the highest of any foreign country, and about 18 percent of all Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad.
Bangladeshi credit card spending in India was BDT 51 crore in September 2024 and the same in August 2024, down from a high of BDT 92 crore in June 2024 before the July student movement, roughly half.
Total Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad was about BDT 421 crore in September 2024, up from BDT 373 crore in August, an increase of BDT 48 crore or about 13 percent.

Bangladeshi credit card spending in Thailand rose from BDT 33 crore in August 2024 to BDT 42 crore in September 2024 (up 9 crore, about 27.25 percent); in Malaysia and the Netherlands it rose by BDT 5 crore each over the same month. Bankers said Thailand and Malaysia had become main travel destinations after India tightened visas.

Domestic credit card spending in Bangladesh was BDT 2,668 crore in September 2024 vs BDT 2,332 crore in August (up 336 crore, 14.40 percent). The report covers 44 card-issuing banks and 1 financial institution.
Abroad, Bangladeshis spent most by credit card at department stores (BDT 116 crore in September 2024) and second most at retail outlet services (BDT 74 crore), both up from August.

headline_en: Saudi Arabia asks about progress in renewing passports of Rohingyas who went there on Bangladeshi passports
summary_en: On 12 May 2024 Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Naser bin Abdul Aziz Al-Dawood met Bangladesh Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan in Dhaka and asked about progress in renewing Bangladeshi passports held by Rohingyas who went to Saudi Arabia in 1973-74 (about 69,000 by the Saudi count). The home minister said they will not be sent back to Bangladesh but their passports must be renewed under a signed MoU, keeping passport details unchanged; he noted Saudi law deports people without valid papers.

facts.statement: Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Naser bin Abdul Aziz Al-Dawood, at a bilateral meeting with Bangladesh Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan at a Dhaka hotel on Sunday 12 May 2024, asked about progress in renewing the passports of Rohingyas who went to Saudi Arabia on Bangladeshi passports in 1973-74.

The Saudi side told Bangladesh that about 69,000 Rohingyas went to Saudi Arabia (on Bangladeshi passports) in 1973-74; Bangladesh's home minister said the exact number was unknown to Bangladesh and could be more or less.

Bangladesh's home minister said Rohingyas living in Saudi Arabia (on Bangladeshi passports) will not be sent back to Bangladesh, but their passports must be renewed, and a memorandum of understanding on this has been signed with Saudi Arabia; the passports will be renewed with their information unchanged.
Under Saudi government law, people without valid papers are sent back (deported).

The Saudi deputy minister came to check whether Bangladesh was moving slowly, facing problems or had loopholes in renewing Rohingyas' passports; the two sides also discussed cooperation to build BGB and police capacity, and Saudi Arabia stressed safe repatriation of Rohingyas to Myanmar as soon as possible.

headline_en: Father who returned from abroad denies us as his children
summary_en: In a legal advice column, a migrant's child writes that their father worked abroad for about 22 years, sending BDT 20,000 a month and beating their mother on each home visit, then returned for good in 2023, stopped paying household costs, abuses the mother and disowns the children. Barrister Miti Sanjana of the Supreme Court explains that this is domestic violence under the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010 and lists the remedies and where to apply.

facts.statement: A letter writer (anonymous) said their father went abroad after marrying about 22 years ago, came home every three years for three months, sent BDT 20,000 a month, and beat their mother on each visit; after returning home for good in 2023 he stopped paying the family's expenses, abuses and beats the mother daily, wants a divorce, denies the children as his, and now wants to file a case against the mother and brother.

Under Bangladesh's Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010, domestic violence means physical, mental or sexual abuse or financial harm by a family member against a woman or child in the family; the Act made domestic violence an offence for the first time and rules under it have been framed. Withholding maintenance (financial deprivation) is covered.
facts.source_in_article: Barrister Miti Sanjana, Supreme Court lawyer

facts.statement: A woman facing domestic violence in Bangladesh can, under the 2010 Act, seek remedies, medical treatment, services from an enforcement officer, and, where applicable, free legal advice and aid under the Legal Aid Act 2000.

An application under the Domestic Violence Act 2010 can be made by the victim or on her behalf by an enforcement officer, service provider or any other person; the court sets a hearing date within seven days of receiving it. The woman can apply for protection to the officer-in-charge of any police station, a women affairs officer, or directly to the court.

Remedies under the Domestic Violence Act 2010: interim protection order (section 13, can be ex parte); protection order after hearing both sides; residence order (section 15, barring the abuser from the home, stopping eviction, arranging safe shelter with consent, bond with or without surety); compensation/maintenance order (section 16, one-off or monthly maintenance for the woman and child at their accustomed standard of living); safe custody order for the child (section 17).

Offences under the Domestic Violence Act 2010 are cognisable, bailable and compoundable; punishment is in section 30, but under section 31 the court may instead order community service for a set period. Separately, Penal Code section 323 punishes voluntarily causing hurt with up to one year in jail or a BDT 1,000 fine or both.

headline_en: How to prepare for higher study abroad: the steps
summary_en: A general guide for Bangladeshi students planning higher study abroad, covering decision and planning (at least a year ahead), language tests (IELTS, TOEFL and others), researching courses and universities, applying to several universities, funding and scholarships, the student visa process, accommodation, and travel preparation.

facts.statement: Going abroad for higher study takes at least a year of well-planned activity; seminars, workshops and counselling on careers and study abroad during the bachelor's can help, but the student must decide.

Most universities in developed countries require proof of English; most accept academic IELTS or TOEFL. Some well-known European universities require other languages, chiefly Mandarin Chinese, German, French, Arabic and Japanese.
The article names the British Council, IDP and the Institute of Modern Languages at Dhaka University as the best places in Bangladesh to sit tests and get language proficiency certificates.

When researching, check course content, research scope, campus life, job prospects, tuition costs and scholarships; Facebook groups on higher study, alumni and teachers are useful sources; shortlist two or three destinations and compare them.

Applicants with a good CGPA apply to several universities, built around their final-year thesis or project paper; follow each university's admission instructions exactly. Some want only digital copies of documents, others also want physical copies by post; information must be consistent across all certificates.

Tuition fees are very high in the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and Singapore; part-time work alone cannot cover study costs, and international students are allowed only a limited number of work hours per week.

According to the article, public universities in Norway, Germany and China give degrees free to all international students regardless of nationality, but living costs are high, so scholarships are the best funding route. Before going, a bank balance must be shown to cover all living costs in that country.

In EU countries short language courses are sometimes allowed on a tourist visa, but almost all courses longer than three months need a student visa. Usually an offer letter from a university is needed before applying; after paying the required admission fee, the institution provides the documents needed for the student visa application. Visa processes differ by country.

Students often face problems arranging housing abroad, so it is best to fix accommodation before leaving; options are university-provided housing (sometimes with scholarships), student dormitories (may share kitchen or bathroom), sharing with local residents (sublet), or a pricier apartment, often shared.

Book flights as early as possible to save money, check cancellation and change policies, arrive well before classes start, follow the airline's baggage limits (extra baggage costs more), and pack student ID, passport and essential medicines.

headline_en: Bangladeshis fifth in setting up second homes in Malaysia
summary_en: As of 31 January 2024, 3,604 Bangladeshis held Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) passes, fifth after China, Australia, South Korea and Japan, according to Malaysia's tourism minister in parliament as reported by Malay Mail. The programme was restructured in December 2023 into Platinum, Gold and Silver tiers with fixed-deposit requirements of 5 million, 2 million and 500,000 ringgit, a minimum age of 30 and a 60-day annual stay requirement. The article notes allegations that laundered money funds such second homes.

facts.statement: As of 31 January 2024, 3,604 Bangladeshis had set up a second home in Malaysia under the Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) programme, fifth among nationalities; Bangladeshis were once third.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Datuk Seri Tiong King Sing in parliament, via Malay Mail

facts.statement: As of 31 January 2024 there were 56,066 active MM2H pass holders (participants and dependants): China 24,765, Australia 9,265, South Korea 4,940, Japan 4,733, Bangladesh 3,604, UK 2,234, and more than a thousand each from Taiwan, the US, Singapore and India.

In December 2023 Malaysia restructured MM2H into three tiers based on financial capacity: Platinum requires a fixed deposit of 5 million ringgit (50 lakh), Gold 2 million (20 lakh) and Silver 500,000 (5 lakh) ringgit; participants in all tiers must live in Malaysia a total of 60 days a year; applicants must be 30 or older. It was said the new scheme would run on trial for one year and be adjusted later.

Bangladesh Bank has so far allowed only a small number of companies to invest abroad; there are long-standing allegations that money laundered from Bangladesh funds 'second homes' in Canada and Malaysia, Singapore star hotels and Swiss bank deposits. An earlier government offer to bring laundered money back for a nominal tax was taken up by no one.

headline_en: Iftar of expatriate engineers and architects in Dubai
summary_en: The Dubai chapter of NRB Engineers and Architects, an association of Bangladeshi expatriate engineers and architects, held an iftar at Asia Royal restaurant in Dubai on Monday (about 25 March 2024), with Bangladesh's Consul General in Dubai and the Northern Emirates, B M Jamal Hossain, as chief guest. Chapters in Sharjah, Fujairah, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain were represented.

facts.statement: As of March 2024, Bangladesh's Consul General for Dubai and the Northern Emirates was B M Jamal Hossain.

NRB Engineers and Architects is an association of Bangladeshi expatriate engineers and architects in the UAE with chapters in Dubai (president engineer Liakat Ali Khan, secretary engineer Moinul Islam), Sharjah (president engineer Maruf Murtala), Fujairah (president engineer Masud Parvez), Abu Dhabi and Al Ain; its Dubai chapter held an iftar at Asia Royal restaurant, Dubai on Monday (about 25 March 2024).

headline_en: Free internship in Japan for Bangladeshi undergraduate and postgraduate students
summary_en: Japan's Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) offers free 2-to-6-month research internships open to undergraduate and postgraduate students from any country, including Bangladesh, with a 15 April deadline. Interns get 2,400 yen per working day, visa support, air tickets, housing and insurance; the internship runs 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2025.

facts.statement: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), Japan, offers free research internships of two to six months for undergraduate and postgraduate students from any country, including Bangladesh; application deadline 15 April (2024).

OIST research interns receive 2,400 Japanese yen per working day (the article converts this to BDT 1,840 at 0.77 taka per yen as of the afternoon of 3 January), plus free visa support, air tickets to and from Japan, housing and insurance.

OIST internship eligibility: students of any country at undergraduate or postgraduate level, with good results and good English. Required documents: a 400-word statement of purpose, academic mark sheets in English, copies of passport and national ID card, and a recommendation letter. Application is online.
OIST gives internships twice a year, selected on research topic, academic qualifications and merit; this round runs from 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2025.

headline_en: Oman migrant Bablu, who brought his family out of hardship, never made it home
summary_en: Md. Bablu (30) of Sonagazi, Feni, a supervisor at a company in Salalah, Oman for eight years, was killed in a road accident around midnight on Thursday (about 15 February 2024), a week before he was due home on 22 February; his family is worried about how to bring the body home and seeks government help. Separately, Mohammad Ali Sohag (30), also of Sonagazi, died on 9 February after falling from the roof of a 10-storey building under construction in Northern Cyprus; his body was brought home on 15 February and buried on 16 February.

facts.statement: Md. Bablu (30), son of Md. Selim of North Char Chandia village, Char Chandia union, Sonagazi upazila, Feni, was killed around 12 midnight on Thursday (about 15 February 2024) in Salalah, Oman, when the private car taking him from home to work was hit by another vehicle; several others with him were injured.

Md. Bablu went to Oman eight years earlier to support his poor family and worked as a supervisor at a company in Salalah; his income supported the family, paid for two sisters' weddings, and about eight months earlier he sent money from Oman to send his younger brother Md. Shiblu to Saudi Arabia. He was due to come home on 22 February 2024.

As of 16 February 2024, Bablu's family were worried about bringing his body home from Oman, did not know how to go about it and sought help from the government and others concerned; the Char Chandia union parishad chairman Md. Mosharraf Hossain said discussions were under way on how to bring the body home.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi youth Mohammad Ali Sohag (30), of Middle Char Chandia, Sonagazi, Feni, died on 9 February 2024 after falling from the roof of a 10-storey building under construction in Northern Cyprus.

Mohammad Ali Sohag's body was brought home from Northern Cyprus on Thursday night (15 February 2024) and buried in the family graveyard after a janaza at his home in Middle Char Chandia, Sonagazi at 10am on Friday 16 February 2024.
